title: Char-2 cancellation ↔ signed ES with a size-controlled negative term
connection: In char 2 two monic denominators of equal minimal degree cancel at ∞ (m = 2), which is what the F₂ identities exploit. Over Z the closest mechanism is 1/x − 1/x' with x' ≈ x, i.e. signed ES where the negative term is tiny.
why: If the F₂ identities lift to signed integer identities whose sign defect is confined to a small term, the remaining task is a 'sign repair' problem, which is a different and more concrete integer statement.
first_step: Lift the F₂[T] identity of Thm 6.1 coefficientwise to Z[T] (T ↦ integer), record which term goes negative, and measure its size relative to 4/n.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Large-q monodromy (Bary-Soroker style) for 'divisor of A·C·P+1 in a residue class'
connection: Over F_q[T] with q → ∞, factorization types of P-tied polynomials such as A·C·P + 1 become equidistributed via full symmetric monodromy; ES Type II needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 in class −1 mod 4C over Z.
why: A large-q theorem would show the 'divisor in class' event behaves like a random permutation event; it localizes which part of the Z problem is genuinely arithmetic (finite q).
first_step: Check whether Bank–Bary-Soroker–Rosenzweig ('Prime polynomials in short intervals and in arithmetic progressions') or Bary-Soroker's divisor results cover 'has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: FF reciprocity sign (−1)^{deg·deg·(q−1)/2} may resurrect a T1-type square obstruction for q ≡ 3 (mod 4)
connection: T1 (empty certificate lines at odd squares) is a quadratic-reciprocity effect over Q. FF quadratic reciprocity carries a sign depending on degrees and q mod 4, so odd-degree squares in F_3[T], F_7[T] may carry a T1 analogue.
why: If a T1 analogue appears exactly when the reciprocity sign is non-trivial, T1 is pinned to the sign in reciprocity, the 'archimedean' part of Q's reciprocity.
first_step: EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD Thm 1.3 already shows squares fail U_q for q ≡ 3 (mod 4) — start there. For q = 3, 7 enumerate certificate lines at P = Q² with deg Q odd vs even (deg ≤ 6) and test emptiness; compare FUNCTIONFIELD_ES2 §3 (degree parity).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Genus-1 coordinate rings: ES over F_q[x,y]/(E) with sign at the point at infinity
connection: Drinfeld–Hayes rings with nontrivial class group: a 'prime' P generates a non-principal ideal in general, so 4/P is not even an element unless P is principal; ES becomes a statement about principal primes or ideal classes.
why: Separates the role of the class group (trivial for Z) from the role of the cone; if ES fails only in non-trivial class-group rings, class number one is part of the mechanism.
first_step: Pick an elliptic curve over F_3 with A = F_3[E∖O], enumerate principal primes of small degree and run the e-slice search with sign-normalized denominators.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Large-degree numerators A = T^k ↔ Schinzel m/n with m → ∞
connection: In FF the numerator degree k plays the role of log m. Families with k→∞ at fixed q correspond to m/n problems with growing m (Schinzel), where Vaughan-type density results still hold over Z.
why: If ES_q(T^k,·) has a uniform-in-k density theorem in FF, it predicts the right uniformity in m for Z, i.e. a quantitative Vaughan for m ≤ (log n)^c.
first_step: From existing FF data, tabulate failure density at fixed q=3 as k = 1..4 grows and compare with Z data for m = 4..12.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Which non-square classes (m, r) admit an ES polynomial identity?
connection: Mordell–Schinzel excludes square r mod m. For non-square r, is there always an identity 4/(mT + r) = Σ 1/X_i(T) over Z[T]? Over 840 Mordell finds identities for all non-square classes; for general m this is the polynomial world's version of ES.
why: A complete answer in Z[T] separates exactly the polynomial-identity (B1) part of ES and would show whether non-square classes are always B1-coverable.
first_step: Brute-force Type I/II identities for m ≤ 2000, all non-square r, recording uncovered (m,r); check Elsholtz–Tao §2 for a stated answer.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over R[T] with lc > 0: the real-closed-coefficient world
connection: Over R[T] with positive leading coefficients there is no integrality of coefficients, so ES becomes a semialgebraic condition on the solution variety, like the q → ∞ limit but with an ordered constant field.
why: Separates 'ordered field at the sign place' from 'finiteness of the constant field'; if R[T]-ES is trivial, the Z difficulty is all integrality.
first_step: Check whether A/P = Σ 1/X_i with monic-real X_i always has solutions for deg A = 1 (dimension count + sign of leading terms).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field large sieve on the ES certificate set (Hsu-type FF large sieve)
connection: The FF large sieve is sharp with explicit constants. Applied to 'P avoiding all certificate classes for moduli ≤ Q', it bounds the FF exceptional set; Z has the same inequality with worse explicit constants.
why: The FF large-sieve bound can be compared directly with the FF exceptional count computed exactly, calibrating how lossy the Z large-sieve route is.
first_step: Compute the FF large-sieve prediction for q=3, A=T, deg ≤ 12 and compare with the exact failure counts in data/ffl.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Drinfeld modular curves X₀(P) point counts as ES solution counters
connection: Type II ES data at P correspond to points on modular-type curves in FF; Drinfeld modular curves have explicit point counts (Gekeler). If the ES count at P equals a Hecke eigenvalue sum, Ramanujan bounds (Drinfeld) give lower bounds.
why: A lower bound from a Ramanujan-type identity is the only FF mechanism that would directly transfer as 'pointwise' information over Z.
first_step: Test numerically in F_3[T] whether #ES-solutions(P) correlates with a_P of some Drinfeld modular form of small level (fit against Gekeler's tables).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Riemann–Roch dimension count of the ES variety at fixed P in FF
connection: The space of solutions of A/P = Σ 1/X_i with bounded degrees is a variety whose expected dimension is −k (BRAINSTORM ff §4). Riemann–Roch on the ES surface's fibration gives exact dimension of families.
why: Over Z the analogue is the log² p expected count; RR gives an FF exact formula that could reveal a hidden term (e.g. a constant correction) that also exists over Z.
first_step: Compute for q = 3 the generating function of #solutions by degree and compare with the expected-dimension prediction; look for a polynomial-in-q correction.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Carlitz cyclotomic fields as the FF analogue of Q(ζ_{4C}) in Type II certificates
connection: Type II certificate conditions over Z are splitting conditions in Q(ζ_{4C}). In FF they become splitting in Carlitz cyclotomic fields K_M, which are abelian with Galois group (F_q[T]/M)^*.
why: Clean class field theory in FF makes the certificate covering problem an explicit set-covering in finite abelian groups; any FF covering bound gives a template for Z.
first_step: Express the FF covering trees of FUNCTIONFIELD_ES as covers of (F_q[T]/M)^* by cosets and compute covering numbers.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Polynomial ES at P = T² + T + 1, T⁴ + 1 and other never-square polynomials
connection: Generalizing the T²+1 test: for each irreducible quadratic/quartic f that is never a square and has values ≡ 1 mod 4, ask for a Z[T] identity. Mordell–Schinzel's obstruction is pointwise at square values, which f avoids.
why: A positive find would be a genuine new infinite certificate family for primes of a polynomial shape.
first_step: Run the same coefficient search as for T²+1 on a list of ten such f; note obstructions at fixed T mod M.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over Z[T]/(T² − D) as Z-module identities = real quadratic world
connection: Identities with denominators in Z[√D] specialize to the real-quadratic world (other_rings Prop 3.3). Viewing them as polynomial identities in T modulo T² − D links the two worlds.
why: Shows whether the real-quadratic universal-divisor identity can be 'traced down' to Z, giving a family over Z of trace-type denominators.
first_step: Take the D = 2 identity of Prop 3.3 and compute Galois traces/norms of its denominators; see if they yield a Z identity with numerator 8 (see trace-descent item).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over Q(T) with denominators in Z[T] but positivity 'for T in an interval' (semi-algebraic cone)
connection: Instead of eventual positivity (lc > 0), require denominators positive on [0, ∞) or on an interval. This cone is not multiplicatively a valuation cone and sits between Z[T]-lc and genuine pointwise positivity.
why: Mordell–Schinzel uses positivity on infinitely many integer points; different positivity notions show exactly how much positivity the obstruction needs.
first_step: Check whether T1 at squares already kills identities whose denominators are positive only for T in a residue class mod M.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: F_q[T] with q → ∞ AND deg P → ∞ jointly: the critical scaling deg P ≈ c·q
connection: Thm 2.1 (fails, q→∞ fixed degree) and Thm 5.3 (density-0 failures, fixed q) bound a phase diagram; along deg P ≍ f(q) there is a critical curve.
why: The critical curve is the FF version of 'expected number of solutions ≍ log² p'; its exact location in FF predicts how close Z is to the threshold.
first_step: Compute failure proportions on a grid q ∈ {3,5,7,9,11,13}, deg P ∈ {3..7} and fit the 50%-failure curve.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over F_q[T] with the extra condition 'distinct denominators' — equivalent or not?
connection: Over Z, distinctness is (believed/known) harmless for n > 2. In F_q[T] char 3, the trivial 3/P = 1/P+1/P+1/P shows repeats matter; with distinctness the char-3 numerator-3 case becomes non-trivial.
why: A distinctness-sensitive FF world is a new problem whose behaviour in char 3 could mimic Z with numerator 4.
first_step: Check whether 'ES_3(T, P) with distinct monic denominators' fails anywhere for deg P ≤ 8.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Dirichlet-density version of ES_q: probability that a random monic P of degree n satisfies ES
connection: Rather than all P, compute the exact probability π_q(n) that random P of degree n is ES-good; integer twin is the density of n ≤ N with a 'short' ES solution.
why: Exact π_q(n) as a rational function in q (if it is one) would be a structural prediction for the Z density of 'easy' n by certificate size.
first_step: Compute π_3(n), π_5(n) for n ≤ 8 and test polynomial-in-1/q fits.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field Type II ↔ binary quadratic forms over F_q[T] (Artin's imaginary quadratic function fields)
connection: Type II ES data encode representations by binary forms; over F_q[T] with q odd, binary forms have class groups of imaginary quadratic function fields (Artin). Class numbers are given by L-function values (RH known).
why: An FF formula 'ES count at P = combination of class numbers' with RH would give exact asymptotics, whose Z twin is a Dirichlet-class-number formula for ES counts.
first_step: Express the FF Type II count at fixed P as a sum over discriminants of class numbers h(D) and test numerically for q = 3.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Real quadratic O_K with N(ε) = −1: positive ES PROVED via inert ℓ ≡ 3 mod 4 and η ≡ −1 mod ℓ
connection: Prop 3.3: a totally positive unit η with ℓ | 1 + η supplies a universal divisor ℓ ≡ 3 (mod 4). Over Z the only units are ±1, so this step has no direct replacement; its integer shadow is a p-independent divisor of a p-tied integer, which only congruence (B1) supplies.
why: This is the proved twin with the most transparent mechanism; any 'unit-like' integer object (e.g. the Pell/unit-orbit families) is a candidate replacement.
first_step: Read UNIT_ORBIT_ES.md for integer replacements of η and list which ones produce divisors of 4Cp+1 independent of p.

title: Gaussian cone ES (Bradford–Ionascu Conj. 1.1) is OPEN — the Z[i] twin of ES
connection: Denominators in Z[i] with Re, Im of equal sign. The cone is discrete at ∞ and has no small units, so the unit-sum mechanism fails, as over Z. The other_rings principle predicts a genuine lottery problem.
why: A second open twin with richer arithmetic (split primes) — progress there (e.g. density-1 results) could be transported.
first_step: Implement a search for the Gaussian cone ES for Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 10^5 and record failures; check whether failures concentrate at squares as over Z.

title: Totally positive ES over arbitrary number fields K with an infinite unit group
connection: Generalize Prop 3.3: if K has a totally positive unit η and a prime ℓ ≡ 3 (mod 4) (rational, inert or split suitably) with η ≡ −1 (mod some prime above ℓ), positive ES holds for rational n. Conjecture: true for every K with unit rank ≥ 1 and a totally positive unit of infinite order.
why: Would show the Z difficulty is exactly 'unit rank 0 + discreteness', i.e. Q and imaginary quadratic fields are the only hard worlds among number fields.
first_step: Try K = Q(√3) (N(ε) = +1) and a cubic field with mixed-sign units; search η^j ≡ −1 mod ℓ numerically (other_rings evidence covers D = 3, 6, 7).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Eisenstein cone: Z[ω] with denominators in the 60° sector
connection: Z[ω] has 6 units; angular sectors are not closed under multiplication (arguments add), so a positive cone must be a semiring such as N-spans of a few units, or a sector cone with a weaker closure requirement. Each choice gives a different Eisenstein ES.
why: Choosing a closed cone in Z[ω] is itself a non-trivial design question that tests which positivity axioms matter.
first_step: Determine the multiplicatively closed cones in Z[ω] discrete at ∞ (e.g. N-span of {1, −ω²}?) and run the e-slice search in each.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Semiring cones Z_{≥0}[α] for α a Pisot or Salem number
connection: For α Pisot, Z_{≥0}[α] is discrete at the dominant place while conjugates shrink — like β-expansions. ES over these cones links to β-numeration (Pisot finiteness property F).
why: If ES-type statements over Z_{≥0}[α] relate to finiteness properties of β-expansions, there is a dynamical-systems literature to borrow.
first_step: Check the Frougny–Solomyak finiteness property (F) and test a numerator-4 ES in Z_{≥0}[golden ratio].
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Erdős–Straus for Gaussian integers / over ℤ[i]: does the analogue hold and does its proof (if any) use something ES lacks?
connection: ES over ℤ[i]: 4/α = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with Gaussian integers; the extra units and the splitting of p ≡ 1 mod 4 (p = ππ̄) change the problem: for p ≡ 1 mod 4, 4/p = (4/π)(1/π̄) — the hard primes split! The question 4/π for a Gaussian prime π of norm p.
why: Over ℤ[i] the analogue might be easier (more structure) or provably different; comparing sheds light on what ℤ lacks. Repo may have this (git grep Gaussian).
first_step: git grep -il 'gaussian integer' -- '*.md'; if absent, compute solutions of 4/π = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z over ℤ[i] for norm(π) ≤ 10⁴ with |x|,|y|,|z| ≤ N(π)² and see whether every π has one.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Positive-definite integer matrices: (4/n)·I = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹
connection: In Sym_k(Z) with the positive-definite cone, diagonal solutions are k copies of ES; non-diagonal X allow far more freedom. For k = 2, is (4/n) I always a sum of three inverses of positive-definite integral matrices?
why: A proof via non-diagonal matrices would be a 'matrix ES' theorem; projecting back (e.g. by the (1,1) entry x₂₂/det X) gives 4/n as a sum of three fractions with structured numerators.
first_step: Search k = 2: enumerate positive-definite integral X with small entries and check whether (4/n)I − X⁻¹ − Y⁻¹ is the inverse of an integral PD matrix, for n = p ≤ 1000.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Units of Z[1/2]: 4 becomes a unit and ES is trivial — the dyadic place carries the problem
connection: If 2 ∈ S the numerator 4 is a unit and ES collapses. Together with the Z[1/p] item: the obstruction is spread over the dyadic place and the place p.
why: Suggests a two-place reformulation: ES as a gluing problem between a 2-adic and a p-adic condition with an archimedean constraint.
first_step: Write ES as 'there exist local solutions at 2, p, ∞ with a common global lift of bounded height' and check it against STRONG_APPROX_ES.md.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Positive ES over O_K for n ∈ O_K with Galois-conjugate denominators only
connection: Require the three denominators to form a Galois orbit (K cubic, x, σx, σ²x): 4/n = Tr(1/x). Then ES becomes 'n/4 is the reciprocal of a trace of a reciprocal' — a norm-form equation.
why: Gives a cubic norm-form reformulation for rational n: Tr_{K/Q}(1/x) = 4/n; such equations are amenable to Thue/Schmidt or to equidistribution of units.
first_step: For cyclic cubic K of small conductor, solve Tr(1/x) = 4/p for totally positive x ∈ O_K, p ≤ 10^4.

title: p-adic sign patterns: which quadratic-character patterns (χ(x), χ(y), χ(z)) occur among local solutions
connection: Z_p carries no order, but a sign can be a quadratic character. ES over Z_p with denominators in a quadratic-character cone is a local question solvable by Hensel; relevant only as local data.
why: Local data are inputs to Bright–Loughran's no-BM result and the singular series; the cone version records which sign patterns of x, y, z occur locally.
first_step: Compute, for ℓ ≤ 30, which (χ(x), χ(y), χ(z)) sign patterns occur for local solutions of 4/n with n ≡ 1 mod 4 — compare with global solutions' patterns.

title: Adelic ES: Bright–Loughran no Brauer–Manin obstruction ↔ strong approximation failure
connection: Integral points on the ES surface are not obstructed by Brauer–Manin; ES is therefore an 'existence of integral points beyond BM' question, like Markoff surfaces where strong approximation fails in a structured way.
why: Markoff surfaces have proven 'almost all' strong approximation (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, W. Chen); an analogous orbit structure on ES surfaces would be a transferable mechanism.
first_step: Check whether the ES affine surfaces have a nontrivial automorphism group acting on integral points (Vieta-like moves); see MARKOFF_ES.md.

title: Real quadratic fields with N(ε) = +1: other_rings evidence shows coverage, find the proof
connection: For D = 3, 6, 7 (N(ε) = +1) the rational classes were covered numerically. The proof of Prop 3.3 used N(ε) = −1 to get ε^{ℓ+1} ≡ −1; for N(ε) = +1 one needs another route (e.g. ℓ split and ε of even order modulo a prime above ℓ).
why: Completing the classification of real quadratic fields would make 'unit rank ≥ 1 ⇒ ES' a theorem for all real quadratic K.
first_step: For D = 3, find ℓ ≡ 3 mod 4 split in K and a prime 𝔩 | ℓ with ε of even order mod 𝔩 and ε^{j} ≡ −1 mod 𝔩 — then need κ totally positive; test.

title: Function-field–number-field bridge: Q(√D) ↔ F_q(T)(√D(T)) real quadratic function fields
connection: Real quadratic function fields (D of even degree with square leading coefficient) have units (Pell polynomial solutions); the unit-sum mechanism applies there too.
why: Shows the unit mechanism is uniform across global fields and identifies Pell-polynomial units as the FF counterpart of η.
first_step: Take q = 3, D = T² + 1, find the fundamental unit (Pell polynomial) and test the mechanism for monic P.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Lipschitz/Hurwitz quaternions with integer coefficients ≥ 0 as cone (semiring N[i,j,k])
connection: The semiring of quaternions with non-negative coefficients is multiplicatively closed? (No: i·i = −1 ∉.) Hence a natural non-commutative cone must be designed (e.g. positive real part + norm conditions).
why: Recording a failed cone design avoids wasted searches and clarifies minimal axioms (multiplicative closure is essential for Lemma 3.1).
first_step: List candidate quaternionic cones and check multiplicative closure; keep only valid ones for a search.

title: Imaginary quadratic fields are the only other unit-rank-0 worlds: Bradford–Ionascu cone is the right twin
connection: Number fields with finite unit group are Q and imaginary quadratic fields. So among number fields the ES-hard worlds (with a sensible cone) are exactly Q and imaginary quadratics.
why: Focuses analogue efforts: Gaussian/Eisenstein cone ES are the only number-field twins, and statements proved for them would be closest to Z.
first_step: State as an Assessment in the cone-classification note; list known results for Gaussian cone ES.

title: Ring of formal power series Z[[T]]: ES for 4/(n + T) trivial by Hensel-type lifting?
connection: Over Z[[T]] with 'positivity' of the constant term, 4/(n + T) = Σ 1/X_i requires ES for n at T = 0 plus solvable higher-order equations; higher orders are linear in the corrections.
why: If every ES solution lifts formally, the variety is smooth at integer points along this deformation — a structural fact about the solution variety.
first_step: Check the Jacobian rank of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) at known integer solutions (is the surface smooth there?).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Quartic residue symbol (A/p)₄ on certificates: hidden finer obstruction?
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4), the quartic symbol refines (A/p). If certificates' quartic symbols are biased (e.g. never i for some class of p), there may be a finer reciprocity structure, as in the Apollonian quartic obstruction.
why: Quartic reciprocity obstructions appeared in HKRS for Apollonian packings. A quartic bias in ES certificates would be a new invariant.
first_step: Note (cheap test): (A/p) = −1 forces A^{(p−1)/4} = ±i, so only the i vs −i split is informative, and it needs a canonical i (e.g. i ≡ a/b mod p from p = a² + b², a odd, b even). With that normalisation, compute the i/−i split over sign-(−1) words, and the ±1 split over sign-(+1) words, for p ≡ 1 (8) < 10⁶.

title: Unit fractions generate a DVR (Epstein): structure of R(D) for D = Z[1/S] and O_K
connection: Epstein shows the subring generated by reciprocals of a Euclidean domain is K or a rank-1 DVR. ES asks for specific 3-term representations; the ring R(D) records which 'unit fraction algebra' each world supports.
why: If R(D) ≠ K exactly in the hard worlds (e.g. F_q[T] where R(D) is the DVR at ∞), it gives an algebraic invariant correlating with ES-hardness.
first_step: Compute R(D) for Z, F_q[T], Z[i], Z[√2] from Epstein's theorem and compare with the hard/easy classification.

title: Egyptian length function ℓ_R(a/b) across domains R
connection: Define ℓ_R(q) = minimal number of unit fractions (with cone) summing to q. ES ⇔ ℓ_ℕ(4/n) ≤ 3. Compare ℓ over Z, F_q[T], O_K: maximal ℓ for numerator-k fractions.
why: A domain-independent invariant enables 'transfer' statements: e.g. ℓ_Z(4/n) ≤ ℓ_{Z[i]}-something.
first_step: Compute ℓ for numerator ≤ 8 fractions in Z and F_3[T] (monic) and compare distributions.

title: The numerator set M(p) is divisor-closed, so ES ⇔ M(p) contains a multiple of 4
connection: Let M(p) = {m : m/p is a sum of three unit fractions}. If m/p = Σ 1/x_i and d | m then (m/d)/p = Σ 1/(d x_i), so M(p) is closed under divisors. Hence ES(p) ⇔ 4k ∈ M(p) for some k ≥ 1.
why: Weakens the target from one numerator to an infinite family; the Luca–Pappalardi/Mond–Portier average |M(p)| ≈ (log p)⁴ (up to loglog factors; Σ_{p≤x}A₃(p) ≍ x(log x)³ divided by π(x)) means typical p have many numerators, and one needs just one divisible by 4.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^5 compute M(p) (from all 3-term representations with any numerator) and record which element divisible by 4 appears first; look for a large-m element that is forced (like p + 1 ∈ M(p) always).

title: All-even ES ⇔ 8/p is a sum of three unit fractions: fails only at p = 17, 241 (p < 2·10^4)
connection: Denominators all even ⇔ 8/p = Σ 1/(x_i/2). In the computation, 'all even' fails only at p = 17 and 241 among 269 primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000. Schinzel's conjecture for m = 8 predicts finitely many failures.
why: 8/p ⇒ 4/p by divisor-closure, so a proof of the m = 8 statement for p > p₀ would prove ES beyond p₀; m = 8 is an 'over-strengthening' whose exceptions are visible and checkable.
first_step: Search for a polynomial/covering family giving all-even solutions for p ≡ 1 (24) and see which residue classes remain; compare with T1 at squares (do even squares-type obstructions exist?).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: z is a common multiple of x and y: fails only at p = 2521 below 2·10^4
connection: Solutions with x | z and y | z exist for every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000 except 2521. This sub-world is almost as rich as ES.
why: A near-complete subfamily with a single small exception is an excellent candidate for a structural theorem 'ES with lcm = max denominator for p > p₀' and indicates a rich parametrisation.
first_step: Still only 2521 below 2·10^4 (data/z52b/analogues_constraints_20000.txt). Parametrize lcm-solutions (z = lcm) explicitly and run to 10^6 to see if exceptions stay sparse; inspect 2521 = 2521 (prime) for special structure.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Denominators ≡ 1 (mod 3) is impossible when 3 ∤ n: a 3-adic obstruction
connection: If x, y, z ≡ 1 mod 3 then 1/x + 1/y + 1/z ≡ 3 ≡ 0 in Z_(3), while 4/n is a 3-adic unit when 3 ∤ n. More generally, with k terms and denominators ≡ 1 mod ℓ, one needs 4/n ≡ k (mod ℓ).
why: Shows that 'number of terms ≡ 0 mod ℓ' interacts with congruence-restricted denominators; a family of worlds where obstructions depend on k mod ℓ.
first_step: Tabulate for ℓ ∈ {3,5,7}, H = subgroup of (Z/ℓ)^*, the classes of n for which ES_H is locally obstructed.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Arithmetic-progression denominators x, y, z in AP never occur (p < 4000)
connection: No solution with y − x = z − y appears for any p. Possibly a provable impossibility (or extreme rarity) via the equation 4x(x+d)(x+2d) = p(…)
why: AP-structured denominators connect to elliptic curves (the equation becomes a curve in (x,d) for fixed p); impossibility would be an elliptic-curve rank/torsion statement.
first_step: Write 4/p = 1/x + 1/(x+d) + 1/(x+2d) as a cubic curve in (x, d) and test for rational points; check whether a local obstruction rules it out.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Schinzel's m/n conjecture: table of the largest exception N(m) for m ≤ 30
connection: For each m, compute the n for which m/n is not a 3-term sum. Schinzel conjectures finiteness for each m. The growth of N(m) in m is the 'numerator direction' of the phase diagram.
why: If N(m) grows like exp(c√m) or polynomially, it constrains any uniform method (a method that works for m = 4 should work for all m with a predictable threshold).
first_step: Use the MO question's suggested n(k) viewpoint: compute largest failures for k=4,5,… over small ranges and test whether the same divisor-in-one-class parametrization extends uniformly in k.

title: Numerator ladder 4 | 8 | 16 | …: ES(4·2^j) ⇒ ES(4) and exceptions grow with j
connection: By divisor-closure, 2^{j+2}/p solvable ⇒ 4/p solvable. The exceptional sets E_j for m = 2^{j+2} grow with j; ES ⇔ E_0 = ∅. Data at j = 1 (m = 8): {17, 241} below 4000.
why: Studying how E_j shrinks as j decreases gives a 'descent' picture; a proof that E_{j} ⊆ (explicit finite set) ∪ E_{j+1}... is not obviously helpful, but the E_j structure may reveal which primes are intrinsically hard.
first_step: Compute E_1, E_2 (m = 8, 16) for p < 10^5 and check whether hard ES primes (few solutions, e.g. 5, 13, 17, 193) are in all E_j.

title: Signed ES with a size-controlled negative term: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z with z ≥ n^{1+δ}
connection: Signed ES is trivial (4/(4k+1) = 1/k − 1/(k(4k+1))). Requiring the negative term to be tiny (z large) interpolates between trivial and ES-like. Find the threshold δ at which signed ES stops being covered by identities.
why: A threshold statement would be a new integer theorem halfway to ES, and the identity families near threshold are candidates to perturb into positive solutions.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4, compute the maximal z over signed solutions with one negative term; check whether z ≥ p³ is always achievable (via identities).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Odd greedy algorithm (open termination problem) ↔ odd-denominator Egyptian fractions
connection: Every rational with odd denominator is a finite sum of distinct odd unit fractions (Breusch / Stewart, to check), but whether the odd greedy algorithm terminates is a famous open problem. ES with odd denominators is impossible (2-adic), but 4/n with an even number of odd terms (two can suffice, e.g. 4/15 = 1/5 + 1/15) is a natural neighbour.
why: Two open problems about restricted Egyptian expansions; techniques from one (e.g. 2-adic descent) may cross over.
first_step: Check the status of the odd greedy problem and of 'minimal number of odd unit fractions for 4/n' (must be even by parity); compute for n ≤ 1000.

title: Shifted-prime denominators (Bloom): 4/n with denominators of the form q − 1, q prime
connection: Bloom proved results on unit fractions with shifted prime denominators (density/Ramsey type). The 3-term restriction 4/n = Σ 1/(q_i − 1) is a sparse constrained world.
why: A sparse world where heuristics predict finitely many solutions overall tests the lottery model calibration (expected count ≪ 1 gives failures).
first_step: Compute the expected number of solutions under the lottery model and compare with brute force for n ≤ 10^4.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Denominators in short intervals (Croot) ↔ size windows for ES solutions
connection: Croot studied unit fractions with denominators in short intervals [N, N + N^θ]. ES solutions have x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4] and y, z in structured ranges; asking for all three denominators in a short window is a size-constrained world.
why: Size windows are central to the repo's window/slice analysis; Croot's techniques give existence for long sums, hinting at what's needed for three.
first_step: Read Croot math/9904181 to see whether his argument has a 3-term component; compute the window widths of ES solutions for hard primes.

title: Covering systems ↔ unit fractions (Z.-W. Sun): ES as a statement about AP packings
connection: Sun relates m-covers by residue classes to sums of unit fractions of moduli. Three pairwise disjoint APs with moduli x, y, z have density Σ 1/x_i; ES ⇔ some disjoint triple of APs has density exactly 4/n (disjointness needs at least pairwise gcd > 1, but this is neither automatic — (2,5,10) is an ES triple at n = 5 with gcd(2,5) = 1 — nor sufficient: periods (6,10,14) admit no three pairwise disjoint APs, since that would need three distinct parities).
why: Imports covering-system technology (Hough, Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba distortion method) into ES via packings.
first_step: Determine for which ES triples disjoint residues exist (a CRT/graph-colouring condition on the gcds) and whether every p has at least one such triple; only then is 'ES ⇔ AP packing' an equivalence.

title: A₃(p)-numerator geometry: the set M(p) as lattice points under a hyperbola
connection: m ∈ M(p) iff m/p = Σ 1/x_i; for each Type II parameter set, the achievable m form arithmetic progressions. M(p) is then a union of APs intersected with [1, 3p].
why: If M(p) is a union of many APs with differences coprime to 4, it contains a multiple of 4 — a pigeonhole route to ES via the numerator direction.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4 compute M(p) and fit it as a union of APs; inspect the differences mod 4.

title: 4/n as a sum of three reciprocals of squares (Graham-type world)
connection: Graham characterized rationals that are finite sums of reciprocals of distinct squares. The 3-term version 4/n = 1/a² + 1/b² + 1/c² is a sparse world with local obstructions.
why: Not equivalent to ES, but a sibling in which local/global behaviour can be determined fully; it tests whether square-type obstructions come back with square denominators.
first_step: Compute for n ≤ 10^5 which n admit 4/n = Σ 1/a_i² (3 terms) and look for congruence patterns.

title: Breusch/Stewart: every rational with odd denominator is a finite sum of distinct odd unit fractions
connection: Solved universal unit-fraction statement under a parity restriction; ES fixed-length with no parity constraint. Note: for odd n, 4/n with all three denominators odd is impossible (4xyz is even but n(xy+yz+zx) is odd), so ES at odd n always uses an even denominator.
why: Parity restrictions change term counts dramatically — a clean feature-flip for the 2-adic side of ES (F29).
first_step: Compute: for primes p ≤ 10⁶, does 4/p always have a 3-term solution with all denominators odd? (Certainly not when … check quickly.)

title: ES restricted to 'Type I only' or 'Type II only': two sub-worlds with known almost-all behaviour
connection: Elsholtz–Tao distinguish Type I (p divides one denominator) and Type II (p divides two). Each sub-world is a constrained ES; which primes need Type II? (Computation: 'y, z both divisible by p' never fails below 4000; 'only z divisible by p' never fails either.)
why: Since both sub-worlds appear complete numerically, each is a strengthening of ES and may be easier to attack structurally (one family of divisor conditions).
first_step: Extend to 10^6: does 'Type II only' (p | y, p | z) ever fail? (Repo has censuses—check I3/Type II data first.)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES for numerators m that are prime vs composite (4 composite, 5 prime)
connection: Divisor-closure links composite numerators to their divisors; a prime numerator m has no proper non-trivial divisor (except 1). Compare exception structures across prime and composite m.
why: If composite m are systematically 'easier' through factor structure, the integer statement 'ES(4) ⇐ ES(2)-type subproblems' may have a useful partial version.
first_step: Using the Schinzel table item, compare exception counts for m prime vs composite at fixed n-range.

title: Engel and Pierce expansions: ES as a length-3 Engel-type representation
connection: Chain solutions (x | y | z) are Engel-like (1/x(1 + 1/a(1 + 1/b))). Engel/Pierce expansions of 4/n are deterministic; their lengths give a dynamical invariant.
why: If a variant of Engel expansion of 4/n always has length ≤ 3 after a single 'reset', ES follows; computing it is cheap.
first_step: Compute the Engel expansion length of 4/p for p ≤ 10^5; correlate with chain-world failures (38 below 4000).

title: Riemann–Hurwitz integrality: a surface subgroup of Δ(x,y,z) of index d needs n | d(n − 4)
connection: For an ES solution, a torsion-free normal subgroup of index d in Δ(x,y,z) yields genus g with 2g − 2 = d(1 − 4/n). Hence n must divide d(n − 4); for prime n ≥ 5 this forces n | d.
why: Translates ES into 'Δ(x,y,z) has a finite quotient of order divisible by n with x, y, z element orders' — a group-theoretic existence statement where e.g. PSL₂(F_q) quotients (Macbeath) are classified.
first_step: For small n list ES triples and check whether PSL₂(F_p) is a quotient of Δ(x,y,z) (Macbeath's criterion); see if a uniform choice like PSL₂(F_p) suggests a construction.

title: Brieskorn links: ES solutions never give integral homology spheres
connection: The link of x^a + y^b + z^c is an integral homology sphere iff a, b, c are pairwise coprime. Pairwise coprime ES solutions are impossible (constraint-world item), so ES links always have non-trivial H₁.
why: Gives a topological invariant (H₁ of the link, related to gcds of the denominators) attached to every solution; the gcd skeleton of Type I/II solutions becomes the torsion of H₁.
first_step: Compute H₁ of Brieskorn links for ES triples of small p and compare with the Type I/II parameters.

title: Star-shaped Dynkin trees T_{x,y,z}: det(Cartan) = xyz(1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 1)
connection: The tree T_{p,q,r} (arms with p, q, r vertices including the centre) has Cartan determinant pqr(1/p+1/q+1/r − 1) (E₈ = T_{2,3,5}: 1; E₆ = T_{2,3,3}: 3). ES ⇔ some T_{x,y,z} has n·det = xyz(4 − n), a hyperbolic lattice of discriminant xyz(n−4)/n.
why: Brings in lattice/root-system tools (discriminant groups, Vinberg reflectivity) and the recent weighted-star-tree classification of Torrente-Lujan.
first_step: Compute discriminant groups of T_{x,y,z} lattices for ES triples of small p; see whether they have a uniform structure (e.g. cyclic of order xyz(n−4)/n).

title: Parallel resistors: ES ⇔ a resistance n/4 Ω made from three integer resistors in parallel
connection: Conductances add in parallel: 1/R = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z. So ES ⇔ R = n/4 is a parallel combination of three integer resistors (equivalently three thin lenses of integer focal length in contact).
why: Electrical networks connect to squared rectangles (Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte) and Kirchhoff matrix-tree counts; a network-theoretic proof of a 'three-branch' realizability statement is conceivable.
first_step: Check the literature on 'realizing resistance values with k resistors' (series–parallel, minimal number of unit resistors) for 3-branch parallel results.

title: Kraft–McMillan / compact trees ↔ sums of unit fractions (Elsholtz–Heuberger–Prodinger)
connection: Compact prefix codes and canonical trees are counted via sums of unit fractions; ES-type identities appear as specific tree shapes with three leaves of weights 1/x_i summing to 4/n.
why: A tree/code interpretation may give a bijective or generating-function handle on solution counts.
first_step: Read arXiv:1108.5964 to see which unit-fraction equations correspond to which trees; check whether 3-leaf subtrees encode ES.

title: Hirzebruch–Jung continued fractions and cyclic quotient singularities ↔ ES₅
connection: ES₅ (continued-fraction length ≤ 3) can be read as a statement about cyclic quotient singularities 1/p(1, q) whose HJ continued fraction (resolution graph) has a specific short shape.
why: Toric geometry gives operations (blow-ups, Wahl/T-singularities) acting on continued fractions; ES might be equivalent to the existence of a short resolution chain.
first_step: Translate λ(p) ≤ 3 into an HJ-continued-fraction condition on some q mod p and check against bsA_toric_ksb_wahl.md.

title: Arithmetic triangle groups (Takeuchi's 85) and ES triples
connection: Only finitely many triangle groups are arithmetic (Takeuchi). An ES triple (x,y,z) giving an arithmetic Δ would carry a quaternion algebra; for large n, ES triples are non-arithmetic.
why: A finite check: which n have an ES triple among Takeuchi's list; quaternion data might connect to the repo's quaternion forms.
first_step: Intersect Takeuchi's list with {(x,y,z) : 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n} and list the n obtained.

title: Tessellations and Wythoff constructions: uniform tilings with vertex configurations from ES triples
connection: A triangle (π/x, π/y, π/z) tiles the hyperbolic plane; vertex/edge/face counts of Wythoff tilings depend on 1/x+1/y+1/z. ES triples give tilings with angle defect 2π·... proportional to (1 − 4/n).
why: Mostly a reformulation; potential value is visual/heuristic (e.g. counting tilings with given defect).
first_step: Low priority: note equivalence; compute angle defects of ES triangles for p ≤ 100.

title: Hypergeometric differential equations: exponent differences 1/x, 1/y, 1/z with Σ = 4/n
connection: Schwarz's list: the hypergeometric equation with exponent differences (λ, μ, ν) has monodromy a triangle group when they are reciprocals of integers; λ + μ + ν < 1 gives hyperbolic monodromy. ES ⇔ some Schwarz triangle with reciprocal angles has angle sum 4π/n.
why: Connects to monodromy/arithmetic of hypergeometric functions (Beukers–Heckman); ES triples give specific hypergeometric families whose arithmeticity could be tested.
first_step: Context; check whether any ES triple gives an arithmetic monodromy group (overlaps Takeuchi item).

title: Markov/Hacking–Prokhorov contrast: ES's surface has NO Vieta involution (linear in each variable)
connection: Markov triples a² + b² + c² = 3abc classify degenerations of P² to P(a², b², c²) and their integral points form Vieta-mutation orbits. The ES surface 4xyz = n(xy + yz + zx) is linear in each variable, so x is determined by (y, z): there is no second root and hence no Vieta involution.
why: Records why Markov-type orbit methods (strong approximation via mutation groups) have no direct ES analogue; any group action on ES integral points must come from elsewhere (e.g. Type I/II reparametrizations).
first_step: Look for other birational automorphisms of S_n preserving integrality (see the next item).

title: Apollonian/Descartes: curvatures with reciprocal relations
connection: Descartes' theorem relates curvatures quadratically; Apollonian packings carry orbit structure (thin groups) with local–global principles (Bourgain–Kontorovich density one; failures found by Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange). ES's reciprocal-sum structure is linear in curvatures 1/x.
why: Apollonian local–global failure via reciprocity (quadratic/quartic obstructions) is the closest known analogue of T1: an orbit problem where a reciprocity obstruction removes a density-zero but infinite set.
first_step: Read Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange (local-global failures in Apollonian packings) and compare their reciprocity obstruction with T1 at odd squares.

title: Egyptian fractions in the Sierpiński triangle / Pascal mod 2
connection: Recent work connects Egyptian fractions to the Sierpiński triangle (De Carli et al.). A 2-adic/Lucas-theorem structure might organize 4/n representations by binary digits of n.
why: The 2-adic structure of ES (coordinate in 4Z ∪ (8Z − p), m = 8 coincidence) could match Pascal-mod-2 patterns.
first_step: Read arXiv:2412.09728 to see the precise correspondence and test whether ES solution counts correlate with binary digit patterns of p.

title: Tropical ES: min(−v(x), −v(y), −v(z)) structure and Newton polytopes
connection: Tropicalizing 4xyz − n(xy + yz + zx) at a prime ℓ gives a tropical surface; ES solutions with given ℓ-adic valuations lie on cells of it. Over each ℓ | n the cell structure forces which denominators carry ℓ.
why: The tropical picture is exactly the Type I/II case split at ℓ = p; at other ℓ it describes the 'gcd skeleton'. Systematizing it gives a finite combinatorial classification of valuation patterns.
first_step: Compute the tropical variety of the ES surface for ℓ = 2 and ℓ = p and list all cells; match with Type I/II and with the 2-adic observations (m = 8, 4 | denominator).

title: Series–parallel networks with k unit resistors realize which rationals? ES as the 3-branch case
connection: The set of resistances of series–parallel networks of k unit resistors is a classical sequence (OEIS). A 3-branch parallel with integer resistors is an ES triple; the general series-parallel set is much larger.
why: Known counts/structure of this set (e.g. via continued fractions) might give a hierarchy argument: n/4 realizable with few resistors ⇒ structure close to ES.
first_step: Look up the OEIS sequence for 'number of distinct resistances with n unit resistors (series–parallel)' and its structural results.

title: Rademacher/Dedekind-sum reciprocity world for the triangle orbifold invariants
connection: Rho/eta invariants of Seifert spaces from ES triples are sums of Dedekind sums with reciprocity laws; T1 is a reciprocity phenomenon. Checking whether T1's congruence can be derived from Dedekind reciprocity applied to ES triples.
why: A second, topological derivation of T1 would show it is a genuine invariant-theoretic constraint and might suggest generalizations (other numerators, other square classes).
first_step: Compute Σ s(1, x_i) (or the Casson–Walker invariant) for ES triples at small p and look for congruences mod small numbers.

title: Toric/polytope view: ES triples ↔ reflexive-like triangles with given lattice data
connection: A lattice triangle with vertices on axes at distances x, y, z (simplex with intercepts) defines the plane X/x + Y/y + Z/z = 1, which contains the diagonal point (t,t,t) iff Σ 1/x_i = 1/t. So ES ⇔ some plane with positive integer intercepts passes through (n/4, n/4, n/4).
why: Lattice-point/geometry-of-numbers view: find a lattice plane with positive integer intercepts through the diagonal point at height n/4. This is a 'plane through a point' problem amenable to geometry of numbers.
first_step: Formalize: planes with integer intercepts through (t,t,t), t = n/4; parametrize by normal vector (1/x, 1/y, 1/z) and relate to the repo's lattice forms.

title: ES in models of IΔ₀: does bounded arithmetic prove 'almost all n'?
connection: Vaughan's density theorem uses analytic number theory; formalizing it in weak arithmetic is unlikely, but elementary 'almost-all' proofs (sieve-free covering arguments) might live in IΔ₀ + Ω₁.
why: A weak-arithmetic analysis isolates which tools are logically necessary, e.g. whether exponentiation (power ladders) is needed.
first_step: Survey: is there any Erdős–Straus-type density statement formalized in bounded arithmetic? (Probably not — low priority.)

title: Beurling generalized integers: build a system where some generalized prime fails ES
connection: ES's Type II needs divisors of the additive shift 4Cp + 1; Beurling systems keep multiplicative structure but destroy additive structure. In a Beurling system with integers 'close to' ℕ (Diamond–Montgomery–Vorhauer type), ES may fail infinitely often.
why: A Beurling counterexample would prove that any ES proof must use additive structure beyond the multiplicative/PNT statistics — a 'barrier theorem'.
first_step: Define ES for Beurling integers N_P (with an addition borrowed from R), construct a random Beurling system and test ES for its primes numerically.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Cramér-type model for 'hard primes': which properties of p predict few solutions?
connection: In the computation, the primes with fewest solutions are 5, 13, 17, 193, 29, 41, 73, 97. Hard primes may be those with p − 1 or p + 3 having few small factors (fewer Type I/II options).
why: A predictive model for the solution count at p (beyond log²p) identifies the regime where a counterexample would live.
first_step: Regress #solutions(p) for p < 2·10^4 on ω(p+3), ω((p+1)/2), smoothness of p − 1, etc.

title: q-deformed rationals (Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko) and the continued-fraction form ES₅
connection: q-deformed rationals [a/b]_q are defined via continued fractions; ES₅ characterizes ES via continued-fraction length. A q-ES₅ statement could be stated for [4/p]_q and tested for positivity of coefficients.
why: q-rationals have total positivity and Jones-polynomial interpretations; a positivity statement for q-ES₅ might be provable and specialize at q = 1.
first_step: Check whether Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko 'q-deformed rationals and q-continued fractions' (Forum Math. Sigma 2020) defines sums; test [4/p]_q against sums of three q-unit fractions.

title: Highly composite p − 1 makes p hard? (2521 = lcm(1..10)+1, 241 = 240+1, 1801 = 1800+1, 601 = 600+1)
connection: Several failures of constrained worlds are primes with p − 1 very smooth (601, 1801, 2521, 241). If p − 1 has many small factors then p ≡ 1 modulo many small moduli, i.e. p lies in square classes (1 is a square) for all those moduli — exactly where T1-type obstructions bite.
why: This links 'hard primes' to T1 directly: p ≡ 1 mod M for highly composite M is the most square-like residue profile, so certificate lines are empty modulo all those M.
first_step: For p < 10^6, compute the largest M with p ≡ 1 mod M among smooth M and correlate with #solutions(p) and with constrained-world failures.

title: Type II with x not divisible by p never fails below 2·10^4
connection: Solutions with p | y, p | z, p ∤ x exist for every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 2·10^4. This is the 'pure Type II' strengthening (Elsholtz–Tao notation).
why: A sub-world that is complete in range and has the cleanest divisor parametrization (divisors of a p-tied integer in one class) is the natural proof target.
first_step: Compare with the repo's existing Type II censuses (Z52_BANKED / I3 censuses) to avoid duplication; then count pure-Type-II solutions vs log²p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Dynamical world: Farey/Gauss map orbits of 4/p and 'three-step returns'
connection: ES₅ (length ≤ 3) asks for short orbits of a map on rationals. In the dynamical world, random rationals have orbit lengths ~ log p; ES needs a 'short-cut' orbit of length 3 for one of many starting points tied to p.
why: Dynamical large-deviation results (orbit lengths of rationals) give probability of short orbits; summing over available starting points recovers the log² heuristic.
first_step: Check repo's z31_dynamics_ergodic.md; compute the distribution of minimal ES₅ lengths over starting points for p ≤ 10^4.

title: Function-field random-matrix model applied over Z: Katz–Sarnak symmetry type of ES counts?
connection: If the FF fixed-P ES count is a trace of a Frobenius on some cohomology (sum over Type II data), its fluctuations follow a symmetry type (U, Sp, O). Over Z the same symmetry type would predict lower-tail probabilities.
why: A symmetry type predicts how often the count is near zero, which is the ES question at a single p.
first_step: Compute FF fixed-P counts for q = 3, deg P = 8, normalize, and compare histogram with Sato–Tate/semicircle/other Katz–Sarnak laws.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Adelic counting: Tamagawa-type volume of ES integral points with bounded height
connection: Integral points on the affine ES surface of height ≤ H should be ~ c·(log H)^r·H^a by a Hardy–Littlewood/Tamagawa heuristic; Bright–Loughran's no-BM result means no Brauer correction at all? (check whether their result is for integral or rational points).
why: If the heuristic constant c(n) is computable and positive for all n, it formalizes 'ES expected to hold'; deviations at hard primes would test it.
first_step: Read Bright–Loughran for the precise statement (integral BM) and compute the singular series at p for the ES surface; compare with actual solution counts.

title: Numerator-8 and 4 | denominator coincidence: test an explicit bijection between the two solution sets
connection: Up to 2·10^4 both 'all denominators even' (⇔ 8/p) and 'some denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' fail exactly at {17, 241}. A map: a solution of 8/p (x', y', z') gives 4/p with (2x', 2y', 2z'); does every solution with 4 | x arise from some all-even solution and vice versa?
why: An exact bijection would be a 2-adic structural theorem about ES; if not exact, the coincidence of failure sets is still a strong hint of a local mechanism.
first_step: For p < 2000, compute both solution sets and test whether 'has a solution with 4 | some denominator' ⇔ 'has an all-even solution' solution-by-solution (not just existence).

title: Prime-power numerators: m = 4 = 2² vs m = 9, 25, 49 — do odd prime squares behave like 4?
connection: Divisor-closure: 9/p solvable ⇒ 3/p solvable (trivial). For m = ℓ², the 'hard part' is ℓ² itself. Compare exception sets for m = 9, 25 with ES.
why: If m = ℓ² is generally easy except for ℓ = 2, then the dyadic nature of 4 matters; if m = 9 has square-class obstructions too, T1 is uniform.
first_step: Compute exceptions of 9/n and 25/n (3 terms) for n ≤ 10^5; compare with Mordell-type identity coverage modulo 840·k.

title: xy + yz + zx = N (Borwein–Choi): a symmetric ternary problem solved up to one possible exception (none under GRH)
connection: Borwein–Choi determine the N not of the form xy + yz + zx (x, y, z ≥ 1) — 18 known exceptions plus at most one more unconditionally, the extra one excluded under GRH — via class numbers of Q(√−N). For an ES solution, xy + yz + zx = 4xyz/n (the pretzel determinant).
why: The same symmetric quadratic in x, y, z appears in ES; their class-number method (representations ↔ forms of discriminant −4N) is a proved-twin technique for a closely related equation.
first_step: Read Borwein–Choi (Exp. Math. 9 (2000)) and identify how r_{σ₂}(n) is written as a class-number sum; look for an analogous expression of the ES count on the slice σ₂ = 4σ₃/n.

title: Croot's colouring theorem and Bloom's density theorem: Egyptian existence in dense sets
connection: Croot proved that any finite colouring of ℕ has a monochromatic set with reciprocal sum 1; Bloom proved that sets of positive upper density contain such sets. The method (Fourier analysis on smooth numbers, many terms) fails for 3 terms.
why: Their 'smooth-number Fourier' technology might yield 'k-term ES with denominators in a dense set' for bounded but large k, a new intermediate theorem.
first_step: Check Liu–Sawhney 'further questions' for bounded-length results with dense denominators.

title: Agoh–Giuga and Egyptian divisibility: Σ 1/p_i − 1/Π p_i ∈ ℤ
connection: Giuga numbers satisfy Σ_{p|n} 1/p − 1/n ∈ ℤ. Egyptian equations over prime denominators with a correction term are another sibling with open status (Agoh–Giuga conjecture).
why: Prime-denominator Egyptian equations are very rigid; a technique for Giuga-type equations might apply to ES with prime-power denominators.
first_step: Low priority; read a survey on Giuga numbers for techniques on Egyptian equations with prime denominators.

title: Harmonic numbers' p-adic valuations (Boyd) and the integrality of Σ 1/x
connection: Boyd's conjecture: J_p = {n : p | numerator(H_n)} is finite; studied via p-adic trees. ES at p is a p-adic statement about which unit-fraction sums have valuation −1 at p.
why: p-adic tree methods for harmonic sums might organize ES solutions by p-adic structure (Type I/II = which denominators carry p).
first_step: Low priority; read Boyd's 'A p-adic study of the partial sums of the harmonic series' for tree technique.

title: Erdős multiplication-table problem ↔ number of distinct products in Type II parametrizations
connection: Ford's resolution of the multiplication-table problem counts distinct products ab ≤ x. ES Type II parameters generate integers as products; overlaps among products reduce effective tickets.
why: The multiplication-table constant (log x)^{−δ} is the same exponent as in divisors-in-intervals; ES heuristics should incorporate it.
first_step: Compute the overlap rate among Type II certificate products for fixed p and compare with Ford's constant.

title: Lehmer's totient problem: Egyptian-type constraints ∏(1 − 1/p) from φ(n) | n − 1
connection: φ(n) | n − 1 implies inequalities and Egyptian-type relations on the prime factors. Another rigid multiplicative/Egyptian sibling with open status.
why: Methods to bound or exclude solutions there might adapt to proving rigidity (non-existence) in constrained ES worlds, i.e. explaining their failure sets.
first_step: Low priority.

title: Erdős–Selfridge/Graham 'Egyptian fractions with denominators in [N, cN]' as size-window sibling
connection: Problems asking for Σ 1/x_i = 1 with all x_i in a dyadic range relate to ES solutions whose denominators are confined to windows (p/4 < x ≤ 3p/4 etc.).
why: Window-confined existence results (Croot) are the closest analytic sibling to the ES window/slice structure.
first_step: Pointer: compare with Croot's short-interval result (batch C).

title: Counting Egyptian fractions (Bettin–Grenié–Molteni): number of k-term representations of 1
connection: Precise asymptotics/lower bounds for the number of k-term Egyptian representations exist; ES counts (Elsholtz–Tao) are the numerator-4 three-term analogue.
why: Their methods (lattice point counting with Dirichlet series) may give secondary terms for ES average counts, sharpening the lottery mean.
first_step: Read arXiv:1906.11986 / 2509.10030 for methods; compare with Elsholtz–Tao's average counts.

title: Waring-type 'every n is a sum of three triangular numbers' (Gauss) ↔ ES via genus theory
connection: Gauss's Eureka theorem follows from three squares. Problems equivalent to ternary quadratic representability are 'easy'; ES's equation 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is cubic. A quadratic slice (fixing one variable) gives binary problems.
why: Fixing x gives the 2-term problem, whose solvability is a binary-form/divisor question; the union over x is ES. Genus theory over the union is the conceptual gap.
first_step: Context; check whether 'union over x of binary-form problems' has a ternary-form encoding (cf. Borwein–Choi item).

title: Hilbert irreducibility / thin sets (Serre): ES failures must lie in a thin set?
connection: Each Type II certificate family gives a polynomial-in-parameters set of good p; a counterexample p must avoid all of them. By Hilbert irreducibility style reasoning, the set of p avoiding a single family of positive density is 'thin-complement'. A union over growing families is the issue.
why: Formalizing 'ES failures form a thin set in Serre's sense' would be a weak but new theorem shape (thin sets have density zero with power savings).
first_step: Test whether depth-K hard primes cluster on values of polynomials (e.g. squares, quadratic polynomials) by fitting.

title: The unit mechanism is NOT finite for fixed S: e·κ = 1 + η has infinitely many instances
connection: In e·κ = 1 + η (other_rings Lemma 3.1) only η is an S-unit; e and κ are not, so S-unit-equation finiteness does not apply. E.g. e = 3 divides 1 + 5^{2j+1} for every j. For a fixed S the mechanism therefore offers infinitely many identities, all of the same congruence type.
why: Corrects an over-reach: the reason fixed-S mechanisms cannot prove integer ES is not finiteness but that they are congruence-type (B1) once translated back to Z.
first_step: Record; check whether the infinitely many instances for fixed S ever produce non-congruence integer families (expected: no).

title: Integer-side statement replacing 'universal divisor': a p-dependent e ≡ 3 (mod 4) with e | 1 + η(p)
connection: In proved worlds e | 1 + η with η a unit. Over Z, the analogous statement is: there exist integers a, b with a·b ≡ −1 (mod e), e ≡ 3 (mod 4), and e·(stuff) = p-tied — which is precisely a Type II certificate. Writing it as 'η(p) = p-tied integer playing the unit' (e.g. η = 4Cp) makes the dictionary explicit.
why: Identifies the Z-object to construct: a family η(p) of p-tied integers such that 1 + η(p) has a divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4) in the right range. The Z[1/ℓ] proof suggests algebraic factorization (Zsigmondy-like) of 1 + η(p) as the mechanism to imitate.
first_step: Search η(p) of the forms a·p^k, a·p^k ± b, with 1 + η(p) having an algebraic factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) for all p ≡ 1 mod 4; check against T1 (must fail at square classes if polynomial).

title: All even with a denominator ≡ 0 mod 8: fails at 13 primes below 8000
connection: The refinement '8/p with a denominator divisible by 4' (i.e. 4/p with all denominators even and one ≡ 0 mod 8) fails at 5, 13, 17, 73, 97, 113, 193, 241, 577, 769, ….
why: Maps the 2-adic fine structure of solutions; combined with the {17, 241} coincidence it suggests a tower of 2-adic strengthenings with growing finite exception sets.
first_step: Build the 2-adic tower: for each (v₂(x), v₂(y), v₂(z)) pattern, list failing primes below 10^4; find patterns with no failures beyond small p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Categorified ES over N[T]: identities with non-negative coefficient polynomials, evaluated at T = 1
connection: If 4/P(T) = Σ 1/X_i(T) with X_i ∈ N[T] and P(1) = n, evaluation at T = 1 gives ES for n and at T = 2, 3, … ES for P(2), P(3), …. So N[T]-solutions are 'categorified' solutions propagating to an infinite family.
why: For a given n, choosing P with P(1) = n freely might make the N[T]-problem easier than ES (more freedom in P), yet it implies ES at n. Conversely Mordell–Schinzel forbids it when P(T) hits square classes at many T.
first_step: For n = 5, 13, 17, search P ∈ N[T] of degree ≤ 2 with P(1) = n and an N[T]-identity of low degree; check what values P(T) take mod 840.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over the ring Z[x]/(x² + x + 1) = Z[ω] with cone N[1, −ω²] (semiring spanned by two units)
connection: The N-span of 1 and −ω² (a 60° wedge spanned by two units) is closed under addition; closure under multiplication needs checking ((−ω²)² = ω⁴ = ω, outside the wedge?). Cone design determines whether an Eisenstein twin exists.
why: If no multiplicatively closed discrete cone exists in Z[ω] with full rank, then the Eisenstein world has no faithful ES twin — a structural fact.
first_step: Enumerate small candidate cones generated by units/small elements and test multiplicative closure computationally.

title: Weighted-variable world: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with (x, y, z) restricted to a 2-parameter algebraic family
connection: Each Type I/II family is a 2-parameter rational surface inside the ES variety. The 'world' of a single family is a ternary divisor problem; ES is the union. Asking which single family is 'closest to complete' gives a ranking.
why: The best single family (fewest failures) is the most promising proof target; the constraint data already show near-complete sub-worlds (lcm = z, pure Type II).
first_step: For each standard Type I/II family, compute failure counts for p < 10^5 and rank.

title: One algebraic denominator: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/α with α ∈ O_K totally positive, x, y ∈ ℕ
connection: Allowing exactly one denominator from a real quadratic O_K (totally positive) while the others are integers. Then 1/α must be rational, so α is rational unless 1/x + 1/y is irrational — impossible. So this world collapses to ES (or to two algebraic denominators).
why: Shows that algebraic denominators come in conjugate pairs at minimum; the minimal interesting mixed world has 2 algebraic + 1 rational denominator (the trace-norm binary-form item).
first_step: Record; pursue the 2+1 world (batch B 'quadratic orbit ES').

title: Dyadic world Z[1/2] variant with 4 NOT a unit: replace numerator by 3 over Z[1/3]
connection: Over Z[1/3] the numerator 3 is a unit, mirroring Z[1/2] for 4. The hard analogue would be '3/n over ℕ' — but 3/n is trivial over ℕ. So the pair (numerator, inverted prime) = (4, 2) is special: 4 is a prime power of the smallest prime.
why: Highlights that ES's numerator is a power of the prime 2 that also controls the parity/2-adic structure; any 'ℓ-analogue' of ES is ℓ²/n with ℓ odd (see prime-squares item).
first_step: Context; tie to the m = 9, 25 computations.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Eisenstein-norm denominators fail for 90% of p: a 3-adic obstruction?
connection: All denominators of the form a² + ab + b² (no prime ≡ 2 mod 3 to an odd power) fails at 451 of 499 primes. Possibly a 3-adic/ cubic-character obstruction like the odd-denominator 2-adic one: norms are ≡ 0, 1 mod 3, and denominators ≡ 1 mod 3 are 3-adically obstructed (batch C).
why: If explained by a local obstruction (sum of three norms ≡ 1 mod 3 forcing a 3-adic contradiction), it's a clean example of the congruence-subgroup obstruction family; otherwise a lottery world.
first_step: Check the 48 surviving primes: do their solutions all involve a denominator divisible by 3? If yes, the obstruction is the 'denominators ≡ 1 mod 3' 3-adic one.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Two-prime world: ES for n = pq simultaneously with prescribed distribution of p, q among denominators
connection: ES(pq) is implied by ES(p), but asking that p | x and q | y (split) is a constrained world that couples two primes. Its failures are pairs (p, q) — a 2-dimensional exceptional set.
why: 2D exceptional sets can be studied with bilinear methods (sums over p and q), sometimes yielding results unavailable in 1D.
first_step: Compute split-solvability for p, q ≡ 1 mod 4 below 500; see if failures form a structured set (e.g. both in square classes).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Hereditary/inductive world: ES(p) from ES of smaller primes via composition laws
connection: COMPOSITION_ES studies composition. A world where solutions compose (e.g. via Seifert-space covers or AP packings) would give induction: if ES(p) follows from ES(q) for smaller q dividing some p-tied integer, ES follows by strong induction.
why: An inductive mechanism is the classical way to prove 'for all p' statements; any composition law with the right divisibility closure would suffice.
first_step: Check COMPOSITION_ES.md for laws of the form ES(q) ⇒ ES(p) when q | f(p); search for f with q < p always available.

title: Toy world: ES restricted to x ≤ p/2 (the 'small first denominator' world)
connection: x ranges in (p/4, 3p/4]; restricting x to the lower half (p/4, p/2] keeps most Type II solutions (x near p/4). A failure in this restricted world identifies p that need x > p/2.
why: Clarifies which part of the x-range is essential; proofs often use x = (p + e)/4 with small e — 'small-e world' is the extreme.
first_step: Compute, for p < 10^5, the minimal e = 4x − p over all solutions; study its growth (this is the repo's slice index — check existing data first).

title: Partial-fraction world: 4/(T(T+1)(T+2)…) in Q(T) — Egyptian decompositions of rational functions
connection: Partial fractions decompose rational functions into sums of simple fractions A/(T − a). An 'Egyptian' decomposition requires numerators 1 and denominators in a semiring (e.g. monic polynomials with positive roots). This is a characteristic-0 FF-like world with residues.
why: Residue calculus gives exact conditions: Σ residues = coefficient conditions; may reveal a residue obstruction analogous to Lemma 1.1.
first_step: Determine when 4/(T − a) = Σ 1/X_i(T) with X_i monic in R[T] having real positive roots; compute residue constraints.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Elliptic-curve ES: '4/P = Σ 1/X_i' in the group law sense (point division) — category check
connection: Unit fractions don't exist in an abelian group of points; replacing 1/x by 'x-coordinate of a point' gives a different problem (sums of x-coordinates). Recorded as a nonsense-adjacent world; only the coordinate-ring version (genus-1 FF world) is meaningful.
why: Prunes a tempting but meaningless analogy.
first_step: None (closed).

title: Zeta-function world: Dirichlet series Σ_n #ES(n) n^{−s} and its analytic continuation
connection: If the generating Dirichlet series of ES counts has a meromorphic continuation with a pole structure (Elsholtz–Tao give average order), its behaviour near s = 1 encodes average counts; zero-free regions control exceptions.
why: A Dirichlet series with an Euler-product-like factorization would turn ES counting into L-function theory (repo: anal_dirichlet_series).
first_step: Pointer: read BRAINSTORM/anal_dirichlet_series.md; compute the series' local factors numerically.

title: Greedy-in-a-different-order world: choose z first (largest), then solve the 2-term problem
connection: Reverse greedy: pick z among divisors-structured candidates and check if 4/p − 1/z is a 2-term sum. Different search orders define different canonical solutions and different 'certificate complexity' measures.
why: If some order gives bounded search depth for all p tested, it suggests the right certificate measure for a proof.
first_step: Implement reverse search with z ∈ {p·d : d | small numbers} and measure depth needed for p < 10^6.

title: Probabilistic number theory world: Erdős–Kac for the number of ES solutions
connection: If #ES(p) is a sum of many weakly dependent indicators, log #ES(p) might satisfy a CLT (Erdős–Kac-type) with mean ~ 2 log log p and variance ~ c log log p.
why: A CLT would quantify lower-tail probabilities, the core ES question at the heuristic level.
first_step: Compute log #ES(p) for p < 10^5 and test normality after centring by 2 log log p.

title: Function-field Gaussian twin: F_q[T][√−T] or F_q[T, i] with a 'sector' sign
connection: The Gaussian cone twin has an FF analogue: an imaginary quadratic function field with a sign on both 'real and imaginary' parts (e.g. leading coefficients). Combining the two analogue directions gives a doubly-twisted world where computation is easy.
why: If the FF-Gaussian twin is proved (by FF methods) while the Z-Gaussian twin is open, the transfer gap is the same as for ES — confirming the gap is archimedean, not about i.
first_step: Define the sign function on F_q[T][√D] for D of odd degree (imaginary quadratic FF) and run the e-slice search.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Poisson-shape heuristic validated in FF large q (p_f(n)·e^{−M_g(n)}): test the same model on Z data
connection: The FF large-q densities match an independent-Poisson-shapes model. Over Z, the I3/U exceptional data could be fit by the same model with integer 'shape masses'.
why: If the same model fits Z, it is a strong unified heuristic; if not, the discrepancy is a Z-specific arithmetic effect worth isolating.
first_step: Take the repo's U(n) exceptional data and fit p_f(n)·e^{−M_g(n)} with integer shape masses; compare residuals.

title: Fixed q = 3 resembles Z (EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD #10): use F_3[T] as the Z simulator
connection: At q = 3, non-square failures vanish at odd n ≤ 15 and are few at even n, with no irreducible failure beyond n = 8 — Z-like behaviour. F_3[T] is the best 'simulator' of Z among FF worlds.
why: Any claimed integer mechanism can be stress-tested in F_3[T] with exact enumeration to large degree, where the analogous statement is checkable.
first_step: Adopt a rule: every proposed ES mechanism gets an F_3[T] translation and a degree ≤ 15 test before Z work.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES modulo p with denominators in an interval [1, H] (Shparlinski-type small solutions)
connection: Count solutions of 4/n ≡ 1/x + 1/y + 1/z (mod p) with 1 ≤ x, y, z ≤ H. For H ≥ p^{1/2+ε} character-sum bounds give many solutions; ES-type statements need H ~ p^{1/3}-ish lifts (the real solutions have x ≈ p/4 though).
why: Determines the minimal box H(p) for modular solvability; integer ES solutions give boxes of size p² for z, so this is a different (stronger) finite question, but its methods (Kloosterman) are those relevant to Type II slices.
first_step: Compute H(p) numerically for p ≤ 2000 and compare with p^{1/3}, p^{1/2}.

title: Signed ES with two negative terms: 4/n = 1/x − 1/y − 1/z — trivial, and what that shows
connection: 1/x − 1/y − 1/z = 4/n with x < n/4: choose x = ⌊n/4⌋ (or nearby) and represent the positive difference by 1/y + 1/z — becomes a 2-term positive problem for the difference, often solvable but not always.
why: Sign patterns (+,+,+), (+,+,−), (+,−,−) form a ladder: (+,+,−) trivial, (+,−,−) reduces to 2-term problems, (+,+,+) is ES. The (+,−,−) case is a natural intermediate.
first_step: For n ≤ 10^4 test (+,−,−) solvability with a bounded first term; list failures.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: k = 4 positive terms with all denominators ≡ 0 mod 4? ⇔ 16/n as a 4-term sum
connection: Generalizing all-even ⇔ 8/p: 4-term representations with all denominators divisible by 4 ⇔ 16/n is a 4-term sum. Divisor-closure across k-term worlds: (4d)/n with k terms ⇒ 4/n with k terms.
why: A k-term numerator ladder with k = 4 might be provable (more freedom), providing 4-term ES for all n — and a 4 → 3 merging step would be needed.
first_step: Compute exceptions of 16/n as a 4-term sum for n ≤ 10^4.

title: Matrix ES with nilpotent perturbations: X = xI + N (unipotent-type) over Z
connection: For X = xI + N with N nilpotent (N² = 0), X⁻¹ = (1/x)I − N/x². Matrix ES with such X reduces to ES plus the linear condition Σ N_i/x_i² = 0 — the dual-number world in matrix form.
why: Connects the dual-number item to matrices: solvable whenever the tangent condition is, so it's a 'first-order' matrix world.
first_step: Record equivalence; test the tangent condition on ES solutions for small p (shared with dual-number item).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Octonions / Cayley integers: non-associative ES — category check
connection: Unit fractions in a non-associative algebra are still defined (x⁻¹ = x̄/N(x)), and sums make sense, integer scalars still associate, so n·x scaling arguments survive; what may fail are arguments multiplying non-real denominators together (products of three octonions). The world is meaningful but its structure theory is thin.
why: Low value except as a test of which ES arguments use associativity (probably none beyond commutative subalgebras).
first_step: Low priority; note.

title: Z[i] without cone: solutions are plentiful; the cone is a 1/4-probability event per solution
connection: If unconstrained Gaussian solutions are many (polylog or more) and angles are equidistributed, the chance that all three denominators land in the cone is ≈ (1/4)³ per solution — so the Gaussian twin is a lottery with known ticket probability.
why: A clean model where the 'lottery' probability is geometric (angles), enabling exact heuristics to compare with the integer lottery.
first_step: Measure the fraction of unconstrained Gaussian solutions with all denominators in the cone for p ≤ 1000.

title: Adelic interpolation: p-adic solution families at 2 and p glued with archimedean windows
connection: ES at p = existence of a global point; locally at 2, p, ∞ the solution sets are open sets (2-adic patterns, Type I/II at p, size windows at ∞). Strong approximation fails (it's a cubic surface integral-point problem), but measuring the adelic volume of the 'window' gives the expected count.
why: The adelic window volume times the global density should reproduce log²p; mismatch identifies missing local factors.
first_step: Compute the product of local densities at 2, p, ∞ (window) and small primes for the ES integral-point count; compare with Elsholtz–Tao's average.

title: Monic F_q[T] with A = 4 (constant) in char 3: trivially true since 4 = 1
connection: In char 3, 4 = 1, so ES_q(4, P) = ES_q(1, P) is trivial (1/P = 1/(P+1) + 1/(P(P+1)) split once more). Constant numerators reduce mod p; only polynomial numerators are faithful.
why: Boundary marker: shows why the faithful FF analogue uses deg A ≥ 1.
first_step: Record.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES along thin exponential sequences: Fermat numbers are trivial, 4·3^k + 1 is not
connection: Thin sequences of special form often admit identities: n ≡ 2 (mod 3) is easy (4/n = 1/n + 1/((n+1)/3) + 1/(n(n+1)/3)), so Fermat numbers 2^{2^a} + 1 ≡ 2 (mod 3) are trivial; but n = 4·3^k + 1 ≡ 1 (mod 3) and ≡ 1 (mod 4) is not automatically easy. Systematically listing thin exponential families where ES is automatic vs hard.
why: Exponential families are where power-ladder certificates live; knowing which families are automatically easy narrows hard ones.
first_step: For families a·b^k + c with small a, b, c and p prime, test which have a uniform identity for all k (cf. Proth item in repo).

title: Gaussian numerator ladder: (1+i)^k/π for k = 1..4 interpolates between 2/n (trivial) and 4/n
connection: In Z[i], 4 = −(1+i)⁴, so the Gaussian-cone ES has numerator (1+i)⁴ up to a unit. The intermediate numerators (1+i)² = 2i and (1+i)³ give worlds 'between 2 and 4' that have no integer counterpart.
why: Locating the first k at which the Gaussian-cone problem becomes hard would show whether difficulty is tied to the full dyadic exponent (v_{(1+i)}(4) = 4) or appears earlier — a dyadic resolution invisible over Z.
first_step: Search for Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 2000 whether (1+i)^k/π (k = 1, 2, 3) is a sum of three cone unit fractions; record failures per k.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Beatty-restricted denominators: 4/n = Σ 1/⌊k_iθ⌋ for irrational θ
connection: Restricting denominators to a Beatty sequence (density 1/θ) is a 'quasi-random' thinning with equidistribution available (Weyl sums). The world sits between ES (θ = 1) and random thinning.
why: Equidistribution makes the Beatty world analytically tractable on average; if heuristics predict a threshold θ_c beyond which failures appear, it calibrates the ES lottery.
first_step: For θ ∈ {√2, φ, e/2} test p ≤ 5000 for Beatty-restricted ES; record failure counts.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Transfer statement B (from N(ε) = −1 fields): 'a p-tied integer surrogate η(p) with e | 1 + η(p), e ≡ 3 (mod 4)'
connection: The real-quadratic proof needs a unit η ≡ −1 modulo a prime ℓ ≡ 3 (mod 4). Over Z, candidates for η(p) are p-tied integers (like Pell solutions for Q(√p), 4Cp, p^k); the statement 'for every p some η(p) in a small explicit family has 1 + η(p) divisible by a suitable e' would replace the unit.
why: This is the precise integer target suggested by the cleanest proved twin; it is a divisor-in-class statement over a structured family.
first_step: List small explicit families η(p) and the resulting ES identities; compute which families cover all p < 10^6.

title: Transfer statement E (from the Gaussian twin): ES ⇐ 'Gaussian-cone ES for rational p' + projection
connection: If a projection Z[i]-solutions → Z-solutions existed, the Gaussian twin (with split-prime divisor abundance) would imply ES. The norm-constrained data (40 failures) show norms are not that projection.
why: Identifies a missing map; proving none exists (e.g. by a dimension/degree argument) closes the direction.
first_step: Look for a Galois-equivariant map from Gaussian solutions of 4/p to rational ones (e.g. via real parts of 1/x); test on data.

title: Galois-cohomology world: ES solutions as rational points of a torsor under a torus
connection: The plane X + Y + Z = 4/n in reciprocal coordinates intersects the 'integrality' conditions; integrality of 1/X is a multiplicative condition, so the integral points are points of a torsor under a split torus (G_m³) restricted to a plane — a log-Calabi–Yau setting.
why: Log-CY integral points have a growing theory (Gross–Hacking–Keel mirror symmetry, cluster varieties); ES might be a cluster-type variety whose integral points have canonical bases.
first_step: Check whether the ES surface (or its log-CY compactification) is a cluster variety; compute its boundary divisor and log-canonical class.

title: ES over Z[√2] with cone 'conjugate ≥ 1' (all embeddings ≥ 1): units excluded, lottery restored?
connection: Elements with all conjugates ≥ 1 form a multiplicatively closed set bounded below by 1 at both places (though dense in [1, ∞) in each embedding) and excluding all non-trivial units. This 'height-positive' cone should behave like ℕ (hard).
why: If computations show ES over this cone fails for some rational p, it is a hard world with richer arithmetic; if it always holds, there is a mechanism beyond units worth extracting.
first_step: Search 4/p = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ Z[√2], x_i, x_i' ≥ 1, for p ≤ 2000, bounded height; compare with integer solution counts.

title: Max-plus/min-plus degeneration families (Maslov dequantization): ES_h for h → 0
