connection: Deform 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n via x ↦ x^{1/h}-type dequantization; as h → 0 the equation becomes a tropical (max-plus) relation of exponents. Intermediate h give real-analytic families connecting ES to its tropical limit.
why: Mostly geometric intuition (size windows); may help visualize which size patterns are forced.
first_step: Low priority; note.

title: Profinite world: ES over Ẑ is locally solvable, but a 'sign' via an Ẑ^×-character can obstruct it
connection: Without restrictions ES is solvable in Ẑ (allowing non-unit denominators). Imposing a profinite 'sign' such as χ_{−4}(x_i) = 1 (denominators ≡ 1 mod 4) is obstructed: the reciprocal sum is ≡ 3 (mod 4) while 4/n ≡ 0 (mod 4) 2-adically for odd n. The sterile-point program, by contrast, studies which profinite points avoid all CERTIFICATE classes — not solutions.
why: Clarifies that profinite obstructions to certificates (sterile points, T1) are different from local obstructions to solutions (which ES lacks); character-type 'signs' produce the latter.
first_step: Record; connect to FF_STERILE_* and the T1 statement.

title: Category-error check: 'ES in the field of p-adic numbers with absolute value positivity'
connection: Q_p has no ordering, and |x|_p ≥ 1 is not closed under addition; so 'positive' p-adic ES with |·|_p-positivity is ill-defined beyond cones of units (collapse) — record as closed.
why: Avoids repeated reconsideration.
first_step: None (closed).

title: World of 'n with prescribed factorization of n + 3': p ≡ 2 mod 3 trivial, p + 3 structure controls the x = (p+3)/4 slice
connection: The slice x = (p+3)/4 leaves 3/(px) = 1/y + 1/z, solvable iff px has a divisor ≡ 2 (mod 3) (or similar). So ES on the e = 3 slice is a statement about the prime factors of (p + 3)/4 modulo 3. Similar for e = 7, 11, … (each slice a 'world').
why: Each slice world is a congruence-on-factors world (a Chebotarev statement for p + e); the union over e is ES. Studying slice-world failure densities gives the per-slice ticket probability.
first_step: Compute, for p < 10^6, the failure density of the e-slice for e = 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and compare with independence predictions.

title: Square-class depth: number of moduli M ≤ X with p ≡ square mod M — a T1-depth invariant of p
connection: T1 says certificate lines are empty at squares; a prime p ≡ 1 (mod M) behaves like a square modulo M. The count D(p) = #{M ≤ X : p is a square mod M} (or the largest smooth M with p ≡ 1 mod M) measures how 'square-like' p is.
why: If #ES(p) anti-correlates with D(p), hard primes are 'locally square-like' — a precise version of the smooth-(p − 1) observation and a direct link between hardness and T1.
first_step: Compute D(p) for p < 2·10^4 and correlate with #ES(p) and with constrained-world failures.

title: ES with denominators from a lacunary set (powers times small factors): 4/p = Σ 1/(a_i 2^{k_i})
connection: Denominators of the form small·2^k: 4/p − Σ … requires p | some denominator, so at least one denominator is p·(small)·2^k; the problem becomes a 2-adic digit problem for (stuff)/p — likely solvable only for special p (p | 2^k − small).
why: A lacunary world tied to the multiplicative order of 2 mod p: ES-type solvability ⇔ conditions on ord_p(2), an Artin-type problem.
first_step: For p < 5000, test solvability with denominators a·2^k (a ≤ 15) times p^{0,1}; correlate with ord_p(2).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Catalog: n = p + 2^a + 2^b (Crocker)
connection: n = p + 2^a + 2^b (Crocker) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ log n. Obstruction: no single-modulus covering; failures come from an explicit sparse family. Status: false infinitely often (Crocker 1971; Pan 2011 gives ≫ x^{1−ε} odd exceptions ≤ x). Mechanism: an explicit sparse family of odd n (check whether it is built from 2^{2^m}−1 and Fermat-number divisibility, as commonly described).
why: Log-count, no covering, still false i.o. — the sharpest warning that 'log² count + no local obstruction' is not enough; ES's count is log² p.
first_step: Read Crocker 1971 (Pacific J. Math.) and isolate the exact structural input; ask whether an ES analogue (p tied to 2^{2^m}) exists among primes.

title: Catalog: Riesel numbers k·2^n − 1 (509203)
connection: Riesel numbers k·2^n − 1 (509203) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: divergent log, periodic parameter. Obstruction: covering. Status: false for specific k; minimality open. Mechanism: covering.
why: Same mechanism as Sierpiński; included for completeness of the covering family.
first_step: Note: ES certificate families are also 'k·m + 1' shapes (4Cp+1): check whether any covering-type identity is impossible for them by B1.

title: Catalog: n − 2^k composite for all k (Erdős; e.g. via covering)
connection: n − 2^k composite for all k (Erdős; e.g. via covering) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: O(1). Obstruction: covering. Status: infinitely many such odd n. Mechanism: covering.
why: Dual phrasing of the p + 2^k problem; witness = prime value of a shifted sparse sequence.

first_step: Compare the Markoff failure mechanism (finite fundamental domain of Vieta moves) with ES and check whether ES has any reduction theory producing a finite 'fundamental set'.

To supply it one could: allow identities in auxiliary forced quantities (two-squares decomposition a, b of p; continued fraction of √p) rather than in p itself
why: Mordell–Schinzel only forbids polynomial identities in n; identities in other p-determined quantities are not covered.
first_step: Run a small symbolic search: rational-function identities 4/(a²+b²) = Σ 1/X_i(a,b) with X_i polynomials (with sign/positivity conditions on regions).

title: Feature: multiple disjoint certificate 'regimes' by size (x near p/4 vs x near p)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'multiple disjoint certificate 'regimes' by size (x near p/4 vs x near p)'. ES HAS distinct size regimes (Type I: one denominator divisible by p; Type II: two). To supply it one could: treat regimes as independent experiments and prove an anti-correlation (if small-x regime fails then large-x regime succeeds)
why: Dichotomy arguments need two regimes with complementary failure conditions.
first_step: Compute regime-wise counts for p ≤ 10^7 and their correlation.

title: Feature: hereditary consistency across scales (ES(p) solutions at p shape solutions at p·k)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'hereditary consistency across scales (ES(p) solutions at p shape solutions at p·k)'. ES HAS trivial scaling. To supply it one could: seek non-trivial 'lifting' from n = pq to p, i.e. a solution for 4/(pq) which is not a scaled 4/p solution, giving info about p
why: Non-trivial composite information might feed back to primes via descent.
first_step: Count non-scaled solutions of 4/(pq) and test whether their existence correlates with R(p).

title: Feature: strong cancellation in a fixed-target character sum (Rickards–Stange)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'strong cancellation in a fixed-target character sum (Rickards–Stange)'. ES LACKS (fibre size log²). To supply it one could: replace the fibre over p by a larger fibre over a p-dependent family (e.g. all n = p·k, k ≤ K) of size power, then extract p
why: The only proved 'squares + sporadic' theorem uses a long character sum over one target's fibre.
first_step: Count solutions of 4/(pk) over k ≤ K that do NOT come from scaling — is that fibre power-size and does it carry p-information?

title: Meta: 'witness profile' taxonomy (trials × success × correlation × structure)
connection: Classify all small-count existence problems by four numbers: log #trials, typical success probability, correlation strength between trials, and presence of algebraic structure. Plot proved/false/open.
why: Moves the dividing-line discussion from anecdotes to a 4-dimensional chart; ES's coordinates can be measured empirically.
first_step: Measure ES's correlation strength between certificate families empirically (pairwise covariance) — the unknown coordinate.

title: Meta: Poisson model predicts largest exception for each m — test at m = 4 by 'virtual exceptions'
connection: Under the PW Poisson model P(fail) ≈ exp(−(log p)³/m · κ), compute the expected number of exceptions beyond 10^18 for m = 4: if astronomically small, ES's verification is 'model-complete'.
why: Clarifies what verification to 10^18 means under the best available model.
first_step: Fit κ from m = 8..15 exception data, compute Σ_{p > 10^18} P(fail) for m = 4.

title: Catalog: n = p + x³ (prime plus cube)
connection: n = p + x³ (prime plus cube) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ n^{1/3}/log n. Obstruction: local mod small primes; algebraic at cubes (n = m³: m³ − x³ factors). Status: open; almost-all expected. Mechanism: —.
why: Same as Conjecture H with cubes: algebraic factorisation at perfect cubes — another 'T1-like' algebraic exceptional family.
first_step: None.

title: Catalog: Erdős: 4/n with x, y, z ≤ C·n²? (size of ES solutions)
connection: Erdős: 4/n with x, y, z ≤ C·n²? (size of ES solutions) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: log² (all solutions have max ≤ n²·const). Obstruction: —. Status: known size bounds (all positive solutions are ≪ n²). Mechanism: elementary.
why: Size bounds make ES a bounded search per n, so 'least witness' questions are well-posed.
first_step: None.

title: AP-avoidance density: CRT classes dodging all Type I families with ad ≤ X
connection: Compute the density δ(X) of residue classes (coprime, ≡ 1 mod 24) that avoid every Type I AP −f mod 4ad with ad ≤ X. ES ⇔ no prime survives all X; the decay rate of δ(X) is the 'covering strength'.
why: If δ(X) decays like exp(−c log² X) it matches Vaughan's exceptional set; slower decay would leave room for many CRT-constructed near-counterexamples.
first_step: Monte Carlo over random large residues, X = 10..2000; fit log δ vs log X.

title: Kubilius-type probabilistic model of R(p) as a sum of weakly dependent indicators
connection: R(p) = Σ_{families} 1[p ∈ AP(family)]; Kubilius models replace dependence by independence across moduli. The model's prediction for P(R(p) = 0) is exp(−(1+o(1))·E R(p)) if dependence is weak.
why: Formal backbone for the 'log² ⇒ true' heuristic; the dividing line is the dependence structure.
first_step: Fit the empirical distribution of R(p)/E[R(p)] for p ≡ 1 mod 24 and compare to Poisson; repo LOWER_TAIL memos have related data.

title: ES as a 'prime covering' dual to Sierpiński: an explicit infinite system that must cover all primes
connection: Sierpiński numbers are k such that a finite covering hits every k·2^n + 1; ES is the claim that an infinite AP system {−f mod 4ad} hits every prime. Both are covering statements, one about a sequence, one about primes.
why: Unifies the failure mechanism of p + 2^k with the success claim of ES: covering theory is the common language.
first_step: Survey: are there theorems that an infinite family of APs with divergent Σ1/modulus and a 'genericity' condition covers all primes (or all integers) except an explicit set?

title: ES certificate as small solution of a congruence: lattice/Thue reformulation with p fixed
connection: For fixed (a, k), Type I asks f | 4a²d+1 with 4ad | p+f: equivalently a pair of congruences in (d, f) — a 2-dim lattice problem modulo p-dependent moduli, solvable by Thue's lemma when moduli and bounds balance.
why: Thue-type pigeonhole proves O(1)-count statements; the obstruction is the divisibility (not congruence) condition f | 4a²d+1.
first_step: Check LONGSHOT_PIGEONHOLE.md and BALANCED_LATTICE.md for this exact form.

title: Arithmetic statistics of 'ES-failing residue systems' (Cohen–Lenstra style)
connection: Model the subgroups H_C ∌ −1 confining N_C's factors as random subgroups; Cohen–Lenstra-type weights might give the right probabilities for simultaneous confinement.
why: Arithmetic statistics heuristics with correct weights often predict exceptional sets accurately (e.g. Stevenhagen's negative Pell).
first_step: Compute the empirical distribution of the subgroup generated by N_C's prime factors in (ℤ/4C)^× for fixed small C over many p.

title: Analogy with Lehmer's question for unit fractions: smallest positive value of 4/p − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z
connection: If ES fails at p, the closest approach |4/p − Σ 1/x_i| > 0 is bounded below by 1/(pxyz). Study the 'Egyptian approximation gap' distribution; ES ⇔ gap = 0 is attained.
why: Converts existence into a Diophantine-approximation statement where Baker/geometry-of-numbers tools might bite.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10^5, the minimal positive gap and the number of near-solutions with gap ≤ 1/(p·xyz)·K.

title: Archimedean variant: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x, y, z ∈ ℤ allowing one negative denominator
connection: With one negative denominator the problem changes count regime (infinitely many solutions?) and becomes identity-solvable; the dividing line between 'all positive' and 'one negative' measures the positivity cost.
why: Isolates positivity as the obstacle (feature item 'positivity as the whole content').
first_step: Find explicit identities for 4/p = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z valid for all p; check known literature (it is classical that signed versions are easy).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Fixed-length words in SL₂(ℤ): Waring problem for SL₂ / word maps
connection: Every element of SL₂(ℤ/p) is a product of ≤ 3 (or bounded) elements of a given type (Waring for word maps; Larsen–Shalev). ES₅ is a fixed-length word condition in SL₂(ℤ) with integrality.
why: Bounded-width results in finite groups are proved by character theory (Frobenius formula) — a 'thick' count over the group — but ES needs integral lifts.
first_step: Check whether the ES₅ word count over SL₂(ℤ/N) is given by a Frobenius character formula and whether lifting to ℤ is the only gap.

title: Erdős–Graham problem on 4/n with distinct denominators all ≤ n^{1+ε}?
connection: Bounding the largest denominator changes count; there might be literature on 'Egyptian fractions with small denominators' (Erdős–Graham book) for 4/n specifically.
why: A family where the count is tunable by the size bound.
first_step: Check Erdős–Graham 'Old and new problems' section on unit fractions for size-bounded ES variants.

title: Correlation with Mordell's quadratic-residue classes: strength of 'residual' structure among hard primes
connection: Mordell's classes are exactly p that are squares mod 840 — the T1 shadow. Within these, does R(p) correlate with further quadratic-residue conditions (mod 11, 13, …)?
why: If the hard primes get progressively harder with more QR conditions, T1's shadow is the governing structure; ES failure would need p to be a QR mod 'everything' (impossible for a non-square), suggesting a proof route via 'p non-square ⇒ some character escapes'.
first_step: Compute mean R(p)/log² p for p in hard classes split by (p/11), (p/13), (p/17), (p/19).

title: Result: CRT avoidance density of ES certificate families decays like exp(−c (ln X)³), c ≈ 0.028
connection: Fraction δ(X) of residues in Mordell's hard classes (prime-like) that avoid every Type I family (p ≡ −f mod 4ad, f | 4a²d+1) and Type II family (p ≡ −e mod 4ab, e | a+b) with ad, ab ≤ X: δ(100) = 7.8e-2, δ(1000) = 1.2e-4, δ(1778) = 9e-6; ln δ/(ln X)³ ≈ 0.025–0.030 stable over X = 56..1778 (2·10⁶ samples).
why: This is exactly the Poisson/independence prediction (expected number of hitting families ~ (log X)³, matching Pomerance–Weingartner's (log p)³/m scaling): ES's certificate families behave like independent events at the level of residues. EVIDENCE only; Chebotarev makes δ(X) the exact density of primes unsolved by families ≤ X.
first_step: Extend to X = 10⁴ with 10⁸ samples (vectorised, memory-bounded) to test whether the exponent 3 persists or creeps.

title: Prediction: least ES family size grows like exp((ln x / c)^{1/3}) — super-polylog, sub-power
connection: If δ(X) ≈ exp(−c (ln X)³), the largest least-family size among hard primes ≤ x is ≈ exp((ln π_hard(x)/c)^{1/3}) ≈ exp(((ln x)/c)^{1/3}): about 5·10⁴ at x = 10¹⁸. This matches the shape of H4_NOT_POLYLOG.md's proven lower bounds exp((log p)^κ), κ < 1/12 (κ < 1/6 relative to (G)), and suggests κ = 1/3 is the true exponent (for this coordinate).
why: Gives a concrete conjectural Linnik-constant law for ES and an explicit target for the proven-lower-bound programme (raise κ towards 1/3) and for any upper bound (which would be ES-strength).
first_step: Compare with the Salez / Mihnea–Dumitru verification data to 10¹⁸ if family sizes are recorded there; check whether the H4 coordinate and s(p) are comparable.

title: Records of least family size: are record-setting primes near squares?
connection: Record primes (830041, 7155121, 7183201, 53049049) are not squares; 830041 = 911² + 120, 7183201 = 2680² + 801. T1 makes certificate lines empty at squares — near-square primes might inherit difficulty.
why: If records concentrate near squares, the T1 shadow governs the tail and the right model is 'random covering conditioned on distance to squares'.
first_step: For hard primes < 10⁸, regress least s(p) on log(distance to nearest square)/log p.

title: Catalog: Gaussian primes in narrow sectors / Hecke Größencharaktere
connection: Gaussian primes in narrow sectors / Hecke Größencharaktere ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power. Obstruction: none. Status: proved for sectors of power width. Mechanism: Hecke L-functions.
why: Angular equidistribution — ES Gaussian liftings would need sector control.
first_step: None.

title: Connection: ES ⟺ Frobenius of p lies in a union of Chebotarev sets of growing level — least-prime-in-Chebotarev theory in reverse
connection: Each certificate family is a Chebotarev condition in Q(ζ_{4ad}) (splitting/residue condition). ES says Frob_p always lands in the union over all levels. Least-prime results answer 'is the first prime in a fixed Chebotarev set small?'; ES asks 'is every prime in the union of growing sets?'.
why: A 'reverse Chebotarev covering' framing makes the dividing feature precise: unions over growing level with total density → 1 at rate exp(−c log³ X).
first_step: Search for theorems of the form 'every prime p lies in some Chebotarev set C_L with L ≤ f(p)' for natural families (e.g. every p splits completely in some field of a family).

title: Connection: Erdős–Hall 'every n has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m for some small m'-type statements
connection: Stewart's criterion makes 'n has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m' central. Ask the pointwise question 'for every n ≡ 1 mod 4p…'; the analogous unconditional results for integers in APs are about divisors in residue classes (Erdős–Hall, Hall–Tenenbaum).
why: Divisor-in-class problems for individual integers are typically almost-all; pointwise results need structure (e.g. n has many prime factors).
first_step: Literature check: 'divisors in residue classes Hall Tenenbaum individual integers'.

title: Ramsey–ES: a monochromatic solution for every finite colouring (stronger statement)
connection: Croot proved every finite colouring has a monochromatic Egyptian representation of 1. Formulate Ramsey–ES: for every finite colouring of ℕ and every large prime p, is there a monochromatic (x,y,z) with 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z? If true, it implies ES and may be accessible to Croot-type density arguments (or be false, which is informative).
why: Strengthenings sometimes have better proofs; falsification would show which colourings are 'ES-hard'.
first_step: Test colourings by 2-adic valuation parity, by residue mod 3, and random 2-colourings for p ≤ 10⁴; look for primes with no monochromatic solution.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Connection: correlation between families measured by survivor statistics
connection: In the residue model, families are independent if δ(X) equals ∏(1 − density of family). Comparing the observed δ(X) with the independent product quantifies correlation exactly (no primes needed).
why: Correlation is the one unknown dividing-line coordinate for ES; this is a direct, cheap measurement.
first_step: Compute ∏_{families ≤ X}(1 − |res|/φ(m)·…) (careful with non-unit residues) vs observed δ(X).

title: Connection: residue model vs actual primes — the only gap is size, not residue
connection: Type I/II parametrisations have no size constraint (Pomerance slides): the residue model is EXACT for each fixed family set. ES ⟺ no prime survives all families; the gap between the model and ES is that X must grow with p (and Chebotarev error terms in level ≈ exp((log p)^{1/3})).
why: Reformulates ES as a uniform Chebotarev/sieve problem at level exp((log p)^{1/3+ε}): far below power level, where Bombieri–Vinogradov-type averages are strong — but needed pointwise for one p.
first_step: Check: is there any pointwise result 'every prime p avoids a sieve of level L = exp((log p)^θ) only if p is in an explicit thin set'? (Least-witness theory for sieves.)

title: Result: ES certificate families are strongly positively correlated (residue model), yet coverage still decays like exp(−c log³ X)
connection: Observed survivor fraction vs product of marginal miss rates (families with s ≤ X): ratio 1.5 at X = 32, 6.5 at X = 100, 4·10² at X = 316, 8.5·10⁵ at X = 1000. Survivors are far more common than independence predicts, but ln δ/(ln X)³ stays ≈ 0.028 while the independent product has ≈ 0.045–0.07.
why: Independence fails badly — the dividing-line 'correlation' coordinate for ES is large — but in a way that only rescales the log³ intensity. This is the empirical form of the T1 shadow: families share quadratic-character conditions. EVIDENCE.
first_step: Identify the correlation source: group families by the quadratic characters their residue sets lie in (χ_{−4d} cosets) and recompute the independence ratio within/between character groups.

title: Prediction: under GRH the 'sign layer' reaches n(p) ≤ 2 log² p, so if s(p) were a function of n(p) alone ES would follow — the data say it is not alone
connection: Bach's bound makes character patterns of p escape square-like behaviour by ℓ ≈ 2 log² p. If ES-hardness were controlled only by n(p) (plus bounded noise), a GRH-conditional pointwise argument would exist. The observed n(p) = 17 record with s = 2814 shows extra (class-layer) difficulty — consistent with the campaign's 'class, not parity' gap.
why: Separates how much of ES's tail is explained by the sign layer (characters) vs the class layer; quantitative version of FRONTIER's F6/G4 split.
first_step: Quantify: fraction of variance of log s(p) explained by the quadratic-character vector of p modulo ℓ ≤ 100 (linear/tree model).

title: Feature: character-sorted family covering — ES as a covering of the 'character cube' {±1}^ℓ
connection: Group certificate families by the quadratic-character pattern they require. ES then needs: for every pattern realised by a prime p (all patterns except 'all +1' for squares), some family compatible with that pattern also hits p's finer class. The coarse layer is a covering of the Boolean cube minus the all-ones corner.
why: Makes T1 (all-ones corner uncovered) and ES (every other corner eventually covered) two parts of one combinatorial statement; the coarse layer may be provable by finite combinatorics.
first_step: Compute, for ℓ ≤ 7 small primes, which corners of {±1}^ℓ are covered by at least one family with s ≤ 1000 (coarse layer), and how the fine layer behaves inside each corner.

title: OEIS anchor: ordered count O(n) = A292581, at primes A292624
connection: O(n) (ordered triples) matches A292581, and O(p) matches A292624; U(p) matches A192789.
why: Three independent OEIS entries anchor the prime-restricted counts used in all correlation items below.
first_step: Pull b-files of A292624/A192789 to extend our prime data past 2·10⁵ for free, if they go further.

title: U(p) ≤ 4 only for p ∈ {2,3,5,13,17}
connection: Among primes ≤ 2·10⁵, U(p) ≤ 4 only at 2,3,5,13,17; for p > 1000 min U(p) is 9 (at 2521), 11, 15, …
why: An explicit lower bound U(p) ≥ c log²p failing only at small p is the kind of statement the BM main-term work (FRONTIER §2.2) predicts; the empirical floor calibrates c.
first_step: Fit min_{p∈[X,2X]} U(p) vs (log X)² for X up to 10⁷ (count program runs in ~1 s per prime at 10⁶).

title: Record lows of U(p)/log²p are 53, 61, 73, 193, 2521
connection: Scanning primes 50 < p < 2·10⁵, U(p)/log²p sets record lows exactly at 53, 61, 73, 193, 2521 (ratio 0.147 at 2521); no further record up to 2·10⁵.
why: Two of the five records are the Type-A (b=1) failures 193, 2521; the record sequence is a compact 'hardness' fingerprint not in OEIS.
first_step: Extend to 10⁷ with the count program restricted to candidates p ≡ 1 (mod 840) or with large least-QNR (cheap pre-filter), to see if 66529 or other A/R failures become records.

title: U(232 792 561) = 276: the lcm(1..19)+1 prime is hard but not extreme
connection: p = lcm(1,…,19)+1 has U = 276, U/log²p = 0.74, U/log³p = 0.039 vs median U/log³p ≈ 0.095 at 10⁷ (below the minimum of 113 random primes at 10⁷); k₁ = 193, k₂ = 83 (k₁/k₂ = 2.3, typical). [An earlier version reported k₁ = 47 < k₂ = 82 — an artefact of a 64-bit overflow in the type classification, fixed after review.]
why: Partially confirms the lcm+1 prediction (hard, ≈ 2.5× below typical) but not 'record-hard'; the Type I/II split is normal, so all-small-primes-split does not starve Type I specifically at this prime.
first_step: Model-guided search for primes ≡ 1 (mod 2520·11·13) ≤ 10¹⁰ with extreme L(1,χ_p); compare their U/log³p with the lcm(1..19)+1 value.

title: log U(p) ≈ const − 0.30·log L_Q(1,χ_p), saturating at Q ≈ 30
connection: Adding log of the truncated Euler product ∏_{q≤Q}(1−χ_p(q)/q)^{−1} to the (log p, loglog p) regression gives α ≈ −0.30 and R²-gain 0.29 (Q=2), 0.40 (Q=3), 0.47 (Q=7), 0.49 (Q=31), 0.48 (Q=1000).
why: About half the residual variance of log U(p) is explained by the quadratic character of p at primes ≤ 30; this suggests (it does not prove) that much of the count's fluctuation is governed by finitely many local data.
first_step: Fit with separate coefficients per small prime q (2,3,5,7,11,13) to get the local weights; compare to the Elsholtz–Tao local densities.

title: (★) count R(p) correlates with h(−4p) (α ≈ +0.38, R²-gain 0.20)
connection: The c=1 Type-II line R(p) = #{4uBC−u−B=p} fits log R ≈ … + 0.38 log L_Q(1,χ_{−4p}) (gain 0.20) and only −0.17 on χ_p (gain 0.09).
why: R(p) is the campaign's central count; a class-number dependence suggests an exact or approximate formula in terms of h(−4p)/Hurwitz numbers (theta-series origin), cf. KUDLA_ES.md.
first_step: Fit log R(p) on log L(1,χ_{dp}) for twists d ∈ {−4,−8,−3,−20,…} jointly (class numbers themselves scale like √p, R like log²p, so only L-values/Euler products can enter); identify the minimal twist set.

title: a_p(32a1) mod 8 is just (2/p)
connection: The strong correlation of U(p) with a_p(y²=x³−x) mod 8 (ρ=+0.55) is identical to that with (2/p) (ρ=−0.55): for this CM curve a_p mod 8 encodes p mod 8.
why: Records a spurious-looking modular-form 'match' and its trivial explanation (guard against false fingerprints).
first_step: None needed; use as a sanity check whenever a CM form correlates.

title: Least primitive root vs U: ρ = −0.57 (proxy check)
connection: The least primitive root g(p) is a QNR, so g(p) ≥ least QNR; its correlation is weaker than least QNR (−0.66).
why: Proxy relationship; recorded to avoid double-counting in multi-feature models.
first_step: Partial correlation of U with g(p) given least QNR.

title: U(p) vs τ((p+3)/4): ρ = +0.59
connection: U(p) residual correlates +0.59 with τ((p+3)/4) and +0.48 with τ(p+3), but only +0.12 with τ(4p+1), +0.12 with τ(p+4), +0.05 with τ(p+12).
why: x = (p+3)/4 is the smallest admissible first denominator; solutions with x=(p+3)/4 come from divisors of (p+3)/4-related numbers; a single shift explains a large share of variance.
first_step: Count solutions by x−⌈p/4⌉ ∈ {0,1,2,…} and measure what fraction of U(p) comes from the first few x; relate to divisors of p+3, p+7, …

title: h(−3p) correlates positively with U(p) (ρ=+0.46)
connection: U(p) residual vs h(−3p) (imaginary quadratic field Q(√−3p)) ρ = +0.46; vs h(−4p) only +0.08 (raw) / +0.14 (normalised).
why: χ_{−3p}(q) = (−3/q)(p/q): another twist; ES identities with denominator 3 (p ≡ 2 mod 3 classes) suggest the −3 twist is natural.
first_step: Fit log U on all of log L(1,χ_{dp}) for d ∈ {1,−1,−3,−4,−8,5,−20,…} jointly and identify the minimal set.

title: minz(p)/p sequence: 1,1,2,2,3,4,6,3,6,8,8,10,… (not in OEIS)
connection: floor(minz(p)/p) at primes; at p≡1(4): 2,4,6,8,10,4,14,9,10,8,28,7,…; minz(p)/p correlates −0.42 with τ(4p+1) and −0.31 with R(p).
why: The cofactor of p in the optimal denominator is a 'height' of the cheapest certificate; small values relate to (★) with small C (divisors of 4Cp+1).
first_step: Identify minz(p)/p with the least C such that 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C) or similar; test equality over our range.

title: minlcm(p)/p at primes not in OEIS; correlates +0.23 with least QNR
connection: The least common denominator over solutions, divided by p, behaves like a cost: larger when small primes are QRs (ρ=+0.23 with least QNR, +0.20 with L(1,χ_p)).
why: Smallest common denominator = smallest N with 4N/p a sum of three divisors of N (Egyptian-fraction 'practical number' view) — links ES to practical numbers / Erdős–Graham denominators.
first_step: Check: is minlcm(p)/p always a practical number? Compute and compare to OEIS A005153.

title: U(n) records at 2,3,6,8,10,12,15,24,30,40,48,60,… vs highly composite numbers
connection: Record positions of U(n) (not in OEIS) are dominated by smooth numbers but are not A002182 (15, 30, 40 appear; 36 does not).
why: Records of a divisor-sum-like count should track the extremal order of a specific divisor function; identifying it gives the right 'max U(n) ≍ ?' growth.
first_step: Compare record positions with records of Σ_{d|n} τ(d)², τ(n)τ(n+1)…; fit max_{n≤X} U(n) vs exp(c log X/log log X).

title: U(p) mod m is equidistributed (small bias at U ≡ 1 mod 6)
connection: For p≡1(4) >100 (n=8 843), U(p) mod 2,3,4,8 are flat within noise; U(p) ≡ 1 (mod 6) is 1361 vs ≈1490 expected (≈3.5σ low).
why: No parity constraint ⇒ no simple involution explains U(p); the mod-6 dip may be a counting artefact (e.g. solutions with y=z).
first_step: Separate solutions with repeated denominators (x=y or y=z) and recount mod 6.

title: k₁(p) can be small while k₂(p) is not — or vice versa?
connection: k₁ and k₂ have residual correlation driven by different characters; tabulating the joint distribution of (k₁(p), k₂(p)) shows whether simultaneous smallness is rarer than independence predicts.
why: Anti-correlation of the types' local obstructions would be the cleanest heuristic for 'one type always works'.
first_step: Compute Spearman(k₁ residual, k₂ residual) and the count of p with both below their 5% quantiles vs 0.25% expected.

title: U(p) at p ≡ 1 (24) vs p ≡ 1 (840) distributions
connection: Spearman of residual U(p) with 1[p≡1 mod 24] is −0.62, with '840-square class' −0.38, with 1[p≡1 mod 840] −0.15 (rare event).
why: Quantifies how much of hardness is the classical Mordell residue structure — a reference point for any proof that treats 'bad residue classes' separately.
first_step: Compute mean U(p)/log²p per class mod 840 (the six square classes 1,121,169,289,361,529) and rank them.

title: Hard primes are p ≡ 1 mod a large smooth modulus — compare with Carmichael/Korselt primes
connection: 2521, 1201, 3361, 20521, 21841, 4201, 14401, 9601 all have p−1 divisible by 2⁴·3·5² or 2⁴·3·5·7 etc.; these are exactly the primes used to build Carmichael numbers (Erdős construction, p−1 | L).
why: Shared extremal structure (p−1 | L for smooth L) — tools for counting such primes (AGP, Erdős) could count ES-hard candidates.
first_step: Test: are ES-hard primes over-represented among prime factors of Carmichael numbers ≤ 10¹²? (Pinch's tables).

title: Campaign hard-prime lists are not in OEIS
why: No hidden classical identity (e.g. 'primes p with property X of p−1') explains them — or OEIS lacks it; submission would expose them to outside pattern-finders.
first_step: Submit the R-zero list with a definition and b-file to OEIS; also add I3 zeros (114 terms) and U failures.

title: 7/n fails only at n = 2 (≤ 10⁵ primes, n ≤ 4000)
connection: Consistent with PW (no 7/n exception in [3, 10¹³]); 7/p counts at primes are small (U₇(p) = 0,1,2,3,2,8,4,…).
why: 7/n is the smallest numerator where the local (mod-m) obstruction picture differs from 4 and 5; any ES method that is numerator-uniform must also handle 7.
first_step: Fit U₇(p) vs log²p and check whether the hardest 7/p primes coincide with the hardest 4/p primes.

title: '4-divisible ES': 16/p last failure ≤ 10⁵ is 83449 — an R-zero
connection: 16/p failures (38 primes ≤ 10⁵) include 193, 577, 1201, 2521, 3361, 3169, 4801, 33601, 36529, 78721 and end at 83449, which is also a (★) failure.
why: Two independent hardness tests pick out the same large prime 83449: suggests a shared 2-adic obstruction (p ≡ 1 mod 16? 83449 mod 16 = 9) worth isolating.
first_step: Compute v₂(p−1), p mod 16/32/64 for all 16/p failures and for the 14 R-zeros; test whether 2-adic depth predicts both.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Divisibility-strengthened ES_k ladder (k | x,y,z): last failures 241, 12241, 83449, 90001, ≥97777, 92401, …
why: PW prove n_m ≥ exp(m^{1/3+o(1)}), so ES_k fails infinitely far out as k grows but each ES_k plausibly has finitely many failures — a quantitative family 'between' ES and false statements, useful to calibrate any method's strength (a method proving ES_k for k=3 would be stronger than ES).
first_step: Pick the smallest k (k=2, 'even ES') and try to push the census to 10¹⁰ with a dedicated sieve; check whether the 8/n exceptions really stop at 241.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Hardness index H(p) = #{m ≤ 48 : m/p fails} correlates with U(p)/log²p (ρ = −0.43)
why: A single prime-level 'obstruction profile' across numerators: if hardness were a local (Euler-product) phenomenon, H(p) should be predictable from p mod small numbers — a cheap test of locality.
first_step: Regress H(p) on Legendre symbols (q/p) for q ≤ 30 and on p mod 8,9,16,25; report R².

title: PW numerics reproduced: for every m ∈ [20,48] some prime in (m², 2m²) fails m/p
connection: Counts of failing primes in (m², 2m²): m=20:6, 21:5, 22:5, 23:5, 24:13, …, 48:70 — consistent with PW's reported numerics for m ≥ 20.
why: Independent confirmation of a 2025 literature claim with our engine; and the counts per m give an empirical density to compare with PW's probabilistic model.
first_step: Compare the counts with PW's predicted number (their Elsholtz–Tao-style density) in (m², 2m²).

title: 15/p failure set contains three of the 30 hardest ES primes (4201, 12601, 20521)
connection: 15/p fails at 25 primes ≤ 10⁵ ending 1103,1171,1367,4201,6301,12601,16831,20521; 4201, 12601, 20521 are top-30 hard for 4/p though 15 is not a multiple of 4.
why: Cross-numerator coincidence not explained by divisibility monotonicity; suggests a shared local cause (p ≡ 1 mod 120 or 840?).
first_step: Compute p mod 840 for 15/p failures and test enrichment of p ≡ 1 (mod 120).

title: Last-failure sequence by numerator m (7..48) is not in OEIS
why: These are lower bounds for Schinzel's n_m (true values may be larger beyond 10⁵); a curated table would let PW-type theory be compared with data.
first_step: Extend each m to 10⁷ (cost drops ∝ 1/m) and submit as 'largest known prime p with m/p not a sum of 3 unit fractions'.

title: U₈(p) = number of all-even ES solutions of 4/p
connection: By scaling, U₈(p) counts solutions of 4/p with x, y, z even; at primes: 0,0,1,3,0,3,0,2,7,4,12,6,…
why: Ratio U₈(p)/U₄(p) is the 'even fraction' of ES solutions — a 2-adic statistic; if it tends to a constant, even-ES is ES with a constant-factor loss.
first_step: Compute U₈(p)/U₄(p) average by p mod 8 and mod 16; compare with the 2-adic local density of the ES surface.

title: Joint failure: no prime ≤ 10⁵ fails both 8/p and 12/p beyond {2,3}
connection: fail(8) ∩ fail(12) = {2,3}; fail(8) ∩ fail(16) = fail(8) by monotonicity; overlaps of non-nested failure sets are small.
why: Different divisibility strengthenings fail on disjoint primes; a covering-by-subfamilies proof (each prime gets an even OR 3-divisible solution) is numerically plausible: 'ES_2 ∪ ES_3 covers all p > 3'.
first_step: Verify 'every prime p > 3 has an ES solution with all-even or all-3-divisible denominators' to 10⁷, and find the minimal such union family.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: 12/25 fails while 12/5 fails: inherited, but 13/14 fails with 13/2, 13/7 failing
connection: Composite failures appear to be products of failing primes (25 = 5², 14 = 2·7, 4 = 2²): consistent with 'fail(m/n) ⇒ each prime factor fails or is tiny'.
why: If 'n fails ⇒ every prime factor of n fails' held for all m it would reduce Schinzel to primes as for ES.
first_step: Test the implication on m ≤ 48 and n ≤ 4000 composite (needs composite runs for m > 13).

title: Schinzel sibling with j unit fractions (PW's generalisation)
connection: PW also treat m/n as a sum of j unit fractions; the analogous fingerprints (failure sets of m/n with j=2,3,4) give a two-parameter table.
why: The j=2 case is purely divisor-theoretic (m/n = 1/x+1/y ⟺ divisors of n² in a class) — an exactly solvable layer whose failure statistics calibrate j=3.
first_step: Note 4/n = 1/x + 1/y is solvable iff n is even or has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4), so its exceptional set (all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4) has density zero — the same set as the isosceles-law failures; compute and the j=4 exceptions for m ≤ 48.

title: 8/n failures 131 and 241 vs ES hardness of 131 (≡ 3 mod 4) and 241
connection: 241 is a top-30 hard prime for 4/p and the last 8/p failure; 131 ≡ 3 (mod 4) is easy for 4/p.
why: Mixed picture: the even-ES failures are not explained by 4/p hardness alone; 131 needs a separate 2-adic explanation.
first_step: Examine all ES solutions of 4/131 and why none has all-even denominators (parity of x,y,z patterns).

title: Word sieve reproduces every campaign census (cheap independent engine)
connection: A 25-line C sieve over n = tuv − u − v (all n ≤ 3·10⁶ in 5 s) reproduces the 114 I3 zeros (max 2 433 600), the R-zeros ≤ 3·10⁶, and the six non-square U failures ≤ 10⁶.
why: A third independent engine for the censuses; also makes per-n counts (not just zero sets) available for fingerprinting.
first_step: Extend to 3·10⁸ with uint16 counters in a memory-bounded segmented version and re-certify the (★) census to that height.

title: 2 433 600 = 1560² is a zero of I3, R, Uv and ESC simultaneously
connection: At n = 1560² every certificate family in the word sieve vanishes (W = 54 but I3 = R = Uv = ESC = 0); same at 1225 = 35² and 105.
why: The largest I3 zero is a square with smooth root; suggests the I3 exceptional set is 'squares with smooth roots + small n' — directly testable.
first_step: Test I3(m²) for smooth m (m = 2^a3^b5^c13^d…) up to 10⁸ via a targeted solver for tuv−u−v = m².

title: R(3^k) = 0 exactly for even k (squares) and k = 1
why: Sanity fingerprint of T1 on prime powers; also the odd-power values (2,2,4,18,10,10) are a small test sequence for any closed formula.
first_step: Compare R(3^{2j+1}) with the BM main term M_BM(3^{2j+1}).

title: Mean R(n)/log²n on n ≡ 1 (4) drifts 0.145 → 0.133 (10³ → 10⁶)
connection: Average of R(n)/(log n)² over n ≡ 1 (4) in [X, 2X]: 0.1446 (10³), 0.1388 (10⁴), 0.1353 (10⁵), 0.1332 (10⁶); FRONTIER lists constants 1/8 = 0.125 (all integers) and 3/(2π²) = 0.152.
why: Drift towards 1/8 with a 1/log correction is a sharp numerical test of the second-order term in the (★) mean.
first_step: Fit mean = 1/8 + a/log X + b/log²X to 10⁸; compare with a second-order term from the divisor-sum asymptotics.

title: R-zeros sit in the low tail of M_BM but not at its bottom
why: A small BM main term is neither necessary nor sufficient for R(p) = 0 — the fluctuation term X(p) (characters of order ≥ 3) matters; quantifies how much a pure-BM argument can miss.
first_step: For each R-zero compute the full character decomposition M_gen and X; record which characters cancel the main term.

title: I3(n) = 1 is rare beyond 1000: 2160, 2316, 3900, 9090, 9408, 30276, 453660
connection: Only seven n in (1000, 3·10⁶] have exactly one I3 word.
why: The single-word survivors are 'almost-zeros'; their structure (all even, smooth) predicts where a hypothetical further I3 zero would lie.
first_step: Factor them (2160 = 2⁴3³5, 453660 = 2²·3·5·7561, 7561 prime) and look for a common shape with 2433600.

title: t=1 and t=2 word counts are τ(n+1) and τ(2n+1) (OEIS A000005, A099774)
connection: The t=1 slice of tuv−u−v=n is (u−1)(v−1)=n+1 → τ(n+1); the t=2 slice is (2u−1)(2v−1)=2n+1 → τ(2n+1) (OEIS confirmed).
why: Sanity anchor for the word sieve, and a reminder that each t-slice is a divisor function of tn+1 restricted to −1 mod t — the 'tied-modulus divisor event'.
first_step: None (anchor); use as unit tests.

title: Joint zeros of R and Uv among n ≡ 1 (4)
connection: Since R (t ∈ 4ℤ) and Uv (v ∈ 𝒞_n) are different slices of the same word equation, their joint zero set among n≡1(4) non-squares should be tiny.
why: A two-line union covering all primes is the most economical certificate statement; FRONTIER notes (★) ∪ b=1 never fails ≤ 10⁸.
first_step: Compute the joint zero set of (R, Uv) and of (R, I3) ≤ 3·10⁶ from words_3e6.npy.

title: R(p) correlates with τ(4p+1)? — divisor-form check
connection: R(p) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cp+1 : d ≡ −1 (mod 4C)}; the C=1 term is #{d | 4p+1 : d ≡ 3 (mod 4)}; minz(p)/p correlates −0.42 with τ(4p+1).
why: Quantifies how much of R comes from C = 1 — if most, the (★) problem is essentially about one integer 4p+1 (a 'single shifted prime' divisor problem).
first_step: Compute the C-profile of R(p): fraction of R from C = 1, 2, 3, … at p ≤ 10⁶.

title: A segmented word sieve to 10¹⁰ for per-n counts
connection: The word sieve is O(N log²N); a segmented version (block in n, loop over (t,u) with v-range intersecting the block) gives counts to 10¹⁰ in hours.
why: Per-n counts (not only zero sets) at large heights allow fingerprinting the minimum count growth, the true test of any log²-lower-bound conjecture.
first_step: Implement segmented z52b_fingerprint_words with uint8 saturating counters for I3, R, Uv; run to 10¹⁰ on primes p≡1(4) only.

title: Poisson test for R(p) given M_BM(p)
connection: If R(p) ≈ Poisson-like with mean ∝ M_BM(p), P(R=0) ≈ exp(−c M_BM) — at M_BM ≈ 3 (p=409) this gives a few % — test against the 14 observed zeros.
why: Calibrates the 'tied-modulus divisor event' independence model of FRONTIER §2.1 against actual zero counts.
first_step: Fit P(R=0 | M_BM) by logistic regression on p ≤ 3·10⁶ (needs M_BM for all p; use the script with chunking).

title: 2-adic depth matters: p ≡ 1 (16) has 9% fewer ES solutions than p ≡ 9 (16)
connection: Among p ≡ 1 (8), residual log U(p) is lower by 0.094 when p ≡ 1 (16) (k₁ −0.098, k₂ −0.080, R −0.051); next level 32 vs 16 only −0.013; 9 vs 3: −0.030; 25 vs 5: −0.021.
why: Not explained by quadratic characters ((2/p) = 1 in both classes) nor by the quartic character of 2 (null): it is the multiplicative depth of p−1 at 2 — local densities of the ES surface at 2 depend on p mod 16.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic local density of {4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z} as a function of p mod 2^k and compare to the observed 9% gap.

title: Neumann–Setzer primes p = u² + 64 among hard primes?
connection: For prime conductor p ≠ 17, elliptic curves with a rational 2-torsion point exist iff p = u² + 64 (Neumann–Setzer; conductor 17 is the exception, LMFDB 17.a); check whether ES-hard primes or R-zeros are of this form (e.g. 409 − 64 = 345 is not a square; 577 − 64 = 513 not).
why: LMFDB fingerprint: an ES ↔ elliptic-curve-of-conductor-p link would show up as over-representation of p = u²+64 among hard primes.
first_step: Test all 14 R-zeros, 3 Type-A failures and the 40 hardest primes for p = u²+64; and correlate U(p) with #isogeny classes of conductor p in LMFDB.

title: Ranks of the genus-1 fibres of the ES surface at hard primes
connection: Fixing one denominator turns 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z into a conic; fixing a linear relation gives cubic curves. Compute the Mordell–Weil rank of natural elliptic fibres for p ∈ {193, 409, 577, 2521, 66529} vs easy primes.
why: If hard primes correlate with rank-0 fibres, a Mordell–Weil/Selmer viewpoint would be a new lever (rank parity via root numbers is computable).
first_step: Construct a genuine genus-one fibration of the ES cubic surface (note: the substitution x = ty only gives conics 4tyz = p(ty + (t+1)z); use e.g. a pencil of plane sections through a line on the surface or a non-linear pencil) and compute ranks with Sage/Magma at the listed p.

title: τ(p+1) and τ(p+4) correlate weakly (+0.12), τ(p+12) not at all
connection: Shifted divisor functions at shifts 1,4,12 carry little information on ES count, unlike shift 3 (+0.48 for τ(p+3)).
why: Highlights the special role of the shift 3 (x = (p+3)/4), i.e. the first greedy step, among all shifts.
first_step: Tabulate ρ(U, τ(p+s)) for s = 1..50 to find the full 'shift spectrum' and compare with which x-values carry solutions.

title: k₁ (Type I) is more sensitive to 5 than k₂: ρ((5/p)) = −0.32 for k₁
connection: Residual k₁ correlates −0.32 with (5/p); k₂ less (not in top list).
why: Different local primes drive the two types; designing a covering argument per type should exploit their complementary local profiles.
first_step: Build a table ρ(type, (q/p)) for q ≤ 50 and both types.

title: minz(p)/p anticorrelates with h(−4p)/√p (−0.19)
connection: The cheapest certificate is lower (smaller height) when L(1,χ_{−4p}) is large.
why: Height of the optimal solution relates to the (★)/Type II side (χ_{−4p}); a height bound and an L-value bound may be linked.
first_step: Regress log(minz(p)/p) on log L(1,χ_{−4p}) and log L(1,χ_p).

title: Real class number h(p) is uncorrelated with U(p) (−0.04)
connection: Since h(p) = 1 for most p ≡ 1 (4) at this size, only the regulator carries the L-value; h(p) alone is uninformative.
why: Negative fingerprint: avoids chasing 'class group of Q(√p)' explanations.
first_step: None.

title: Which ternary quadratic form's r_Q(p) best predicts U(p)?
connection: Compute-and-check: for all reduced positive ternary forms Q of discriminant ≤ 200, compute r_Q(p) at p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 10⁵ and the Spearman with U(p) residual.
why: If some Q stands out, ES counts might be (asymptotically) a theta coefficient — the Kudla/Siegel–Weil route (KUDLA_ES.md).
first_step: Use pari qfrep on the Brandt–Intrau list (discriminant ≤ 200) and rank by correlation.

title: Sum of two squares p = a² + b² and the Hecke-angle of p vs ES-hardness
connection: Primes p ≡ 1 (4) have a Gaussian angle θ_p (p = a² + b²). Hecke Grössencharacters equidistribute θ_p. If ES-hardness (e.g. large least certificate level, or λ(p) large) correlated with θ_p, ES would interact with ℤ[i]-arithmetic.
why: It is cheap and tests whether the Gaussian structure that p ≡ 1 (4) brings carries ES information. A null result rules out a class of approaches.
first_step: For p < 10⁸, correlate min certificate level / λ(p) / N₋(p) with θ_p and with a mod small numbers.

title: ord_p(2)/(p−1) correlates +0.45 with U(p)
connection: Higher multiplicative order of 2 mod p ⇒ more solutions; partly via (2/p) (2 is a QNR ⇒ index odd…), partly via p−1 smoothness.
why: Artin-type data (order of 2) is a cheap proxy that might enter ES via 2-power denominators (TWO_POWER_LADDER.md).
first_step: Partial correlation controlling for (2/p) and τ(p−1); compare with ord_p(3), ord_p(5).

title: R-zeros have small h(−4p): 13 of 14 below the median (nominal binomial tail ≈ 0.0009)
why: Confirms the χ_{−4p} fit's prediction: (★)-hard primes have small class number of Q(√−p); the extreme version (Siegel-zero-like L(1,χ_{−4p})) would be the hardest (★) instances — ties the campaign's Siegel-dichotomy memo to data.
first_step: Extend to R-zeros beyond 10¹⁰ if the census is extended; compute the joint (h(−4p), L(1,χ_p)) quantile and see whether R-zeros are extreme in the joint distribution.

title: Euler-product weights per prime q for log U(p)
connection: Fit log U(p) residual = Σ_q β_q χ_p(q) for q ≤ 50 (at p ≡ 1 (4), χ_{−4p}(q) = (−1/q)χ_p(q) is collinear, so a joint χ_p/χ_{−4p} per-q fit is unidentifiable — only one coefficient per q is meaningful).
why: The fitted β_q, γ_q profile is a 'local-density fingerprint' that a heuristic count (Elsholtz–Tao style) should reproduce exactly; mismatches pinpoint missing local factors.
first_step: Done in data/z52b/qweights.json (χ_p only); compare β_q with −c/q (naive Euler factor slope).

title: Variance of log U(p) after removing the χ_p effect: what is left?
connection: After the Euler-product fit (R² gain ≈ 0.49), the remaining residual variance can be tested against τ((p+3)/4), τ(p−1), and pure noise.
why: Quantifies how much of ES count fluctuation is 'genuinely global' (divisor coincidences) vs local — the global part is what any proof must control pointwise.
first_step: Fit the full model log U ~ log p + Euler(χ_p) + Euler(χ_{−4p}) + log τ((p+3)/4) + log τ(p−1) and report residual variance.

title: ρ(U, I3(p)) = +0.46, ρ(U, W(p)) = +0.32
connection: Word counts at the same prime predict the ES count moderately; I3 more than all words.
why: I3 words (t,u,v ≥ 3) are a 'bulk' certificate family; strong correlation means I3 sees most of the arithmetic driving U.
first_step: Check whether I3(p) also follows χ_p (it does weakly: α ≈ −0.12) and whether its residual is mostly noise.

title: ES counts at Sophie Germain / safe primes
connection: Safe primes (p = 2q+1) have p−1 maximally non-smooth; predicted to be ES-easy. Compute mean U(p)/log²p over safe primes vs all primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) (safe primes > 7 are ≡ 3 (mod 4)… so compare within class).
why: Tests the p−1 smoothness axis independent of p mod 4 (within p ≡ 3 (4), which is always ES-easy but count still varies).
first_step: Compute on p ≡ 3 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵: ρ(U, P⁺(p−1)) and mean over safe primes.

title: Proth-type primes k·2^n + 1 with small k as an ES-hardness test bed
connection: Primes k·2^n+1 (k ≤ 15) have deep 2-adic structure and controllable p−1; scanning U(p)/log² over them separates 2-adic depth from other effects.
why: Large known families (Proth primes) give hard-ish test primes at sizes 10⁶–10¹² where generic censuses are too expensive.
first_step: List Proth primes ≤ 10⁸ and compute R(p), U(p) via targeted solvers.

title: p mod 5 and p mod 7 as integers are uninformative (|ρ| ≤ 0.07)
connection: Raw residues p mod 5, p mod 7 show tiny correlation; the information is in the Legendre symbols (5/p), (7/p) (and for 7 even that is null).
why: Sanity: ES local dependence is via characters, not the residue's numeric value.
first_step: None.

title: Number of distinct x vs number of solutions per x: concentration index
connection: U(p)/nx(p) (solutions per first denominator) is a concentration fingerprint; Gini coefficient of the x-profile per prime.
why: If solutions concentrate on few x, ES at p reduces to few divisor problems — relevant to POINTWISE strategies.
first_step: Compute U/nx at p ≤ 2·10⁵ (both in data) and its dependence on χ_p.

title: U(p) for p ≡ 3 (4): correlation profile mirrors p ≡ 1 (4)?
connection: All correlations above were computed for p ≡ 1 (4); for p ≡ 3 (4) ES is trivial but counts still fluctuate — compare the χ_p fit.
why: If the same Euler-product law holds, the count law is uniform across classes — a sign it comes from the surface's local densities, not from ES-specific structure.
first_step: Rerun z52b_fingerprint_lfit.py restricted to p ≡ 3 (4).

title: U(p²) and U(p³): prime powers fingerprint
connection: Compute U at prime squares and cubes (in range: p² ≤ 30 000): odd squares kill all certificate lines (T1) but ES(p²) holds via p — how big is U(p²)?
why: T1 says line counts vanish at squares; U(p²) shows how many 'non-line' solutions exist — a measure of what T1-avoiding methods must capture.
first_step: Extract U(m²) for odd m ≤ 173 from the data and compare with U at neighbouring non-squares.

title: Candidate explanation of the q mod 3 dichotomy: p ≡ −3 (mod q) forces (p/q) = (−3/q)
connection: The strongest single shift is x = (p+3)/4 (ρ(U, τ(p+3)) = +0.48); q | p+3 ⟺ p ≡ −3 (q), which forces (q/p) = (p/q) = (−3/q) = +1 iff q ≡ 1 (mod 3). So for q ≡ 1 (3) 'q is a QR' is positively confounded with 'q divides p+3' (more solutions), cancelling the generic negative QR effect.
why: Candidate mechanism (not yet tested by the controlled regression in the first step): the greedy first step x = ⌈(p+1)/4⌉ couples ES counts to the cubic-residue-flavoured symbol (−3/q). Every first-denominator shift s similarly couples via (−s/q).
first_step: Verify by adding 1[q | p+3] features; then search for the full 'shift ⊗ character' structure: weight of (q/p) ≈ Σ_s w_s·(−s/q)·(…).

title: Sign flip between p ≡ 1 and p ≡ 3 (mod 4): QR-ness of small primes helps at 3 (mod 4), hurts at 1 (mod 4)
connection: β_q are uniformly positive for p ≡ 3 (4) and mostly negative for p ≡ 1 (4) (for U, k₁, k₂, Uv).
why: At p ≡ 3 (4), (q/p) = χ_{−p}(q) (imaginary field Q(√−p)) and enters positively: U grows with L(1,χ_{−p}) ∝ h(−p)/√p; at p ≡ 1 (4), (q/p) = χ_p(q) (real field Q(√p)) and enters negatively: U shrinks as L(1,χ_p) = 2h(p)log ε_p/√p grows. Imaginary-quadratic L-values help, real-quadratic ones hurt.
first_step: Fit a model U ∝ L(1,χ_{−p})^{a} at p ≡ 3 and L(1,χ_p)^{b} at p ≡ 1 and compare |a|, |b| (≈ 0.4 vs ≈ 0.3?).

title: I3 count has β₇ = +0.039 (p ≡ 1 mod 4): QR at 7 helps I3
connection: Unlike U, I3(p) gains when 7 is a QR mod p; k₂ and Uv have β₇ ≈ −0.045.
why: Different certificate families have opposite responses at the same local prime — evidence for complementary families (union arguments) at the level of local densities.
first_step: Tabulate sign(β_q) per family for q ≤ 50 and find pairs of families with opposite sign at many q.

title: Prime squares p²: what fraction of ES solutions is inherited from 4/p?
connection: Data: U(9) = 6, U(25) = 10, U(49) = 18, U(81) = 46, U(121) = 24, U(169) = 24, U(289) = 27; test for p² ≤ 30 000 whether every solution of 4/p² arises by scaling a solution of 4/p or from the divisor structure of p².
why: Inheritance is not universal ((4, 6, 36) for 4/9 is not a scaled solution of 4/3), so the inherited fraction is a real statistic; if it tends to 1, T1 is 'lines see only primitive solutions'.
first_step: Dump solutions for 4/p² (p ≤ 173) and test inheritance by gcd structure.

title: Proth primes are not hard: 65537 (ratio 0.96), 786433 (0.92), 5767169 (1.44), 104857601 (1.62)
connection: Deep 2-adic structure alone (p ≡ 1 mod 2^k) does not make ES hard; 193 = 3·2⁶+1 (0.22), 97 (0.38), 769 (0.41) moderately hard at small size.
why: Separates 2-adic depth from the full smooth-p−1 profile; ES hardness needs many small primes simultaneously ≡ 1-ish, not one deep prime power.
first_step: Regress U(p)/log² on v₂(p−1), v₃(p−1), v₅(p−1) jointly with the χ_p Euler product to apportion.

title: Reversal: does the count law predict which numbers m/p fail (Schinzel)?
connection: Use the fitted ES-count Euler product with numerator-m analogue to predict log U_m(p); compare predicted lowest values with actual failures m ∈ [8, 48].
why: A successful prediction would show the Schinzel failures are exactly 'local-density-small' primes — supporting PW's probabilistic picture with arithmetic content.
first_step: Fit per-q weights for each m (data on disk) and compute AUC of predicted log U_m for failure vs non-failure.

title: Continued fraction of 4/p and its partial quotients vs U(p)
connection: 4/p has a short CF; ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3 is about CF lengths of p/A for certain A. Correlate U(p) with the CF length/max partial quotient of p/A over small A.
why: Bridges the CF formulation (Zaremba-type, ZAREMBA_TRANSFER.md) to the count; a strong correlation would suggest Zaremba/Bourgain–Kontorovich density tools apply.
first_step: For each p compute #{A < p : CF length of p/A ≤ 3} (the five-slice count) and Spearman with U(p).

title: Hirzebruch–Jung length fingerprint of hard primes
connection: λ(p) (minimal HJ/CF length certificate) for hard primes vs random: are hard primes the ones with λ(p) = 3 exactly (no length-2 certificates)?
why: λ(p) is a discrete hardness grade; its distribution conditional on χ_p would connect CF dynamics with the Euler-product count law.
first_step: Compute λ(p) for p ≤ 10⁵ (existing scripts? check scripts/*hj*) and cross-tabulate with U(p)/log² quantiles.

title: Hard-prime 'deficit vectors' over local primes
connection: For each hard prime compute the vector ((q/p))_{q≤47} and 1[q | p+3], 1[q | p−1]; cluster hard primes by these vectors.
why: If hard primes form a few clusters (e.g. 'all small q QR' and 'p−1 smooth'), each cluster may need a different certificate family.
first_step: k-means on the 200 hardest primes ≤ 2·10⁵ with these binary features.

title: Least C with a (★) certificate vs p mod small numbers
connection: Cmin(p) (least C with a divisor d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)) should depend on p mod 3, 5, 7 via which C make 4Cp+1 divisible by small primes.
why: A table of E[Cmin | p mod 840] is a direct, computable covering-cost fingerprint.
first_step: Compute Cmin for p ≤ 10⁶ and average by p mod 840.

title: Pairwise union conjecture: (★) ∪ U covers every non-square n ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶ except 105
connection: Joint zeros of R and Uv among non-square n ≡ 1 (mod 4), n ≤ 3·10⁶: only {105}. Same for R ∩ I3 = {105} and Uv ∩ I3 = {105}.
why: Any two of the three word families jointly certify ES on all non-square n ≡ 1 (4) in range (squares are T1-dead for all lines). A two-family statement is the most economical union target and stronger than FRONTIER's (★) ∪ b=1 at primes.
first_step: Extend the joint census to 10⁹ with the segmented sieve; try to find the local reason the families' failure sets are disjoint (different shift/character profiles, cf. per-prime weights).

title: Independence heuristic predicts unbounded Vmin; data show a plateau at 116 — test it
connection: If fail_v events at a prime were independent with P(fail_v) ≍ C_v(log p)^{−1/2}, the probability that all v ≤ 116 fail is tiny but the number of primes is huge; compute the expected number of primes ≤ X with Vmin > 116 under the model and compare with 0 observed.
why: A discrepancy would quantify positive dependence/repulsion between shifts (FRONTIER's joint-failure discussion) using a sharp observable.
first_step: Use the single-shift law constants from EXSET_SHIFT_DIVISORS §2 to compute E#{p ≤ 3·10⁶ : Vmin(p) > V} for V = 31, 87, 116.

title: Boundary-only (★) primes as a second hardness list
connection: Compute-and-check: primes p ≡ 1 (4) where every (★) triple has u = 1 or B = 1 (trivial divisor of 4Cp+1 near the boundary); expect them to contain 184837 and be ~10× more numerous than R-zeros.
why: FRONTIER counts R(p) including boundary; interior counts are what equidistribution arguments control — so the interior-zero list is the real target of such arguments.
first_step: Modify the word sieve to count interior (★) words (u, B ≥ 2) and list zeros at primes ≤ 3·10⁶.

title: Mean (★) certificate size ≈ 2 and U size ≈ 4: most primes are certified by C ∈ {1,2}
connection: Cmin(p) = 1 for 76.6% of primes ≡ 1 (4) with a certificate and ≤ 2 for 91.8% (reviewer rerun): i.e. 4p+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4), or 8p+1 one ≡ −1 (mod 8), for ≈ 92% of primes.
why: The (★) problem is mostly 'one or two shifted integers have a divisor in a class' — quantitative law: P(Cmin > c) decays fast; the tail (c ≥ 10) contains all hardness.
first_step: Fit P(Cmin > c) for c ≤ 50 and compare with the product of single-event failure probabilities ∏_{C≤c} P(4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C).

title: 105 is the unique non-square n ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶ killing all three word families
connection: R(105) = Uv(105) = I3(105) = 0 and ESC(105) = 0; every other non-square n ≡ 1 (4) has at least two families alive.
why: 105 = 3·5·7 is 'locally square' modulo 8 and small primes? (105 ≡ 1 mod 8, 105 ≡ 0 mod 3,5,7) — its divisibility by 3,5,7 kills shifts; a structural characterisation would explain uniqueness.
first_step: Check whether n = 3·5·7·m² or other 'n ≡ 0 mod 105' families have systematically few words.

title: x | z ⟺ y | z for every solution at a prime (proved from the normal form)
connection: Since p | z, 4z/p = z/x + z/y + 1 is an integer identity: if x | z then z/y is an integer, and conversely. Data agree (identical failure sets and share 0.377).
why: Suggests a structural lemma: at a prime, x | z forces y | z (and conversely), i.e. z = lcm(x, y) — a rigid sub-family amenable to a parametrisation by divisors of z/p.
first_step: Use the lcm-closed family z = lcm(x, y) as a parametrisation by divisors of z/p (three divisors a, b of z with a + b + 1 = 4z/p).

title: All-squarefree solutions: fail only at 71, 191, 21 169 among primes ≤ 10⁵
connection: Every prime ≤ 10⁵ except 71, 191, 21169 has an ES solution with x, y, z all squarefree (share 0.15); x squarefree alone never fails (all n ≤ 3000 too).
why: Squarefree denominators are the natural setting for local-global arguments (no prime-power local conditions); a three-exception family is a candidate 'squarefree ES' conjecture. 71 and 191 ≡ 3 (mod 4)!
first_step: Explain 71 and 191 (≡ 7 mod 8, easy for ES but every solution has a square factor); extend census to 10⁷.

title: Height: every prime ≤ 10⁵ has a solution with z ≤ p², but 50 primes need z > p^{1.75}
connection: z ≤ p² never fails; z ≤ p^{1.75} fails at 50 primes (241, 269, 367, 449, 577, 601, …, last 95327); z ≤ p^{1.5} fails at 7 109 primes.
why: A height-bounded ES ('z ≤ p²') is a finite search per prime with a clean conjectural exponent between 1.75 and 2 — the right scale for effective/lattice approaches (LATTICE_MEETING.md).
first_step: Compute max_{p≤X} log(minz(p))/log p up to 10⁷ and check whether it tends to 2 from below.

title: Coprime-pair solutions fail at 1 285 primes (13, 37, 61, 97, 109, 181, 193, …)
connection: Solutions with gcd(x,y) = 1 (equivalently some coprime pair, identical failure set) are absent at 1 285 primes ≤ 10⁵, all apparently ≡ 1 (mod 12).
why: Pairwise-coprime structure fails generically on p ≡ 1 (12): every ES solution there shares factors — consistent with the 'multiplicative' Type I/II constructions.
first_step: Verify the mod-12 claim and compute the failure density in p ≡ 1 (12).

title: Power-of-2 denominators are rare (fail at 9 483 of 9 592 primes)
connection: Only ≈ 1.1% (109) of primes ≤ 10⁵ have a solution with a power of 2 among x, y, z (TWO_POWER_LADDER.md studies such ladders).
why: Calibration for any approach via 2-power denominators: it can certify only a thin set of primes.
first_step: List primes with a 2-power solution and compare with the ladder families in TWO_POWER_LADDER.md.

title: 'Only z divisible by n' fails at all powers of 2 (composites ≤ 3000)
connection: At n = 2^k every solution has ≥ 2 denominators divisible by n (or none); at odd primes the k₁-shape always exists.
why: Powers of 2 are the ES 'easy' case but structurally degenerate; sanity fingerprint for the normal-form lemma.
first_step: None.

title: Union of restricted families: smallest set of shapes covering all primes
connection: Shapes with tiny failure sets ≤ 10⁵: lcm-closed {2521}; all-squarefree {71, 191, 21169}; none-div-by-3 {3, 241}; some-denominator-div-by-4 {2, 17, 241}. lcm-closed ∪ none-div-by-3 covers every prime ≤ 10⁵ (lcm-closed certifies 3). Not all pairs are disjoint: none-div-by-3 and 4-divides-some both fail at 241.
why: Each shape has its own local structure; a proof of 'every p has an lcm-closed or 3-free solution' might be easier than ES if the two obstructions are incompatible (2521 vs 241 are different local profiles).
first_step: Find the local reason for each single exception and test whether any prime can fail two shapes simultaneously (search to 10⁷).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Primitive-failure primes vs R-zeros and Type-A failures
connection: 193 is a primitive failure; check overlap of the 110 primitive failures with the hard lists (R-zeros 409, 577, 5569, 9601, 23929, 83449 are p ≡ 1 (24); some are ≡ 1 (12)).
why: If primitive failures and line failures overlap strongly, the lines are 'primitive-solution detectors'.
first_step: Intersect the sets (variants.json) and compute the hypergeometric p-value.

title: The χ_p correlation persists out of sample at 10⁶ and 10⁷
connection: Spearman(U(p), log L₃₁(1,χ_p)) = −0.62 (156 primes ≡ 1 (4) in [10⁶, 10⁶+4000]) and −0.69 (113 primes in [10⁷, 10⁷+4000]); k₁ −0.66/−0.75, k₂ −0.38/−0.36 — same strength as at ≤ 2·10⁵ (rank correlations; the fitted exponent α ≈ −0.30 itself was not re-estimated).
why: The correlation is scale-stable, so the χ_p dependence is not small-number noise; whether the exponent is stable needs the refit in the first step.
first_step: Push to 10⁹ windows (count program ≈ 100 s per prime there) and track whether the exponent α ≈ −0.3 drifts.

title: Rédei 4-/8-rank of Cl(−4p) has no effect (h(−4p) mod 16 strata differ by ≤ 0.016 in residual log counts)
connection: For p ≡ 1 (8), residual log U, k₁, k₂, R by h(−4p) mod 16 ∈ {0,4,8,12}: |differences| ≤ 0.016.
why: Another higher-character null: 8-rank (Barrucand–Cohn: p = x²+32y²) governs quartic/octic symbols, which the data already showed are irrelevant.
first_step: None; record.

title: Does any prime > 2·10⁵ beat 2521's U/log³p?
why: If 2521 stays the global minimum of U/log³p, ES hardness is bounded below in normalised form — a strong empirical lower bound U(p) ≥ 0.019 log³p.
first_step: Model-guided search (previous item) for p ≤ 10¹⁰ with U/log³p < 0.03.

title: BM residual correlation with U persists at 20 000–30 000: +0.58
connection: Residual Spearman(M_BM, U) = 0.65 (≤ 12 000) and 0.58 (20 000–30 000); with R only 0.10 / 0.10.
why: Robust: the campaign's BM main term is a strong predictor of the *total* ES count but not of its own (★) count fluctuations — suggests reorganising the BM analysis around U(p) or ESC(p).
first_step: Recompute the BM-type main term for the ESC family (all coordinates) and check whether it predicts ESC(p) fluctuations.

title: Markov primes vs 12/p failures: {2, 5, 13, 29, 433} = Markov ∩ fail(12) ≤ 10⁵
connection: Markov primes ≤ 10⁵: 2,5,13,29,89,233,433,1597,2897,5741,7561,28657,33461,43261,96557; five lie in the 22-element 12/p failure set (and the same five in fail(24)); 433 is the notable one.
why: Probably small-number coincidence, but Markov numbers m have −1 and other small quantities as QRs mod m (m | a²+b² with structured a, b) — a quadratic-residue profile like ES-hard primes; MARKOFF_ES.md explores Markov ↔ ES.
first_step: Compute the least QNR / L(1,χ_m) quantile for Markov primes and test enrichment in all m/p failure sets with a permutation test.

title: Primes of the form m² + 1 (Landau) as an ES-hardness family
connection: p = m² + 1 has p − 1 a square (τ(p−1) odd) and p ≡ 1 (4); 577 = 24² + 1 is an R-zero. Compute mean residual log U over p = m²+1 ≤ 2·10⁵ vs all p ≡ 1 (4).
why: A polynomial family where p−1 has structured divisors: tests whether 'p−1 has many square factors' matters beyond τ(p−1).
first_step: Run after the data refresh (misc script); report mean residual and the R-zero count among m²+1 primes ≤ 3·10⁶.

title: Function-field analogue of the χ_p Euler-product law
connection: Over F_q[T], fit the ES count at monic irreducible P against Σ_{deg Q ≤ d} χ_P(Q)/|Q| (quadratic character of small-degree irreducibles mod P).
why: If the same law (negative α for 'P ≡ 1 mod 4'-analogue) holds, the count mechanism (Brauer/Hilbert symbol) is characteristic-free and the function-field proofs might reveal how to beat it.
first_step: Pick q = 3, deg P ≤ 10 (≈ 6 000 irreducibles); reuse the F_q[T] solution counters.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sibling 4/n with denominators in an arithmetic progression or geometric constraints
connection: Solutions with y − x = z − y or y² = xz (geometric) are 'rigid' sub-families; their existence sets at primes are new exception sets.
why: Rigid families are where polynomial-identity constructions live; their failure sets indicate which residue classes each rigid family covers.
first_step: Add the two flags to the variant counter and list failures at primes ≤ 10⁵.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Hard primes vs Wilson / Wolstenholme-type congruences: null test
connection: Wilson quotients (p−1)!+1)/p mod p and Wolstenholme quotients are p-adic invariants of small integers collectively; test correlation with residual U(p).
why: Expected null (ES counts depend on quadratic data); a non-null would be surprising and important.
first_step: Compute Wilson quotient mod p for p ≤ 2·10⁵ (O(p) each — use p ≤ 2·10⁴) and Spearman.

title: Erdős–Graham style: least common denominator of ES solutions vs smooth numbers
connection: minlcm(p)/p (least common denominator over solutions, divided by p) — is it always smooth (all prime factors ≤ p^{1/2})? Practical?
why: Egyptian-fraction denominators tend to be smooth; a smoothness law for minlcm would give a search space ('only smooth L need be tried') for certificates.
first_step: Factor minlcm(p)/p for p ≤ 2·10⁵ and record the max of log P⁺/log p.

title: U(n) at Sylvester-sequence-related n (2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, …)
connection: Sylvester numbers s_k satisfy 1 = Σ 1/s_i + 1/(s_k − 1); n = 43, 1807 = 13·139: compute U and compare to neighbours.
why: Numbers with built-in unit-fraction identities might have anomalously many ES solutions (an 'easy family' mirror of lcm+1).
first_step: Look up U(43), U(1807) in f4_all_30000.txt; extend to 3263443 = s₅ with the count program.

title: Cohen–Lenstra heuristic for h(p) irrelevant; regulator heuristics (Hooley) relevant
connection: Since ES counts follow L(1,χ_p) and h(p) is mostly 1, the distribution of ES counts at p ≡ 1 (4) inherits the distribution of log ε_p/√p (Hooley's conjecture on the average of real quadratic class numbers × regulators).
why: Gives a 'distribution of hardness' prediction: P(U(p) small) ≈ P(L(1,χ_p) large) which is doubly-exponentially small in the size (Granville–Soundararajan distribution of L(1,χ)).
first_step: Compare the empirical tail of residual log U with the Granville–Soundararajan tail for log L(1,χ_p) scaled by α ≈ 0.3.

title: Siegel-zero scenario check: what if L(1,χ_{−4p}) is tiny?
connection: k₂ and R correlate positively with L(1,χ_{−4p}); an exceptional (Siegel) discriminant −4p would make Type II/(★) starve; Type I is χ_p-driven and unaffected.
why: Suggests ES is robust to Siegel zeros via Type I (complementarity), aligning with the campaign's 'Siegel dichotomy' discussion.
first_step: Look at the primes with the smallest h(−4p)/√p ≤ 2·10⁵ and check that their k₁ is normal.

title: Autocorrelation of residual log U(n): lag 840 → 0.60, lag 120 → 0.49, lag 1 → −0.28
connection: The ES count sequence is strongly periodic with period 840 and anti-correlated at lag 1 (consecutive integers have opposite parity / mod-4 behaviour).
why: Ramanujan-expansion structure: U(n) ≈ Σ_q a_q c_q(n) with significant a_q for q | 840 — a clean target for a 'singular series' heuristic for the count over all n (not only primes).
first_step: Fit U(n)/log³n by Ramanujan sums c_q(n), q ≤ 120, and report the top coefficients (are they multiplicative in q?).

title: No Type I / Type II complementarity: residual corr(k₁, k₂) = +0.70
connection: At p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵, residual log k₁ and log k₂ correlate +0.70; 250 primes have both below their 5% quantiles vs 22 expected under independence.
why: Kills the hope that 'when Type I is starved Type II is fed' in general — the types share the dominant hardness axis (χ_p, p−1 smoothness); even at lcm(1..19)+1 the split is typical (k₁ = 193, k₂ = 83; an earlier 'Type II overtakes' claim was an overflow artefact).
first_step: Partial correlation of k₁, k₂ after removing the χ_p Euler product: is the residual dependence then ≈ 0 (types independent given local data)?

title: Class ordering within Mordell classes vs 3-adic depth
connection: 1 (mod 840) is hardest, 289 (mod 840) least among the six; p ≡ 1 (mod 9) vs 4,7 (mod 9) inside each class should explain part of it (9 vs 3 depth effect −0.03 measured earlier).
why: Gives the 'next layer' of Mordell's analysis: which further congruence (mod 9, 16, 25, 49, 11, 13) splits each hard class most.
first_step: Within p ≡ 1 (mod 840) primes, compute mean residual by p mod 9·16·25·11·13 factors one at a time.

title: Partition function parity p(p) mod 2 vs ES counts (null test)
connection: Brief asks for partition-type comparisons: compute p(n) mod 2 and mod 3 for n ≤ 2·10⁵ (Euler pentagonal recurrence) and correlate with residual U at primes.
why: Expected null (no known link); a positive result would be a genuine surprise linking ES to modular forms of weight −1/2.
first_step: Implement the pentagonal recurrence mod 2/3 in numpy and run the Spearman test.

title: Type number of quaternion orders vs ES counts
connection: The type number of B_{p,∞} has class-number correction terms (h(−4p), h(−8p), h(−3p)) whose weighting resembles our twist fits; QUATERNION_ES.md relates ES to quaternion orders.
why: If ES counts correlate with the *correction terms* (after removing (p−1)/12 growth), the quaternion picture has a quantitative fingerprint.
first_step: Compute type numbers via Pizer/Eichler formulas for p ≤ 10⁵ and correlate their corrections with residual U, k₂.

title: Rank of y² = x³ − p²x / congruent-number curve at p vs ES count
connection: Congruent number curve E_p: y² = x³ − p²x; Tunnell's criterion decides positive rank / congruence (sufficiency conditional on BSD; it does not give the rank); primes p ≡ 5, 7 (8) are congruent (Heegner/Monsky). Compare U(p) by Tunnell class.
why: Tunnell's criterion counts ternary-form representations (x²+2y²+8z² = p) — a theta-series fingerprint; ES may correlate with these ternary counts.
first_step: Compute Tunnell's counts A(p), B(p) for p ≤ 10⁵ and Spearman with residual U(p).

title: ES counts vs number of ideal classes of order 2 / genus characters of Q(√−p·m)
connection: Genus theory of Q(√−4p·m) for small m produces characters χ_m·χ_p; our fits show only χ_p-type and χ_{−4p}-type Euler products matter. Test twists by m ∈ {3, 5, 7, 15, 21, 35, 105}.
why: Maps which genus fields 'see' ES hardness; 105 = 3·5·7 appears as a universal small exception elsewhere.
first_step: Fit log U on log L(1, χ_{−mp}) for the listed m jointly.

title: Exception counting functions per decade stop early
connection: (★) zeros per decade 10²…10¹⁰: 2,2,2,3,5,0,0,0 (last 8 813 281 in a search to 10¹⁰); U failures: last 978145 (to 10⁹); I3: last 2 433 600 (to 3·10⁶ here; campaign to 1e9); Type A: last 66529 (to 10¹¹); 8/p: last 241.
why: Under a dispersion model where P(count = 0) ≈ exp(−c·mean²/var), exceptions die out super-polynomially — consistent with finite exceptional sets for every line; the decade profile is a fit target for c.
first_step: Fit c for (★) using the empirical mean/variance of R(p) at 10⁵–3·10⁶ and predict the expected number of zeros beyond 10⁷ (should be ≪ 1).

title: Cross-numerator residual correlations: U₄ vs U₅ 0.23, U₆ 0.50, U₇ 0.16, U₉ 0.26, U₁₃ 0.15
connection: Residual log counts at primes 10³–10⁵ correlate weakly across numerators except 6 (6/p = (4/p)·(3/2) shares structure with 4/p).
why: Different numerators see largely different arithmetic: a joint 'all numerators hard' prime must be p ≡ 1 mod a smooth modulus — 12601 = 2³3²5²7 + 1 is hardest for 4, 5 and 7 simultaneously.
first_step: Cluster primes by their vector of residuals over m = 4..13; identify the universal-hard cluster.

title: Numerator-6 tracks numerator-4 (residual corr 0.50)
connection: 6/p solutions include (3/2)·… rescalings of 4/p-type structures; hardest 6/p primes 1657, 6481, 16561, 21841, 1873, 2521, … overlap 4/p hard lists (21841, 2521, 1873, 20521).
why: 6/p is 'ES with a 2-adic/3-adic twist'; its failure-free status (no 6/p failure ≤ 10⁵) plus shared hardness makes it a natural sibling to prove first.
first_step: Check whether every ES solution family (Type I/II parametrisations) has a 6/p analogue and compare counts.

title: Census design: compute U only at model-predicted hard primes
connection: Since n mod 840 explains 64% and the χ_p Euler product most of the rest, a census of the hardest primes can target ≈ 1% of primes (p ≡ 1, 121, 361, 169, 529, 289 mod 840 with many small QRs).
why: Turns the global lower-envelope question into a feasible computation up to 10¹² for the candidate set.
first_step: Implement the pre-filter (840-class + q ≤ 23 QR count ≥ 6) and run the count on survivors in [10⁹, 10⁹ + 10⁷].

title: OEIS A392469 = records of min k (p | y = kp) over primes p ≡ 1 (mod 24) — reproduced
why: Identifies the entry's implicit restriction (p ≡ 1 mod 24) — a possible clarification for OEIS — and links its comment '(q/p) = 1 for q ≤ 13 for all late terms' to our χ_p Euler-product law.
first_step: Email/edit suggestion for A392469: state the p ≡ 1 (24) restriction or add the all-prime variant; compare k(p) with Cmin(p) of the (★) line.

title: A139665 (primes x² + 840y²) = Mordell's six hard classes, because 840 is idoneal
connection: Primes of the form x² + 840y² are exactly the primes ≡ 1, 121, 169, 289, 361, 529 (mod 840) (entry comment; Knott links to Mordell 1969); 840 is an Euler idoneal number, so each genus of discriminant −3360 has one class and the principal genus is a congruence condition.
why: Recasts Mordell's obstruction as 'p splits completely in the genus field Q(i, √2, √−3, √5, √−7) of Q(√−210)'; our class ordering (1 ≻ 121 ≻ 361 ≻ 169 ≻ 529 ≻ 289) is then a statement about which ring-class-field data refine hardness; the largest known idoneal number 1848 suggests a mod-1848 analogue.
first_step: Check the 'idoneal' framing: does a Mordell-type covering mod 1848 (or 1320, 1365) leave exactly the principal genus uncovered? Compute which classes mod 1848·5 have polynomial identities.

title: A396825/A397366 (van Tol): integers not in the 'S(n)' triangle — 12, 28, 33, 60, 96, 124, 193, 228, 288, 336, 385, …
connection: van Tol's S(n) = {A ≤ 4n−2 : A·X + W ≡ 0 (mod 4n−1) for divisors X, W of n}; complement A396825 contains all squares, all ≡ 0,1,4,9 (mod 12), and includes 193 (a Type-A failure) and 288, 336 (A287116), 12, 28, 60, 96, 124, 228 (our U-zero set Uv = 0).
why: Another divisor-class formulation whose exceptional set overlaps ours: aligning the three (A396825, A287116, our Uv/ESC zero sets) could reveal they are the same obstruction at different normalisations.
first_step: Compute the symmetric differences between A396825 ∩ [1, 3000] and our Uv/ESC/R zero sets; explain 33 and 193.

title: A213340 / A213686 / A213687: value sets of the bilinear polynomials 5+8t+12k+16kt etc.
connection: These OEIS entries list the values of ES identity polynomials (Type-like families a + bt + ck + dkt); their union is a covering-by-bilinear-forms description of ES-solvable n.
