why: Bilinear value sets are exactly the shape n = tuv − u − v-type words after substitution; their complements in p ≡ 1 (24) should match our hard sets — a direct test of which bilinear families matter.
first_step: Compute the union of the listed bilinear families' values ≤ 10⁶ and compare its complement with the R-, U-, I3-zero sets.

title: A400619's record prime 8 803 369 is ES-hard (U/log³p = 0.034) but not a (★) zero (R = 16)
connection: U(8803369) = 140 (k₁ = 94, k₂ = 46; overflow-corrected), U/log³p = 0.034 — below the 10⁶/10⁷ window minima 0.044/0.055 and below lcm(1..19)+1 (0.039); words: W = 107, I3 = 68, R = 16, Uv = 11. The nearby R-zero 8 813 281 has W = 127, R = 0.
why: Greedy-depth records are genuinely hard for the full count, while (★) zeros are line-specific: two independent hardness notions pick different primes at the same height.
first_step: Compute the χ_p Euler product and p mod 840 for 8803369 and 8813281; predict which notion each satisfies.

title: 105 = 3·5·7 vs 385 = 5·7·11: products of consecutive odd primes in exceptional sets
connection: 105 is a zero of all our word families; 385 is in A396825 but our families certify it; 33 = 3·11 likewise.
why: Squarefree products of small odd primes are 'locally saturated' (n ≡ 0 mod many small q kills many shifts); a cheap structural family to test any certificate system on: 15015, 255255, …
first_step: Compute R, Uv, I3, ESC at products of consecutive odd primes up to 3·10⁶ (105, 1155, 15015, 255255) and at 3·5·7·m² forms.

title: Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n) grows faster than N log³N in range (ratio 7.6 → 19.6 for N = 10³ → 3·10⁴)
connection: Over all n (composites included) the ordered-count partial sums outgrow N log³N; composite n with many divisors carry large counts.
why: Composite counts are dominated by divisor-rich n; irrelevant to ES existence but important if one uses averages over all n as a proxy for primes (wrong normalisation by a log² factor).
first_step: Check ET's statement for Σ_{n≤N} f(n) (if any) and fit the exponent of log.

title: ES count vs number of prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) of n
connection: For composite n, fit log U(n) on ω₁(n) = #{p | n : p ≡ 1 (4)} and ω₃(n); the isosceles law says ω₃ = 0 kills degenerate solutions for odd n (even n have them anyway); does ω₃ also boost the bulk count?
why: Quantifies how the 'sum of two squares' structure of n influences ES counts beyond the isosceles locus.
first_step: Regress on f4_all_30000.txt.

title: Distribution of x/p over all solutions (the 'x-profile')
connection: Histogram of x/p ∈ (1/4, 3/4] over all solutions at primes 10⁴–2·10⁵; expect mass near 1/4 (greedy) with a 1/(4x − p)-type law.
why: The x-profile is the density a sieve over x must reproduce; deviations (e.g. secondary peaks at x/p = 1/3, 1/2) show identity families.
first_step: Extend the count program to histogram x/p and y/p.

title: Ratio y/x and z/y spectra as fingerprints of identity families
connection: Polynomial identity families produce solutions with rational ratios y/x → constants as p grows (e.g. y ≈ 2x); peaks in the empirical distribution of y/x identify which identities fire.
why: A data-driven way to rediscover Mordell-type identities and to see which ones the hard classes lack.
first_step: Histogram log(y/x) over all solutions at p ≤ 2·10⁵ split by class mod 840.

title: Quasi-identities: ratio buckets present for a positive proportion of a hard class
connection: In the six hard classes, find solution families (ratio buckets) present for ≥ 30% of primes; each corresponds to a conditional identity (valid when some auxiliary divisibility holds).
why: Conditional identities with complementary conditions could jointly cover a hard class — a 'covering by conditional identities' strategy whose obstacles the data would show.
first_step: Mine the solution lists of primes ≡ 1 (mod 840) ≤ 2·10⁵ for frequent ratio buckets and their auxiliary conditions.

title: ES counts for p in Chebotarev classes of the 2-part of the class group of Q(√−p)
connection: For p ≡ 1 (8), the 4-rank of Cl(−4p) is 1 iff p ≡ 1 (8) and 8 | h iff p = x² + 32y² … — null observed for h mod 16; extend to the 2-class field tower data of Q(√−2p), Q(√−6p).
why: Rules out (or finds) dependence of ES on 2-class-group data beyond genus — completing the 'only genus characters matter' fingerprint.
first_step: Compute h(−8p), h(−24p) mod 16 and test as for h(−4p).

title: Hardness vs the order of 10 mod p (decimal period) — category check
connection: Decimal period of 1/p is ord_p(10); a correlation would only reflect (2/p), (5/p) structure already captured.
why: Guards against 'recreational' fingerprints; if a residual correlation remains after controlling for (2/p), (5/p), that is a genuine surprise.
first_step: Partial Spearman of U-residual with ord_p(10)/(p−1) given (2/p), (5/p).

title: ES count of the Fermat quotient-free / 'ES-easy' family p ≡ −1 (mod 840): exact identities
connection: Record-easy primes are ≡ −1 (mod 840); since p ≡ 3 (4) is trivially ES-solvable, the count excess there measures how many extra identity families fire at −1 modulo 3, 5, 7, 8.
why: The easy-side structure (all identities fire) quantifies the 'maximum covering multiplicity' — the dual of the hard side.
first_step: Mean U(p)/log³p over p ≡ 839 (mod 840) vs other p ≡ 3 (4).

title: Lag-840 correlation at primes: residual log U(p) vs U(p+840) = 0.64 (3 425 pairs); lag 5880: 0.58
connection: Among primes p ≡ 1 (4) with p + 840 also prime, residuals correlate 0.64 — the mod-840 class carries ≈ 60% of the variance at primes too.
why: Confirms at primes what the all-n spectrum showed: ES counts are dominated by a mod-840 periodic component plus a character (q ∤ 840) component.
first_step: Decompose the remaining 40% by p mod 11, 13 and by the χ_p Euler product over q ≥ 11.

title: Easy class −1 (mod 840): mean U/log³p = 0.70 vs 0.19 for other p ≡ 3 (4)
connection: Primes p ≡ 839 (mod 840) have 3.6× more ES solutions than other primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) (p > 1000).
why: Quantifies the covering multiplicity at the 'all identities fire' class — the dual extreme to p ≡ 1 (mod 840).
first_step: Count which classical identities apply at p ≡ −1 (mod 840) and check that their solution counts sum to the observed excess.

title: U(p) vs U((p+3)/4): raw Spearman 0.66; vs U(4p+1): 0.36 (size-confounded)
connection: Raw rank correlations between ES counts at p and at the p-tied integers (p+3)/4 and 4p+1 (p ≤ 30 000 / 7 500).
why: Most of this is the common size trend; the residual correlation (after log n terms on both sides) would show whether difficulty propagates along the greedy map p ↦ (p+3)/4.
first_step: Recompute on residuals; if positive, ES-hardness is 'inherited' along the greedy forest (FOREST_*.md).

title: Proposed 'hall of fame' test set for ES ideas
why: Breadth lanes generate hundreds of candidate connections; a fixed, diverse hard set makes cheap falsification uniform across lanes.
first_step: Add a script that, given a candidate certificate family (as a predicate on (x,y,z) or words), reports which hall-of-fame primes it certifies.

title: Degenerate-locus obstruction as a model for T1
connection: The isosceles locus of 4/p is obstructed exactly on p ≡ 1 (4) by a mod-4 factor-class argument on 2p²; T1 (all certificate lines empty at odd squares) is a reciprocity obstruction on p-tied integers.
why: Both are 'a fixed integer built from p has no divisor in a required class' — the isosceles case is the 0-dimensional toy model of the line obstructions, fully understood; studying how the obstruction disappears when one moves off the degenerate locus could illuminate why lines fail only at squares.
first_step: Parametrise near-isosceles solutions (y − x small) and compute when their divisor-class condition becomes solvable for p ≡ 1 (4).

title: Residual factor pairs
connection: Fixing x turns 4/p−1/x=a/b into (ay−b)(az−b)=b²; connect ES to complementary divisors in simultaneous residue classes.
why: This is an exact two-unit-fraction reformulation rather than a counting analogy.
first_step: For primes below 500, enumerate x up to p and record the successful residue pairs.

title: Primitive projective triples
connection: View denominator triples as rational points up to common scaling, with p recovered from their reciprocal sum.
why: Scaling explains why prime cases are central and may separate shape from arithmetic size.
first_step: Enumerate primitive triples with coordinates below 100 and sort the resulting reduced values of 4xyz/(xy+xz+yz).

title: Near-equal denominator perturbations
connection: Write y=z+h and study the exact residual equation as h varies, connecting ES to near-square factorization.
why: Small h gives structured, checkable subfamilies without claiming they cover every prime.
first_step: Enumerate the smallest attainable difference z−y for primes below 1000.

title: Weighted mediants
connection: Compare residual fractions from neighboring x with Farey mediants, looking for intervals where a two-term decomposition persists.
why: Farey adjacency controls numerator-denominator determinants exactly.
first_step: Compute Farey neighbors of residual fractions for the first 50 difficult primes.

title: Cluster-style mutations
connection: Search for involutions on auxiliary ES parametrizations analogous to replacing one root of a quadratic while fixing other variables.
why: An exact positive integral mutation could propagate certificates across a connected graph.
first_step: For three existing elementary parametrizations, solve for each coordinate and test whether another integral branch exists.

title: Saturation and boundary components
connection: Study the ideal of 4xyz−p(xy+xz+yz) after excluding zero coordinates and compare its components under congruence restrictions.
why: Removing degenerate solutions is essential before algebraic parametrizations are interpreted arithmetically.
first_step: Compute the saturation by xyz for a small symbolic specialization and inspect the nonzero locus.

title: Height functions on certificates
connection: Compare max(x,y,z), xyz, and auxiliary-parameter height as costs on the same certificate space.
why: A proof-producing descent may work for a height unrelated to the smallest denominator.
first_step: For bounded triples, build move graphs and test which heights decrease along known identity transformations.

title: Newton polytope viewpoints
connection: Compare monomial supports of the ES surface and auxiliary divisor equations to find sparse elimination orders.
why: Sparse structure can reduce symbolic-search complexity without implying integer-point existence.
first_step: Draw the exponent support and test elimination with two variable orders in a computer algebra system.

title: Conic bundles
connection: Choose auxiliary coordinates that leave a conic equation over one parameter and study its local solvability and integral points.
why: Conics admit explicit parametrizations once a rational point is supplied.
first_step: Search linear substitutions that make one residual equation quadratic in two remaining variables.

title: Class-group bookkeeping
connection: When a divisor condition factors in a quadratic order, distinguish principal from nonprincipal ideal factors.
why: This identifies an arithmetic constraint that could guide which auxiliary field is useful.
first_step: For a small negative discriminant arising from a slice, compare ideal factorizations with actual integral certificates.

title: Quaternion multiplication as composition
connection: Ask whether quaternion norm identities compose two partial ES certificates into a full one.
why: Four-square identities offer explicit polynomial relations whose congruences can be checked.
first_step: Choose a small norm identity and symbolically test whether its cross terms match an ES residual equation.

title: Continuants modulo powers of two
connection: Analyze short continuant recurrences modulo 8,16,32 and compare reachable states with the admissible coordinate classes.
why: Finite parity information may guide an otherwise unbounded integer construction.
first_step: Build the exact transition graph for continuants modulo 16 with coefficient residues as labels.

title: Euclidean quotient parity
connection: Track parity of Euclidean quotients together with remainder size when processing p and an auxiliary parameter.
why: Parity-decorated Euclidean descent could interact with the required classes modulo four.
first_step: Compute quotient-parity strings for certificates found by a fixed divisor search and compare with controls.

title: Hensel lifting with size control
connection: Lift auxiliary congruence solutions modulo prime powers while tracking whether representatives stay inside useful positive intervals.
why: Local lifting is only a component, but controlled representatives could feed a global construction.
first_step: Lift one divisor-family congruence from modulus q to q² and measure least positive representatives.

title: Rational reconstruction
connection: Use modular solutions plus height bounds to reconstruct candidate rational parametrizations of ES certificates.
why: Rational reconstruction is an exact computational tool when the bounds are justified.
first_step: For a fixed prime, reconstruct small ratios y/z from modular solutions at successively larger moduli.

title: Fundamental domain boundary crossings
connection: Follow a moving residue target through lattice fundamental domains as p changes and record when short representatives appear.
why: Boundary crossings may explain abrupt changes in the cheapest certificate.
first_step: Track nearest lattice representatives for consecutive admissible primes in one explicit two-variable model.

title: Divisor posets
connection: Organize divisors of each p-tied integer by divisibility and study where the target residue first occurs.
why: Poset structure may reveal that a few prime-factor toggles suffice to reach the target.
first_step: Construct divisor Hasse diagrams for 20 auxiliary integers and color nodes by target residues.

title: Zero-sum theory for divisor residues
connection: Take discrete-log coordinates when available and compare target divisor residues with zero-sum sequence phenomena.
why: Multiplicative divisor selection becomes additive combinatorics in finite abelian groups.
first_step: For cyclic unit groups of small moduli, compute the exponent multiset and shortest subsequences hitting the target.

title: Complement involutions on divisors
connection: Use d↔N/d as an involution on candidate residues and look for forced pairs or fixed points.
why: The involution is exact and may reduce search or create parity constraints on failures.
first_step: For each residue r modulo a small modulus, calculate how complementary divisors transform r when it is invertible.

title: Composition of partial certificates
connection: Define a partial certificate as satisfying the equation and some integrality conditions, then seek operations that complete missing conditions.
why: Separating algebraic validity from integrality may make complementary constructions visible.
first_step: Create a table of rational identities with their exact integrality requirements and test pairwise compatible substitutions.

title: Cancellation across auxiliary parameters
connection: Sum character errors over C before taking absolute values, looking for cancellation lost in parameterwise bounds.
why: Different certificate lines may compensate each other's arithmetic biases.
first_step: Compute signed nonprincipal-character contributions for C≤30 over a sample of primes.

title: Singular-series fluctuations
connection: Build a candidate Euler-product heuristic from local densities and compare it with observed certificate counts.
why: A varying local factor may explain low-count primes better than a single average.
first_step: Compute truncated products using primes up to 31 and compare with bounded-search counts.

title: High moments of certificate counts
connection: Expand third and fourth moments of a bounded certificate count to distinguish thin tails from heavy correlations.
why: Higher moments retain information that the average and variance can miss.
first_step: Compute the first four empirical moments with the same cutoff for all sampled primes.

title: Janson-style avoidance models
connection: Model bounded auxiliary choices as witness events and investigate whether an avoidance inequality can be justified from their dependencies.
why: A bound below one on an actual finite avoidance probability would certify at least one witness for that fixed instance.
first_step: Specify a finite probability space of auxiliary choices and compute all pairwise event intersections for small p.

title: Lopsided dependence of failures
connection: Ask whether failure events exhibit one-sided dependence more favorable than their raw correlations suggest.
why: Avoidance estimates sometimes use conditional probabilities rather than symmetric independence.
first_step: Compute conditional failure frequencies for pairs and triples of parameter choices without extrapolating to a theorem.

title: Smooth auxiliary values
connection: Favor parameters for which the p-tied integer has many small prime factors, then inspect whether their divisor residues cover the target.
why: Smoothness supplies many selectable factors but does not by itself settle residue coverage.
first_step: Search C≤100 for primes below 1000 and correlate smoothness with target-residue success.

title: Least quadratic nonresidue steering
connection: Use small quadratic nonresidues to choose auxiliary parameters that escape symbol restrictions of one family.
why: A character witness supplies arithmetic information beyond p modulo a fixed integer.
first_step: For each sampled prime, correlate its least nonresidue with the smallest successful auxiliary parameter.

title: Splitting fields of auxiliary polynomials
connection: For polynomial subfamilies of auxiliary values, relate factor-residue behavior to splitting in explicitly computed number fields.
why: Field structure may organize observed factor patterns, though integer prime divisors need separate analysis.
first_step: Compute a splitting field for one quadratic auxiliary polynomial and state precisely which finite-field splitting event is relevant.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Pretentious character diagnostics
connection: Compare stubborn divisor-residue biases with multiplicative functions that mimic simple characters on small primes.
why: A structured bias could suggest a complementary family tailored to that character.
first_step: Compute distances between empirical factor-sign patterns and a small library of Dirichlet characters.

title: Sum–product mixing across parameters
connection: Compare multiplicative divisor generation with additive changes in the auxiliary parameter.
why: Alternating two different operations may escape concentration that persists under either alone.
first_step: Build a small state graph with factor multiplication and valid parameter-shift edges, checking each edge algebraically.

title: Spectral gaps of certificate transitions
connection: Construct a finite transition matrix from verified certificate transformations and inspect its bottlenecks.
why: A spectral picture may identify missing moves or separated families, not prove connectivity on its own.
first_step: Enumerate bounded certificates for one p and compute transition components before estimating eigenvalues.

title: Polynomial recurrence selectors
connection: Ask whether a parameter sequence chosen by polynomial recurrence repeatedly enters a sufficient residue pattern.
why: Recurrence could replace an unstructured search if its visits can be made effective.
first_step: Choose one exact sufficient congruence pattern and compute visits of quadratic parameter sequences modulo its modulus.

title: Beatty-sequence denominators
connection: Choose candidate denominators from complementary floor sequences and inspect exact reciprocal residuals.
why: Complementary sequences offer a systematic way to couple rounding errors without claiming an identity.
first_step: For slopes with simple quadratic irrational values, test the first two denominators and factor the residual numerator.

title: Sieve parity diagnostics
connection: Check which certificate predicates depend only on roughness and which depend on the parity or residue of factor products.
why: This identifies information a chosen sieve model must retain, without discarding the connection.
first_step: Construct two auxiliary integers with matching small-prime divisibility data but different target-divisor behavior.

title: Dense-model questions for divisor residues
connection: Ask whether a normalized divisor-residue measure resembles a simpler measure on the test functions relevant to ES.
why: Only the relevant tests need approximation, so a tailored model might be more useful than global uniformity.
first_step: Specify a finite test-function family and solve for a simple measure matching its moments.

title: Rare prime strata as separate models
connection: Partition primes by combinations of small character values and build separate count models for sparse strata.
why: Mixture distributions can hide strong structure in an exceptional tail.
first_step: Choose three small character labels and compare the full count histogram within each nonempty stratum.

title: Moment inversion for zero counts
connection: Use finite-support moment bounds to estimate the possible mass at zero under measured or proved count moments.
why: This makes the distinction between average abundance and universal positivity explicit without rejecting the approach.
first_step: Solve the small linear program maximizing zero mass subject to the first three empirical moments.

title: Witness hypergraphs
connection: Build a hypergraph whose vertices are auxiliary choices and whose edges are jointly compatible pieces of a certificate.
why: Compatibility may be more naturally expressed by small tuples than by one successful parameter.
first_step: For one exact parametrization, separate its constraints into three pieces and enumerate compatible triples for a small prime.

title: Matroids for family diversity
connection: Treat residue tests supplied by candidate families as feature vectors and use independence to choose a diverse search portfolio.
why: Linear independence is a cheap surrogate for avoiding many near-identical families.
first_step: Build a binary family-by-test matrix on small primes and compare independent subsets with greedy coverage subsets.

title: VC dimension of certificate families
connection: View each parametrized identity as a subset of sampled primes and estimate the combinatorial complexity of that set system.
why: Low complexity might explain why small representative samples reveal much of the coverage structure.
first_step: Search for shattered subsets of size up to five in a bounded incidence matrix.

title: Discrepancy-balanced family splits
connection: Color certificate families into two portfolios whose coverage counts stay close across sampled primes.
why: Balanced splits can reveal genuine diversity and create independent-looking diagnostic datasets.
first_step: Solve a small discrepancy-minimization problem on the family-prime incidence matrix.

title: Sunflower patterns among constraints
connection: Search for families of certificate conditions sharing a common core and disjoint extra congruence requirements.
why: A sunflower structure may identify a reusable common lemma with several interchangeable completions.
first_step: Represent each small family by its set of atomic congruence conditions and detect common-core collections.

title: Arithmetic progressions inside witness sets
connection: Look for long arithmetic progressions of successful auxiliary parameters and derive the conditions responsible.
why: Progressions may signal a hidden congruence family rather than random abundance.
first_step: For fixed small primes, find maximal progressions of successful C and compare their differences with the factorization of p−1.

title: Residue graph homomorphisms
connection: Map an integral certificate-transition graph to its reductions modulo several small integers.
why: Fibers and missing lifts can reveal exactly what information a residue graph forgets.
first_step: Construct the reduction map for a bounded transition graph and inspect fibers of successful residue states.

title: Automatic pattern diagnostics
connection: Test whether experimentally observed family selectors have low-complexity digit behavior.
why: A short automaton would suggest a recursive selector, though finite data cannot establish automaticity.
first_step: Infer minimal automata from initial selector labels and test them on a disjoint larger range.

title: Weighted automata for word height
connection: Add costs measuring coefficient size or word length to the congruence automaton.
why: Shortest accepted paths can find economical candidate certificates while respecting exact finite-state constraints.
first_step: Run shortest-path search with logarithmic coefficient cost and compare candidates against direct enumeration.

title: Carry cellular automata
connection: View the multiplication and addition in the cleared ES equation as local carry interactions on digit strings.
why: Local update rules may reveal impossible digit patterns or efficient branch propagation.
first_step: Implement a bounded-width carry propagation diagram for a toy prime and compare its pruning with naive digit search.

title: Digit lifting of identities
connection: Try extending a certificate for a truncated base expansion of p when one more digit is appended.
why: This is an induction proposal with exact algebraic correction terms, not an assumption that prime prefixes behave well.
first_step: Substitute p′=bp+r and x′=bx+a into the cleared equation and solve the first correction constraints.

title: Multivariate certificate generating functions
connection: Weight certificates by denominator height, gcd type, and parameter size in a formal generating series.
why: Different projections of one series can compare search costs and arithmetic strata.
first_step: Compute a truncated series for p=13 and inspect which coefficients are invariant under denominator permutation.

title: Restricted additive bases of divisors
connection: Ask when the divisor set of a chosen common denominator is an additive basis for the specific target 4L/p.
why: This reframes the problem as a constrained three-sum problem with tunable ambient integer L.
first_step: For L=p times a small smooth number, compute D(L)+D(L)+D(L) near the target.

title: Ehrhart families of auxiliary polytopes
connection: When a parametrization reduces to linear inequalities and congruences, study its integer-point count as the bounds dilate.
why: Quasipolynomial counts can give exact finite-family information without addressing nonlinear cases automatically.
first_step: Isolate one linear parameter region and compute its first several dilation counts.

title: Markov bases for certificate fibers
connection: Seek finite move sets connecting all nonnegative solutions of a fixed linearized parameter constraint.
why: Connectivity of the linear fiber could reduce enumeration before nonlinear conditions are imposed.
first_step: Compute a kernel basis for a toy exponent-allocation matrix and test which moves preserve positivity.

title: Matrix-tree determinants
connection: Compare determinant expressions from the forest formulation with graph Laplacian cofactors.
why: A graph realization could make positivity or combinatorial multiplicity transparent.
first_step: Construct small weighted trees and check which Laplacian minors reproduce short tuv−u−v expressions.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Electrical network interpretation
connection: Interpret a denominator or continued-fraction identity as series-parallel resistance reduction.
why: Exact rational network laws may suggest composition operations whose integrality can then be checked.
first_step: Translate short continued fractions into resistor networks and mark operations preserving the required residue classes.

title: Interlacing under adding families
connection: Compare spectra of finite incidence matrices before and after adding a new certificate family.
why: Spectral changes may quantify genuinely new coverage directions rather than raw success counts.
first_step: Compute singular values of a family-prime matrix and rank additions by their effect on the smallest nonzero values.

title: Discrete Morse reductions
connection: Assign a combinatorial gradient to a bounded certificate complex and collapse redundant regions.
why: A reduced complex might isolate the essential obstructions to moving between certificate families.
first_step: Build a small complex from compatible local moves and test elementary collapses with explicit free-face checks.

title: Nerves of parametrization charts
connection: Construct the nerve whose vertices are exact parametrizations and whose simplices record shared certificates.
why: Intersections may expose a small core of identities linking otherwise separate approaches.
first_step: Compute pairwise and triple intersections for five small parametrization families over a finite prime sample.

title: Termination orders for identity search
connection: Seek a well-founded monomial or lexicographic order that decreases under selected ES transformations.
why: A genuine termination argument could turn heuristic rewriting into a reliable normalization procedure.
first_step: Try lexicographic orders on denominator height and gcd data for three verified rewrite rules.

title: Combinatorial games on residual fractions
connection: Define legal moves as exact split-and-merge operations and winning positions as positive three-term decompositions.
why: A strategy theorem on a specified class of positions could produce constructive identities.
first_step: Write precise game rules, enumerate small positions, and look for a decreasing potential on winning strategies.

title: Rhythmic subdivisions as identity generators
connection: Translate exact unit-fraction splitting into subdivisions of a common rhythmic cycle, then search for regroupings into three parts.
why: The musical picture is only a representation of rational identities, but may prompt overlooked regroupings.
first_step: Enumerate subdivisions of a 60-slot cycle and retain only regroupings that verify an exact three-unit-fraction equality.

title: Certificate partition functions
connection: Introduce a fugacity for auxiliary size and form a finite partition function whose coefficients count verified certificates.
why: Different fugacities emphasize economical witnesses or high multiplicity without changing the underlying exact count.
first_step: Compute the partition polynomial for a small prime and compare its low-degree coefficients across primes.

title: Cluster expansions for factor dependence
connection: Group interacting prime-factor selections into connected clusters instead of treating them as independent residue choices.
why: A convergent or finite exact expansion could organize corrections to naive randomness.
first_step: For an auxiliary integer with at most six distinct factors, calculate connected correlation terms explicitly.

title: Cavity messages on factor graphs
connection: Represent local valuation and congruence constraints as a factor graph and pass approximate marginal messages.
why: Belief propagation can suggest assignments, while exact substitution verifies every output.
first_step: Build a small factor graph for residue-factor selection and compare message marginals with exhaustive enumeration.

title: Search-budget phase diagrams
connection: Plot witness existence and multiplicity against two independent cutoffs, such as C and allowed denominator height.
why: A two-dimensional diagram may distinguish families that look identical under a single budget.
first_step: For a fixed prime sample, compute coarse grids of success rates over both cutoffs.

title: Renormalization by eliminating small factors
connection: Integrate out the choices involving the smallest prime factors to obtain an effective residue distribution for the remaining factors.
why: This is exact convolution on a finite group before any approximation is introduced.
first_step: Eliminate prime factors one at a time and track support size, entropy, and target mass.

title: Annealing with exact repairs
connection: Combine stochastic descent on a congruence energy with deterministic repair of one remaining divisibility condition.
why: A repair step ties the physical analogy to exact arithmetic output.
first_step: Implement a toy annealer on one residual parametrization and verify every reported zero by integer arithmetic.

title: Density of states near valid certificates
connection: Count parameter assignments by exact residual size and divisibility defect rather than only success or failure.
why: Near-zero abundance might suggest a correction lemma or reveal that approximate solutions are misleading.
first_step: Compute the joint histogram of residual numerator and gcd defect for a small parameter box.

title: Random-matrix baselines for family incidence
connection: Compare singular values of the actual family-prime incidence matrix with matrices preserving its row and column sums.
why: This can detect collective arithmetic structure beyond individual family success rates.
first_step: Generate degree-preserving shuffled matrices and compare their leading singular values with the original.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Quantum-walk-inspired exploration
connection: Compare coherent-walk-inspired search heuristics with classical walks on a finite residue graph, without assuming hardware speedups.
why: Interference patterns may suggest new deterministic orderings of candidate residues.
first_step: Simulate a very small unitary walk and compare the high-amplitude states with shortest target-reaching paths.

title: Tensor-network contraction of residue constraints
connection: Represent factor choices and congruence checks as small tensors and contract along a low-width graph.
why: Contraction order can exploit sparse dependencies in exact witness counting.
first_step: Construct a residue-selection tensor network for at most ten factors and compare contraction widths.

title: Holographic changes of basis
connection: Test whether a basis change simplifies local tensors in a finite certificate constraint network.
why: Some encodings become easier after transforming the local representation, but all arithmetic constraints must survive.
first_step: Apply small invertible basis changes to a toy residue tensor and compare sparsity and contraction cost.

title: Toda-like recurrences of continuants
connection: Compare determinant recurrences of tridiagonal matrices with short continued-fraction certificate expressions.
why: Shared determinant algebra may suggest bilinear recurrence identities useful for composition.
first_step: Compute adjacent tridiagonal minors symbolically and test their identities against a short continuant parametrization.

title: Symplectic coordinates for matrix words
connection: Use the area-preserving action of SL₂ on pairs of coordinates to track certificate-related invariants.
why: An invariant determinant can constrain possible moves more cleanly than expanded polynomials.
first_step: Choose two column vectors from a short word and compute which parameter changes preserve their determinant and residue labels.

title: Horocycle sampling of congruence states
connection: Study elementary unipotent matrix orbits modulo small integers and their integer-height growth.
why: These are explicit orbits that could generate systematic candidate families.
first_step: Enumerate products of two unipotent flows modulo 16 and track the least integer height realizing each target state.

title: Interval-exchange selectors
connection: Use interval maps associated with rational approximation to partition parameter choices into symbolic regimes.
why: A finite partition might yield a small list of exact denominator formulas on each regime.
first_step: Compute return itineraries for a simple interval map and test whether an exact residual formula is constant in symbolic type.

title: Return-time distributions
connection: Measure first visits to admissible residue states in deterministic certificate-generating dynamics.
why: Return-time tails are directly connected to the cost of the resulting search procedure.
first_step: For several initial states, record first-hit times and compare them with orbit component sizes.

title: Escape to the cusp
connection: Interpret unusually large minimal denominators as possible degeneration of an associated lattice basis.
why: This can distinguish missing certificates from certificates hidden in highly anisotropic regions.
first_step: For difficult bounded instances, compute successive minima of a relevant small lattice and compare them with denominator imbalance.

title: Arithmetic tori from norm-one units
connection: Use norm-one units to move along a norm-equation slice while preserving its right-hand side.
why: The remaining question becomes whether the orbit reaches the positivity and congruence region needed for ES.
first_step: For a small real quadratic norm equation, compute unit-orbit residues modulo the required modulus.

title: Convex relaxations of bounded searches
connection: Relax selected bilinear constraints using valid convex envelopes inside a finite parameter box.
why: The relaxation can prune impossible boxes or reveal promising corners, without supplying integer witnesses by itself.
first_step: Apply McCormick envelopes to one bounded auxiliary equation and compare feasible boxes with exact enumeration.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Curvature-adapted sampling
connection: Sample near the real solution surface with density adjusted to local curvature and rounding sensitivity.
why: This may propose integer candidates more efficiently than sampling a rectangular box.
first_step: Compute the Hessian of z=pxy/(4xy−p(x+y)) and compare two bounded sampling schemes.

title: Optimal transport of divisor-residue measures
connection: Compare residue distributions from two auxiliary parameters using a cost based on allowed residue moves.
why: A low-cost transport plan might identify concrete transformations connecting complementary families.
first_step: For a small modulus, solve a finite transport problem between two divisor-residue histograms and inspect its dominant edges.

title: Harmonic analysis beyond the unit group
connection: Use the full multiplicative residue monoid when auxiliary factors are not units, rather than forcing a group model.
why: A monoid representation can retain valuation strata that ordinary character expansions omit.
first_step: Construct multiplication operators on residues modulo 12 and decompose their invariant subspaces.

title: SMT over mixed integer structures
connection: Combine integer arithmetic, divisibility, and bit-vector residue constraints in a bounded solver model.
why: Different theories may cooperate better than one large expanded polynomial equation.
first_step: Model one auxiliary divisor family with explicit finite bounds and compare integer-only with mixed-theory formulations.

title: Counterexample-guided identity synthesis
connection: Alternate proposing symbolic denominator formulas with finding primes or parameter values violating their claimed domain.
why: Counterexamples refine the synthesis grammar while every accepted identity requires symbolic verification.
first_step: Run a small CEGIS loop over affine numerator and denominator templates restricted to one residue class.

title: Equality saturation for rational identities
connection: Store equivalent rational expressions in an e-graph and extract forms with simpler integrality conditions.
why: Equivalent formulas can have very different arithmetic usability even when their real values agree.
first_step: Build an e-graph from a few verified reciprocal identities and score expressions by denominator-factor complexity.

title: Constraint propagation on factor domains
connection: Maintain finite domains for factor residues and remove choices that cannot participate in a valid complementary pair.
why: Arc consistency can sharply reduce bounded search while preserving every actual solution.
first_step: Apply AC-3 to a three-variable factor-residue model and compare remaining domains with exhaustive solutions.

title: Proof-carrying witness search
connection: Make each search result carry the integer arithmetic needed to verify positivity and the cleared identity independently.
why: This decouples experimental algorithms from trust in their implementation.
first_step: Specify a compact witness record and a verifier using only exact integer operations.

title: Grammar compression of certificates
connection: Compress a finite certificate database using shared identity templates and parameter substitutions.
why: A short grammar can reveal repeated constructions hidden among many individual triples.
first_step: Cluster exact triples by common rational-expression templates and compare compressed description lengths.

title: Minimum-description-length family selection
connection: Balance the coverage of a formula against the complexity of its exceptional-case conditions.
why: This discourages overfitting while keeping every mathematically valid family available.
first_step: Encode formula syntax and residue exceptions with an explicit code, then compare several portfolios on held-out primes.

title: Treewidth of arithmetic factor graphs
connection: Measure the width of a factor graph after separating valuations, carries, and residues.
why: Small treewidth would support exact dynamic programming for that bounded encoding.
first_step: Construct three alternative factor graphs for the same tiny instance and compare elimination widths.

title: FFT convolution on cyclic residue coordinates
connection: Use discrete-log coordinates in a cyclic unit group to turn divisor-selection convolution into cyclic convolution.
why: Fast convolution can count residue witnesses exactly with suitable integer reconstruction.
first_step: For a small prime modulus, compare direct dynamic programming with an exact convolution implementation.

title: Decision diagrams for factor subsets
connection: Compress repeated residual subproblems using zero-suppressed decision diagrams or related shared DAGs.
why: Many distinct divisors can share the same remaining residue problem.
first_step: Build a small decision diagram for target-residue divisor selection and compare its node count with the number of divisors.

title: Arithmetic-circuit complexity
connection: Compare expanded polynomial identities with compact straight-line arithmetic circuits.
why: A low-complexity circuit may expose composition structure that expansion obscures.
first_step: Represent three candidate families as circuits and count multiplication gates after common-subexpression elimination.

title: Modular interpolation of identities
connection: Recover candidate polynomial coefficients from evaluations modulo several primes and reconstruct rational coefficients.
why: This can make symbolic discovery cheaper, followed by exact identity checking.
first_step: Recover a known low-degree numerator identity from modular samples as a pipeline sanity check.

title: Approximate common divisors as hints
connection: Explore cases where several auxiliary values are near multiples of an unknown useful factor.
why: Shared approximate divisibility might reveal a factor-selection strategy if the error model is justified.
first_step: Construct exact small examples from known certificates and test whether the useful factor is recoverable from the proposed hints.

title: Partial factor bits from congruence constraints
connection: Use the required residue of a useful divisor as partial information in a factorization problem.
why: A residue class supplies genuine bits of structure, though it may be far too weak for existing algorithms.
first_step: For small auxiliary integers, measure how much the target congruence shrinks the divisor search and check partial-factor recovery literature.

title: Elliptic-curve factorization as a probe
connection: Use small factoring budgets to sample auxiliary factors and ask whether easily found factors already yield many certificates.
why: This measures whether complete factorization is unnecessary for exploratory coverage.
first_step: Apply equal small ECM budgets to a bounded list of auxiliary values and verify all certificates obtained from partial factorizations.

title: Factor-base relations for certificate search
connection: Collect auxiliary values smooth over a chosen factor base and record their residue-selection structure.
why: This borrows a relation-collection viewpoint without assuming factorization-style linear algebra directly solves ES.
first_step: Build a tiny factor-base relation matrix and determine what additional condition turns a relation into an actual target divisor.

title: Factoring-free gcd certificates
connection: Search for constructions where a useful divisor is produced as a gcd of two explicit expressions.
why: A gcd can supply a verified factor without requiring complete factorization.
first_step: Try short polynomial gcd expressions in p and C and retain only cases where the gcd provably has the target residue.

title: Las Vegas certificate discovery
connection: Allow random candidate generation but accept outputs only after deterministic exact verification.
why: Randomness then affects runtime rather than the correctness of reported witnesses.
first_step: Design a randomized parameter sampler with explicit timeouts and an independent certificate checker.

title: Perfect-hash-style family isolation
connection: Use hash partitions to isolate one witness among many candidate factors, simplifying a bounded search subproblem.
why: Isolation can aid algorithm design, while an exact check prevents the hash mechanism from inventing witnesses.
first_step: Apply a small family of residue hashes to known multi-witness instances and measure isolation rates.

title: Cache keys as mathematical assumptions
connection: Key cached computations by the full parametrization, modulus, positivity convention, and search bounds.
why: This prevents results from one mathematical model being silently reused in a different one.
first_step: Audit a toy search cache and construct two deliberately incompatible configurations that must not share entries.

title: Factor-graph neural heuristics
connection: Use a graph model whose nodes represent prime factors, residues, and valuation slots to rank partial assignments.
why: The architecture mirrors actual arithmetic constraints, while final outputs still require exact verification.
first_step: Train only on tiny exhaustively solved factor-selection instances and test ranking quality on larger held-out ones.

title: Decision trees as conjecture extractors
connection: Fit shallow trees using residue and character features, then translate each leaf into a proposed arithmetic lemma.
why: A transparent leaf condition is a concrete object for proof or counterexample search.
first_step: Fit a depth-three tree for one family's success and exhaustively test each leaf condition in a larger range.

title: Rational-function recognition in families
connection: Group certificates by a discrete template label and attempt exact rational interpolation of their parameters as functions of p.
why: Recovered formulas can be verified symbolically and their integrality domains derived.
first_step: For one visually coherent cluster, interpolate low-degree rational functions from exact data and test unused points.

title: Active learning at family boundaries
connection: Choose new examples near the boundary where a simple family selector changes its prediction.
why: Boundary cases may expose missing congruence hypotheses more quickly than uniform sampling.
first_step: Train a shallow selector, query its most ambiguous bounded inputs, and inspect the exact divisibility reasons for each outcome.

title: Calibration of success predictions
connection: Measure whether predicted success probabilities for a fixed search budget match observed frequencies.
why: Well-calibrated uncertainty is useful for scheduling, but cannot turn a probability estimate into a proof.
first_step: Build reliability curves on held-out primes and separate calibration by small-residue strata.

title: Explaining count outliers
connection: For primes with unexpectedly few witnesses, decompose the prediction error into factorization, local-density, and family-overlap features.
why: An explanation may suggest a targeted new identity instead of merely another statistical model.
first_step: Select ten low-count outliers and compare each feature against matched primes of similar size.

title: Nonnegative latent mechanisms
connection: Factor a nonnegative count matrix into a few latent family and prime components, then seek arithmetic interpretations.
why: Unlike a proof, the factorization only suggests which mechanisms might be shared.
first_step: Fit ranks two through five and inspect whether components align with known gcd or character labels.

title: Motifs in proof graphs
connection: Mine repeated small subgraphs in graphs of exact algebraic derivations.
why: Recurring proof fragments may become reusable lemmas or identity-generation macros.
first_step: Encode ten elementary derivations as operation DAGs and identify repeated three-operation motifs.

title: Language-model analogy proposals with algebraic gates
connection: Use a language model only to propose cross-domain encodings, then require a written map and a checked toy instance.
why: The algebraic gate separates a useful analogy from merely similar terminology.
first_step: Prompt for five encodings of the same residual factor equation and discard only those lacking a well-defined map.

title: Citation-graph bridges
connection: Trace papers that connect two relevant areas, such as restricted divisor problems and finite-group zero-sum theory.
why: Bridge papers may supply a transferable lemma not indexed under Egyptian fractions.
first_step: Search for a paper using both topic vocabularies, verify it exists, and inspect its cited technical tools.

title: Positivity proof certificates
connection: Attach explicit positive-factor decompositions to every symbolic denominator expression.
why: An algebraically correct identity can still fail as an ES construction if denominators are nonpositive.
first_step: For three candidate formulas, rewrite each denominator into products or sums whose signs follow from stated hypotheses.

title: Replayable symbolic proof traces
connection: Export each algebraic simplification as a sequence of exact transformations rather than only a final yes/no answer.
why: A small checker can replay discovery-tool output independently.
first_step: For one rational identity, record clearing denominators, ring normalization, and hypothesis use as separate trace steps.

title: Metamorphic tests from scaling
connection: Use exact transformations such as scaling a valid triple along with n to generate consistency checks.
why: If 4/n=Σ1/x, scaling all four quantities by a positive integer preserves the identity.
first_step: Specify a test transforming a valid witness at n into one at kn and verify all fields update consistently.

title: Bloom-related density increments
connection: Investigate whether work associated with Bloom on unit-fraction problems offers a density-increment mechanism adaptable to structured divisor sets.
why: The potentially transferable object is a lemma about reciprocal mass, not an assumed three-term theorem.
first_step: Find the relevant paper, verify its hypotheses, and compare its denominator set with divisors of a p-tied integer.

title: Lüroth-style digit systems
connection: Check whether a rational expansion with consecutive-product denominators can be converted into a useful three-term ES ansatz.
why: The digit system offers a different exact decomposition grammar, not an automatic short representation.
first_step: Verify the precise Lüroth expansion formula and test finite rational examples for algebraically valid regroupings.

title: Odd-denominator greedy variants
connection: Compare a greedy rule restricted to odd denominators with unrestricted greedy search on related residual fractions.
why: Restrictions can expose parity mechanisms even if they make termination harder.
first_step: Define a precise odd-denominator choice rule and compute its first three residuals on a bounded set of admissible rational inputs.

title: 8/n and k/n siblings: Kahn–Kalai threshold across the numerator k
connection: Varying the numerator k (k/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z) changes the expected solution count; Schinzel–Sierpiński-type problems are open for each k ≥ 4.
why: A threshold picture across k (where 'almost all' becomes 'all') calibrates ES's position.
first_step: Compute failure counts of k/n for k = 4..12, n ≤ 10^6 (excluding trivial obstructions) and fit expected-count vs failure-rate curves.

title: Primitive-to-scaled transfer
connection: Track how primitive denominator shapes generate certificates for composite n and which shapes first appear at prime n.
why: This may reveal composition laws without confusing the easy scaling direction with a converse.
first_step: Canonicalize triples by their common gcd and map the resulting primitive shapes to the reduced fraction they represent.

title: Polynomial continued fractions
connection: Compare short continued fractions over Fq[T] with the integer word formulations, retaining coefficient degree and unit information.
why: The Euclidean algorithm survives, but ordering and parity constraints change substantially.
first_step: Compute length-three expansions over F5[T] and identify which coefficient conditions correspond to the integer formulation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Boundary divisors and integral points
connection: Compactify a rational parametrization and identify which boundary components correspond to zero, infinite, or nonintegral denominators.
why: The boundary may explain why rational abundance does not directly imply useful integer points.
first_step: For one explicit chart, homogenize its equation and label every boundary component by its arithmetic meaning.

title: Real components and positivity chambers
connection: Partition the real auxiliary variety by signs of all denominator factors and analyze each chamber separately.
why: Only certain chambers yield positive unit fractions; chamber transitions may suggest controlled transformations.
first_step: For a two-parameter rational family, draw the zero sets of denominator factors and label every positive chamber.

title: Genus-two slices as stress tests
connection: Impose a simple additional relation and check whether a higher-genus curve appears with a few explicit certificate points.
why: Such slices can reveal which constraints make a family too rigid while still providing concrete finite examples.
first_step: Try a cubic relation between two denominators, compute the curve genus, and inspect the known points without assuming completeness.

title: Infinitesimal deformations and exact correction
connection: Compute tangent directions at a certificate, then ask which directions extend to rational curves with controllable denominators.
why: Tangent data can propose families, but exact substitution is required beyond first order.
first_step: Linearize the cleared equation at one small triple and test two tangent directions with quadratic correction terms.

title: Enumerating low-degree curves on the surface
connection: Search directly for lines or conics contained in a chosen compactification rather than guessing denominator formulas individually.
why: Coefficient equations turn the family search into a finite symbolic problem at each degree.
first_step: Substitute a general affine line with rational coefficients and solve the resulting coefficient equations.

title: Indefinite quadratic-form orbits
connection: Study indefinite quadratic slices using reduction and automorphisms rather than finite ellipsoid enumeration.
why: Infinite orbits may generate recurrent witnesses, with positivity handled along the orbit.
first_step: For one binary indefinite form arising from a slice, compute a fundamental automorphism and its residues modulo 8.

title: Eisenstein and cusp contribution separation
connection: For a valid modular count, separate an explicit main contribution from the cusp contribution before assessing positivity.
why: The decomposition could reveal the exact estimate needed for one slice, without assuming it is available.
first_step: Locate the modular space for a concrete theta series and determine whether its Eisenstein projection can be computed at low level.

title: Spinor-genus diagnostics on quadratic slices
connection: Check whether local representation conditions for a selected quadratic form split into globally different arithmetic classes.
why: The goal is to understand that slice's representation pattern, not to infer an obstruction for ES as a whole.
first_step: Compute small representation data for a concrete ternary form and check literature on its genus and spinor genus.

title: Local zeta functions of certificate congruences
connection: Count solutions of a fixed auxiliary polynomial system modulo powers of a prime and package the counts in a generating function.
why: The local zeta data may reveal stable lifting patterns and singular branches.
first_step: For a small odd prime q, count solutions modulo q and q² in a bounded-dimensional model and separate singular from nonsingular classes.

title: Motivic comparison as a bookkeeping lead
connection: Ask whether several auxiliary varieties share a common geometric decomposition that explains repeated finite-field count formulas.
why: A decomposition could transfer exact counting identities, but any motivic interpretation remains to be checked.
first_step: Compute point counts of two related charts over several small odd fields and seek an explicit cut-and-paste decomposition.

title: Finite-field incidence bounds
connection: Represent a reduced certificate relation as incidences between points and curves over a finite field.
why: Incidence geometry can estimate modular witness abundance, with integer lifting kept as a separate problem.
first_step: For the residual factor equation modulo q, identify the point and curve sets and count incidences directly for small q.

title: Reciprocal additive energy modulo q
connection: Study additive relations among inverses of a structured denominator set in a finite field.
why: This is a direct modular analogue of the reciprocal sum and can identify concentration or additive structure.
first_step: Choose an odd prime q not dividing p; compute the additive energy of inverses of a short nonzero interval in Fq and compare its three-fold sums with 4/p modulo q.

title: Lemma barter across communities
connection: Package one arithmetic lemma and one potentially useful external theorem hypothesis as a two-way translation task for specialists.
why: The exchange can expose a missing hypothesis or a tractable substitute without asking for a verdict on ES.
first_step: Draft separate finite-group and quadratic-form versions of one concrete subproblem, each with a worked example and an explicit desired conclusion.

title: Transfer-matrix / partition-function view of the ES certificate set
connection: The set of e-slices e ≡ −p (mod 4) with −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N} ↔ a 1-D statistical-mechanics chain whose 'spins' are the prime factors of N and whose Boltzmann weight is the indicator of the product landing in −1 mod e.
why: Positivity of a partition function (Z > 0) is exactly ES(p); stat-mech has tools (Lee–Yang zeros, cluster expansions) for proving positivity/non-vanishing that number theory does not routinely use.
first_step: Write Z_p(β) = Σ_e Σ_{ab|N} exp(−β·dist(ab⁻¹, −1 mod e)) and numerically locate its complex-β zeros for p ≤ 10⁵; check whether zeros avoid the real axis uniformly (Lee–Yang-type) and whether the pattern differs at odd squares.

title: Random matrix statistics of the ES solution-count sequence f(p)
connection: f(p) (number of 4/p solutions) ↔ eigenvalue-count statistics; ask whether the normalized fluctuations of f(p)/log²p follow a known RMT law (GUE/GOE/Poisson) or a Selberg-class law.
why: If f(p) behaves like a 'spectral count' of some operator, then a lower bound f(p) ≥ 1 could be a spectral gap statement instead of a sieve statement.
first_step: Compute f(p) for primes up to 10⁷ (repo has data), fit the distribution of f(p)/E[f] and its two-point correlation along primes; compare to Poisson and to divisor-function moments (Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum arcsine law).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Quantum-chaos / Berry–Tabor view of the e-slice as an integrable billiard
connection: The levels x = (quantity with p in it) of an integrable system have Poisson statistics (Berry–Tabor); the ES certificate x values for fixed p might be modelled by a 2-torus billiard's level set.
why: Poisson statistics would make f(p) ~ Poisson(log²p) with P(f=0) = exp(−c log²p), which is the heuristic ES already relies on; a rigorous Berry–Tabor-type theorem for a suitable flow would be a 'new input'.
first_step: Read Marklof's survey on Berry–Tabor for values of quadratic forms; check whether the e-slice set {(a,b): ab | N, ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 mod e} can be stated as values of a binary form at lattice points.

title: Sandpile/abelian-network identity element and divisors of 4Cp+1
connection: Chip-firing on the cycle graph ℤ/e with e ≡ −p mod 4 has a group structure (sandpile group ≅ ℤ/e); the e-slice condition −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹} is membership of −1 in a subset-product set inside this group.
why: Sandpile identities have surprising explicit structure (Levine–Propp); seen in repo as bsA_selling_sandpile but the specific 'subset-product set hits −1' angle may not be.
first_step: git grep sandpile in BRAINSTORM; then check whether the subset-product set {ab⁻¹ : ab | N} mod e is ever a subgroup or a coset (compute for p ≤ 10⁴).

title: Renormalization-group flow on the Mordell residue classes mod 840·k
connection: Mordell's covering by identities reduces hard primes to 6 square classes mod 840; iterating to larger moduli (840·k) is an RG-like coarse-graining; the fixed point structure (what fraction of classes stay hard as modulus grows) is a computable 'critical exponent'.
why: Mordell–Schinzel says squares are never covered, but the *rate* at which non-square hard classes are absorbed by polynomial identities is a measurable quantity; a scaling law might suggest a non-polynomial identity family.
first_step: Using verification-style filters, measure fraction of primes surviving modulus-M filters for M in a geometric sequence; fit decay exponent.

title: Dyson's 'sphere-packing of unit fractions' metaphor: energy minimization over Egyptian fraction triples
connection: Treat (x,y,z) as particles with energy E = |4/n − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z|; ES is 'ground state energy is 0 for every n'. Energy-landscape methods (basin-hopping, simulated annealing) find ground states fast; the landscape's funnel structure might reveal a deterministic descent rule.
why: A deterministic descent that never gets stuck would be a proof; even failing that, the funnel geometry around the global minimum may suggest an invariant.
first_step: Run basin-hopping on E over (x,y,z) ∈ [1, n²]³ for 1000 primes; record the sequence of local minima visited and check whether they correspond to continued-fraction convergents of 4/n.

title: Entropy of the ES solution set as a function of p: 'thermodynamic limit' test
connection: Define S(p) = log f(p). Is S(p) ≈ 2 log log p + c with bounded fluctuations (like an extensive quantity) or heavy-tailed? Thermodynamic self-averaging would give concentration; concentration is the enemy of counterexamples.
why: If S(p) concentrates with sub-Gaussian tails around 2 log log p, counterexamples are 'large deviations' and a large-deviation principle could be a route to an unconditional bound at least for 'typical' primes in explicit sets.
first_step: Use the repo's f(p) data (p ≤ 10⁸) to fit the tails of S(p) − mean; compare with Erdős–Kac-type normal law for ω(4Cp+1).

title: KAM-type persistence: solutions of 4/n persist under small perturbation of n
connection: A solution for n yields solutions for multiples of n; conversely, do solutions 'persist' from n to n+1, n+2 via small rational moves (the way KAM tori persist)? ES across consecutive integers is a 'persistence' problem.
why: Elsholtz–Tao's identities for n ≡ 2,3 mod 4 are such persistence rules; a complete persistence rule along primes ≡ 1 mod 24 would be a proof; partial rules give covering systems (B1 — but we are breadth-first).
first_step: Compute, for consecutive primes p < q ≤ 10⁵, the minimal 'edit distance' between solution sets (e.g. number of solutions for q within Hamming distance 1 in (x,y,z)/scaled coordinates); look for structure.

title: Coupling-from-the-past / exact sampling of ES solutions to detect non-uniformity
connection: Propp–Wilson exact sampling of a uniformly random solution of 4/p; the sampling chain's mixing time as a function of p is a measurable complexity of the solution set.
why: If exact sampling is easy (chain couples fast), solution sets are 'structured'; structure is what a proof can exploit.
first_step: Design a Markov chain on solutions (moves: change one of (c,d,f) parameters in the Type I form) and measure coupling time for p ≤ 10⁵.

title: Hyperbolic lattice-point counting in a 'thin' cone: ES as a Selberg-pretrace positivity
connection: ES's Type II condition ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 is a 'determinant = 1' condition on a 2×2 integer matrix [[f, 2c], [2cd, f′]]... (up to normalization); counting such matrices with congruence constraints is hyperbolic lattice point counting.
why: Lattice-point problems in SL₂(ℤ) have error terms via spectral theory; the campaign's B3 says the main term is only log²p, but spectral *positivity* (not counting) might still apply to a cleverly weighted sum.
first_step: Verify exact matrix form: find integers such that det [[f, α],[β, f′]] = 1 encodes ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 (α β = 4c²dp); then check whether the congruence f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd is a Γ₀/Γ₁-type condition.

title: Ehrenfest-style 'recurrence': ES solutions along the sequence p → p+24k as a Poincaré recurrence
connection: Fix a solution template (c,d,f) and ask for which k it still works for p+24k; the recurrence set is an AP-union (polynomial identity) or empty. The density of 'recurrence times' is a dynamical invariant.
why: Quantifies how much of ES is 'covered by local identities' vs genuinely new at each prime.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴ and each solution, compute the set of k ≤ 10³ for which the same (c,d) with the forced f works for p+24k; histogram.

title: Turbulence-style intermittency statistics for f(p)
connection: Multifractal/intermittent behaviour of f(p) across p (moments ⟨f^q⟩ scaling anomalously) would indicate heavy tails; the campaign only has means and almost-all results.
why: Moment scaling exponents distinguish 'log-normal' from 'Poisson' models of f(p); the lower tail (f = 0) is the whole question.
first_step: Compute ⟨f(p)^q⟩ for q = −2..4 over primes in dyadic ranges up to 10⁸ using repo data; fit scaling exponents.

title: Spectral gap of the 'ES Laplacian' on the forest reformulation
connection: Repo mentions a forest reformulation. Forests have Laplacians; Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem counts spanning forests as determinants. Ask whether f(p) (or an e-slice count) is a determinant/minor of a p-dependent Laplacian.
why: Determinant formulas are exact and sometimes provably nonzero by congruence/sign arguments.
first_step: git grep -il forest -- '*.md' to find the repo's reformulation; test whether the count equals a Laplacian minor for p ≤ 100.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Statistical mechanics of covering systems: 'temperature' at which Mordell-style covers fail
connection: Each polynomial identity covers an AP of primes; covering systems have a Hough-type threshold (minimum modulus bounded). Translate: a complete ES cover by identities with moduli ≤ M is impossible (Mordell–Schinzel), but a cover with density 1 − δ(M) is possible; δ(M) is a 'free energy'.
why: The rate δ(M) → 0 quantifies B1 precisely; a slow decay says identities are not the way, a fast decay says the residual set is tiny and maybe handleable differently.
first_step: Compute δ(M) = density of residues mod M not covered by identities of degree ≤ 2 with parameter modulus ≤ M, for M = 840, 1680, 2520, …; fit.

title: Gravitational lensing time-delay identities and unit fractions
connection: Fermat's principle for multiple images gives sums of reciprocals of distances; integer-distance lensing configurations are an unexplored source of Egyptian fraction identities (pure lead-check).
why: Cheap search; probably nothing.
first_step: Web search 'reciprocal distances integer identities lens equation Egyptian'; drop if nothing.

title: Hydrodynamic limit of Elsholtz–Tao's f(n) along short intervals
connection: Σ_{n∈[N,N+H]} f(n) for H = N^θ: short-interval averages (Matomäki–Radziwiłł technology) of multiplicative-like functions. f is not multiplicative, but its Type I count is a divisor-type sum.
why: Short-interval results for divisor-type functions are strong (every short interval of length N^{0.5+ε} has its expected count); pushing H down to log^A N along primes would be 'almost pointwise'.
first_step: Search 'divisor function short intervals every interval' (Ivić, Matomäki); check what H is attainable for d(n) restricted to residue classes and whether the Type I count fits.

title: Entanglement-entropy-style 'area law' for solution counts across Type I/Type II
connection: f_I(p) and f_II(p) are counted separately; their mutual information (over p) measures how independent the two mechanisms are. If nearly independent, P(f=0) ≈ P(f_I=0)·P(f_II=0), squaring the exponent in the heuristic.
why: A quantitative independence statement (even EVIDENCE) sharpens the target: proving only f_I ≥ 1 or only f_II ≥ 1 may be the better-defined problem.
first_step: From repo data, compute correlation of f_I(p), f_II(p) and of their indicator-of-zero across p ≤ 10⁸; compare conditional distributions.

title: Self-organized criticality: is the distribution of C_min(p) a power law?
connection: If C_min(p) (first winning C) has a power-law tail, the 'rare hard primes' are scale-free and adversarial search at 10¹⁸ would find larger C_min than seen; if exponential, pointwise proofs 'should' exist with C ≤ (log p)^A.
why: Directly calibrates the shape a proof must take (bounded C ⇒ covering, polylog C ⇒ sieve-like).
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁷ and fit tail; check repo (git grep 'C_min\|smallest c' DISPROOF_AVENUES.md STATUS.md).

title: Factoring with hints (Rivest–Shamir, Maurer): ES as 'one divisor with 1/2 of the bits known'
connection: If a divisor f of 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 mod 4C, then its low bits (mod 4C) are known; Maurer/Rivest–Shamir show factoring with half the bits known is polynomial. Conversely the *existence* of such a 'half-known' divisor for some C is ES.
why: The crypto literature's reverse question — for which N do such hint-structured divisors exist for a given hint modulus — may have been studied for key-generation (e.g. 'RSA keys with prescribed residue primes').
first_step: Search 'divisors in a prescribed residue class existence density Lenstra' (Lenstra 1984, 'Divisors in residue classes'): Lenstra bounds the NUMBER of divisors in a class by a constant when M > N^{1/3}; check what this says about ES's counting shape (at most O(1) certificates per large C).

title: Presburger/automatic-sequence test: is the set of (p, C_min(p)) k-automatic in any base?
connection: Automatic sequences and k-regular sequences are decidable by Walnut; if the first winning C (or Type I minimal c) were k-regular in p, Walnut could *prove* ES in that regime. Almost certainly not, but the negative result would be informative: it shows ES is 'non-automatic' which rules out all finite-automaton covering proofs.
why: Cheap and decisive one way or the other; connects to B1 in automaton language.
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁶, test for 2-/3-/10-regularity with a k-kernel rank test (compute subsequences C_min(k^e p + r) and check linear dependence).

title: Kolmogorov complexity of the solution 'script' (c,d,f) across primes
connection: For each p, encode the lexicographically first Type I/II solution as a string; measure compressibility across consecutive primes (gzip of the concatenation, or a learned model's perplexity). Low complexity = hidden rule.
why: Direct test for 'there is a simple hidden rule the campaign has not found'. Cheap.
first_step: Produce the (c,d,f) first-solution sequence for p ≤ 10⁶, compress with xz/zpaq, compare with compressibility of a surrogate random sequence with the same marginals.

title: Symbolic regression on f(p) to find a closed-form main term with explicit arithmetic corrections
connection: Fit f(p) ≈ A log²p + B log p · g(p) + ... where g ranges over arithmetic features (number of prime factors of p−1, p+1, class number h(−p), h(−4p), least QNR, Legendre symbols of small primes).
why: If a class-number or L-value feature explains a large part of the variance, it hints that f(p) is 'really' a class-number-type quantity (which would be an exact-formula route).
first_step: Build a feature table for primes ≤ 10⁶ (h(−4p), h(−p), ω(p±1), (2/p),(3/p),(5/p),(7/p), smallest prime factor of 4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1 …); run PySR/LASSO on f(p)/log²p; report R².

title: Transformer trained on (p → first solution) to test for learnable 'algorithm'
connection: Train a small transformer on digit sequences p ↦ (x,y,z) for p ≤ 10⁶; test extrapolation to larger p. Charton-style experiments show some arithmetic tasks (GCD, modular arithmetic) are learnable with interpretable circuits.
why: If a model generalises beyond training range, mechanistic interpretability might extract an algorithm; if it cannot, that's weak evidence of no simple algorithm.
first_step: Replicate Charton's GCD-transformer setup with ES targets; measure out-of-range accuracy.

title: Hidden-shift/period structure in the e-slice subset-product sets
connection: The set S_N(e) = {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N} is a 'sumset' in log coordinates; Freiman/Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers structure theorems describe sets with small doubling, and the group-theoretic Kneser theorem gives |S + S| bounds. ES needs −1 ∈ S for some e.
why: Additive-combinatorics structure of S_N could show S_N(e) is 'almost a subgroup' for many e — then membership of −1 is a character-sum question.
first_step: Compute |S_N(e)| and |S·S| relative to e for p ≤ 10⁵ and all admissible e ≤ 4p; look for e where S is a near-subgroup.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz for the ES polynomial on a product set
connection: Alon's CN: a polynomial of degree Σ d_i with nonzero coefficient on Π x_i^{d_i} has a non-root on any product set S_1×S_2×S_3 with |S_i| > d_i. ES wants a *root* of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) in a product set — the dual question, but CN-type 'non-vanishing then counting' arguments (e.g. for Cauchy–Davenport) sometimes yield existence of roots of auxiliary polynomials.
why: Listed in the repo's deep-lane catalogue; the free-lane twist: apply CN to an auxiliary polynomial whose non-vanishing implies an ES root (e.g. Π over candidate (x,y) of (something)).
first_step: Try: fix n, consider F(x,y) = Π_{z ∈ Z}(4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx)) over a set Z; CN gives a non-root of F in product sets, i.e. (x,y) such that no z ∈ Z works — the wrong direction. Try instead the polynomial method over F_q with q | some 4Cp+1.

title: Mine the Lean 'Erdős problems' formalisation project for ES-adjacent lemmas
connection: Erdős problems site + Lean formalisation efforts (e.g. Erdős #306 nearly formalised). ES is Erdős problem #… (check the erdosproblems.com number) — see what lemma infrastructure exists for unit-fraction problems there.
why: Infrastructure reuse; cheap.
first_step: Visit https://www.erdosproblems.com and search 'Straus'; check the associated GitHub for Lean files.

title: Knuth–Bendix / term rewriting view of the 'Egyptian fraction identities' and confluence
connection: The family of identities (e.g. 1/n = 1/(n+1) + 1/(n(n+1))) forms a rewriting system on multisets of unit fractions; ES asks whether 4/n rewrites to a 3-element multiset. Confluence/termination theory could classify reachable lengths.
why: Formal rewriting makes 'what can be derived from splitting identities' a decidable question in restricted cases; the known tiny families (Bleicher–Erdős) would fit.
first_step: Define rewriting rules: split 1/a → 1/(a+1) + 1/(a(a+1)), merge 1/a + 1/b → 1/c when possible; compute reachable 3-term representations from the greedy 4-term one for n ≤ 1000.

title: Streaming/sketching: minimal information about p needed to construct a solution
connection: Communication-complexity framing: Alice knows p mod M, Bob knows ⌊p/M⌋; how much communication is needed to agree on an ES solution? If O(1) bits suffice for some M, that's a covering system; if Θ(log p), solutions are 'global'.
why: A clean quantitative version of 'ES is not local' (Mordell–Schinzel says polynomial-local fails; this asks for any protocol).
first_step: Empirically: for M = 840, compute for each residue class r the size of the smallest 'dictionary' of solution templates (c,d) needed to cover all primes ≡ r up to 10⁶; growth with the range.

title: LLL on the 3-variable ES equation directly: find small solutions to 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) = 0 via Coppersmith bivariate
connection: After fixing x (≈ n/4 + small), the equation in (y,z) is a bivariate integer polynomial of bidegree (1,1): (4x − n)yz − nx(y+z) = 0 ⇒ ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = n²x². So solutions are divisor pairs of n²x² in classes — Coppersmith's bivariate method finds small roots.
why: The factorisation ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = n²x² is the classical two-term reduction; the 'small root' regime y,z ≤ n^{1+ε} may be exactly where solutions live. Quantify.
first_step: Check numerically: for p ≤ 10⁶, what is min over solutions of max(y,z)/p? Does a solution with max ≤ p^{3/2} always exist? (Relates to known bounds on denominators.)

title: Constraint-propagation / arc-consistency on the (c,d,f) space to prove 'no solution' is contradictory
connection: CSP solvers find contradictions by propagating constraints; for a *symbolic* p (represented by its residues mod many small moduli), propagation might derive that 'no solution for any C ≤ K' contradicts p being prime ≡ 1 mod 24 for some K.
why: This is the covering-system search re-done with a general-purpose propagator that can also use quadratic-residuosity constraints (not just congruences) — which Mordell–Schinzel does not forbid.
first_step: Compute, for each q ≤ 200, the allowed residues of p mod q given all certificates with modulus q; multiply densities.

title: Automated theorem proving on the 'two-term' lemma with a free parameter: Vampire/E on the divisor form
