connection: First-order provers can sometimes prove number-theoretic lemmas given axioms about divisibility; the lemma 'if p ≡ 1 mod 24 and p < 2^k then ∃C ≤ K ...' is a bounded statement they might handle for small k.
why: Low chance, but the prover's search traces for small k might reveal which lemmas are reused — a proof-skeleton extraction.
first_step: Encode the divisor form in TPTP with Peano arithmetic axioms + bounded quantifiers; try Vampire for k ≤ 8.

title: Union-find / disjoint-set structure of 'solution sharing' between different primes
connection: Two primes share a template if the same (c,d) with the forced f gives solutions for both. Build the graph on primes ≤ X with edges = shared template; connected components and their growth describe how 'global' the solution structure is.
why: Giant-component formation would indicate a Markoff-like 'strong approximation' phenomenon; many tiny components would indicate per-prime independence.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, list templates (c,d) of all solutions, build the bipartite prime–template graph, compute component structure.

title: Quantum annealing formulation of ES as QUBO — purely to inspect the energy landscape
connection: Encode the bit-blasted equation as a QUBO; the spectrum of the Ising Hamiltonian (gap between ground state and first excited) across p measures 'hardness'; a gap that scales mildly suggests structure.
why: Cheap curiosity test; may reveal p-dependence of the landscape.
first_step: Build QUBO for p ≤ 200 via standard multiplication gadgets; exact-diagonalise small instances; plot gap vs p.

title: Model-checking a finite abstraction: ES for p 'with all small primes' residues fixed' as a finite transition system
connection: Abstract p by its residues mod all primes ≤ B and by its Legendre symbols; a finite-state system over these abstractions can be model-checked for the property 'some C ≤ K yields a divisor in class'. Counterexample traces are candidate hard residue profiles.
why: Finds the exact abstract profile of a potential counterexample; such profiles could then be hunted at 10¹⁸ (adversarial search guidance).
first_step: Enumerate profiles of p mod 840 and Legendre symbols (q/p) for q ≤ 31; for each profile, compute the empirical fraction of primes with C_min ≤ 10; find worst profiles.

title: Database cross-reference: OEIS sequences around f(n), C_min, and Egyptian-fraction lengths
connection: OEIS has A073101 (number of solutions of 4/n), A192787, etc. Looking at the 'sequences that reference these' and their formulas/comments may reveal a connection the campaign missed.
why: Cheap and occasionally very fruitful.
first_step: Fetch OEIS A073101, A192787, A192788, A192789 and all sequences citing 'Erdős–Straus'; read comments and formulas; list any with unexpected cross-references (e.g. to class numbers, Bernoulli, Markoff).

title: Is C_min(p) actually bounded? (sanity question separating covering from identities)
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids *polynomial* identities on square classes but does not forbid 'for every prime p ≡ 1 mod 24 some C ≤ 10⁶ works'. If C_min is empirically bounded (e.g. ≤ 1000 up to 10¹⁸) that is a striking structural fact; if it grows like log p, there is no finite cover at all.
why: This is the single most basic calibration of the 'covering' approach and the question is sharp and cheap.
first_step: git grep -il 'C_min\|bounded C\|smallest C' -- '*.md'; if absent, compute max_{p ≤ 10⁸} C_min(p) with C in Type II form and in e-slice form.

title: Bit-level pattern mining on winning C in binary (are winning C's 'smooth'? 'prime'? 'powers of 2'?)
connection: The multiplicative structure of winning C matters (4C is the modulus); test whether winning C are biased toward smooth numbers, primes, or specific residue classes mod 3, 5, 7.
why: A bias (e.g. winning C is often a multiple of 3 for p ≡ 1 mod 3) is a candidate identity direction; cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ collect all winning C ≤ 1000; compare their distribution of ω(C), smoothness, C mod 12 against the uniform baseline.

title: Reed–Solomon-type interpolation: can the map p ↦ (x,y,z) be interpolated by a low-degree polynomial over a finite field F_q?
connection: Over F_q (q a prime of size ~ range), the 'first solution' map restricted to primes is a function; its degree as a polynomial over F_q (via interpolation) compared to the number of points measures 'algebraicity'.
why: If the map had degree far below the number of points for structured subsets (e.g. primes in a fixed class mod M), those subsets are covered by an algebraic rule — a new identity family.
first_step: Take primes ≡ 1 mod 840 up to 10⁵, interpolate C_min(p) mod q as a polynomial in p mod q, check the degree vs number of points; expect full degree (no structure) — a negative result calibrates B1.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sylvester's 1880 sequence and Egyptian fraction 'denominator growth': why 3-term is the hard case
connection: Sylvester's greedy gives 4/n in ≤ 4 terms always; the gap between 4 (easy, greedy) and 3 (open) is the whole conjecture. Historically, similar 'one fewer term' gaps were closed by divisor-structure lemmas (e.g. Nagell's results on 2/n, 3/n).
why: Revisit how the k = 2 and numerator 2, 3 cases were resolved (they are theorems); the proof pattern for 3/n (always ≤ 2 terms? no: 3/n = 2 terms iff n has a divisor ≡ 2 mod 3; else 3 terms) suggests that ES is the first case where the 'iff' divisor criterion is not local — which is exactly Mordell–Schinzel. Document the exact historical sequence of results.
first_step: Search and read: Nagell 1922/23 on a/n = 1/x + 1/y; Mordell's chapter 30; list which cases (numerator a, k terms) are theorems and by what method.

title: Rosati 1954 / Bernstein 1962 / Webb 1970 / Vaughan 1970: trace the lineage of exceptional-set bounds for the 'thin' idea that was dropped
connection: The exceptional-set line (Webb, Vaughan, Elsholtz–Tao, Elsholtz–Planitzer) improved E(N) by better sieving; each paper's 'what we could not do' section records the pointwise obstruction in the author's words.
why: Someone in 1970 may have had an idea for pointwise bounds that was abandoned for being 'too hard', not wrong.
first_step: Read Vaughan 1970 Mathematika §4 (final remarks) and Webb 1970 Proc. AMS; note any conditional or partial pointwise statement.

title: Ask Christian Elsholtz / Stefan Planitzer directly what they consider the current frontier
connection: People item: the authors of the almost-all lower bound f(n) ≥ (log n)^{log 6 + o(1)} are the closest active experts; a short email with the campaign's barrier map attached could elicit either a known dead-end or a tip.
why: Human expert input is cheap relative to the search cost; the campaign's FRONTIER.md is a ready-made attachment.
first_step: Draft a 10-line email summarising the single-integer lower tail (FRONTIER §2) and asking (i) is this reduction known, (ii) any route they abandoned; send.

title: Contact Bright and Loughran about an integral-Brauer–Manin *refinement* at the ES fibre
connection: BL showed no BM obstruction; the campaign found the Brauer class dies at the ES fibre k = 0. Ask them whether any finer invariant (descent obstruction, étale-Brauer, or 'integral points on log K3 / cubic surfaces with 3 A₁ singularities') applies to U_n.
why: The surface people know what finer obstructions exist; cheap to ask.
first_step: Email summarising Z52_BANKED 'why the obvious Brauer class dies at k = 0'; ask about étale-Brauer and about Harpaz–Wittenberg fibration method for integral points.

title: Conference lens: which 2026–27 meetings have unit fractions / Egyptian fractions sessions (Integers, CANT, ELAZ)?
connection: CANT (Combinatorial and Additive Number Theory, NYC), the INTEGERS conference, and ELAZ host unit-fraction talks regularly; abstracts there may contain unpublished partial results.
why: Cheap scan.
first_step: Fetch the abstracts of CANT 2024–2026 and INTEGERS 2025; grep for 'unit fraction', 'Egyptian', 'Straus'.

title: Geometry of numbers: Minkowski's theorem on the 'Type II' lattice to force a divisor pair
connection: Type II: ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd. For fixed (c,d), the set {(f, f′)} is a congruence sublattice; Minkowski's theorem guarantees a nonzero lattice point in any convex body of volume 2^k det Λ; the hyperbola ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 is not convex, but regions between hyperbolas are.
why: Pigeonhole/Minkowski is the classic 'existence for every n' tool (two-squares theorem); it fails here because the target is a single hyperbola, but a 'union over (c,d)' body might have enough volume. Quantify.
first_step: For fixed p, compute the total 'volume' Σ_{(c,d) ≤ X} (area of the region 4c²dp < ff′ < 4c²dp + 2 inside the congruence conditions) vs the lattice determinant; see at which X Minkowski-type volume exceeds the threshold (expect: never by a polylog factor — document the gap).

title: Gauss composition / Bhargava cubes for the Type II identity ff′ − 4c²dp = 1
connection: ff′ − (2c)²dp = 1 is a 'norm form equals 1' type equation: ff′ − D·1 = 1 with D = 4c²dp; i.e. the matrix [[f, 2c√d],[2c√d·p... ]] — more precisely it says f·f′ ≡ 1 mod 4c²dp. Bhargava's parametrisation of ideal classes by 2×2×2 cubes might organise the triples (f, f′, 4c²d) with product structure.
why: Composition laws give group structure on solution sets of quadratic-type equations; a group structure on ES certificates for fixed p would be a huge structural input (cf. Markoff).
first_step: Check whether the set of Type II certificates for fixed p carries a natural binary operation (e.g. via the ideal (f, p + 2c√−d) composition); test on p = 1009: list certificates and look for closure.

title: Explicit infinite family inside the square classes via Bateman–Horn-free arguments: p with 4p+1 having a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4
connection: 4p + 1 (C = 1) has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4 iff 4p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4 (since 4p+1 ≡ 1 mod 4, it has an even number of such factors, so ≥ 2 if any; any prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4 is itself a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4). So C = 1 wins iff 4p + 1 is not a product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4 — i.e. iff 4p+1 is not a sum of two squares in the 'all factors 1 mod 4' sense.
why: This is a clean, non-polynomial criterion: ES(p) holds whenever 4p+1 is not entirely composed of primes ≡ 1 mod 4. The complementary set (4p+1 all of whose prime factors are ≡ 1 mod 4) has density → 0 (Landau–Ramanujan-type, ~ 1/√log p). Likewise C = 2: 8p+1 not all factors ≡ 1 mod 8 ... each C removes a 1/√log-density set; the intersection is the real target. Document this chain explicitly as the cleanest statement of 'why the heuristic count is log²p but no proof'.
first_step: Verify the claim (C = 1 Type II wins iff 4p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4) against the repo's divisor form; compute the density of primes p ≤ 10⁷ with 4p+1 having only factors ≡ 1 mod 4; then for C=1..K the joint density.

title: Kummer/Galois reformulation: ES ⟸ ∃C: some prime factor q of 4Cp+1 has Frobenius outside a fixed subgroup of Gal(ℚ(ζ_{4C})/ℚ)
connection: If the subgroup criterion holds, then C wins whenever some prime q | 4Cp+1 has q mod 4C ∉ H for every −1-free subgroup H... Simplest: q ≡ −1 mod 4C directly (then q itself is the divisor). So a sufficient condition: 4Cp+1 has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C. Over C, this is 'the polynomial values 4Cp+1 (C varying, p fixed) have a prime factor in the class −1' — a statement about prime divisors of a linear polynomial in C at a fixed 'twist' p.
why: Prime divisors of values of linear forms in residue classes is a well-studied topic (e.g. Bang–Zsigmondy for a^n − 1, and 'prime factors of n! ± 1' type results); the fixed-p twist is unusual but concrete.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁶ the smallest C such that 4Cp+1 has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C (the 'prime-divisor' certificate); compare to C_min; search 'prime divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C'.

title: Monks–Moore style 'hypergraph' of Egyptian-fraction decompositions and Hall's marriage theorem
connection: Hall's theorem gives existence of systems of distinct representatives from counting conditions; for the family of sets S_C = {divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C}, ES needs ONE non-empty set, not an SDR — a much weaker requirement. But Hall-type 'defect' versions (König) give lower bounds on how many sets are non-empty from global counts.
why: Trivial direction: Σ_C |S_C| ≥ 1 ⟹ some S_C ≠ ∅; the campaign's M_BM is exactly the average of Σ_C |S_C| over p. The marriage-theorem lens asks instead for *structural* reasons (a bipartite graph between C's and divisor classes with a perfect matching for all p) — equivalent to a 'universal' witness assignment.
first_step: Note that it reduces to the counting statement; record as a reminder that 'structure beyond counting' is what's needed; cheap to drop.

title: Lines on the ES cubic surface: do the lines correspond to the known polynomial identities?
connection: Polynomial identities (Mordell families) are rational curves on U_n parametrised by n; lines on the cubic surface are the simplest rational curves. Conjecture: each degree-1 identity in n is a line, and Mordell–Schinzel's non-existence on square classes is a statement that no line defined over the function field ℚ(n) meets the integral locus there.
why: Translates the 'identities' question into the (finite!) geometry of 27 lines; new identities might be found among non-obvious lines or conics (degree-2 rational curves).
first_step: Compute the lines on 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) over ℚ(n) in Sage/Magma; match with the known identity list.

title: Jacobsthal function analogue: longest run of C with 4Cp+1 'bad'
connection: The Jacobsthal function j(m) is the longest gap between integers coprime to m; here, define J(p) = C_min(p) − 1 = the longest initial run of bad C. Jacobsthal-type upper bounds (Iwaniec: j(m) ≪ log²m) are *pointwise*, proved by sieve.
why: If 'bad C' could be modelled as 'C hitting a residue class mod each small prime' (like non-coprimality), Iwaniec's method would bound C_min(p) ≪ log²p pointwise — a proof! The model is wrong (badness is not a congruence condition in C) but the degree of mismatch is the question.
first_step: Test empirically whether badness of C is 'locally determined': for fixed p, is the set of bad C periodic mod small moduli? (Compute correlation of bad(C) with C mod q.)

title: Choose C = (p−1)/4 or C = (p+3)/4 etc.: 'self-referential' C that make 4Cp+1 factor algebraically
connection: If C is a polynomial in p, 4Cp + 1 is a polynomial in p which may factor: e.g. C = p gives 4p² + 1 (irreducible); C = (p² − 1)/4 ... gives p³ − p + 1; C = 2p+1... Algebraic factorisations give guaranteed divisors; the residue condition then is a polynomial congruence — i.e. this IS the polynomial-identity route (B1), but with quadratic/cubic C. Mordell–Schinzel covers all polynomial C? It covers polynomial x,y,z; polynomial C ⟹ polynomial (x,y,z). So yes.
why: Still worth listing: identities with C = polynomial of degree ≥ 3 are not in Mordell's table, and the theorem forbids them only on square classes — maybe they cover *more* of the non-square classes (reducing the residual set to exactly the squares mod a larger modulus?).
first_step: Enumerate C = aP(p) for small polynomials P of degree ≤ 3, factor 4Cp+1 symbolically, check which residue classes mod 840·k get covered.

title: Egyptian fraction 'Engel expansion' and 'Pierce expansion' of 4/p: alternative canonical expansions with ≤ 3 terms?
connection: Engel expansion writes x = 1/a₁ + 1/(a₁a₂) + 1/(a₁a₂a₃) + …; Pierce alternates signs. For 4/p, the Engel expansion's length and the possibility of truncation/modification to 3 unit fractions is an unexplored canonical form.
why: Canonical expansions with algebraic structure (Engel: a_{k+1} determined by a_k) might make 'length 3' a tractable condition like ES₅'s CF length.
first_step: Compute Engel expansions of 4/p for p ≤ 10⁴; count lengths; check whether a length-3 Engel expansion exists for all p (unlikely) or whether the Engel denominators relate to Type I/II parameters.

title: Music/tilings: 4/p as a rhythm — Euclidean rhythms and unit-fraction tilings of the circle
connection: Tiling a circle of circumference 4 by three arcs of lengths p/x, p/y, p/z... i.e. 4 = p/x + p/y + p/z — a tiling of [0,4] by rational lengths with a common 'p' numerator. Euclidean rhythms (Toussaint) relate to Bjorklund's algorithm = Euclid's algorithm = continued fractions.
why: Recreational lens that lands on continued fractions again; perhaps a rhythmic 'evenness' measure corresponds to CF length ≤ 3.
first_step: Just note the reformulation; compute whether the Bjorklund rhythm E(4, p) decomposes into 3 'regular' sub-rhythms iff ES solution exists with specific structure — 15 minutes.

title: The word form p = tuv − u − v with t ∈ 4ℤ: 'every prime is tuv − u − v with 4 | t' as a multiplicative-additive representation problem
connection: p + u + v = tuv with t = 4C ⟺ 4Cp + 1 = (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1): so 'some 4Cp+1 factors as a product of two numbers ≡ −1 mod 4C' is a SUFFICIENT condition for ES (it is the c = 1 sub-case of Type II; it gives x = Cuv, y = pCv, z = pCu). Full Type II is ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 with the weaker congruence f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd). Sanity computation (scripts/z52b_free_fable_sanity.py): the C-form is strictly weaker — p = 409, 577, 5569, 9601 have no C-form certificate with C < 1500 although they have Type II certificates (409: c=2, d=1, f=7, f′=935).
why: The C-form is the cleanest 'tied-modulus' statement (N = 4Cp+1, modulus 4C | N − 1) and covers all but a thin set of primes; the exceptions are themselves a lead (what distinguishes 409, 577, 5569, 9601?). 5569 ≡ 529 and 9601 ≡ 361 (mod 840) are Mordell-hard.
first_step: Extend the census: primes p ≤ 10⁶ with no C-form certificate for C ≤ 10⁴; density (→ 0? constant?); Legendre profiles of the exceptions; then the general question G(m,k): does mk+1 have a divisor ≡ −1 mod m.

title: Model theory: is ES expressible in a decidable theory after fixing the structure of (ℕ, +, ·|_{divisors of 4Cp+1})?
connection: Full arithmetic is undecidable, but fragments like Presburger + 'is a power of 2' (Büchi) or Skolem arithmetic (ℕ, ·) are decidable. ES mixes + and · minimally: 4Cp + 1 = ab, a ≡ b ≡ −1 (4C). Determine the weakest theory in which ES is expressible and whether any known decidability/undecidability result applies to its ∀∃ fragment.
why: Calibration: if ES lies in a decidable fragment, there's an algorithm to decide it (in principle); more realistically it identifies ES's logical complexity relative to e.g. Zaremba (also ∀∃ with bounded searches).
first_step: Write ES in the language (ℕ, +, ·, <) and try to reduce the number of multiplications; note that 'a ≡ −1 mod 4C' and 'ab = 4Cp+1' need two products with shared variables; check against the known decidable fragments (e.g. 'one multiplication' theories are already undecidable? — Robinson).

title: Closure of winning C under multiplication: if 4Cp+1 = ab with a,b ≡ −1 mod 4C, what about C' = Ck?
connection: 4Ckp + 1 — relation to ab: 4Ckp + 1 = k(ab − 1) + 1 = kab − k + 1. No obvious divisor. But via the (x,y,z) form: a solution for p from C gives (x,y,z); scaling doesn't change C. So no direct closure; but the e-slice form (e ≡ −p mod 4) might have closure: if e works, does e·k work? Check.
why: Any closure property on the certificate set would be a group-like structure (cf. Markoff orbits); worth 10 minutes of computation.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, list winning e-slices and winning C; test closure under multiplication by small k and under 'e ↦ 4N − e'-type involutions.

title: Matroids / linear algebra over F₂: the 'sign vectors' of divisors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^×/squares
connection: (ℤ/4C)^× modulo squares is an F₂-vector space; prime factors of 4Cp+1 give vectors; −1 is a target vector; subset-product hits −1 in the quotient iff −1 ∈ span (a linear algebra question!). The full condition (−1 as a subset product, not mod squares) is harder, but the F₂-relaxation is linear and decidable by rank.
why: The F₂-relaxation is a necessary condition for a win that is *linear* — and its failure probability is exactly 2^{−(rank deficiency)}; it isolates the 'genus-like' part (characters of order 2) from the rest. Repo's 'genus layer is pointwise free' lemma may be this.
first_step: git grep -il 'genus layer' -- '*.md' and compare; then compute for p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 100: does the F₂-relaxation hold (−1 ∈ span of factor vectors mod squares) and how often does the full condition fail when the relaxation holds?
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Representation theory: the count of divisors in class −1 mod 4C is a trace of a permutation representation
connection: #{d | N : d ≡ r mod m} = (1/φ(m)) Σ_χ χ̄(r) Σ_{d|N} χ(d); the inner sum is a 'twisted divisor function' σ₀(N, χ) which is the Fourier coefficient of an Eisenstein series E(χ, χ̄). Summing over C (with N = 4Cp+1, m = 4C) is summing coefficients of a *varying-level* Eisenstein family at the arguments 4Cp+1 — a 'horizontal' sum across levels.
why: Varying-level sums of Eisenstein coefficients have appeared in the theory of 'moments of L-functions over a family of levels' (e.g. Conrey–Iwaniec); positivity results for such family sums exist on average over the argument but here the argument is tied to the level.
first_step: Write Σ_{C≤X} σ₀(4Cp+1; χ_C-component) explicitly; look for a Petersson/Kuznetsov-type formula that handles 'argument = 4Cp+1 tied to level 4C'; search 'Eisenstein series coefficients at n ≡ 1 mod level'.

title: Type I with d = 1 only: the 'sum of two squares' subfamily of ES
connection: Setting d = 1 in Type I gives p² + (2c)² = f·g with f ≡ −p (mod 4c). Since p ≡ 1 mod 4, p = u² + v² (Fermat); p² + 4c² = (p + 2ci)(p − 2ci) in ℤ[i] — f corresponds to an ideal divisor of (p + 2ci). The Gaussian integer structure is fully explicit: f = N(α) for α | p + 2ci. The congruence f ≡ −p mod 4c is then a condition on α mod 4c in ℤ[i].
why: This subfamily lives entirely in ℤ[i], where everything is computable via Gaussian factorisation; a complete analysis (which p have a d=1 Type I solution? density? structure of failures?) is a clean sub-problem; failures are the input to the general problem.
first_step: Compute the set of p ≤ 10⁷ with no d=1 Type I solution for c ≤ 10⁴; density, structure (do they correlate with p's Gaussian factorisation u + vi?).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Mock modular forms / Zagier's weight-3/2 Eisenstein series for class-number generating functions evaluated at the ES data
connection: The generating function Σ H(n)q^n is a mock modular form (Zagier). The ES Type I count relates to H(p² + 4c²d) (previous item). Mock modularity gives asymptotics with *explicit* error terms for sums of H over quadratic sequences (via holomorphic projection / shadow).
why: Explicit error terms for 'class numbers along quadratic sequences p² + 4c²d in c' might, for a single p, give a positive main term exceeding the error — a pointwise statement! The size: main term ≍ X·√(p)... vs ES's count log²p — the class-number sum counts ALL divisors, not the residue-class-constrained ones; the constraint costs 1/φ(4cd), summing to ≈ log X. So the error term must be < log X — hopeless unless the error is tiny. Record the calculation.
first_step: Compute Σ_{c ≤ X} H(p² + 4c²) for p = 10⁶+3 and compare with main term; then the constrained count; tabulate the ratio.

title: Noncommutative: quaternion orders of discriminant tied to p — the repo's quaternion reformulation and the 'Eichler mass formula' as a positive main term
connection: Repo lists quaternion orders. Eichler's mass formula gives Σ 1/|O_i^×| = explicit (positive) sum over classes; representation numbers of orders are theta-series coefficients. If ES certificates are 'optimal embeddings' of a quadratic order into a quaternion order (as in Eichler's embedding theory), the count is a product of local embedding numbers × class number — exactly a formula with a positive main term.
why: Optimal-embedding counts are *exact* (Eichler) when summed over the genus; the pointwise count for one maximal order has a spectral error (Gross–Zagier-type). Positivity for one order at level p... the 'one order' is the issue (B2 again), but the embedding-number formula may reveal which local conditions matter.
first_step: git grep -il quaternion -- '*.md' and read the repo's reformulation; then check whether Type I/II certificates are optimal embeddings of ℤ[√−d]-type orders into a definite quaternion order of discriminant related to p or 4C.

title: Shifted divisor problem at fixed shift p: Σ_{C ≤ X} τ(4Cp+1) with X ≪ p^ε — the 'short range' regime
connection: Classical: Σ_{n ≤ X} τ(an + b) ~ (main) for X ≫ a^{1+ε} or so; ES needs C only up to polylog(p) ideally (so X ≪ a^ε, far below the classical range). In the short range, the sum is dominated by the structure of the specific p — i.e. exactly the pointwise regime. Known results: for X ≥ a^{1/2+ε}? (Friedlander–Iwaniec, divisor function in APs to large moduli; Fouvry). For X < a^{1/2} essentially nothing is known pointwise.
why: Pins down the exact analytic barrier: ES(p) with C ≤ p^θ requires understanding τ(4Cp+1)-type sums with C ≤ p^θ; θ < 1/2 is beyond current technology for the *unrestricted* divisor sum, let alone the class-restricted one. But θ ≥ 1 (C up to p) IS within technology for the unrestricted sum — so 'ES with C ≤ p' might be attackable via large-modulus divisor results if the class restriction can be handled by characters (log-many characters…).
first_step: Read Fouvry–Iwaniec / Friedlander–Iwaniec on τ in APs to moduli q ≤ x^{2/3}; map to Σ_{C ≤ X} τ(4Cp + 1) with p as the 'modulus' and X as the range: need X ≥ p^{3/2}? Record the exact requirement.

title: Erdős–Rényi random graph threshold: at what 'connectivity' does the prime–template bipartite graph lose isolated vertices?
connection: An isolated prime (no template among those used by primes ≤ X) is a 'locally unique' solver; the growth of the number of isolated primes vs X measures the entropy of the solution structure.
why: If isolated primes vanish (every prime shares a template with another), the templates form a 'cover with reuse', a weak form of structure.
first_step: Build the bipartite graph (primes ≤ 10⁶, templates = (C, a mod 4C) or (c,d)); count isolated vertices as a function of X.

title: Semigroup orbit reformulation: Type II certificates as products of two 'elementary' matrices in a congruence semigroup
connection: 4Cp + 1 = (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1). Consider matrices M_C(u) = [[4Cu − 1, ?],[?, ?]] in SL₂? E.g. the matrix [[4Cu−1, −u],[−4C·?..]] — find a representation where the product M_C(u)·M_C(v) has p as an entry. Try: A_u = [[1, u],[0, 1]]·[[1, 0],[−4C, 1]]·... Standard: the continued fraction [0; 4C, u, ...]? Let's just make it an experiment.
why: If Type II certificates are entries of products in a 2-generator semigroup (parametrised by C), then 'p appears as an entry' is a thin-orbit problem with the level 4C — same shape as Zaremba (where the semigroup is fixed and q is the entry). The novelty: the semigroup depends on C, but p must appear for SOME C — a union over C of thin orbits.
first_step: Find matrices in SL₂(ℤ) whose (1,1)-entry of a length-2 product is (4Cu−1)(4Cv−1) − 1)/(4C) = p for integers u,v (e.g. [[4Cu−1, u],[4C·?, ?]] with det 1 forces entries); if found, compare with the ES₅ word of length 3.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES for primes in a fixed Chebotarev class of a big compositum: a 'conditional on splitting' infinite family
connection: Fix the splitting of p in K = ℚ(i, √2, √3, √5, √7, …) (finitely many Legendre symbols); for a given profile, does a *fixed* Type I/II template (with d, c chosen by the profile) always work? That would be an identity depending on Legendre symbols — not polynomial, so not excluded by Mordell–Schinzel.
why: Legendre-symbol-dependent identities are a natural, unexplored (?) class strictly larger than polynomial identities. Even partial coverage (e.g. all profiles except those where p is a square mod all small primes — which includes squares!) would be a beautiful structural statement matching T1.
first_step: For primes ≤ 10⁷ with profile (p mod 840, (p/q) for q ≤ 31), check whether the first winning template (C, a mod 4C) is constant on the profile class; count profile classes with a constant template.

title: Composite n and the 'certificate from a factor' loophole: ES(n) for n = pq follows from ES(p); but are there composites with NO Type I/II solution other than squares and the sporadics?
connection: The U(n) list (105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145) are exactly such sporadics (for the U(n) statement). Understanding WHY 105 = 3·5·7 fails the direct Type I/II test while 3, 5, 7 each succeed — a 'non-transfer' of certificates to products — is a small concrete structure question.
why: Sporadics are the fingerprints of the mechanism; their factorisations (105 = 3·5·7; 2961 = 3²·7·47; 3985 = 5·797; 25305 = 3·5·7·241; 111969 = 3·37·1009? check; 978145 = 5·...?) might share a pattern (many small primes ≡ 3 mod 4? products of a square and something?).
first_step: Factor all six sporadics; compute their Legendre profiles; list which small C fail and why (subgroup type or few factors); see if a common structural reason emerges.

title: Is f_II(n) (or any ES count) a *multiplicative* or 'quasi-multiplicative' function?
connection: Egyptian-fraction counts are not multiplicative (solutions for pq are not products of solutions for p and q), but there may be a sub-count (e.g. 'primitive' Type II certificates, coprimality-restricted) that is multiplicative or satisfies a Hecke-type relation f(pq) = f(p)f(q) + correction.
why: Multiplicativity would make f a Dirichlet-series coefficient with an Euler product — immediate structure; Hecke-type relations would be modular-form-like.
first_step: Compute f_II(n) for n ≤ 10⁴ and test f(mn) vs f(m)f(n) for coprime m,n; look for a correction term pattern.

title: Gate G4 quantified: 'subgroup generated by factors contains −1' vs 'subset product hits −1' disagree in ~20% of (p, C) pairs
connection: Sanity computation: for primes p < 3000 (p ≡ 1 mod 4) and C < 40, the subgroup generated by the prime factors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^× contains −1 but no subset product (with multiplicities) equals −1 in 1695 of 8229 cases (~21%). So the 'Galois/subgroup' relaxation is far from tight: multiplicity (few factors) matters a lot.
why: Quantifies the repo's gate G4 ('class, not parity'): any proof via 'some prime factor lands outside a subgroup' loses ~20% of the certificates per C, which matters when the expected count per C is < 1.
first_step: Break down the 21% by ω(4Cp+1) (expect: mostly ω ≤ 2); check whether for ω ≥ 4 the two notions agree ≥ 95%; if so, 'C with 4Cp+1 having ≥ 4 prime factors' is a regime where the Galois relaxation is essentially exact.

title: Meta: maintain a single 'dictionary of forms' table (Type I, Type II, C-form, e-slice, word, ES₅, U_n, quaternion) with exact equivalence scopes
connection: This lane found that one popular form (C-form) is strictly weaker than Type II; the repo has ≥ 8 reformulations and their mutual implications are scattered. A one-page table 'form A ⟹ form B (scope, proof pointer, counterexample if not ⟺)' prevents wasted lanes.
why: Cheap, high-leverage: half the items in any breadth lane depend on which form they silently assume.
first_step: Create REFORMULATIONS.md with a matrix of implications among the 8 forms, each entry with a pointer or a small counterexample (e.g. 409 for C-form vs Type II).

title: Meta: switch the primary object from 'f(p) ≥ 1' to 'the failure set F_K = {p : no certificate with parameters ≤ K}' and study F_K as K grows
connection: F_K is a well-defined, computable set for each K; ES says ∩_K F_K ∩ primes = ∅. The sequence F_K (density, structure, smallest elements, Legendre profiles) is a richer object than f(p) and directly mirrors 'squares + sporadic' phenomena (F_∞ ⊇ odd squares).
why: Reframing from 'count' to 'nested exceptional sets' matches how Rickards–Stange and HKRS state results and may expose structure (e.g. F_K is eventually a union of thin sets).
first_step: Compute F_K for K = 1..50 (parameter = c²d or C) on n ≤ 10⁶ (all n); plot density vs K; list the structure of F_50.

title: Meta: adopt 'squares + sporadic' as the official conjecture shape for Type II alone and for Type I alone
connection: Instead of ES itself, state: 'f_II(n) = 0 iff n is an odd square or n ∈ S_II (finite)'; similarly Type I. These are stronger, type-separated conjectures with their own sporadic lists, cheaper to test, and their mechanism (reciprocity obstruction only at squares) is more precisely what HKRS/RS handle.
why: Separating types might reveal that one type has a *provable* 'squares + sporadic' structure (e.g. Type I via class-group/ternary-form theory, Duke–Schulze-Pillot style) even if the other doesn't.
first_step: Compute S_I and S_II (n ≤ 10⁷, all n) and see if they stabilise; then check Type I's structure against representation-by-ternary-forms theorems.

title: Experimental: 'd = 1 ∪ d = 2 ∪ d = 3' — do three fixed imaginary quadratic fields already certify all primes ≤ 10⁸ (Type I)?
connection: If yes, ES on that range follows from three class-group-structured problems; the question 'is there a p with no Type I solution for d ≤ 3' becomes the sharpened target with full algebraic structure (ℤ[i], ℤ[√−2], ℤ[ω]).
why: Fixed-field problems admit Chebotarev/ray-class analysis; a fixed finite set of fields with 'all p' coverage would be a new, cleaner conjecture.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁷ whether a Type I certificate with d ∈ {1,2,3} exists (c unbounded up to p); list failures and their count growth.

title: Composite exceptions to the C-form: which non-square n < 10⁵ have no 4Cn+1 = ab, a ≡ b ≡ −1 (4C)?
connection: The C-form does not use primality, so it's a statement about all n. Odd squares fail (T1). Which other n fail? Among primes 409, 577, 5569, 9601 (C < 1500). Composite failures would show whether the C-form exceptional set is 'squares + sporadic' or has infinite non-square families.
why: Cheap census that characterises a natural sub-conjecture; the structure of composite exceptions (do they factor as square × something? products of C-form exceptions?) is informative.
first_step: Compute for all n ≤ 10⁵ (n ≡ 1 mod 4; also check n ≡ 3 mod 4 which has a different parity structure) whether a C-form certificate exists with C ≤ 2000; list non-square failures; factor them.

title: Recreational: the 'Egyptian fraction game' (players alternately subtract unit fractions from 4/n; last mover wins) — its P-positions
connection: Combinatorial game whose P-positions are governed by the two-term representability of remainders; ES is 'the first player can win in 3 moves'. Game-theoretic analysis (Sprague–Grundy) of unit-fraction subtraction games may have been studied.
why: Recreational lens; may surface a known structural result on unit-fraction subtraction.
first_step: Define game: position r (rational), move: subtract 1/x with r − 1/x ≥ 0; player who reaches 0 at move ≤ 3 wins. Compute outcomes for 4/p.

title: Mathematical-olympiad lens: known olympiad problems 'show 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n ≡ r mod m' and their solutions as identity sources
connection: Many olympiad/Putnam problems ask for specific residue classes (e.g. n ≡ 2 mod 3, n ≡ 3 mod 4); their solutions are identities already in Mordell's list, but the *techniques* (e.g. choosing x = (n+1)/2…) occasionally differ.
why: Cheap; the AoPS archive is searchable.
first_step: Search AoPS for 'Erdős–Straus' and '4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z'; collect all identities; diff against the repo census.

title: Analogy: Goldbach's 'every even n is p + q' vs ES's 'every p has a certificate' — the Hardy–Littlewood singular series as the ES 'local factor' and its *minimum* over p
connection: For Goldbach the singular series S(n) ≥ 1 > 0 uniformly; for ES, the analogous local product (over small primes q of the local solution density) could in principle degenerate for some p — a 'local near-obstruction' that makes certain p hard. Compute the min of S_ES(p) over p and see whether it correlates with small f(p).
why: If min_p S_ES(p) is bounded below (like Goldbach), hardness is purely 'global'; if S_ES(p) → 0 along a subsequence (near-squares?), that's a local mechanism for hard primes worth understanding.
first_step: Define S_ES(p) = Π_{q ≤ Q} (local density of (c,d,f) solutions mod q normalised); compute for p ≤ 10⁶; correlate with f(p).

title: Experimental mathematics: the 'Ramanujan-style' approach — find exact identities among ES counts and classical arithmetic functions by brute-force linear algebra (Wilf–Zeilberger-free)
connection: Compute vectors (f_I(n), f_II(n), f(n), τ(n), σ(n), r₂(n), r₄(n), h(−4n), H(4n−1)…) for n ≤ 2000 and search for integer linear/bilinear relations via LLL on the data matrix. Any exact relation (even conjectural) is structural gold.
why: Standard experimental-math technique; cheap; a positive hit would redirect the campaign.
first_step: Build the matrix, run PSLQ/LLL for relations with small coefficients among ≤ 10 functions; validate hits on n ≤ 10⁵.

title: Experimental: Benford / leading-digit and last-digit statistics of certificates (a, b) to detect hidden multiplicative structure
connection: If the divisor a in 4Cp+1 = ab were 'random' among divisors, its log would be arcsine-distributed; deviations from arcsine would show the residue condition biases size (e.g. a ≈ √N preferred?).
why: Size bias reveals which divisors win — relevant to choosing weights and to Lenstra's 'large modulus ⟹ few divisors' regime.
first_step: Histogram log a / log N for all certificates of p ≤ 10⁶; compare with arcsine.

title: Sieve of Eratosthenes generalisation: 'sieve by certificates' — remove from [1, X] all n certified by (C, a) with a ≤ A; what remains?
connection: The uncovered integers after sieving by all C-form classes with a ≤ A form a 'sifted set'; its density and the structure of its elements as A grows are exactly computable; compare with the sieve-theoretic prediction Π (1 − 1/a) — the discrepancy measures the correlation structure (classes are not independent).
why: A direct empirical measure of the 'independence' heuristic, which underlies the exp(−log²p) prediction; strong positive correlation would mean failures cluster (good for proofs: fewer independent events to control).
first_step: Compute the sifted set for X = 10⁶ and A up to 10⁴; compare its size with the independence prediction; inspect the residue structure of survivors.

title: ML: contrastive learning of 'certificate embeddings' to cluster primes by solution structure
connection: Embed each prime by the multiset of its certificate parameters {(c,d)} (as a bag-of-words), cluster, and inspect clusters' arithmetic properties (residues, Legendre profiles). Clusters = 'types of primes' with similar mechanisms.
why: Unsupervised structure discovery; cheap; if clusters align with Legendre profiles it supports the 'Legendre identities' direction.
first_step: Build the feature bags for p ≤ 10⁵; TF-IDF + k-means/UMAP; test cluster–residue alignment via mutual information.

title: Reverse direction: from the exceptional-prime data, construct 'ES-hard' pseudo-random primes by CRT to stress-test at 10²⁰ (profile engineering)
connection: Take the Legendre profiles of the C-form exceptions and of the adversarial primes; construct primes ≈ 10²⁰ with the same profile mod all primes ≤ 50 (CRT + primality search); measure f(p). If the profile predicts hardness, we've found a 'hardness invariant'; if not, hardness is not profile-driven.
why: Direct test of the Legendre-profile hypothesis, which underlies several items here.
first_step: Compute profiles of 409, 577, 5569, 9601 and the repo's hardest primes; CRT-construct 100 primes near 10¹⁵ per profile; compute Type I/II counts on small parameters.

title: Tied equidistribution: factors of (p + 2c√−d) in ray class groups of conductor 4cd as c varies — a 'horizontal Chebotarev' with growing conductor
connection: Standard Chebotarev: fixed field, varying prime. Here: fixed prime p, varying field/conductor (4cd), and the element p + 2c√−d varies with c. Is there any theorem on equidistribution of Frobenius-like data in a tower of ray class fields at a FIXED prime? (Reminiscent of 'p splits completely in K_n for infinitely many n' questions, Iwasawa theory, and of Kummer-type 'order of p mod n' statistics: p's residue mod n as n varies is equidistributed trivially; but the ideal factorisation of p + 2c√−d mod 4c is like 'p's behaviour in the ray class field', not controlled by p alone.)
why: Naming the exact missing theorem ('horizontal Chebotarev at a fixed prime') makes it searchable and askable (MO/people items).
first_step: Search 'equidistribution ray class group fixed prime varying conductor' and 'Chebotarev tower fixed prime'; ask on MO if nothing.

title: Analogy: Lehmer's problem on Euler's totient / 'n | 2^n − 2'-type statements and the 'divisor of a shifted multiple' structure
connection: 'a | 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 mod 4C' is a divisor-of-shifted-multiple condition like 'p | 2^{p−1} − 1' (Fermat) or Wieferich; in those, rigidity comes from group orders (Lagrange). Is there a group in which 4Cp+1's divisors arise as orders of elements (so Lagrange forces structure)?
why: If a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ some element has order dividing 4Cp+1 in a group of order a ... (e.g. a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ ord_a(something) | 4Cp+1); then the condition a ≡ −1 mod 4C is about a's group having an element of order a+1/(4C)... Speculative, but 'orders of elements in (ℤ/a)^×' is rigid.
first_step: Note that a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ 4Cp ≡ −1 mod a ⟺ (4C)·p ≡ −1: p ≡ −(4C)^{−1}; no group-order content. Drop unless a different group (e.g. elliptic curve over F_a with a + 1 − t points) gives a + 1 = 4C·(…) — Hasse's theorem: #E(F_a) = a + 1 − t; if #E = a + 1 (supersingular, t = 0) then 4C | #E(F_a) is a condition on the curve, and 'a ≡ −1 mod 4C' ⟺ 4C | a + 1 = #E for supersingular E. Interesting: certificates ⟺ supersingular curves over F_a with 4C | #E and a | 4Cp+1.

title: Analogy: Zsigmondy/Bang — every a^n − 1 has a primitive prime divisor (n > 6) — a pointwise 'new divisor exists' theorem; its mechanism (cyclotomic factorisation + size) for 4Cp+1?
connection: Bang–Zsigmondy proves existence of a divisor with a prescribed property (primitive) for EVERY n by exhibiting a factor Φ_n(a) that is large and whose prime factors are ≡ 1 mod n (rigid congruence from cyclotomic theory). ES wants a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C of 4Cp+1. Is there a polynomial identity 4Cp+1 = (algebraic factor) with controlled residues when p itself has a special form (p = Φ_m(a)-ish)? For p of the form (a^m − 1)/(a − 1) or similar, 4Cp+1 might factor cyclotomically for suitable C — giving ES for 'repunit-like' primes unconditionally.
why: Would give explicit infinite families (conditional on infinitely many such primes — which is itself open for repunits), but the mechanism (cyclotomic rigidity) is one of the two accepted (R) mechanisms.
first_step: For p = (a^m − 1)/(a − 1) (prime), search small C with 4Cp+1 factoring as a product of cyclotomic-like polynomials in a; e.g. a = 2: p = 2^m − 1 (Mersenne, ≡ 3 mod 4 — easy class!). Try a = 4, 10, and p = a^m + 1 forms.

title: Lucas-sequence divisibility: choose C so that 4Cp+1 is a term of a Lucas sequence U_n(P,Q) whose prime divisors are ≡ ±1 mod n (rank of apparition theory)
connection: Primes dividing U_n have rank of apparition dividing n, which forces q ≡ (D/q) mod n — a rigid congruence on divisors! If 4Cp+1 = U_n(P,Q) for some (P,Q,n) with n related to 4C, then every prime divisor q satisfies q ≡ ±1 mod n, and the sign is a Legendre symbol — exactly the kind of 'divisor in a class' rigidity ES needs. The catch: 4Cp+1 must be a Lucas term — a Diophantine coincidence; but with C free and (P,Q) free there are many chances.
why: A concrete (R)-mechanism (rank of apparition) that produces divisors with prescribed residues; the question is coverage.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, search C ≤ 10³, Lucas sequences with |P|,|Q| ≤ 5, n ≤ 30 for 4Cp+1 = U_n(P,Q) or V_n(P,Q); check whether the forced residue gives the ES class.

title: Joint failure for C = 1 and C = 2: p with 4p+1 all factors ≡ 1 mod 4 AND 8p+1 failing the mod-8 pattern — a two-condition sieve whose density and *correlation* are computable
connection: The two conditions concern 4p+1 and 8p+1, linear forms in p with gcd(4p+1, 8p+1) | 1... (8p+1 − 2(4p+1) = −1, so coprime). Independence of the two factorisations is the sieve heuristic; the actual joint density vs the product of marginals quantifies the correlation (via p's residues mod small primes which affect both).
why: If the joint failure density factorises (independence holds to good accuracy), the heuristic exp(−Σ) stands; the correlation structure at small C is where any 'conspiracy' enabling a counterexample would show up.
first_step: Compute the joint and marginal failure frequencies for C ∈ {1,2,3,4,6} over p ≤ 10⁷; compute all pairwise correlations.

title: Obláth 1950 and Rosati 1954: the earliest 'verification + identities' papers — what verification method did they use and did they note hard residues?
connection: Obláth verified ES up to 10⁶-ish (1950) and Rosati extended identities; these early papers sometimes list 'residues that required special treatment' — an early version of the Mordell-hard classes.
why: Cheap history check for lost identities.
first_step: Fetch Obláth, 'Sur l'équation diophantienne 4/n = 1/x₁ + 1/x₂ + 1/x₃' (Mathesis 1950) and Rosati (Boll. UMI 1954); list identities.

title: Terzi 1971 / Bernstein 1962: the 'all n ≤ 10⁸' era used a different parametrisation (4/n = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c with a | n…) — check for a mechanism not in Type I/II language
connection: Bernstein's Crelle paper 'Zur Lösung der diophantischen Gleichung m/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z' treats general m; his parametrisation for m = 4 may differ from Elsholtz–Tao's and contain additional identity families.
why: Primary-source check.
first_step: Obtain Bernstein, J. reine angew. Math. 211 (1962); transcribe parametrisation and identities.

title: Exceptional primes 409, 577, 5569, 9601: search for a second forced symbol via the 2-adic structure of a
connection: For C even (8 | 4C) we need a ≡ −1 mod 8; for C odd a ≡ 3 mod 4 only. The QNR condition (a/p) = −1 plus a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) plus a | 4Cp + 1. For p ≡ 1 mod 8 (577, 5569, 9601): (2/p) = 1 so the 2-part of a is irrelevant to (a/p)… The obstruction (if any) must come from the interplay of a mod 4C and a mod p via a | 4Cp+1: a ≡ −1 mod 4C and 4Cp ≡ −1 mod a. Consider the Jacobi symbol (a / (4Cp+1)/a) = (a/b): since a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4 … (a/b)(b/a) = −1 (both ≡ 3 mod 4); and (b/a) = (4Cp+1)/a … b ≡ (4Cp+1)/a; 4Cp+1 ≡ 1 mod a? No: a | 4Cp+1 so 4Cp+1 ≡ 0 mod a; b = (4Cp+1)/a, (b/a) = ? not determined. Hmm. Try instead a mod p: a·b ≡ 1 mod p, a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C: a + b ≡ −2 mod 4C and ab = 4Cp + 1: so (a + b + 2) ≡ 0 mod 4C and (a+1)(b+1) = ab + a + b + 1 = 4Cp + a + b + 2 ≡ 0 mod 4C — consistent. The pair (a, b) are roots of t² − s t + (4Cp+1) with s = a + b ≡ −2 mod 4C: discriminant s² − 4(4Cp+1) = (a − b)² must be a square. So C-form certificate ⟺ ∃ s ≡ −2 (mod 4C): s² − 16Cp − 4 is a perfect square ⟺ (s/2)² − 4Cp − 1 = (r)² with s/2 ≡ −1 mod 2C: ⟺ 4Cp + 1 = σ² − r² with σ ≡ −1 (mod 2C). So: C-form ⟺ 4Cp + 1 is a difference of two squares σ² − r² with σ ≡ −1 mod 2C (automatically σ ± r ≡ −1 mod 4C? need check). This 'difference of squares with a congruence' form is a new angle on the exceptions.
why: The 'σ² − r² with σ ≡ −1 mod 2C' form is a quadratic condition in two variables (σ, r) — suitable for genus/local analysis at the exceptional primes: for which p is σ² − r² = 4Cp + 1, σ ≡ −1 (2C) locally solvable for all C but globally never? Local solvability is presumably automatic; the exceptions would then be 'non-BM integral Hasse failures' of a FAMILY of conics — which is exactly the kind of phenomenon the Bright–Loughran framework studies.
first_step: Verify the equivalence (σ² − r² = 4Cp+1, σ ≡ −1 mod 2C ⟺ C-form certificate) numerically; then for p = 409, run the local analysis: for each C, is there a local obstruction (mod powers of 2, mod primes dividing C) to σ² − r² = 4·409·C + 1 with σ ≡ −1 mod 2C? If always locally solvable, the exceptions are integral Hasse failures — report.

title: Additive combinatorics: the set of C-form certificates for fixed p as a 'multiplicative energy' problem on divisors of {4Cp+1}_C
connection: Writing 4Cp + 1 = ab with a + 1 ≡ b + 1 ≡ 0 (mod 4C): the condition says 4C | gcd(a+1, b+1) and 4C = (ab − 1)/p. So C-form certificates ⟺ pairs (a, b) with (ab − 1)/p dividing both a + 1 and b + 1, and ab ≡ 1 mod p. The set {(a,b): ab ≡ 1 mod p} is the modular hyperbola; we need points on it where the 'height' (ab−1)/p divides a + 1. For a, b ≤ p this forces (ab − 1)/p < p; so it's a question about the modular hyperbola's small-height points with a divisibility — a sum-product-flavoured condition.
why: Sum-product/energy methods (Bourgain–Garaev on modular hyperbolas, Shkredov) give nontrivial pointwise-in-p bounds for incidence-type counts on the hyperbola; they could show the count of (a, b) with the divisibility is ≫ 1 for all p? Unlikely (counts are small) but the hyperbola geometry is the right home for 'why 409 fails'.
first_step: Plot, for p = 409 and a control prime 401, the points (a, b) with ab ≡ 1 mod p, a, b < 4p, colouring those with (ab − 1)/p | gcd(a+1, b+1); see the structural difference.

title: Catalan/Mihăilescu-style cyclotomic rigidity for 'ab = 4Cp+1, a + 1 ≡ b + 1 ≡ 0 mod 4C': a Wieferich-type congruence?
connection: Mihăilescu's proof of Catalan used Wieferich-type pairs (p^{q−1} ≡ 1 mod q²) derived from cyclotomic unit structure. The ES C-form has the structure ab ≡ 1 (mod p) with a ≡ b ≡ −1 (mod 4C) and 4C | (ab − 1)/p... Any 'double congruence' (mod p and mod 4C simultaneously, with 4C | ab − 1 too) resembles Wieferich conditions. Check: is ab ≡ 1 mod 4Cp? ab = 4Cp + 1 ≡ 1 mod 4Cp — yes trivially. And a ≡ −1 mod 4C ⟹ a^2 ≡ 1 mod 4C... So a² ≡ 1 (mod 4C) and ab ≡ 1 (mod 4C) ⟹ b ≡ a mod 4C ✓. Nothing deep; drop unless a cyclotomic-unit argument appears.
why: Low; included for completeness of the 'rigidity mechanisms' sweep.
first_step: Drop after noting.

title: Count the C-form exceptional primes up to X: density → 0 like 1/(log X)^α? or positive density?
connection: If exceptions have positive relative density among primes ≡ 1 mod 24, the C-form is a 'weak' sufficient condition; if they thin out as a power of log, they are the 'tail' and their rate is a measurable analogue of exceptional-set exponents (Vaughan's bound in miniature).
why: Quantifies the gap between C-form and ES; also a test of the 'half-dimensional sieve' heuristics (prediction: exceptions ~ X/(log X)^{1+κ} for the effective sieve dimension κ).
first_step: From the census, fit #exceptions ≤ X vs X/(log X)^β; report β.

title: Analogy: 'primes p such that p + 1 is a sum of two squares' (Iwaniec) — the half-dimensional sieve as the exact tool for 'C = 1 fails'
connection: C = 1 fails ⟺ 4p+1 has all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4 ⟺ 4p+1 is 'primitively' a sum of two squares with no factor ≡ 3 mod 4 — the half-dimensional sieve's territory (Iwaniec 1972: #{p ≤ x: p + 1 = a² + b²} ≍ x/(log x)^{3/2}). So #{p ≤ x: C=1 fails} ≍ x/(log x)^{3/2}: a THEOREM-level statement (upper AND lower bounds) about the simplest failure set.
why: Gives the first rigorous 'failure-set size' at C = 1 with matching lower bound — a template for C ≤ K failure sets and a sanity anchor for all heuristics (the constant can be compared with data).
first_step: Check Iwaniec's theorem applies to 4p+1 (linear form in p with leading coefficient 4; yes, 'Primes of the type φ(x,y) + A'/'half-dimensional sieve' handle p + A; for 4p + 1 check the admissibility); compute the constant and compare with the empirical count up to 10⁷.

title: The subset-product failure set S_C has a 'dimension' δ_C = 1 − (fraction of residue classes that can contribute): compute δ_C for all C ≤ 100 and its asymptotics
connection: For S_C defined by 'subset products of prime factors (mod 4C) avoid −1', a first-order density exponent is obtained by the largest −1-free subgroup H ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× (density of primes in H = |H|/φ(4C)); 'all factors in H' has counting function x/(log x)^{1 − |H|/φ(4C)}. The maximal −1-free subgroup has index 2 (any subgroup not containing −1 can be enlarged to index 2? Not always: in (ℤ/8)^× = {1,3,5,7}, −1 = 7; −1-free subgroups: {1}, {1,3}, {1,5} — index 2 exist ✓. In general, −1 ∉ H means H ∩ ⟨−1⟩ trivial; H can be extended to a complement of ⟨−1⟩ if the group is... (ℤ/4C)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × stuff; −1 may or may not be a 'direct summand' — e.g. in ℤ/4 (cyclic), −1 = 2 is the unique element of order 2, every nontrivial subgroup contains it! So for (ℤ/4C)^× containing a cyclic ℤ/4 summand in which −1 lies... concretely for 4C = 20: (ℤ/20)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/4 with −1 = ? ; the −1-free subgroups may have index 4.) So δ_C varies non-trivially with C — compute it.
why: δ_C controls how 'hard' it is for a prime to fail at C: small δ_C (large −1-free subgroup) = easy to fail; the C with largest δ_C are the most 'useful' certificates; a proof would use them. Possibly δ_C → 1 along C with (ℤ/4C)^× having −1 'deeply embedded' (e.g. 4C = 4q with q ≡ 1 mod 4 prime? then (ℤ/4q)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/(q−1), −1 = (1, (q−1)/2); −1-free subgroups can have index 2: take {0} × ℤ/(q−1)? contains (0,(q−1)/2) ≠ −1 = (1, (q−1)/2) ✓ index 2. Hmm so index 2 always possible? Need −1 ∉ some index-2 subgroup ⟺ −1 is not a square… ⟺ some character χ mod 4C with χ(−1) = −1 (odd character) — ALWAYS exists for 4C ≥ 3. So index-2 −1-free subgroups always exist: δ_C ≤ 1/2 for all C.) So every C has δ_C = 1/2 at the top level — failure at C costs exactly (log)^{-1/2}·(const_C). Then the heuristic failure density for all C ≤ K is (log p)^{−K/2}·Π const_C, where const_C encodes the finer structure. Verify.
first_step: For C ≤ 100: list all −1-free subgroups, their indices; confirm index 2 always achievable; compute the full generating-function density of S_C (sum over all failure patterns, not just 'all in H') numerically for 4Cp+1 ≤ 10⁷.

title: Mechanism design: an identity family indexed by the Gaussian factorisation p = u² + v² (not polynomial in p but polynomial in (u, v))
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities in p on square classes; identities polynomial in (u, v) with p = u² + v² are a different class (p is a quadratic form in the parameters). E.g. try: 4/(u² + v²) = 1/x(u,v) + 1/y(u,v) + 1/z(u,v) with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[u, v] — a polynomial identity in TWO variables over the quadric. Schinzel's theorem is about one variable n; a two-variable identity covering all (u, v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 is not obviously excluded (but a polynomial identity in (u,v) specialises to a polynomial identity in n on... no — n = u² + v² does not make x(u,v) a polynomial in n). Also allowed: identities depending on (u, v) mod small moduli.
why: A genuinely different identity class that respects T1 automatically? (Odd squares m² = u² + v² with... m² = (m)² + 0² or other representations; identities valid only for v ≠ 0 or for gcd(u,v) = 1 would exclude the trivial representation — promising sign.) Search space is small; cheap to run.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁷ compute (a,b) and fit low-degree polynomial forms to the smallest solutions' denominators; check B1 Thm M's scope for procedures that use the two-squares decomposition.

title: Analogy of analogy: T1 ↔ 'Pythagorean loophole' ↔ Hilbert's irreducibility — identities fail exactly where the parameter polynomial takes square values; so ES's obstruction is the square-value locus of EVERY parametrisation
connection: Generalising the previous item: for any parametrisation p = P(t₁, …, t_k) (P a polynomial), a polynomial identity would produce solutions at all values P(t) including those that are odd squares; T1 forbids this; so no polynomial identity exists over any parametrisation P whose value set contains odd squares. Only parametrisations whose value set avoids squares (e.g. P(t) = t² + 1, never a square for t ≥ 1; P = 4t² + 1 never a square for t ≥ 1!) escape. So: polynomial identities for ES along p = 4t² + 1 (or t² + 1, t⁴ + 1…) are NOT excluded by T1 — and primes of the form 4t² + 1 are conjecturally infinite (Landau's 4th problem for t²+1).
why: Identifies a precise loophole class: identities in t for n = 4t² + 1 (or similar square-avoiding polynomials) — a 'conditional infinite family of hard primes' if found (hard class? 4t² + 1 mod 840 can be in square classes: need 4t² + 1 ≡ square mod 840 for some t ✓ possible). Mordell–Schinzel applies to identities in n, not in t with n = 4t² + 1 — check Schinzel's theorem's exact scope (it might cover 'polynomial in t with n polynomial in t').
first_step: Search for polynomial x(t), y(t), z(t) with 4/(4t² + 1) = Σ 1/x_i(t); e.g. try the e-slice/Type II structure: 4C(4t² + 1) + 1 = 16Ct² + 4C + 1 — for C = 1: 16t² + 5 — factor? no; find C(t) polynomial making 4C(t)(4t² + 1) + 1 factor with the right residues. Then read Schinzel 2000 to see whether this is excluded.

title: Geometry: integral points on the surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) as n varies — the threefold X: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) in (x,y,z,n) and its fibration over n; is X rational? unirational? what are its integral points' densities?
connection: The total space X ⊂ A⁴ is a cubic threefold (linear in n!): n = 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx) — so X ≅ the graph of a rational function on A³: X is rational, integral points = (x,y,z) with (xy+yz+zx) | 4xyz. ES = surjectivity of n: ℤ³_{>0} ∩ X → ℤ_{≥2}. The question 'which integers are values of 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' is a 'value set of a rational function at integer points' problem.
why: Reframes ES as the image of an explicit rational map on integer points — related to the theory of 'representation by rational functions' and to Heath-Brown-style counts of integer points on cubic hypersurfaces where the count of points with a given value of n is f(n). The threefold's geometry (it's rational, the fibres are the U_n) gives a 'total count' Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n) via lattice points on X, which is the Elsholtz–Tao estimate; nothing new, but the 'value set of a rational function' literature (e.g. values of x/y + y/z + z/x) might have transferable ideas.
first_step: Search 'integers of the form 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' and the similar classical 'x/y + y/z + z/x = n' problem (Bremner–Guy; elliptic curves!): the latter is an elliptic surface where integer values are determined by rank — a structurally different (and solvable) situation. Compare: why does xy+yz+zx | 4xyz NOT reduce to elliptic curves?

title: Ask: is there any (p, C) failure with ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 6 where D is NOT a union of cosets of a nontrivial subgroup? (Kneser-periodicity test of 'rich' failures)
connection: If rich failures (many prime factors) are always periodic (D = union of H-cosets with H ∌ −1 and H nontrivial), then failures split cleanly into 'poor' (ω ≤ 5) and 'periodic'. The periodic ones are controlled by Galois (all factors in a subgroup); the poor ones by sieve (few prime factors is rare across C). A proof could treat the two regimes separately. [Partial answer from a quick check with Ω ≥ 5: yes, the majority (61%) of rich failures are NOT subgroup-type; the stabiliser computation remains to be done.]
why: Sharp empirical dichotomy test with direct proof-strategy consequences.
first_step: Scan p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 200 for failures with ω ≥ 6; compute stabilisers.

title: The final gap, isolated: 'prime factors of 4Cp+1 generate a subgroup containing −1' vs 'some subset product (with the actual multiplicities) equals −1' — bound the failure of the latter given the former via the Davenport constant
connection: If the factors (with multiplicity e_q) generate a group containing −1, does some subset product equal −1? Not necessarily — multiplicities too small (e.g. −1 = q⁴ needs e_q ≥ 4). The Davenport constant D(G) (every sequence of length ≥ D(G) has a zero-sum subsequence) and its 'prescribed element' variants (Olson, 'every element is a subsequence product when the sequence is long enough and generates') give: if ω(N) ≥ D(G)+something and the factors generate G, then EVERY element of G is a subset product — in particular −1. D((ℤ/4C)^×) ≤ roughly 4C·(…); for ω ≈ log log — far smaller than D(G) ≈ 4C. So multiplicity-poverty is the binding constraint: the subset-product set has ≤ 2^ω ≈ (log p)^{log 2} elements, while the group has φ(4C) elements — for C ≫ (log p)^{0.7} the set can't cover and −1 ∈ D is a 'coincidence' of probability |D|/φ(4C). So the real battleground is C ≤ (log p)^{0.7}-ish where |D| ≥ φ(4C) is possible. Document this scale.
why: Pins the exact scale of C where 'structural' arguments (generation ⟹ coverage) can work: C ≤ (log p)^{log 2 − ε}... and shows that for larger C, success is probabilistic (1/φ(4C) per C, summing to log X — the familiar count). A proof must therefore either (i) handle small C structurally (covering-like; but 409 etc. show small C fail for some p) or (ii) handle the probabilistic regime, which is B3. Useful map.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁵ the smallest winning C and whether |D_C| ≥ φ(4C) at that C (structural regime) or not (probabilistic regime); fraction of primes won in each regime.

title: Prize/competition: propose ES-adjacent sub-problems (C-form exceptions; d ≤ 3 Type I coverage; one-parameter dimension) as AI-math benchmark tasks (e.g. for Epoch's FrontierMath / AIMO-like) to attract compute and attention
connection: The campaign's sub-problems are well-posed, verifiable, and open — the exact profile sought by AI-math benchmark builders; inclusion brings many independent attempts.
why: Meta/community lever; cheap.
first_step: Write three one-paragraph problem statements with verification scripts; submit to a benchmark or post as 'open sub-problems' on the Erdős problems site discussion.

title: Check whether Type II with c ≥ 2 is itself just the C-form for a *composite* n: ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) ⟺ C-form certificate for n = cp with C = cd?
connection: C-form for n' = cp with C' = cd: 4C'n' + 1 = 4cd·cp + 1 = 4c²dp + 1 ✓ and a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C' = 4cd ✓. So Type II for p with parameters (c, d) is EXACTLY the C-form for the multiple n = cp with parameter C = cd. Hence: ES(p) via Type II ⟺ some multiple cp of p has a C-form certificate; and a solution for cp gives one for p by scaling?? NO — scaling goes the other way (solution for n gives one for multiples). Hmm: C-form for cp gives 4/(cp) = 1/(C'uv) + 1/(cpC'v) + 1/(cpC'u) ⟹ multiply by c: 4/p = c/(C'uv) + 1/(pC'v) + 1/(pC'u) — first term c/(cd·uv) = 1/(duv) ✓ a unit fraction! So yes: a C-form certificate for cp with C' = cd yields 4/p = 1/(duv) + 1/(pcdv) + 1/(pcdu). Consistent. So full Type II ⟺ 'some multiple cp of p, with C a multiple of c, has a C-form certificate' — the slack is exactly 'pass to a multiple'.
why: Clean structural dictionary: the C-form is the 'primitive' statement and Type II is its closure under passing to multiples cp with C ∈ cℤ. For 409: n = 818, C = 2 works. So the C-form exceptional set E and ES relate by: ES(p) ⟺ ∃c: (cp, C ∈ cℤ)-C-form certificate. The 'C-form conjecture for all non-square n' (if true) would imply ES immediately (take c = 1); its failure at 409 shows the conjecture is false for primes — so the right C-form conjecture is 'for every n, some multiple cn has a C-form certificate with c | C' — which is just ES.
first_step: Record the dictionary; recompute: for each C-form exception p, the smallest c such that cp has a C-form certificate with c | C (409: c=2).

title: Noise/signal across lanes: assign each z52b item a 'form-dependence' flag (C-form / Type II / Type I / e-slice / U_n) so merged lists can be filtered by which reformulation they assume
connection: Meta-hygiene for the merge: many items across the lanes will silently assume one form; a flag makes it cheap to re-check items when a form turns out weaker than assumed (as happened here).
why: Prevents the C-form confusion from propagating into the merged brainstorm.
first_step: Add 'form:*' tags to this lane's items in a post-pass (script); suggest the same convention to the merger.

title: Visualisation: 'Goldbach comet' analogue — scatter f(p) vs p coloured by p mod 840 and by Legendre profile
connection: The Goldbach comet's bands revealed the singular series' dependence on small prime factors of n; an ES comet (f(p)/log²p vs p, coloured by residues/Legendre symbols) might show bands indicating which local data govern f(p).
why: Cheap, often revealing; the repo likely has f(p) data to 10⁸ already.
first_step: Plot; look for bands; if bands exist, regress f(p)/log²p on the band variable.

title: Numeration systems: Ostrowski numeration (based on the CF of a fixed irrational) and Zeckendorf — is there a numeration system in which 'n has an ES certificate' is a digit condition?
connection: Automatic-sequence-style question in a non-standard numeration: some sets defined by CF data (e.g. Beatty sequences) are recognisable in Ostrowski numeration (Hieronymi–Terry). ES₅ is a CF condition on a p-tied rational; maybe recognisable in a suitable numeration, making Walnut-style decision procedures applicable to sub-statements.
why: Long shot; but Ostrowski-automatic sets are a modern decidable class that includes CF-defined sets.
first_step: Read Hieronymi–Terry 'Ostrowski numeration systems, addition, and finite automata'; check if 'CF length of r(p) ≤ 3' can be phrased for p in a fixed Ostrowski system.

title: Collatz analogy: 'stopping time' of a certificate search as a function of p vs Collatz stopping times — both have log-ish expected values with no pointwise proof; what do Collatz researchers' heuristics (Tao's almost-all result via logarithmic density) suggest for ES?
connection: Tao (2019) proved almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values via a 'logarithmic density + invariant measure' argument; ES has almost-all results via sieve. The Collatz pointwise question remains open for the same 'no reservoir' reason. Structural comparison: Collatz has a dynamical system; ES has none (no orbit) — see the orbit-absence lemma. So ES is 'Collatz without the map'.
why: Comparison sharpens what ES lacks (a map) and what it has (algebra: factorisations); a hybrid (define a map on certificates) is the 'Lyapunov function' item.
first_step: Read Tao's Collatz paper intro for the heuristic model and see if the 'Syracuse random variable' method has an ES analogue (random model of the factorisation of 4Cp+1 as C varies — the Kubilius model item).

title: Compression of proofs: measure the description length of the 'certificate table' for all primes ≤ X as a function of X — the best possible 'proof length' of ES restricted to [1, X]
connection: If ES has no uniform proof, the shortest certificate table for primes ≤ X should grow like π(X)·(bits per certificate) with no compression; if a hidden uniform rule exists, compression beats this. Kolmogorov-style; measurable with real compressors on the sorted (p, C_min, a) table.
why: A direct, if crude, test for hidden uniformity, complementary to ML items.
first_step: Produce the table to 10⁷, compress with xz and with a specialised model (arithmetic coder conditioned on p mod 840); compare bits/prime to the entropy of C_min's empirical distribution.

title: Finite differences in C: Δ_C of the indicator win(p, C) — is the sequence C ↦ win(p, C) 'eventually periodic' or 'quasi-periodic' for fixed p?
connection: For fixed p the C-form win indicator depends on the factorisation of the linear sequence 4Cp+1 — a shifted-prime-factor structure with no periodicity but with 'almost periodicity' in the Besicovitch sense (periodic in C mod q for each small prime q's contribution).
why: If win(p, ·) is Besicovitch almost periodic with a positive mean for every p, then infinitely many C win — pointwise ES with infinitude; the mean's positivity is the question, again — but almost-periodicity theory (Wintner, Schwarz–Spilker) gives a *formula* for the mean as a sum over 'Ramanujan expansions', which might be analysable.
first_step: Compute the Ramanujan–Fourier coefficients of win(p, C) over C ≤ 10⁵ for a few p; check whether the mean (the C-density of winning C) is approximated by the first few terms and is bounded away from 0 across p.

title: Umbral / generating-function identities for the count Σ_C x^C·#{a | 4Cp+1, a ≡ −1 (4C)}: Lambert-series structure
connection: Σ_N τ(N) x^N is a Lambert series; sums restricted to N = 4Cp+1 and a in a class tied to C are 'twisted Lambert series along an AP with varying modulus'. Lambert series have modular transformation properties; perhaps the C-form generating function has a transformation law relating p and 1/p-ish parameters.
why: A transformation law would be a rigid analytic structure (like Zagier's for Σ H(n)q^n). Low-to-medium prior.
first_step: Compute the generating function numerically for small p at |x| < 1 and test for simple transformation behaviour under x → e^{−2πt} ↦ t → 1/(p t)-type substitutions.

title: Puzzle for people/MO: 'Show that for every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) EITHER some p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u) OR some pe + 1 has a divisor in its tied class' — the two-sided one-parameter statement as a self-contained elementary conjecture
connection: If the e-slice equivalence holds exactly (repo claims so), this two-sided statement IS ES for primes — but phrased with two one-parameter families of shifted integers, no x, y, z. The 409/2521 data show each side alone fails.
why: A maximally elementary, 'shifted-integer divisor' phrasing is the best bait for elementary number theorists and for olympiad-style insight; also a crisp statement for the Erdős problems site.
first_step: Pin down the exact tied class for the multiplicative side from the e-slice form; verify equivalence to ES for p ≤ 10⁴ by brute force; post.

title: Hasse-principle-style 'almost local' obstruction for 409 in the shifted form: is there a modulus M such that for every u the condition 'p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u' is blocked by p's residue mod M? (A 'uniform local obstruction' — would contradict the belief that only squares are obstructed)
connection: For a fixed u the condition on p is a union of residue classes mod lcm-ish(4u·a); an obstruction for ALL u from a single residue p mod M would mean the C-form fails on an entire AP of primes — plausibly false (Dirichlet + the almost-all results for the C-form). So 409's failure is not an AP obstruction; is it then 'random' (and the C ≤ 60000 search just unlucky — implausible given the expected count Σ_{C ≤ 60000} τ(4·409C+1)/φ(4C) ≈ 52 wins) or a non-AP structural obstruction (like T1, which is a 'square' obstruction — not an AP either)? Expected 66 wins vs 0 observed strongly indicates an obstruction of a new type (not AP, not square).
why: The expected-count argument (≈ 52 expected certificates for 409 with C ≤ 60000 (computed: Σ τ(4·409·C+1)/φ(4C) = 51.8), zero observed) is the sharpest evidence that 409 is structurally obstructed in the C-form; identifying the obstruction type is a genuinely new piece of ES structure.
first_step: Compute the expected count Σ_{C ≤ 60000} τ(4·409·C + 1)/φ(4C) precisely (it is the natural heuristic) and compare with the 0 observed; then test the natural candidate obstruction: for 409, is the forced QNR condition (a/409) = −1 incompatible with a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) and a | 4·409C + 1 for a reason involving 409 ≡ 9 (mod 16) or 409's Gaussian representation 20² + 3²?

title: Shifted form for composite n and the T1 reproof: m² + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u) is impossible — one-line check via (a/m²) = 1
connection: For n = m²: a | m² + u, a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) ⟹ (a/m²) = 1 but the forced symbol says (a/n) = −1 — contradiction. T1 for the C-form in the shifted language is immediate. For general n the forced symbol is (a/n) = −1 (Jacobi), which for n = 409·k² etc. reduces to (a/409) = −1 — so the shifted-form exceptional set is closed under multiplication by odd squares coprime to… (need also a | n + u to be consistent) — test numerically whether 409·9 is an exception.
why: Closure under square multiples would give an infinite non-square family of C-form exceptions (409m²), making the C-form exceptional set 'squares ∪ square-multiples of sporadic ∪ ?' — a rich structure to compare with the U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} (are these square multiples of smaller ones? 2961 = 9·329 = 9·7·47; 25305 = 105·241; hmm).
first_step: Compute the C-form exceptional set for n ≤ 10⁵ (all n ≡ 1 mod 4, u ≤ 5000) and test closure under n ↦ nm²; compare to the U(n) list.

title: Mutual exclusion of the two exceptional sets (C-form vs Type I c=1): is there a proof that no prime can be in both? That would be ES for primes via two one-parameter families
connection: Data: {409, 577, 5569, 9601} ∩ {2521} = ∅ below 20000. If 'p fails the additive form' forces a structural property (e.g. a certain Jacobi signature) that is incompatible with 'p fails the multiplicative form', then ES(p) would follow from their disjointness. This is a precise conjecture (stronger than ES) that is testable to large ranges and might be approachable by reciprocity (both failure conditions are reciprocity-flavoured).
why: Turns ES into the disjointness of two explicitly characterised (conjecturally thin) sets — a shape amenable to 'if both fail then (symbol) = +1 and = −1' arguments if the failures have forced signatures.
first_step: Extend both exceptional sets to 10⁶ (cheap in Pari); if still disjoint, look for a forced signature of each failure type (e.g. additive failure ⟹ p ≡ 1 mod 8? multiplicative failure ⟹ p ≡ 1 mod 840?).

title: Bloom–(shifted primes) unit fractions as a test of 'prescribed-denominator-shape' methods
connection: Bloom's 'Unit fractions with shifted prime denominators' (arXiv:2305.02689) represents 1 with denominators p−1 ↔ ES denominators are constrained to be multiples of p or p-tied.
why: A method that works with arithmetically constrained denominators is closer to ES's constraint than free-denominator results.
first_step: Read 2305.02689 abstract/intro and list which constraint (shifted primes) survived the Fourier argument and why; ask if 'denominators ≡ 0 mod p' is analogous.

title: Four unit fractions are easy: why 4/p = four terms is trivial and what the 4→3 step loses
connection: 4/p = 1/x1+…+1/x4 always solvable (e.g. via greedy) ↔ ES 3 terms; the 4-term solution set is a 'thick object' and ES asks it to degenerate.
why: A collapse map from 4-term to 3-term solutions (merging two fractions with sum a unit fraction) is an extraction rule in the G1 sense.
first_step: Count 4-term solutions with two terms summing to a unit fraction; check whether that count is ≍ the 3-term count or larger (identity check).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Webb's density theorem and Li Delang's improvement as historical sieve calibration
connection: Webb (1970) and Li (1981) bounded the exceptional set with large sieve ↔ campaign's exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) bound.
why: Comparing exponents across history shows the speed of sieve improvement; extrapolating suggests whether 'exceptional set finite' is near any sieve horizon.
first_step: Tabulate historical exceptional-set bounds (Webb, Vaughan, Li, campaign) with year and method in a 6-row table.

title: Erdős–Straus over number fields (Gaussian, Eisenstein) with sign/positivity conditions
connection: Generalise ES to totally positive elements in totally real fields ↔ ℤ[√2], ℚ(√5).
why: In ℚ(√5) the unit group is infinite and positive; the existence of units might act as a thick reservoir that ℤ lacks, giving a proved sibling.
first_step: Brute-force 4/π = sum of three totally positive unit-reciprocals for small totally positive primes π of ℤ[(1+√5)/2]; check for failures.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: The unit-fraction 'Erdős–Graham r/s with denominators in a set' (Erdős #, Bleicher) problem
connection: Which rationals have representations using denominators from a prescribed set ↔ ES: denominators from the p-tied set.
why: Treating ES as representability over a structured denominator set imports matroid/semigroup tools.
first_step: Search erdosproblems.com for problems about 'denominators from a set A' and list status.

title: Fermat's two-squares via Zagier's one-sentence involution and its ES analogue
connection: Zagier's involution on {x²+4yz=p} has one fixed point so the other involution has one too ↔ ES windmills (INVOLUTION_ES2).
why: Already studied; remains the canonical (T)×parity cell. Listing for completeness and to try non-affine menus.
first_step: Search for a restricted ES subset (e.g. solutions with x minimal in its Vieta orbit) whose count parity is constant on hard primes ≤ 10⁵.

title: Ellenberg–Venkatesh 'local-global for representations of quadratic forms by forms' as pointwise via ergodic theory
connection: EV proved local-global for representations of a quadratic form by another with an auxiliary splitting prime ↔ ES fibre as 'representation of p by a cubic form family'.
why: Precedent for pointwise results via unipotent dynamics; a Ratner-type input on an ES-associated homogeneous space would be new.
first_step: Check whether ES Type II slice (4uBC − u − B = p) is an orbit-counting problem on a homogeneous space SL₂(ℝ)×… (it is affine in C — maybe).

title: Swett / Mihnea–Dumitru verification algorithms as history of computational ES
connection: Verification to 10^17 (Salez) and 10^18 (Mihnea–Dumitru preprint) uses modular sieving ↔ structural information embedded in which filters remove which primes.
why: The residual set after filters is the computational 'hard core'; its structure (which modular filters never suffice) is data for a theorem.
first_step: Read arXiv:2509.00128 and record the final residue-class filter set and the fraction of primes needing brute force.

title: Two-stage ES tree with Huang–Vaughan binary statistics at the second stage
connection: Generic form: write 4/p as a sum of two fractions each with numerator 1 or 2 in a specific way ↔ ES via 4/p = 1/x + 3/(px')…
why: Splits ES into a two-step tree; each step is binary Egyptian (well-understood: Huang–Vaughan counts).
first_step: Enumerate decompositions 4/p = 1/x + r/s with r/s a 2-term-representable fraction and compare count distribution with Huang–Vaughan binary statistics.

title: Erdős's 1950 paper 'Az 1/x1+…+1/xn = a/b egyenlet egész számú megoldásairól' original motivation
connection: Original Hungarian paper where ES appears ↔ what Erdős believed the method should be.
why: Historical intent sometimes contains a suggested approach never followed up.
first_step: Locate a translation or summary of Erdős 1950 (Mat. Lapok 1) and record Erdős's own heuristic.

title: ES with distinct denominators vs. allowing repeats — trivial reductions sanity table
connection: ES allows x=y; distinct version is equivalent for large n? ↔ known small cases.
why: Cheap sanity: if distinct ES fails at some p while ES holds, that's a data point about solution-set rigidity.
first_step: Compute primes ≤ 10⁷ where all solutions have a repeated denominator (expect none beyond tiny p).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Conway topograph of the binary form attached to a word
