connection: Each word gives SL₂ data γ_w = [[A,p],[t,A*]] and hence binary quadratic forms (e.g. the form fixed by γ_w, discriminant (A+A*)² − 4). The topograph shows values on the Farey tree and the 'river' for indefinite forms.
why: Conway's topograph turns representation questions into tree navigation, and ES might become 'a value p appears on a well at depth 3 with prescribed sign'.
first_step: For p < 500 draw topographs of the forms fixed by γ_w; look for a common location of p and the sign.

title: Dirichlet series of ES solution counts and multiple-zeta-like structure
connection: Multiple zeta values have Egyptian-fraction-flavoured sum structure ↔ generating functions of ES solution counts.
why: Generating function Σ_n f(n) n^{-s} for ES counts may be expressible via double/triple Dirichlet series with MZV-like structure.
first_step: Check whether a paper on Dirichlet series Σ f(n)n^{-s} of Egyptian counts exists (search 'Dirichlet series number of Egyptian fraction representations').

title: Cox ring of the minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic, fibred over n
connection: The Cayley cubic's Cox ring is known explicitly (Derenthal et al. list Cox rings of singular del Pezzo surfaces) ↔ ES fibre is a hyperplane section x3 = const·n.
why: Explicit Cox ring coordinates for this family would give the 'right' variables in which ES might become a norm or divisor problem with new symmetry.
first_step: Look up Derenthal 'Singular del Pezzo surfaces whose universal torsors are hypersurfaces' and identify Cayley's cubic (4A1) entry.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Fundamental group of the complement of the ES boundary and Kummer covers
connection: U_n's boundary consists of lines/conics; π₁ of complement gives covers ↔ Type I/II divisibility conditions may be torsor conditions under μ_k.
why: Interpreting d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C as a μ_{4C}-torsor condition would explain the tied modulus geometrically.
first_step: Compute H¹_et(U_n, μ_m) for small m via the boundary configuration and match classes with the ET congruence conditions.

title: Elliptic fibrations of the ES surface: for fixed x, (y,z) lie on a conic; for fixed ratio, on an elliptic curve?
connection: Slicing U_n by x = const gives a hyperbola (binary divisor problem); slicing by y/z = const gives curves of genus ? ↔ elliptic fibration may give rank-based infinitude.
why: If some pencil of curves on U_n has genus-1 fibres with positive rank uniformly, integral points might be forced via descent heights.
first_step: Compute the genus of the curves cut by y = t·z on the ES projective surface and check if any pencil is elliptic.

title: Néron–Severi lattice of the ES surface and lattice-theoretic obstructions
connection: NS lattice of a minimal resolution ↔ integral points via intersection pairing constraints.
why: An arithmetic invariant from NS (e.g. discriminant group twisted by n) might be the hidden 'prime T1' carrier.
first_step: Compute NS of the resolved projective closure of 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)w (with w homogenising) and its Galois action as a function of n.

title: Hecke eigenvalues at p as a certificate source (trace formula identity)
connection: R(p) = trace of some Hecke-like operator? If R(p) = Σ over a set of a_f(p) with f in a fixed space, Deligne's bound would control it.
why: A finite-dimensional space would give R(p) = main + O(p^{1/2-ish}·dim) error — but main is log², so need dim growth; still worth seeing if R(p) has any modular generating function.
first_step: Compute Σ_p R(p) q^p partial sums? Rather: test whether p ↦ R(p) − M(p) correlates with a_f(p) for small-level newforms over primes ≤ 10⁶.

title: Rademacher-type exact formula for a mock modular generating function of R(n)
connection: If Σ R(n) q^n (or a twist) were mock modular, Bringmann–Ono-style exact formulas give coefficients as convergent Kloosterman–Bessel series.
why: Exact formulas with positive main term and explicitly bounded tails are how partition-function positivity facts are proved pointwise.
first_step: Check growth: R(n) is polylog, inconsistent with the exponential growth of weight-<0 mock forms; so look for weight-1 or weight-0 objects (logarithmic growth plausible for weight 1 Eisenstein-like). Test whether n ↦ M₀(n) matches a weight-1 Eisenstein coefficient shape.

title: Class number of ℚ(√−p) and ES: correlation test
connection: h(−4p) controls representations of p by binary forms of discriminant −4p ↔ ES solutions involve binary forms 4uB·…
why: If R(p) correlates with h(−4p) or h(4p)·log ε_p, a class-number formula identity might lurk.
first_step: Compute Pearson/Spearman correlation of R(p)/log²p with h(−4p)/√p and with L(1, χ_p) over primes ≤ 10⁷.

title: Tropicalisation of the ES equation and valuations at p
connection: Tropical variety of 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) under p-adic valuation ↔ which valuation patterns (v_p(x),v_p(y),v_p(z)) are allowed (Type I/II).
why: Tropical geometry classifies degenerations; may reveal hidden Type III-ish patterns for composite n and their absence for primes.
first_step: Compute the tropical variety for v_p(n) = 1 and list cones; match with Type I/II.

title: Additive combinatorics: sum-product phenomena in (ℤ/p)^× and ES Type I
connection: Type I: f | p²+4c²d, f ≡ −p mod 4cd ↔ product sets {ab⁻¹ : ab | N} hitting −1 mod e.
why: Sum-product/Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin: product sets of moderate size in (ℤ/q)^× cover everything; e-slice form needs the divisor-ratio set mod e to contain −1.
first_step: For the e-slice form, measure |{ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N}| / e as function of e for hard primes; check whether it is large enough for generic covering results.

title: Sidon/B_h sets: are ES solution denominators 'too structured' to avoid?
connection: Sets avoiding solutions to 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n-type linear-in-reciprocals equations ↔ Ruzsa's theory of sets without solutions of linear equations.
why: Ruzsa-type extremal results for reciprocal equations might give: the set of 'certificate parameters' is too large to avoid the ES hyperplane.
first_step: Search literature: 'sets without solutions to 1/x + 1/y = 1/z' density (Erdős problem) — record what's known.

title: Polynomial method (Dvir, Croot–Lev–Pach) for existence over F_p
connection: Polynomial method proves existence/size bounds pointwise at each q ↔ ES has a fibre over F_p? (local solvability is trivial).
why: The polynomial method proves things at every prime with no averaging; a polynomial-method argument would need a finite-field shadow of 'integral positive' certificates.
first_step: Find a finite-field statement (over F_p) whose truth implies ES(p) — e.g. 'a certain set S ⊂ F_p² of size ≫ p contains a point of a curve' — and test if the polynomial method applies.

title: Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace: counting F_q-points of the ES surface with p-adic shadow
connection: #U_n(F_q) given by cohomology traces ↔ integral point existence is not a point count, but mod-q counts of the 'certificate variety' (with tied modulus) could vary with q in a structured way.
why: If the certificate variety V_p has an ℓ-adic cohomology computable as a function of p, Lefschetz numbers might encode R(p) mod something.
first_step: Count F_q points of {(u,B,C): 4uBC − u − B = p} for small q, p and see the dependence on (p mod q) — compare with genus/BM layer.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Bourgain–Gamburd expansion in SL₂(ℤ/q) for ES₅ words
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd (and Bourgain–Varjú for composite q) prove Cayley graphs of SL₂(ℤ/q) w.r.t. Zariski-dense generators are expanders; ES₅ / SL₂-word forms of ES express solutions as length-3 words in a fixed generating set.
why: Expansion gives equidistribution of long words; ES fixes length 3, so the relevant input is the short-word distribution — a known barrier (B3) recorded rather than judged.
first_step: Compute the image of all length-≤3 ES₅ words mod q in SL₂(ℤ/q) for q ≤ 200 and measure how much of the target coset they cover.

title: Stern–Brocot / Calkin–Wilf tree paths of 4/p
connection: 4/p's position in the Stern–Brocot tree is encoded by its CF ↔ ES₅ continued-fraction length condition.
why: Tree-path combinatorics (run-length encoding) gives a visual/automaton description of when short Egyptian decompositions exist.
first_step: Compute SB paths of 4/p and of (4x−p)/(px) for successful x; look for a pattern in path run-lengths.

title: Geodesic flow on the modular surface and closed geodesics of discriminant tied to p
connection: Closed geodesics correspond to real quadratic forms; ES certificates might correspond to geodesics passing through a cusp neighbourhood.
why: Equidistribution of closed geodesics (Duke) holds for each large discriminant pointwise — a rare pointwise equidistribution theorem.
first_step: Identify a discriminant D(p) and a target set in the unit tangent bundle such that 'some geodesic of discriminant D(p) visits the set' ⟹ ES(p); check if target set size is ≫ D^{-δ}.

title: Pell equations and ES: x² − D y² = ±4p via units
connection: Representations of 4p or p by norm forms of real quadratic fields always exist when the class group is trivial ↔ ES certificates as norms.
why: Norm-form existence is pointwise (class field theory: p splits ⟹ represented by some form in class group). ES would need a norm-form whose class group is trivial and whose representation yields a certificate.
first_step: Look for D (fixed, small) with h(D) = 1 such that every representation p = N(α) produces an ES certificate via an explicit formula; test D = 5, 8, 12, 13.

title: Binary cubic forms: Delone–Faddeev and ES certificates as cubic rings
connection: Binary cubic forms ↔ cubic rings; 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is a ternary cubic, but its slices are binary cubics.
why: Bhargava-style parametrisation might identify ES solutions with ideal classes in cubic rings of discriminant tied to n; existence via class group nontriviality?
first_step: Compute the binary cubic obtained by fixing z in 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) and its discriminant as function of n,z.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Root number parity forcing: Dokchitser-style 'rank is odd ⟹ point exists' for a certificate curve
connection: If ES(p) ⇐ E_p(ℚ) has a point of a certain type and w(E_p) = −1 for all relevant p, parity conjecture would force rank ≥ 1.
why: Parity forcing is a genuinely pointwise existence source (R-type, conditional on finiteness of Sha or parity conjecture).
first_step: Search for a family of elliptic curves E_p over ℚ indexed by p with w(E_p) = −1 for every p ≡ 1 mod 24 and with points that map to ES solutions.

title: Gross–Zagier singular moduli factorisation as divisor-structure input
connection: Norms of differences of singular moduli have explicitly known prime factorisations (all primes ≤ D1D2/4) ↔ ES needs divisors of p-tied integers in a class.
why: An integer tied to p with explicitly controlled factorisation (only small primes, with Legendre-symbol constraints) is exactly what the 'class gate' wants.
first_step: Compute N(j(τ_{−4p}) − j(τ_{−3}))-type quantities for small p and check if they produce divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C of 4Cp+1-type integers.

title: Abc conjecture consequences for ES failures
connection: ABC controls radicals ↔ an ES counterexample p forces all 4Cp+1 (C ≤ polylog) to avoid divisors in −1 mod 4C; does that force smoothness/radical patterns contradicting abc?
why: Implications from abc to Diophantine non-existence are standard; here we want abc ⟹ existence, which is unusual but possible via 'no huge prime-power structure' arguments.
first_step: Check whether the failure of (★) for p forces 4Cp+1 to be prime or a prime power for many C — and whether that's restricted by known results (it isn't by abc; record negative).

title: Arakelov / heights: ES certificate size as a height and slopes of an arithmetic bundle
connection: Minimal certificate size vs p ↔ successive minima of an Arakelov vector bundle attached to p (Bost's slopes).
why: Slope inequalities give existence of small sections pointwise (Siegel lemma); ES needs a 'section' landing in an integrality cone.
first_step: Model the (u,C) search space as a hermitian ℤ-module and compute slopes for p ≤ 10⁴; compare with minimal certificate heights.

title: R(p) as a partition function: Z(β) = Σ over trial pairs of exp(−β·cost) and the β→∞ limit
connection: Statistical mechanics: count of certificates = zero-temperature limit of a partition function over the trial set 𝓡 with energy = 'distance from divisibility' ↔ R(p).
why: Smooth relaxations (finite β) are analytically tractable (sums of exponentials of residues) and could be bounded below; the question is whether a β-interpolation lower bound survives β → ∞.
first_step: Define E(u,C) = ((p+u) mod (4uC−1))/(4uC−1) and compute Z(β) = Σ e^{−βE} for p ≤ 10⁵; check monotone behaviour of log Z(β) vs log R(p) at large β.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Large deviations: rate function for lower tail of R(p)
connection: Lower tail P(R(p) ≤ εM) in a random model ↔ Janson inequality for sums of dependent indicators.
why: Janson's inequality gives exp(−μ²/(2Δ)) bounds; computing Δ (pair correlation of certificate events) explicitly for ES yields a falsifiable heuristic and identifies dangerous correlations.
first_step: Compute Δ = Σ_{i~j} P(A_i ∧ A_j) for ES certificate events empirically (pairs of (u,C) sharing a modulus factor) at p ~ 10⁷.

title: Random matrix statistics of the sequence R(p)/M(p)
connection: Fluctuations of arithmetic counts often match RMT (e.g. L-function zeros) ↔ R(p) normalised.
why: If fluctuations are Gaussian with variance ~ (log p)^a, the lower tail model sharpens; RMT mismatch indicates hidden structure.
first_step: Compute variance of R(p) − M_BM(p) in windows and its scaling with log p for p ≤ 10⁸ (repo data).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Percolation on the divisor graph: does p 'percolate' to a certificate?
connection: Divisor-lattice percolation ↔ ES certificate as a connection path in a graph whose nodes are p-tied integers and edges are divisibility in classes.
why: Percolation has sharp threshold theorems (Friedgut–Kalai); a giant-component argument could give existence when density exceeds a threshold.
first_step: Define graph G_p on {4Cp+1 : C ≤ T} ∪ divisors with edges by residue condition; compute component sizes for hard vs easy p.

title: Transfer-matrix method for counting certificate words
connection: Count words tuv − u − v = p via a transfer matrix over residues ↔ ES₅/I3 words.
why: Transfer matrices make counting mod q exact and expose eigenvalue gaps; might give the main term and fluctuations as eigenvalue contributions.
first_step: Build the mod-q transfer matrix for words (t,u,v) with tuv − u − v ≡ p mod q and compute its spectrum for q ≤ 50.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Ising-like spin model: the BM character as a spin and T(p) as magnetisation
connection: T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) is a weighted sum of ±1 spins over pairs ↔ magnetisation of a spin system with couplings from multiplicativity.
why: Spin-glass bounds or correlation inequalities (Griffiths/GKS) give pointwise inequalities for ferromagnetic systems; multiplicativity (−uB/p) = (−u/p)(B/p) is a product spin structure (Mattis model).
first_step: Write T(p) = Σ_{u,B} s_u s'_B w(u,B) with s_u = (u/p): it's a Mattis-type bilinear form; compute the max over arbitrary sign patterns vs actual to see how far from worst case.

title: Brownian / random-walk model for the greedy remainder chain
connection: Successive remainders in Egyptian expansions as a Markov chain ↔ probability the chain hits numerator 1 at step 2.
why: Gives a heuristic per-p probability that simple algorithms succeed; separates algorithmic from existential difficulty.
first_step: Simulate the 'first-term then remainder' chain over all first terms x ∈ [p/4, 3p/4] and record the success probability distribution per p.

title: Kolmogorov complexity argument: a counterexample p would be 'simple'?
connection: Incompressibility method: if every p ≤ X of high complexity has a certificate, counterexamples must be low-complexity ↔ disproof search direction.
why: Adversarial searches already target structured p; formalising 'low complexity' (short description) to prioritise searches is a meta improvement.
first_step: Rank candidate primes by description length (e.g. p = a·b^k + c with small a,b,c) and search ES hardness there first.

title: Mixing of the map p ↦ (p mod 4uC−1) as u,C vary: equidistribution of residues of a single integer
connection: Residues of a fixed p modulo a growing family of moduli ↔ ES needs p ≡ −u mod (4uC−1) for some pair; this is 'one integer vs many moduli' — Erdős–Turán type discrepancy.
why: Discrepancy of {p/m} for m in a structured set is a classic (Vinogradov-type) problem; known results (e.g. on p mod m for m ≤ √p) might give existence in some ranges.
first_step: Measure discrepancy of fractional parts {(p+u)/(4uC−1)} over the trial set and compare with random; the ES event is the fractional part being exactly 0.

title: Quantum unique ergodicity analogy: certificates as 'mass' of a p-dependent state
connection: QUE for Hecke eigenforms gives pointwise equidistribution in the eigenvalue aspect ↔ ES certificate counts as 'mass in a small set'.
why: QUE is pointwise in the spectral parameter (Lindenstrauss, Soundararajan); a QUE-type statement for a p-indexed family would give pointwise counts, but the target set must be fixed-size.
first_step: Find whether R(p)/M(p) can be written as ⟨φ_p, 1_A φ_p⟩ for some natural p-family of states φ_p and fixed set A.

title: Extreme value theory for max over p ≤ X of (minimal certificate size)
connection: Gumbel/Fréchet laws for maxima of iid ↔ max_p min-certificate as function of X.
why: If the max grows like (log X)^a with EVT-consistent fluctuations, extrapolate beyond 10¹⁸; deviations flag structure.
first_step: From repo census data, extract record-setting primes for 'least u in I3 word' and fit EVT growth.

title: Fokker–Planck / diffusion model of log R(p) along p
connection: log R(p) as a stochastic process in p ↔ smooth main term plus noise.
why: Autocorrelation of R across nearby primes (p, p+840k) shows whether difficulty is local in residue or random.
first_step: Compute autocorrelation of R(p)/M(p) between primes in the same class mod 840 with lag k.

title: Harmonic-mean interpretation: p/4·3 is the harmonic mean of x,y,z
connection: 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z ⟺ harmonic mean H(x,y,z) = 3p/4 ↔ means inequalities (H ≤ G ≤ A) give box constraints.
why: Box constraints from mean inequalities are already used; the 'harmonic mean of three integers equals 3p/4' phrasing might connect to integer means literature.
first_step: Search 'integers with prescribed harmonic mean' literature for existence theorems.

title: Mechanical analogy: springs in series (compliance adds) and integer stiffness
connection: Springs in series: 1/k = Σ 1/k_i ↔ same algebra as resistors; equivalent reformulation.
why: Duplicate of resistor item in algebra but different community (mechanics puzzles); keep as outreach variant.
first_step: Combine with resistor outreach note (no separate work).

title: Second moment method over primes in short intervals: positive proportion with R(p) ≥ 1 in every interval
connection: Paley–Zygmund on R over primes in [X, X+H] ↔ ES almost-all in short intervals.
why: Repo has interval results; second moment at H = (log X)^A would be a new 'every short interval contains many ES primes' result (weak but new form).
first_step: Check repo's (D)30 interval result range of H; compute what second moment would need for H = (log X)^A.

title: Littlewood conjecture analogy: inf n‖nα‖‖nβ‖ = 0 vs ES certificates as simultaneous small values
connection: Both ask for simultaneous small values of products of distances ↔ ES Type II p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB is a multiplicative Diophantine approximation condition.
why: Littlewood is open too, with measure-zero exceptional set (EKL) — a parallel of 'almost all' ES results; methods might transfer in either direction.
first_step: Write ES Type II as a product-of-distances condition and compare its structure with Littlewood's.

title: Annealed vs quenched averages for certificate counts
connection: Disordered systems: quenched average E[log Z] vs annealed log E[Z] ↔ log R(p) average vs log of average.
why: A large gap indicates rare-event dominance (some p with huge counts, e.g. via Linnik), which affects lower-tail heuristics.
first_step: Compute E[log(1+R(p))] vs log E[R(p)] over primes in dyadic ranges up to 10⁸.

title: Hydrodynamic limit of certificate count as p → ∞ along residue classes
connection: Limit shape of the set of successful (log u/log p, log C/log p) ↔ the main-term density.
why: A limit shape theorem (empirical measure of certificates converges) for almost all p is plausibly provable and would describe where certificates live.
first_step: Plot the empirical measure of (log u, log C)/log p for successful pairs over many p; compare with 1/(uC) density prediction.

title: Quantum algorithm: Grover search for certificates and complexity of certification
connection: Grover gives √ speedup for unstructured search ↔ ES certificate search space ~ p log p trials, polylog winners.
why: Not a proof route; clarifies computational complexity of finding a certificate (classical best ~ ?).
first_step: Determine the best classical algorithm complexity for finding one ES solution for a given p (repo/verification code) and record whether it's polylog-time heuristically.

title: Factoring with hints: ES as 'find a factor of 4Cp+1 in a residue class' (Coppersmith known-MSB/LSB attacks)
connection: Coppersmith factors N given half the bits of a factor; ES wants a factor of N_C = 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C — i.e. the low bits (mod 4C) of the factor are known.
why: Known-LSB factoring (factors in a prescribed class mod M with M ≥ N^{1/4}) is polynomial time via lattices; ES's modulus 4C is tiny relative to N^{1/4}, but summing over C gives many tries.
first_step: Quantify: for which C is 4C ≥ (4Cp+1)^{1/4}? (C ≥ p^{1/3}) — then Coppersmith decides existence of a factor ≡ −1 mod 4C exactly; check whether the large-C range alone has certificates often (data).

title: Witnessing theorem contrapositive: if certificate-finding is hard (e.g. needs factoring), ES is not provable in weak arithmetic
connection: Divisor-form certificates need factoring 4Cp+1 ↔ if every certificate search needs factoring, ES ∉ provable in S¹₂ (under crypto assumptions).
why: Gives a meta-theorem: proofs must use non-constructive or strong tools; clarifies why elementary attempts fail.
first_step: Check whether ES certificates can be found without factoring (e.g. via the Type I trial form, which needs only divisibility tests, poly-time per trial). If yes, the obstruction vanishes.

title: Program synthesis: search for a short program f(p) → (x,y,z) correct for all p ≤ 10⁸
connection: Program synthesis (e.g. enumerative, stochastic superoptimisation, LLM-guided) ↔ a uniform algorithm with provable termination would be ES.
why: Any synthesised program with a bounded loop is a finite menu (B1, must fail i.o. under Dickson); but unbounded-loop programs with simple invariants could suggest a proof structure.
first_step: Run a DSL search (loops over small parameter, modular tests) for programs certifying all primes ≤ 10⁶ with minimal description length; inspect top programs for invariants.

title: Lattice attacks on 'hidden number problem' as a model for finding u with p ≡ −u mod (4uC−1)
connection: HNP: recover hidden α from approximations of α·t mod q ↔ ES conditions as simultaneous approximations.
why: Cryptanalysis has fine-tuned lattice dimensions/bounds for such problems; reuse could design efficient certificate finders for huge p.
first_step: Write ES Type II as approximations of p/(4uC−1) to integers; try a BKZ-based search for certificates at p ~ 10^40 and compare yield with brute force.

title: Index calculus analogy: smooth relations and linear algebra over (ℤ/4C)^×
connection: Index calculus finds discrete logs by collecting smooth relations ↔ ES gate: express −1 as a product of factor-base primes' classes, with the factor base = small primes dividing p-tied integers.
why: Linear algebra over exponent vectors mod the group exponent makes 'is −1 in the generated subgroup' decidable; collecting relations across many C might show the subgroup is always everything.
first_step: For hard p, collect smooth parts of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10³; for each C compute the subgroup generated mod 4C; record when it's proper.

title: Model checking / BDDs for residue-class coverage up to large modulus
connection: Binary decision diagrams represent huge residue-class sets compactly ↔ the uncovered set after modular filters.
why: Exact representation of the uncovered set mod M (M huge) enables precise density of residual primes and structure detection.
first_step: Represent uncovered residues mod 840·Π small primes as a BDD over CRT digits; measure size growth.

title: Dual certificates of failure: what does a 'proof of no Type II (★) solution' look like for p = 409?
connection: Each (★)-failing prime has a finite proof of failure (exhaustion) ↔ shortest such proof structure (via sieving modulo few primes?) reveals what a counterexample to ES would require.
why: If (★)-failures always have short structured proofs (e.g. via a few congruences), then ES-failure needs a similar compact obstruction pattern, which might be ruled out.
first_step: For the 14 (★)-failing primes, compute the minimal set of residue checks proving failure (it's a covering of the trial set); look for common shape.

title: GPU kernel for (★)/I3 census to 10^12
connection: Repo census to 10^10 single engine ↔ GPU acceleration for residue-filter checks.
why: Extends CERTIFIED data for I3_𝒞 and (★) failures; tests growth of least u.
first_step: Port scripts/z52_bank_i3c.c inner loop to CUDA; benchmark on 10^10..10^10+10^8.

title: Gradient-boosted classifier predicting (★)-line failure from residues: feature importance
connection: ML classifier on p's residues mod m ≤ M predicting low R(p) ↔ which local data matter.
why: Feature importance reveals unexpected moduli or quadratic characters that drive difficulty, possibly a new invariant.
first_step: Train XGBoost on primes ≤ 10⁸ with target log R(p)/log²p, features = p mod m for m ≤ 200 and (q/p) for q ≤ 100; list top features.

title: Mechanistic interpretability of a model that 'solves' ES on all tested p
connection: If a network generalises perfectly on out-of-range p, its circuit is an algorithm ↔ a candidate uniform proof idea.
why: Grokking literature shows networks learn modular arithmetic via Fourier features; an ES-solving network would reveal which characters/moduli matter.
first_step: After training (previous item), apply Fourier analysis to embeddings (as in Nanda et al. grokking) to find dominant frequencies.

title: Satisfiability modulo theories with nonlinear integer arithmetic: prove 'ES for n ≡ r mod M' identities automatically
connection: SMT (Z3 NIA) can verify polynomial identities with divisibility ↔ automatic discovery of Mordell-type identities for new classes (non-square).
why: Automated rediscovery of all identity classes mod larger moduli maps exactly which classes have identities (Mordell–Schinzel says square classes never do).
first_step: Use a template x = (a n + b)/c etc. and let a solver search coefficients making 4/n = … an identity on a residue class mod 4·k; enumerate classes covered mod 9240.

title: Hash-based birthday search for collisions between Type I and Type II slices
connection: Birthday paradox: two large lists collide ↔ ES via matching a Type I partial with a Type II partial (meet-in-the-middle).
why: Meet-in-the-middle reformulations sometimes convert existence into collision guarantees (G1 collision column).
first_step: Find a decomposition ES(p) ⟺ L1(p) ∩ L2(p) ≠ ∅ with |L1|,|L2| ≍ √p range; test sizes and collision counts.

title: Kolmogorov–Arnold / sparse regression on Fourier coefficients of 1[R(p) small]
connection: Fourier analysis over (ℤ/M)^× of the indicator of hard primes ↔ which characters correlate with difficulty.
why: Large Fourier coefficients identify characters (e.g. quartic residue symbols) beyond quadratic ones that influence R(p).
first_step: Compute Σ_{p hard} χ(p) for all characters χ mod M ≤ 10⁴ (normalised) and list outliers.

title: Smooth values of 4Cp+1: certificate abundance when some level is smooth
connection: If 4Cp + 1 has many prime factors whose classes in (ℤ/4C)^× are in general position (smoothness alone is not enough: factors all ≡ 1 mod 4 never give a level-4 certificate), its divisors cover (ℤ/4C)^× (subset products), so a certificate exists. ES would follow from 'for every p some C ≤ (log p)^A has 4Cp + 1 with ≥ k prime factors in general position'.
why: Smooth-number theory (Canfield–Erdős–Pomerance; smooth values of linear forms, Harman; Balog–Wooley) gives existence of smooth values in short families. One value with many factors is a pointwise target with a native toolbox.
first_step: Compute, for hard primes, min over C ≤ 10⁴ of the largest prime factor of 4Cp+1 relative to the requirement Ω ≥ D((ℤ/4C)^×) ; record gap.

title: Dirichlet hyperbola method for R(p) with exact error tracking
connection: R(p) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cp+1 : d ≡ −1 mod 4C} ↔ split d ≤ √ and d > √; symmetry d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d preserves class (since product ≡ 1 mod 4C ⇒ cofactor ≡ −1).
why: Already used (R even). Exploit further: the pairing is an involution with no fixed points (squares excluded) — parity of half-count R/2 has no forced value (EVIDENCE fair coin). Record as done.
first_step: Check whether a refined involution (e.g. using d ↔ (4C'p+1)/d across different C) produces a fixed-point-only-at-squares structure.

title: Rational points of bounded height on the ES fibre counted by circle method in 3 variables? (Not enough variables) → use delta method on 4uBC − u − B = p
connection: Heath-Brown delta method counts representations by forms in ≥ 3 variables ↔ 4uBC − u − B = p is a cubic in 3 variables (degenerate: linear in each).
why: Multilinear forms are amenable to the circle method with fewer variables because of their structure (e.g. Kloosterman refinement for xy − zw); R(p) ~ main term log² p might be derivable but error bounds are the issue.
first_step: Set up delta-method counting of 4uBC − u − B = p with smooth weights; compute the singular series and integral; compare with M₀.

title: Reverse the roles: for each modulus m = 4C, list p for which some d|4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 mod m — a 'dual sieve' table
connection: Duality between p and modulus ↔ the set S_C = {p : C-slice succeeds} is a union of residue classes mod d for d ≡ −1 mod 4C.
why: S_C is periodic only if bounded d; with unbounded d it's a 'multiplicative' set. ES ⟺ ∪_C S_C ⊇ primes. Studying S_C's density and correlations between S_C, S_{C'} is a sieve-dimension question.
first_step: Compute densities of S_C among primes ≤ 10⁷ for C ≤ 30 and correlation matrix corr(1_{S_C}, 1_{S_{C'}}); test near-independence.

title: Chen's theorem analogue: 4Cp+1 is P₂ for some small C
connection: Chen-type: for each p, some 4Cp+1 with C ≤ polylog is a product of ≤ 2 primes? ↔ unproven at fixed p; Chen is about averages over p.
why: Calibration: shows even 'some 4Cp+1 has a specific factorisation shape' at fixed p is out of reach of sieves — ES needs such fixed-p statements.
first_step: Record as barrier-calibration: list fixed-p statements about {4Cp+1 : C ≤ (log p)^A} that are known (e.g. not all prime? trivially: some is divisible by 3) and the strongest such.

title: Prime-modulus certificate family as a covering-by-primes question (Erdős covering with prime moduli)
connection: From previous: ES ⟸ p ∈ ∪_ℓ ∪_{C | (ℓ+1)/4} {−(4C)^{-1} mod ℓ} ↔ covering the primes by residue classes mod distinct primes ℓ with τ((ℓ+1)/4) classes each.
why: Covering systems with distinct prime moduli cannot cover ℤ when Σ (#classes)/ℓ converges or by Hough-type results; here Σ τ((ℓ+1)/4)/ℓ diverges — so covering is not excluded by density; but CRT construction evades finite subsets (B1).
first_step: Formalise 'prime-modulus covering with τ((ℓ+1)/4) classes per ℓ' and check whether known results (Erdős, Simpson–Zeilberger on coverings with prime moduli?) exclude covering all integers (likely yes via CRT) — then all primes is a different question (record).

title: Ternary divisor problem: R(p) as τ₃-like count of factorisations 4uBC − u − B = p
connection: R(p) counts restricted 'three-factor' decompositions ↔ τ₃(n) has mean (log n)²/2 — matches R's log² scale!
why: Natural to compare R(p) with τ₃ of a p-tied integer (e.g. τ₃(4p+…)); maybe R(p) = Σ over a bounded set of τ₃(N_i(p)) restricted to classes.
first_step: Compute correlation between R(p) and τ₃(p+1), τ₃(p+3), τ(…) etc. for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Multiplicative energy of the divisor set of 4Cp+1
connection: Additive/multiplicative energy of divisor sets ↔ structured sets cover subgroups faster.
why: Divisor sets have maximal multiplicative structure (they're 'cubes' {Π p_i^{e_i}}); covering results for 'generalised geometric progressions' in (ℤ/q)^× are precise.
first_step: Model divisors as a generalised GP with k generators; compute the minimal k for which such sets cover −1 mod q generically; compare with Ω(4Cp+1).

title: Hidden constraint: the product of all prime factors of 4Cp+1 is ≡ 1 mod 4C — subproduct ≡ −1 ⟺ complementary subproduct ≡ −1
connection: Since 4Cp+1 ≡ 1 mod 4C, d ≡ −1 ⟺ N/d ≡ −1: symmetric ↔ random-model must condition on total product ≡ 1.
why: Getting the conditioning right changes the predicted zero probability (repo's evenness). Sanity for all random models above.
first_step: Incorporate total-product conditioning into the subset-product model of the previous item and recompute probabilities.

title: Identities in terms of sum-of-two-squares representation p = a² + b²
connection: Every p ≡ 1 mod 4 is a² + b² ↔ search for x,y,z polynomial in (a,b) with 4/(a²+b²) = 1/x+1/y+1/z holding identically or on an explicit infinite set.
why: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities in n on residue classes containing squares, but identities in (a,b) are a different object: n = a²+b² is a polynomial in two variables. Does the obstruction persist? (Probably yes via specialisation b=0 giving squares a² — T1 obstruction! then need identities that avoid b = 0 ... record.)
first_step: Check: any identity in (a,b) specialises at b=0 to n = a² (odd square) where Type I/II solutions don't exist (T1) — so any (a,b)-identity must produce non-Type-I/II or fail at b = 0 — test whether rational functions with a pole at b = 0 escape this.

title: Quaternion / sums of four squares representations: many representations (r₄(p) = 8(p+1)) as thick object
connection: p = a²+b²+c²+d² has 8(p+1) representations — a thick object at p ↔ certificate extraction from some representation.
why: Thick object × extraction rule (G1): we need a rule mapping some 4-square representation to an ES certificate; the thick set has size ≍ p, so a rule with success probability ≫ 1/p per rep suffices.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, enumerate four-square representations and test simple formulas (e.g. x = (a²+b²)·k...) for producing certificates; record any rule with high success.

title: Binary quadratic forms of discriminant −4p·k: reduced forms as thick objects (class number h(−4pk) ≈ √p)
connection: Reduced forms (a,b,c) with b² − 4ac = −4pk are ≍ √p in number ↔ ES certificate from a form whose coefficients satisfy a congruence.
why: Type II: 4uBC − u − B = p resembles forms with ac − b²-type relations; a bijection between certificates and special reduced forms would place ES inside class-group combinatorics (where Gauss genus theory and Cohen–Lenstra live).
first_step: Search for (k, map) such that each ES Type II certificate gives a reduced form of discriminant −4pk with a ≡ … ; enumerate for p ≤ 10³.

title: 2-rank / Rédei symbols: 2-part of class groups and the −1-class event
connection: Is −1 a product of classes of prime factors: −1 is a 'genus character' object; Rédei matrices compute 4-ranks via Legendre symbols ↔ ES gate may be a Rédei-type matrix condition.
why: Smith's work on 4-ranks (Alexander Smith 2017, distribution of 2^∞ Selmer/class groups) handles exactly such Legendre-symbol matrices statistically.
first_step: Express 'some subproduct of primes q_i ≡ −1 mod 4C' using characters of (ℤ/4C)^× of 2-power order: a linear algebra condition over F_2 on (χ(q_i)) — compute the F_2 matrix for hard p.

title: Sterile points as profinite objects: x** in Ẑ where all ET identities fail
connection: A sterile point is a profinite integer (point of Ẑ) where no ET identity class contains it ↔ compactness: if no sterile prime-like points exist in the closure of primes in Ẑ, ES would follow from finitely many identities — contradicting B1 — so sterile points must exist; their structure is the obstruction.
why: Classifying sterile profinite points (are they all squares in Ẑ? i.e. locally squares everywhere) would connect B1 to T1: sterile ⟺ 'locally a square' would be a clean theorem.
first_step: Test: are all known sterile points squares in ℤ_ℓ for every ℓ checked? Compute for x** its square-class in ℤ_ℓ for ℓ ≤ 50.

title: Ultraproduct / nonstandard primes: a nonstandard counterexample p* in an ultrapower
connection: If ES is true, it's true in all models of PA where it's provable; a nonstandard model with ES failing at a nonstandard p* would show independence from weaker systems.
why: Model-theoretic view: properties of p* (e.g. p* ≡ square mod every standard m ⟹ p* a 'locally square' prime) mirror sterile points; a structural link between nonstandard counterexamples and profinite sterile points.
first_step: Write: p* nonstandard with no standard-size certificate ⟺ p* ∈ K (sterile set) for all standard moduli ⟹ p* is locally a square at all standard primes? Check logically.

title: Shifted-square obstruction: why squares fail Type I/II via Jacobi symbols, and 'almost squares' (p = m² + small) as stress tests
connection: T1 kills odd squares; primes p = m² + k for small k are 'close to squares' ↔ maybe low certificate counts for small k.
why: If R(m² + k)/M is systematically small for small k, T1's influence leaks to neighbours — a quantitative T1 continuity phenomenon to explain or exploit.
first_step: Compute R(p)/M_BM(p) for primes p = m² + k, k ∈ {4, 16, 36, …} (to keep p ≡ 1 mod 4) vs random p; m ≤ 10⁴.

title: Bateman–Horn densities for primes in hard families as test of B1-type evasion
connection: Bateman–Horn predicts counts of primes in polynomial families ↔ quantify how many primes in a family each certificate class covers.
why: Calibration for which polynomial families are ES-hardest.
first_step: For families f(m) = am² + bm + c generating primes ≡ 1 mod 840, compute average R(f(m))/M; find hardest family.

title: I3 extremal function: least u over primes, as a 'Jacobsthal function' analogue
connection: Least certifying interior endpoint u(p) ≤ 39 to 10⁹ ↔ Jacobsthal function j(m) (max gap in integers coprime to m) controls CRT evasions.
why: Jacobsthal bounds (Iwaniec: j(m) ≪ (log m)²) are pointwise results on CRT-evasion lengths — exactly the B1 cost question; growth of max u(p) should be compared with Jacobsthal-type predictions.
first_step: Model: to evade u ≤ U requires p avoiding certain classes mod moduli depending on u; compute the 'Jacobsthal-type' minimal evader size and compare with observed max u = 39 at 10⁹.

title: One-parameter form: R(p) = #{m ≡ 3 (mod 4) : r_p(m) | (m+1)/4}, r_p(m) = (−p mod m) (CHECKED p ≤ 1009)
connection: Trial form (4uC−1) | p+u with m = 4uC−1 forces u = r_p(m) (as 1 ≤ u < m), so R(p) counts moduli m ≡ 3 mod 4 whose ceiling-remainder divides (m+1)/4 ↔ a single-variable search over m.
why: A one-variable reformulation makes 'remainder of one integer modulo a running modulus' the whole problem — the classical object of the Dirichlet divisor problem and of p mod m statistics (Vinogradov), possibly opening Voronoi/exponential-sum tools.
first_step: Verified numerically (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check1.py, p ≤ 1009 incl. 409 → 0). Next: plot r_p(m)/m against m for hard p and study the arcs where r_p(m) is small (m just above p/q).

title: Consecutive-integer rigidity on (p, p+Q]: can a block of integers avoid all divisors ≡ −1 mod 4(n−p)?
connection: Shift form asks whether every block p+1..p+Q contains n with a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4(n−p) ↔ Erdős–Selfridge/Sylvester–Schur-type theorems on prime factors of consecutive integers are pointwise.
why: The catch (recorded): each n needs a divisor in a class tied to its own offset, so CRT can make p+B avoid it for B ≤ Q (B1); but for B ~ √p the condition becomes 'n = p+B has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4B in [4B−1, ...]', i.e. a factorisation near-square — Sylvester–Schur-type large-prime-factor results could interact.
first_step: Compute for hard p the distribution of contributing B (as fraction of √p); if many come from B ≍ √p, study whether 'consecutive integers near p have near-square factorisations with prescribed class' has literature (search 'divisors close to square root of consecutive integers').

title: Ask Christian Elsholtz which ideas he tried and abandoned
connection: Elsholtz (Graz) co-authored ET 2013 and many unit-fraction papers ↔ unpublished negative results.
why: Experts' graveyard of failed approaches is the cheapest way to avoid repeats and may contain half-working ideas.

connection: The campaign's meta-finding (no known every-n theorem with polylog main term and no averaging) ↔ MO community may know counterexamples.
why: A single counterexample theorem would be a method precedent; a well-posed MO question is cheap and high-information.

title: Polymath-style open collaboration on a bounded sub-problem (e.g. 4^s + 297 family)
connection: Polymath projects (Tao, Gowers) solved bounded problems by crowd effort ↔ open thin families in repo.
why: A well-scoped, verifiable target with computational components suits crowd/AI collaboration.

connection: Repo's Elsholtz–Tao log-log removal claims need expert scrutiny ↔ submitting to a journal or arXiv.

connection: Each barrier theorem has stated scope; scopes have complements (hatches) ↔ enumerate hatch × thick-object pairs mechanically.

connection: A ↔ B ↔ C chains: ES ↔ three cubes ↔ (Heath-Brown) density heuristics; ES ↔ Markoff ↔ Chen's theorem; ES ↔ HKRS ↔ Rickards–Stange.
why: Second-order analogies sometimes connect to solved problems not linked directly.

title: Meta: ES-strength statements ranked by 'how much stronger than ES' — look for the weakest ES-implying statement
connection: I3_𝒞, (★)∪b=1, ES₅, … are ES-implying ↔ which is weakest (most likely provable) while still implying ES.
why: Explicit lattice of ES-implying statements by inclusion of certificate sets clarifies where to aim.

title: Music: Egyptian fractions as rhythms (tuplets) and polyrhythm decompositions
connection: Splitting a measure of length 4/p into three unit-length subdivisions ↔ polyrhythmic tuplets in music notation.
why: Outreach and pattern-hearing; sonification of certificate counts over p could reveal periodicities the eye misses.
first_step: Sonify R(p) over primes ≤ 10⁵ (pitch = R/M) and listen for regular structure; or render tuplet patterns.

title: Multiplicative Egyptian variant: 1 + 4/p = (1+1/x)(1+1/y)(1+1/z)
connection: Products of superparticulars ↔ a 'multiplicative ES'.
why: A sibling problem with different arithmetic; if it has known failures or a proof, it calibrates ES-type behaviour.

connection: The Rhind 2/n table chooses specific decompositions (Gillings' rules) ↔ ES 4/n choices; ancient heuristics = small-denominator preference.

connection: Hundreds of connections with tags ↔ cluster and find under-explored tag combinations.

connection: Citation graph forward search ↔ new techniques applied to ES-adjacent problems since 2024.

why: Outreach lever; not mathematics.

connection: Repo has many equivalent forms (divisor, SL₂, words, lattices, quaternions, theta) ↔ a single conversion library lets each new idea be tested in every form.

connection: Forecasting competitions surface the best models of the count's fluctuation ↔ quantifies how much structure is unexplained.

title: Meta: 'one-sided lower tail' theorem hunt across all of mathematics
connection: FRONTIER: needed form is R(p) ≥ εM at every p ↔ search for any theorem of shape 'count ≥ ε·mean for every member' with polylog mean.
why: Repo found none; widening search to combinatorics (e.g. Ramsey-type guaranteed counts, Kővári–Sós–Turán, supersaturation) may produce precedents: supersaturation theorems give pointwise lower tails for counts!
first_step: Look at supersaturation (Erdős–Simonovits): once density exceeds threshold, the number of copies is ≥ c·expected — pointwise in the host structure. Ask whether ES's thick object admits a supersaturation formulation.

title: Topological degree / index argument: a map whose degree counts certificates mod 2
connection: Brouwer degree gives existence when degree ≠ 0 ↔ ES certificate as a zero of a map from a disk/torus built from p.
why: Degree arguments are the continuous analogue of parity involutions; discretised (Sperner's lemma) they give combinatorial existence.
first_step: Search for a Sperner-type labelling of a triangulated region (indexed by (u,C) or (x,y)) where fully-labelled cells are ES certificates and the boundary labelling forces odd count.

title: Borsuk–Ulam / necklace splitting as existence via equivariant topology
connection: Necklace splitting existence via Borsuk–Ulam ↔ ES as fair division of something?
why: Curiosity; equivariant topology proves existence without construction (PPA-type).
first_step: Look for a ℤ/2-equivariant map whose zeros are ES certificates (e.g. using symmetry y ↔ z).

title: Category-theoretic: ES as existence of a morphism in a category of 'Egyptian decompositions'
connection: Operads/categories of fraction splittings ↔ composition of decompositions.
why: Probably vacuous, but an operadic view might show ES is about generators of an operad being 'enough'.
first_step: Define operad O(k) = k-term decompositions; check whether 3-term decompositions of 4/p arise as composites of 2-term of other fractions (they do: 4/p = 1/x + (4x−p)/(px)).

title: Knot theory / linking numbers: Legendre symbols as linking numbers of primes (arithmetic topology)
connection: Mazur–Morishita arithmetic topology: primes ↔ knots, Legendre symbol ↔ linking number mod 2, Rédei symbol ↔ Milnor triple linking ↔ T1 obstruction is a reciprocity (linking) statement.
why: If T1 is a 'linking number' obstruction, the prime case might be a 'link is not split' statement — Milnor invariants at higher order could give finer obstructions or non-obstructions.
first_step: Express the T1 obstruction as a Legendre-symbol identity and translate into linking numbers à la Morishita; check whether Rédei triple symbols appear in the 4-rank analogue.

title: Waring-type problems in finite groups: −1 as a product of elements from a set
connection: Waring problems in groups (every element is a product of k elements from a conjugacy class) ↔ −1 as subproduct.
why: Abelian case reduces to zero-sum; noted for completeness.
first_step: Merge with zero-sum items; no separate step (check abelian Waring results for subset products).

title: Erdős primitive set conjecture (Lichtman 2022) as structure for failures of related numerator problems
connection: For m/n problems with exceptions (m = 8), the minimal exceptions form a primitive set ↔ Σ 1/(n log n) ≤ that of primes (Lichtman).
why: For m ≥ 5 exceptions, primitive-set bounds constrain how exceptions are distributed; tells whether exceptions are 'prime-like'.
first_step: List minimal 8/n exceptions ≤ 10⁶ and compute Σ 1/(n log n); compare with primes' value.

title: Khinchine flatness theorem for convex pieces of the certificate region
connection: A convex body with no lattice points has bounded lattice width (Khinchine flatness). The hyperbolic certificate region splits into convex pieces, so if ES fails at p, every convex piece is lattice-free and thin in some lattice direction.
why: Flatness-type arguments are the geometry-of-numbers native way to derive structure from emptiness. Here 'thin in a direction' might contradict the known shape of the region.
first_step: For a fixed (u,C) box, the certificate set is a coset of a lattice of determinant ~ uC; apply flatness to decide when a box must contain a coset point (it must if box is large relative to modulus) — computes 'guaranteed' boxes and shows the tied-modulus problem.

title: Local-global principle for systems of linear divisibilities (Lipshitz/Bel'tyukov)
connection: Existential (ℤ,+,|) theory satisfies a local-global principle: a system of divisibilities among linear forms is solvable iff solvable mod all primes powers (with conditions) ↔ ES Type II: (4uC − 1) | p + u is a divisibility between non-linear forms; but u fixed gives linear in C.
why: If ES (or a sufficient condition) could be phrased as a system of linear divisibilities with finitely many unknowns, a local-global principle would decide it — and locally ES is always solvable!
first_step: Find: with u fixed as a parameter, is '∃C: (4uC − 1) | p + u' a linear divisibility system? It is: ∃C,k: k(4uC − 1) = p + u — non-linear (kC). Search for a linear-divisibility sufficient condition, e.g. '∃C: (4C − 1) | (p + 1)' (u=1): linear in C! Then local-global says solvable iff locally solvable — but local solvability of 4C − 1 | p + 1 as C varies ⟺ p+1 has a divisor ≡ 3 mod 4 … check the theorem's precise statement (it may need the divisor to be a linear form in the variables on both sides).

title: Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa (Gowers–Green–Manners–Tao) for divisor quotient sets
connection: PFR (Marton) over 𝔽₂ⁿ and torsion-free groups: small doubling ⇒ covered by few cosets of a subgroup; the set of prime factors of N mod e generates the ES quotient set.
why: If the ES quotient set has small doubling it is near a subgroup H, and −1 ∈ Q reduces to −1 ∈ H — a cleaner (parity-like) test.
first_step: Measure doubling |Q·Q|/|Q| of divisor quotient sets at hard primes; when small, identify H and check −1 ∉ H cases.

title: Dimension theory: Hausdorff dimension of p-adic limits of failing primes (if infinitely many)
connection: If infinitely many (★)-failures existed, their closure in Ẑ is a compact set ↔ its dimension measures 'how sterile'.
why: Gives a quantitative profinite object for (★) failures (which are known to exist: 14 ≤ 10¹⁰); compare with sterile set K.
first_step: Compute residues of the 14 (★)-failing primes mod small moduli and see whether they lie in a small profinite set (e.g. all squares mod 3·5·7·…).

title: Teichmüller / mapping class group dynamics: SL₂(ℤ) words as Dehn twists on a torus
connection: SL₂(ℤ) = mapping class group of the torus; ES₅ words as products of Dehn twists ↔ curves on a torus with intersection numbers tied to p.
why: Geometric reformulation: ES(p) ⟺ some simple closed curves with prescribed intersection numbers exist — curve-complex combinatorics might give existence arguments.
first_step: Translate an ES₅ word [[a,p],[c,d]] into a pair of simple closed curves on the torus with intersection number p; examine the constraint 'c ∈ 4ℕ, a ≡ d ≡ −1 mod c' geometrically.

title: Combinatorics on words: the Christoffel word / Sturmian structure of continued fraction certificates
connection: Christoffel words encode rationals a/b and their CF ↔ ES₅ CF length ≤ 3 words.
why: Word combinatorics (palindromes, standard factorisation of Christoffel words) may produce a combinatorial proof of existence of a short factorisation.
first_step: Compute Christoffel words of 4/p and of certificate rationals; look for standard factorisations corresponding to ES solutions.

title: Small-q pieces: B = q small ⟹ condition u | p + B with u ≡ −p mod B, i.e. divisors of p+1, p+2, … in classes
connection: For small B the C-equation reads: p + B has a divisor u ≡ … Actually p + B = u(4BC − 1) ⟹ the cofactor 4BC − 1 ≡ −1 mod 4B divides p + B ↔ the shift form at small B.
why: Small-B slices are 'divisors of p+B for B ≤ K in class −1 mod 4B': these are K concrete integers next to p. The union over B ≤ K gives a fixed menu (B1 applies), but how fast does coverage grow with K?
first_step: Compute fraction of primes ≤ 10⁸ covered by B ≤ K slices for K = 1..100; fit coverage curve.

title: Iterated Landau–Ramanujan: B-slice fails iff all prime factors of (p+B) avoid a set of classes mod 4B — a 'multiplicatively constrained' integer
connection: Generalising: slice B fails iff the subgroup/subset-product structure of prime factors of p+B avoids −1 mod 4B ↔ for B where (ℤ/4B)^× has a quadratic character separating −1, failure ⟸ all prime factors in its kernel: Landau–Ramanujan-type density (log)^{−1/2}.
why: Each slice fails with probability ~ (log p)^{−δ_B}; joint failure of K slices ~ product if independent — gives a clean heuristic exponent for 'K slices all fail' and connects to sieve dimension.
first_step: Compute δ_B (the density exponent of slice-failure) for B ≤ 30 theoretically (via Chebotarev in (ℤ/4B)^×) and compare with data.

title: Triangles with integer exradii and inradius n/4
connection: For any triangle 1/r = 1/r_a + 1/r_b + 1/r_c, and every positive triple (r_a,r_b,r_c) is realised by a unique triangle (Ravi substitution). So ES(n) ⇔ there is a triangle with integer exradii and inradius exactly n/4.
why: An exact, unrestricted Euclidean-geometry form. Triangle geometry has its own integrality theory (Heronian triangles, integer exradii), and a Heronian strengthening gives testable variants.
first_step: Verify the 'any positive exradii ⟹ triangle' claim; then compute, over ES solutions for p ≤ 10⁴, how often e₂(x,y,z) is a perfect square (rational semiperimeter) and search literature for 'integer exradii triangles'.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Cubic polynomial T²(T − s) + e(T − n/4) with three positive integer roots
connection: x,y,z are the roots of T³ − sT² + e₂T − e₃ with 4e₃ = n·e₂, i.e. of 4T²(T−s) + e₂(4T − n). So ES(n) ⇔ for some (s, e₂) this cubic splits completely over ℤ with positive roots.
why: It is a 'totally split specialisation' problem for a 2-parameter family of cubics. Hilbert-irreducibility counting and 'polynomials with many split values' (Schinzel-type) are the native field.
first_step: Compute the Galois group over Q(s,e) (generic S₃) and the discriminant surface. Check whether split points lie on a subvariety with a parametrisation (they should be exactly U_n).

title: Witten-index analogue: a deformation-invariant signed count of certificates
connection: In physics an index (signed count of ground states) is invariant under deformations, so it can be computed at an easy point ↔ a signed ES count depending only on p mod M would be computable from small primes.
why: A deformation-invariant signed count nonzero on the hard classes would prove existence; T1 forces it to vanish at odd squares, which constrains the candidate (it must 'see' squareness, e.g. through Jacobi symbols).
first_step: Using the signed-count data from the previous item, test which signed sums S(p) are periodic in p (depend only on p mod M); any periodic nonzero one on all p ≡ 1 mod 840 classes is a candidate.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Ramanujan-sum expansion of the trial indicator: 1[m | N] = (1/m) Σ_{d|m} c_d(N)
connection: R(p) = Σ_{(u,C)} (1/m) Σ_{d|m} c_d(p+u) with m = 4uC−1 ↔ Ramanujan–Fourier expansion separates main term (d = 1) and oscillation (Ramanujan sums c_d(p+u)).
why: Ramanujan sums are explicit; regrouping by d gives R(p) = Σ_d (Σ_{m ≡ 0 (d)} …) c_d(·) — possibly revealing a d-level where cancellation fails exactly at squares (T1).
first_step: Compute the contribution of each d ≤ 100 to R(p) for hard p and for odd squares; see which d carry the T1 cancellation.

title: Small-solution strengthening: ES with max(x,y,z) ≤ p·(log p)^A — when does it first fail?
connection: Strengthenings with size bounds ↔ certificates with small C (C ≤ polylog) correspond to small denominators.
why: Determines the 'natural size' of certificates; if a polylog-bounded version holds to 10⁹ with small A, it's a sharper conjecture with possible structure; if it fails, failures are informative.
first_step: For primes ≤ 10⁸, compute min over solutions of max(x,y,z)/p and record max over p; fit growth vs log p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Near-miss gap g(p) = min{4/p − (1/x+1/y+1/z) > 0} and its distribution
connection: Egyptian under-approximations ↔ ES ⟺ gap 0 attainable; the minimal positive gap measures how 'close' p is to failure in a continuous sense.
why: If hard primes have systematically larger minimal positive gaps, gap-based potential functions might guide search or reveal a continuous invariant.
first_step: Compute g(p)·p³ (or appropriately normalised) for primes ≤ 10⁵ restricted to small denominators; compare hard vs easy primes.

title: First-term offset k: x = (p + 4k + 3)/4 and the binary remainder (4k+3)/(px)
connection: Choosing x = ⌈p/4⌉ + k leaves (4k+3)/(p·x) to be written as 2 unit fractions (Rav criterion: divisors d₁,d₂ of p·x with (4k+3) | d₁ + d₂) ↔ a 1-parameter family of binary problems.
why: Gives a simple 'search depth' measure k*(p); a bound k*(p) ≤ (log p)^A would be an ES-strength conjecture with a clean shape for probabilistic modelling (each k succeeds with probability ~ τ(px)/(4k+3)).
first_step: Compute k*(p) for primes ≤ 10⁸ and its max growth; model success probability per k via divisor counts of px.

title: Transport between nearby primes: 4/p = 4/q + 4(q−p)/(pq)
connection: If q close to p has a solution and the correction 4(q−p)/(pq) combines nicely ↔ continuity-type arguments (rare in arithmetic).
why: Likely dead (corrections need extra terms), but checking whether 'ES(q) + small structure ⟹ ES(p)' for q − p ∈ {4, 8, 12} ever works is cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, test whether some solution of 4/q (q = p+4k prime) shares two denominators with a solution of 4/p; record frequency.

title: Bernstein 1962 (Crelle) polynomial families for 4/n as historical identity catalogue
connection: L. Bernstein's 1962 paper on m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z (esp. m = 4) gives families of solutions ↔ repo's identity tables.
why: Cross-check that the repo's identity catalogue includes Bernstein's families; may contain families on non-residue-class sets.
first_step: Check whether 'L. Bernstein, J. Reine Angew. Math. 211 (1962)' is the right citation and extract its families.

title: Mordell's 'Diophantine Equations' (1969) chapter on 4/n: his stated obstructions and hopes
connection: Mordell's book section where the mod-840 reduction appears ↔ his remarks on why identities can't cover squares.
why: Primary-source check of the Mordell–Schinzel narrative; might contain an overlooked suggestion.
first_step: Read the relevant section of Mordell's book and record his remarks verbatim (with page).

title: Covering-radius analogy: CRT evasion as covering radius of a 'certificate code'
connection: Residue classes avoided by an adversarial p ↔ a word at maximal distance from a code; B1 = covering radius > 0 for any finite code.
why: Coding theory has tight covering-radius bounds; might quantify 'how many certificate classes needed to cover primes ≤ X' as a function of X.
first_step: Define code C_B = set of certificate class vectors for moduli ≤ B; compute empirically the fraction of residue vectors not covered as B grows (ties to set-cover item).

title: Divisors ≡ −1 mod m of numbers ≡ 1 mod m: forced when the number has a 'twisted' structure (e.g. N = a² − b² with a ≡ 0, b ≡ 1?)
connection: If N = (A − 1)(A + 1)/k-type factorisations with A ≡ 0 mod m, then A − 1 ≡ −1 mod m is a divisor ↔ ES: 4Cp+1 = (A−1)(A+1)/… would need 4Cp + 1 + 1 = A²·… hmm: 4Cp+1 = d·d' with d ≡ d' ≡ −1 mod 4C; d = A − 1, d' = A' − 1.
why: Clarifies: ES Type II ⟺ 4Cp+1 = (4uC − 1)(4BC − 1); writing as difference of squares, 4Cp+1 = ((d+d')/2)² − ((d−d')/2)² — a representation as difference of squares with constraints mod 4C on the sum — a quadratic-form representation question.
first_step: Rewrite ES Type II as: 4Cp + 1 = X² − Y² with X ≡ −1 (mod 4C)... (X = (d+d')/2 ≡ −1 mod 2C) and test whether this binary-quadratic view yields anything beyond divisor form.

title: Quadratic sieve / CFRAC structure: smooth values of X² − 4Cp − 1 as a thick object at p
connection: QS finds many smooth X² − N (thick object of size ~ N^{1/2} smooth values per sieve interval) ↔ combine smooth relations to get a factorisation of N with prescribed class of factors?
why: Combining relations yields congruences of squares, i.e. a nontrivial factor gcd(X − Y, N) — whose class mod 4C is uncontrolled. But one can sieve over C as well (many N): a 2D thick object.
first_step: Prototype: for C ≤ 50 run a tiny QS on 4Cp+1 and record the classes mod 4C of the factors found; is −1 hit at least as often as random?

title: Cunningham-chain-like structures: p with 4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1, … all prime or class-constrained
connection: Simultaneous primality of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ K (Dickson-type tuple) ↔ the B1 construction of hard primes.
why: Searching for primes with long runs of prime 4Cp+1 gives naturally hard test cases for (★) (not for ES itself).
first_step: Search p ≤ 10¹² for the longest run C = 1..K with every 4Cp+1 prime; compute R(p) and full ES count for the record holders.

title: Symmetric-function view: e₂/e₃ = 4/n and the power-sum moments of solutions
connection: For solutions (x,y,z), power sums p_k relate to e_i via Newton ↔ distribution of (x/p, y/p, z/p) shape statistics.
why: Shape statistics (e.g. ratios y/x) of all solutions across p might show a limiting distribution consistent with the main-term density; deviations hint at structure.
first_step: Compute the empirical distribution of (log y/log p, log z/log p) over all solutions for p ≤ 10⁵ and compare with the predicted density from parametrisations.

title: Induction on p via 'certificate inheritance' along chains p → (p+1)/2 or similar
connection: Look for maps φ on primes with φ(p) < p such that ES(φ(p)) plus local data ⟹ ES(p) ↔ a descent/induction proof.
why: Most such maps fail (ES isn't hereditary) but checking simple candidate maps on data is cheap; a map that works empirically to 10⁸ would be surprising and informative.
first_step: Test candidate maps φ(p) ∈ {(p+3)/4, (p−1)/4 odd part, largest prime factor of p+3} for 'certificate transfer' rules on primes ≤ 10⁶.

title: Kernel-method / Gaussian process regression for R(p)/M(p) with arithmetic kernels
connection: Kernels k(p,q) based on shared residues (e.g. Σ_m w_m 1[p ≡ q mod m]) ↔ GP regression predicts R(p).
why: Learned kernel weights w_m identify the moduli that carry structure; residual variance quantifies randomness.
first_step: Fit a GP with arithmetic kernel on 10⁴ primes; inspect learned w_m.

title: Sylvester 1884 coin problem as the t = 1 ancestor of ES words: history link Sylvester ↔ Erdős–Straus
connection: Sylvester's Educational Times result (largest non-representable = uv − u − v) is the t = 1 case of the ES word shape tuv − u − v ↔ ES is a 'Sylvester-type' question about which primes are k-Frobenius numbers.
why: A historical bridge; the Frobenius-number literature (Ramírez Alfonsín's monograph) might have studied the inverse problem 'given n, find semigroups with g_k = n'.
first_step: Read Ramírez Alfonsín, 'The Diophantine Frobenius Problem' (OUP 2005) index for 'inverse problem' and 'k-Frobenius'; note any result on which integers are Frobenius numbers of 2-generated semigroups with multiplicity constraints.

title: Apéry sets and the gap structure of ⟨u,B⟩: p as the maximal element of a 'level-(4C−1)' Apéry-type set
connection: Numerical semigroup S = ⟨u,B⟩: the set of n with exactly k representations has a known structure (shifted Apéry sets) ↔ p must be the top element of the k = 4C − 1 layer.
why: Semigroup-theoretic language may let one treat (u,B) as an unknown semigroup and p as a forced invariant — e.g. counting semigroups of given 'k-Frobenius number' (an inverse problem) could have a generating-function solution.
first_step: Compute, for n ≤ 10⁴, the number of pairs (u,B, t) with g_t(u,B) = n, t ≡ 0 mod 4, and compare with R(n); then look for a semigroup-enumeration generating function.

title: Representation-count symmetry N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t on [0, g_t] (CHECKED): an involution attached to every ES word
connection: For coprime u,v and g_t = tuv − u − v, the denumerant satisfies N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t for all 0 ≤ n ≤ g_t (generalising symmetry of ⟨u,v⟩ at t = 1) ↔ every ES word p = g_t(u,v) carries the involution n ↦ p − n on representation data.
why: An explicit involution attached to each certificate is the raw material for windmill/parity arguments (G1 parity column); here the involution lives on representations of integers below p rather than on certificates — a different thick object (size ≍ p).
first_step: Verified for u,v ≤ 8, t ≤ 4 (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check3.py). Next: look for a global involution on pairs (n, representation) over all (u,v) whose fixed points correspond to certificates of p; test fixed-point parity on p < 10³.

title: Barvinok short generating functions for ES certificates up to height B
connection: Barvinok's algorithm encodes lattice points of rational polyhedra as short rational generating functions. ES certificates at fixed level C are lattice points in a union of polyhedra intersected with a hyperbola, which needs a polyhedral approximation.
why: Short generating functions allow evaluation of counts mod 2, character-weighted sums, etc., quickly. This is a computational-native route to exact sign sums.
first_step: Approximate the region by polyhedra (dyadic pieces), compute the Barvinok representation (LattE), and test evaluating weighted sign sums for p ~ 10⁶.

title: Grechuk's systematic catalogue of Diophantine equations: where does 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) sit?
connection: B. Grechuk's book/papers order polynomial Diophantine equations by size and record solved/open status ↔ ES family and its nearest solved neighbours by 'size'.
why: Nearby equations in a size-ordered catalogue that were solved suggest methods; ES-like families with parameter n might appear among his open problems.
first_step: Check whether Grechuk, 'Polynomial Diophantine Equations: A Systematic Approach' (Springer, 2024) exists as cited, and look up equations of the form axyz = n(xy+yz+zx) or xyz − x − y = n there.

title: Mining the repo's ~470 brainstorm memos for dangling 'first steps' never executed
connection: Many memos end with proposed cheap tests ↔ some were never run.
why: Executing forgotten cheap tests is high-yield housekeeping.
first_step: Grep BRAINSTORM/*.md for 'first step', 'cheap test', 'TODO', 'next:' and cross-check against data/ and scripts/ for evidence of execution; list unexecuted ones.

title: Real cyclotomic subfield ℚ(ζ_{4C})⁺: divisors split there but inert/ramified-ish in the CM extension
connection: From previous: d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) ⟺ d ≡ ±1 (split in ℚ(ζ_{4C})⁺ for primes) and not +1 ↔ the CM extension ℚ(ζ_{4C})/ℚ(ζ_{4C})⁺ and its relative class group / Stickelberger.
why: CM-field arithmetic (relative class numbers, Stickelberger) is a rigid R-type toolbox; ES's '−1 not +1' distinction is a CM-type sign, possibly linked to the BM character χ_{−4uB}.
first_step: For small C, express R(p)'s C-slice via characters of Gal(ℚ(ζ_{4C})/ℚ) odd under complex conjugation; check whether the odd characters' contribution is a relative-class-number-like quantity.

title: Weighted projective line: ES(★) ⟺ O(p) ≅ ω ⊗ π*O_{P¹}(4C) on the stacky curve P(u,B)
connection: On P(u,B) one has h⁰(O(n)) = N(n; u,B) (denumerant), ω = O(−u−B), and O(uB) = π*O(1) from the coarse P¹ ↔ p = 4C·uB − u − B is exactly deg(ω) + 4C·deg(π*O(1)).
why: Puts (★) into algebraic-geometry language where Riemann–Roch/Serre duality on stacky curves is the Popoviciu formula and the denumerant symmetry N(n)+N(g_t−n) = t is Serre duality. Type I might then correspond to stacky curves with three orbifold points — a uniform geometric home for both types.
first_step: Verify the Serre-duality derivation of N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t on P(u,B); then test whether Type I certificates correspond to line bundles of the form ω ⊗ (pullback) on P(a,b,c)-type stacky curves (three orbifold points).

title: Torus knots T(u,B): 2g(T(u,B)) = (u−1)(B−1) and the (★) relation p + 1 = 2g + (4C−1)uB
connection: The semigroup ⟨u,B⟩ is the semigroup of the plane-curve singularity x^u = y^B (link = torus knot); its conductor is 2g = (u−1)(B−1) ↔ (★): p = 4CuB − u − B ⟺ p + 1 − 2g(T(u,B)) = (4C − 1)uB.
why: Links (★) to singularity theory (Milnor number μ = 2g) and knot invariants (Alexander polynomial exponents = semigroup); speculative, but singularity theory has deformation/adjacency structures that might act on certificates.
first_step: Check the identity and ask whether the condition '(p + 1 − μ) ≡ 0 mod uB with quotient ≡ 3 mod 4' has a meaning for the Milnor fibre or for the Alexander polynomial evaluated at roots of unity.

title: ES certificates for record-size Mordell-hard primes (Proth/generalised Fermat primes in square classes mod 840)
connection: Find a known huge prime p (≥ 10⁵ digits) in a Mordell-hard class and search small certificates (4uC−1) | p + u by trial division ↔ ES verified at a 'random' gigantic prime.
why: Cheap, publicity-friendly, and an adversarial data point at astronomically large p (does a small certificate always exist? the model predicts ≍ log² p ≈ 10¹¹ certificates but small ones are what is cheap to find).
first_step: Take primes from the Top-20 Proth list, reduce mod 840 to find one in a hard class, and run trial division of p + u by 4uC − 1 for uC ≤ 10⁶ using GMP.

title: Self-similarity: does R(p) for p in the hardest classes look like R of smaller primes rescaled (renormalisation in modulus)?
connection: Compare the distribution of R(p)/M(p) within p ≡ 1 mod 840 with that within p ≡ 1 mod 840·k for growing k ↔ scale-invariance of difficulty.
why: If deeper residue restriction keeps reducing R/M without bound, extremely structured primes could be dangerous (quantifies B1 drift); if it saturates, ES is robust.
first_step: Compute mean R/M over primes ≤ 10⁸ in nested classes p ≡ 1 mod 840, 840·11, 840·11·13, … (all-QR classes) and plot vs modulus.

title: Generating 'ES-like' random problems with tunable expected count to locate the existence threshold empirically
connection: Synthetic problems: replace p by random integers in classes and restrict menu so expected count μ varies ↔ empirical P(no solution) as a function of μ.
why: Gives an empirical law P(0) ≈ f(μ) for ES-shaped problems; plugging μ ≈ M_BM(p) estimates the risk at any p and calibrates the (J)97 zero law independently of siblings.
first_step: For random odd n ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁸, count (★) certificates with u,B ≤ U for varying U (thus varying μ) and fit P(R_U = 0) vs μ.

title: ES words are exactly Frobenius numbers of glued semigroups ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩
connection: Johnson/Brauer–Shockley gluing gives g(⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩) = t·g(u,v) + (t−1)(u+v) = tuv − u − v when gcd(u,v) = gcd(t,u+v) = 1 (checked by brute force on 488 triples, scripts/z52b_signature_frob_check.py). So the (★) line (words p = 4C·u·B − u − B, which implies ES but itself fails at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰) ⟺ p is the Frobenius number of a 3-generated numerical semigroup ⟨4Cu, 4CB, u+B⟩; for (★) words gcd(4C, u+B) = gcd(4C, p) = 1 automatically. The other ES word slices (coordinate in 8ℤ − p, or the 4ℤ coordinate not in the t slot) need a different semigroup family.
why: Rosales–García-Sánchez–García-García–Jiménez Madrid proved every positive integer is the Frobenius number of SOME 3-generated semigroup: the (★) slice of ES is a restriction of a solved universality theorem to a structured sub-family (complete intersections glued from a 2-generated piece); finding semigroup families for the other ES slices would give a full semigroup reformulation of ES.
first_step: Read Rosales et al. (Math. Scand. 94 (2004) 5–12): which 3-generator family does their construction use for odd g, and can it be forced into the shape ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ with 4 | t?

title: Rødseth/Greenberg 3-generator Frobenius algorithm vs. ES₅ continued-fraction length
connection: The Rødseth algorithm computes g(a,b,c) via a negative-continued-fraction (Euclid) expansion of a ratio mod a; for ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ that expansion is short. Compare with λ(p) ≤ 3 (F17).
why: If the Rødseth expansion of the glued semigroup is exactly the length-3 negative CF of the ES₅ form, the semigroup literature (Kannan, Ramírez Alfonsín) becomes a dictionary for ES₅.
first_step: Run Rødseth's algorithm symbolically on ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ and record the CF; check against the BOARD2_SLATE ES₅ slice definitions.

title: Genus/Sylvester count of the ES semigroup as a second invariant attached to each witness
connection: Each ES witness (t,u,v) gives a symmetric semigroup S with genus (gaps) (g+1)/2 = (p+1)/2 and an Apéry set of size min generator; these invariants are fixed by p, so ES asks for a semigroup with prescribed Frobenius number and prescribed shape.
why: Counting numerical semigroups by genus is a mature field (Kaplan, Zhai's Fibonacci-like growth); ES asks for one member of a structured subclass among ~φ^g semigroups of genus g — a sparse-subfamily existence question.
first_step: Check OEIS/semigroup tables (e.g. GAP package numericalsgps) for counts of complete-intersection semigroups with given Frobenius number.

title: Shi (2026): local-global also false for generalized circle packings — more reciprocity-obstruction templates
connection: Extension of HKRS to four further packing types (J. Number Theory 2026). Each new packing type is a new data point for 'which orbit structures admit reciprocity obstructions'.
why: A classification of when reciprocity obstructions arise could decide whether ES-type word sets beyond Type I/II can carry them.
first_step: Check whether Shi gives a general criterion (e.g. existence of a quadratic form invariant mod squares along the orbit).

title: Ford-style 'anatomy' model: which levels C can host a witness
connection: A random N with k = ω(N) prime factors has ≤ 2^k divisors; their residues mod 4C hit the class −1 with probability ≈ 1 − exp(−2^k/φ(4C)). With ω ≈ log log p, only levels C ≲ (log p)^{log 2} are 'likely' — an anatomy prediction for where ES witnesses live (cf. Ford's H(x,y,2y)).
why: Ford solved the divisor-in-interval problem via the anatomy of prime factors; the analogous divisor-in-class statistic would give a sharp prediction for the distribution of the smallest working level.
first_step: Compute, for hard primes p ≤ 10⁹, the smallest C with a (★) witness and compare its distribution with (log p)^{log 2}; regress on ω(4Cp+1).

title: Maier's matrix method for ES: build primes where the Poisson model under-predicts failures
connection: Maier showed the Cramér model fails in short intervals because small-prime biases correlate events. For ES, choose p in progressions modulo products of small primes (p a square mod many ℓ) and measure R(p) relative to M_BM(p).
why: If R(p)/M_BM(p) is systematically smaller on such 'Maier primes', the one-sided H⁻_BM is at risk; if not, it is evidence the BM normalisation already absorbs the Maier effect.
first_step: Take primes p ≡ 1 mod 840·∏ℓ with p a QR mod every ℓ ≤ 50, p ≈ 10¹²; compute R(p)/M_BM(p) vs. random primes of same size.

title: Least quadratic non-residue: exists iff n is not a square — the exact reciprocity shape of T1
connection: For n > 1, some prime ℓ has (n/ℓ) = −1 iff n is not a square; the least one is ≪ log²n under GRH (Ankeny/Bach) and ≪ n^{1/(4√e)+ε} unconditionally. ES's BM layer is pointwise free iff n is not a square (SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9 Prop 2.2).
why: This is the only fully solved problem whose failure set is exactly the squares; ES's remaining difficulty is the 'one more character' step beyond it.
first_step: Quantify: for hard primes ≤ 10⁹ correlate ℓ(p) (least non-residue) with R(p) and with the smallest working level; check whether R(p) is small exactly when ℓ(p) is large.

title: Crocker: infinitely many odd n ≠ p + 2^a + 2^b — polylog expected count yet infinitely many failures
connection: Expected count ≍ log n (polylog), like ES, but Crocker exhibits infinitely many exceptions. Shares F04, F24w.
why: Key calibration: a polylog expected count alone does not imply finitely many failures. Learn what structure Crocker's exceptions exploit and check that ES cannot be attacked the same way.
first_step: Check whether Crocker's exceptions come from a covering-type construction (e.g. n = 2^{2^m} − 1) and whether an ES analogue (n in a sparse algebraic family) has abnormally small R(n).

title: Tunnell-type criterion: a ternary-form count whose vanishing ⇔ ES failure
connection: Tunnell expresses the congruent number property, conditionally on BSD, via the difference of counts of two ternary forms (via Waldspurger). An ES analogue would be an identity N₋(p) = (count of form Q₁) − ½(count of Q₂)-type.
why: It is the textbook example of a sign/existence problem translated exactly to ternary-form counts. SIGN_IDENTITY rules out holomorphic forms by size, but a Tunnell-shaped identity for a related 0/1 quantity (not the full count) is not excluded.
first_step: Search for ternary forms Q₁,Q₂ with det ∝ 4·2^k whose representation counts at p correlate with the indicator [λ(p) ≤ 3] or with N₋(p) mod 2.

title: ES ⇒ m/n is a sum of m − 1 unit fractions for every m ≥ 4 (and 'm−1 terms' is a ladder)
connection: m/n = (m−4)·(1/n) + 4/n, so ES gives m − 1 terms (with repeats). Flip: m/n in m − 2 terms is Sierpiński's 5/n problem for m = 5 (3 terms); for general m it trivially fails at small n (e.g. n = 1), and whether it holds for all large n is to be checked (for fixed 3 terms, Schinzel exceptions grow like exp(m^{1/3+o(1)}), Pomerance–Weingartner). F11, F12.
why: Places ES as the first rung of a ladder 'm/n in k(m) terms'; the threshold function k(m) is a natural object whose known values constrain methods.
first_step: Tabulate, for m ≤ 12 and n ≤ 10⁴, the least k with m/n a sum of k unit fractions; record the first m where k = m − 2 fails.

title: Vose: every m/n is a sum of O(√log n) unit fractions — bounded vs. unbounded term counts
connection: Vose's theorem gives a uniform term bound growing with n; ES fixes 3 terms (F12). Erdős conjectured O(log log n) suffices.
why: Methods that achieve O(√log n) (smooth-number denominators) might give 3 terms for numerator 4 if the smoothness budget is tuned to p.
first_step: Re-read Vose's construction and compute the number of terms it produces for 4/p, p hard, p ≤ 10⁹.

title: Feature flip: allow one negative unit fraction — 4/p = 1/((p−1)/4) − 1/(p(p−1)/4) trivially
connection: Positivity (F27) is the whole difficulty: with signs, two terms suffice for p ≡ 1 mod 4. The positive cone is the 'boundary' making the surface log K3-like.
why: Suggests attacking positivity directly: start from the trivial signed solution and move inside the positive cone by symmetries of the cubic surface (Vieta moves / Cremona maps).
first_step: Enumerate signed 3-term solutions with exactly one negative term for hard p and test whether some explicit birational move lands in the positive cone.

title: Descartes/Soddy: three mutually tangent circles of radii x,y,z have inner Soddy curvature 1/x+1/y+1/z + 2√((x+y+z)/xyz)
