connection: ES fixes the linear part to 4/n; rationality of the Soddy curvature additionally needs (x+y+z)/(xyz) to be a rational square. Links ES to Apollonian-type curvature questions (F08 via HKRS).
why: A sub-family of ES solutions inside integral Apollonian configurations would inherit thin-orbit tools.
first_step: Count ES solutions (p ≤ 10⁵) where (x+y+z)·xyz is a square; if non-empty, look for Apollonian structure.

title: Wilsch: integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold — check if the ES threefold is of that type
connection: Wilsch counted integral points on a specific log Fano threefold with torus-like structure. ES's threefold is a cubic with an (S₃ × scaling) symmetry.
why: A matching asymptotic with explicit leading constant would be a cross-check on ET's log³ constant and on the BM-corrected local densities.
first_step: Check the definition of Wilsch's threefold and whether 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is birational to it or to a toric variety.

title: Borwein conjecture (Chen Wang, Adv. Math. 2022): sign pattern of q-product coefficients by saddle-point + finite check
connection: ES ⟺ positivity/nonvanishing of coefficients of an explicit theta-quotient level series at prime indices (F19). Wang proved a coefficient sign pattern for all n analytically.
why: Feature flip: Wang's coefficients have an exponentially dominant main term; ES's are divisor-sized. Clarifies that an ES q-series proof needs a positivity mechanism, not asymptotics.
first_step: Look for a manifestly positive (product/sum-of-squares) expression of Σ_n R(n)q^n restricted to a progression, e.g. via Andrews-style identities.

title: Derandomised Janson: P(no certificate) ≤ exp(−μ + Δ/2) in a pseudorandom model
connection: Janson's inequality bounds the probability that no event occurs among weakly dependent monotone events. For fixed p, with μ = expected certificates ≍ log²p and Δ the pair-dependency sum, a derandomised Janson (pseudorandomness of p's residues) would give R(p) > 0 when μ − Δ/2 → ∞.
why: Connects the campaign's Poisson zero-law heuristics to a precise inequality; the measured zero law (≈ 1.5–2.8 × swap-Poisson) says what Δ must be.
first_step: Compute μ and Δ for the (★) events (indexed by (u,B,C)) at test p, and compare exp(−μ + Δ/2) with the observed zero probability at the same M.

title: Continuants: p = K(a,b,c) = abc + a + c (positive CF) vs ES's negative continuant tuv − u − v
connection: Length-3 continuants K(a,b,c) = abc + a + c represent every n > ? trivially (a = c = 1: b + 2), while the negative-CF version with a 4ℤ constraint is ES. The sign flip is the feature (F16, F27).
why: The positive version is trivially universal; ES lives exactly between positive and negative continuants — a mixed-sign continuant 'abc + a − c' family may interpolate.
first_step: For the 4 sign patterns of abc ± a ± c with a 4ℤ constraint on one coordinate, compute failure sets among primes ≤ 10⁷.

title: Primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 as norms: ES-hardness vs. splitting in many imaginary quadratic fields ℚ(√−uB)
connection: M_BM(p) small ⟺ χ_{−4uB}(p) = +1 for many small pairs, i.e. p splits in many ℚ(√−uB) — Chebotarev in a large compositum. Hard primes are 'maximally split' primes (F20, F29).
why: Gives an explicit adversarial family (primes totally split in the compositum of ℚ(i, √−ℓ) for ℓ ≤ L) and connects ES lower bounds to the least prime not totally split (Linnik/Lagarias–Odlyzko).
first_step: Compute R(p) for the first primes totally split in ℚ(i, √−3, √−5, √−7, √−11, …) (L up to 40) and compare with random p of same size.

title: Absorption method (Ringel, Erdős–Faber–Lovász): approximate structure + absorber ⇒ exact
connection: Combinatorial ∀n∃ conjectures were solved by building most of the object randomly and absorbing the leftovers. ES analogue: '4/p − (a cheap unit fraction) has a 2-term decomposition' succeeds for almost all choices; the absorber is the freedom in x.
why: Forces the question: is there an 'absorbing' set of x values (depending on p only through simple data) guaranteed to contain a good one?
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁸ find the minimal set X(p) of x-values (in terms of p mod small numbers) that always contains a working x; test stability.

title: ES as a Hurwitz-type equation with a Vieta group: orbit counts per n
connection: Hurwitz equations Σx_i² = a·Πx_i have finitely many fundamental solutions per (n,a) generating trees under Vieta moves; ES's word set has a forest structure (F39). Counting fundamental solutions vs. n is a solved problem type. Caveat: tuv − u − v and the ES cubic are multilinear, so classical Vieta root swaps do not exist on them; the analogue must use other involutions/birational moves.
why: If ES words admit a finite 'fundamental domain' per p, existence reduces to existence of a fundamental solution with bounded size.
first_step: Search for involutions or birational moves on (t,u,v) preserving tuv − u − v = p (e.g. moves through the divisor pairing d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d, swaps across levels) and compute orbit structure for p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Feature flip F02: problems without multiplicative closure (Goldbach) can't reduce to primes — ES's prime reduction as an asset
connection: ES(n) ⇐ ES(d) for d | n reduces to primes; for primes the multiplicative structure of n is gone. Conversely, composites have MORE solutions (Elsholtz–Planitzer).
why: Suggests 'prime-free' proofs: use auxiliary composites m = p·k with ES(pk) solutions having k | all denominators (equivalent to ES(p)).
first_step: For hard p, find the smallest k such that 4/(pk) has a solution with k dividing all three denominators — equals ES(p) — but study the distribution of 'near-misses' (k dividing two denominators).

title: Feature flip F17: CF length ≤ 2 — which primes are length-2 (two-term) representable — fully explicit
connection: λ(p) ≤ 2 corresponds to 2-term-type representations, characterised by divisor conditions (Rav). ES₅ is the length-3 rung.
why: Explicit rung below ES; the step 2 → 3 adds one free parameter, which is where the log² count appears.
first_step: Compute the density of primes with λ(p) ≤ 2 (under ES₅ constraints) — should decay like a power of 1/log.

title: Precedent search: theorems giving r(n) ≫ (log n)^c for ALL n (polylog pointwise lower bounds)
connection: Examples to check: number of prime factors-related counts, r(n) for sums of a prime and a square-free?, number of divisors in a dense set; the 'every n has ≫ log n representations as p + 2^a + 2^b' type (false). F04 + F21.
why: If no natural polylog-scale pointwise lower bound has ever been proved, ES's required statement is unprecedented — a strong strategic datum.
first_step: Ask MathOverflow-style search: 'every integer has at least log n representations'; check Erdős–Fuchs-type and additive-basis-order results.

title: Gauss Eureka (n = Δ + Δ + Δ ⟺ 8n + 3 = sum of three odd squares): linear change of variable to a local-global problem
connection: ∀n statement solved by transforming n ↦ 8n + 3 and invoking three squares. ES's divisor forms also transform p ↦ 4Cp + 1, p + 4d (F10).
why: A single fixed affine transformation sufficed there; ES needs a family of transformations (one per C) — the cost of the extra quantifier.
first_step: Look for an ES equivalent with a single affine transform (e.g. a statement about 4p + 1 alone with a richer witness) — e.g. via the Frobenius semigroup item.

title: Chen's theorem (p + 2 = P₂) and 'almost-ES' with a relaxed term
connection: Chen circumvented parity by allowing almost-primes. ES analogue: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + a/z with a small, or with one denominator only 'almost integral' (z ∈ ½ℤ). Note numerator 2 makes ES trivial for p ≡ 1 mod 4 (4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 2/z).
why: Find the weakest relaxation that is not trivial — that marks where the parity-type barrier sits.
first_step: Check triviality for relaxations: (i) z ∈ ½ℤ, (ii) one denominator may be divisible by p², (iii) a/z with a = 3; record first nontrivial one.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Elliott–Halberstam-type level of distribution for divisor-in-class counts (Fouvry–Iwaniec, Friedlander–Iwaniec d₃)
connection: Distribution of τ-type functions in APs beyond √x is known for d₂ (Selberg/Hooley/Heath-Brown) and d₃ (Friedlander–Iwaniec, Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel). ES sums divisor-in-class counts over p-tied integers.
why: These give averages over moduli (B2); pointwise not. Still the best tools for the averaged ES problems (exceptional set).
first_step: Check whether the 3/4 exceptional-set barrier (F40) can be moved by a d₃-in-APs level beyond 1/2 input.

title: Bach–Sorenson explicit GRH least-prime bounds
connection: The least-prime-in-a-class problem has a single-input/single-witness formulation (F01,F21), and a finite exceptional regime controlled by explicit estimates. Its class-group characters resemble the character sums in ES (F20).
why: The explicit constants and effective character-sum machinery may help replace qualitative ES average results with a pointwise count bound.
first_step: Read Bach–Sorenson's explicit GRH bounds and identify the exact zero-sum inequality; test its analogue on the finite character expansion defining R(p).

title: Cramér–Maier matrix method for pointwise short intervals
connection: The matrix method extracts pointwise irregularities at polylogarithmic scales (F04w,F21,F37), sharing ES's delicate pointwise-versus-average issue (F05,F21).
why: It supplies a warning and a tool: organize many correlated residue-class counts in a matrix rather than infer pointwise behavior from a mean.
first_step: Build the analogous residue-class-by-C matrix for R(p) over a modest prime range and test whether Maier-style row/column discrepancies appear.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Tunnell's theta-series criterion for congruent numbers
connection: Tunnell gives a computable ternary quadratic-form criterion for a rational-point question (necessary; sufficient assuming BSD), matching ES's quadratic-form reformulations and theta-series coefficient lens (F19,F31).
why: It is an exact arithmetic criterion whose failure can be tested cheaply, making it a useful model for turning ES into a coefficient-vanishing problem.
first_step: Read Tunnell's theorem statement and compare the two weighted representation counts with the ES theta-quotient coefficient; seek an analogous exact criterion.

title: Smith's positive proportion of congruent numbers via Selmer groups
connection: A positive-proportion theorem for a thin arithmetic property shares ES's local solubility and global integral-witness divide (F06,F07,F31), but is density-level rather than pointwise (F05w).
why: The Selmer-group distribution method could provide a new way to quantify how often arithmetic obstructions vanish in a family of surfaces.
first_step: Check Smith's Selmer distribution theorem hypotheses and ask whether a 2-Selmer-like object exists for the ES cubic surface family.

title: Chen Wang's proof of Borwein's coefficient-positivity conjecture
connection: A coefficient-nonvanishing/positivity problem in q-series is close to ES's theta-quotient coefficient criterion (F19), while requiring control at each index (F01,F21).
why: A successful q-series positivity method could directly inform the ES coefficient lens rather than merely its Diophantine parametrizations.
first_step: Fetch Wang's paper; extract the coefficient recurrence/positivity mechanism and test the first recurrence terms of ES's generating function.

title: Hooley's GRH result for x²+y²+z³
connection: A conditional pointwise representation by mixed-degree forms resembles ES's affine surface family and pointwise integral-witness problem (F01,F13,F21), with analytic prime-distribution input.
why: A hybrid quadratic/cubic representation is close enough geometrically to make its circle-method and L-function tools worth checking for ES's conic fibration.
first_step: Verify the exact Hooley theorem and hypotheses, then inspect its treatment of local factors and compare them with the ES surface's local densities.

title: Finite congruence obstruction tests for universal forms
connection: Local representability is checked prime-by-prime, then a finite criterion can settle universality (F01,F03,F06); ES also has a finite congruence cover but no global witness criterion.
why: It suggests auditing whether ES's known finite modular cover can be strengthened by a local-to-global theorem on the corresponding family of forms.
first_step: For each ES residue class modulo 840, compute the local densities of the associated ternary form and test whether a finite criterion set can control all classes.

title: Least-nonresidue square failure as ES feature flip
connection: Least quadratic nonresidue existence is pointwise away from squares, while squares are exactly where the quadratic character degenerates (F01,F08w). This feature flip isolates a natural thin exceptional set rather than an analytic failure.
why: ES's square-class failures might similarly come from a character becoming principal, suggesting a decomposition by square-free kernel before applying character bounds.
first_step: Compute the real-character contribution to R(p) separately on p's square classes and test for an analogue of the principal-character degeneration.

title: Universal quadratic form escalation as an ES covering strategy
connection: The 290 proof escalates from local representation data to a universal form, while ES combines a finite congruence cover with parametrized certificate families (F03,F09,F34).
why: An escalation analogue might iteratively enlarge certificate families whenever an uncovered residue class remains, providing a disciplined alternative to guessing isolated identities.
first_step: Translate each ES certificate line into a representation vector and simulate escalation on residue classes modulo 840, tracking which new line covers each uncovered class.

title: Markoff orbifold semi-integral Hasse principle
connection: The arXiv:2411.02629 study of local-global principles for semi-integral Markoff-type orbifold pairs matches ES F01/F06/F13 and F07: an integral-point existence problem on a surface with local-global and approximation questions.
why: This is a close surface-arithmetic analogue, and the abstract specifically reports semi-integral Hasse-principle results rather than a generic rational-point theorem.
first_step: Read the theorem statements in arXiv:2411.02629 and compare their semi-integrality conditions with the denominators and positivity constraints in ES.

title: Approximation off a finite set and ES residue families
connection: The strong-approximation results for Markoff orbifold pairs in arXiv:2411.02629 connect ES F06/F07/F13 with F03's congruence coverage: local approximation data may suggest congruence-class subfamilies, though not itself guarantee integral points.
why: The paper treats the interaction of local conditions and global integral-type points on a surface, providing a precise model for organizing ES congruence tests.
first_step: Extract its local-place conditions and test whether analogous conditions on ES denominator triples reproduce known Mordell classes modulo 840.

title: Integral Hasse failure despite dense rational points
connection: The Markoff-type K3 examples of arXiv:2504.10992 share ES F13/F07 and F21: global integral existence can fail despite abundance at the rational level, unlike the pointwise positive-integer target.
why: This establishes a close negative control for proposed ES arguments that pass from rational parametrization to integral solutions.
first_step: Compare the authors' obstruction with the denominators in a rational parametrization of the ES cubic; determine where integrality is lost.

title: Use Markoff K3 obstructions to audit local tests
connection: The Hasse-failing Markoff-type K3 family in arXiv:2504.10992 shares ES F06/F07/F13 and demonstrates why checking all local conditions need not supply a global integral point.
why: It is a concrete test case against overinterpreting ES's known local solubility.
first_step: Read the local-solubility verification in the paper and list which parts depend on the Markoff form, then test their analogues on ES modulo small prime powers.

title: Near-miss identities as an ES obstruction detector
connection: ArXiv:2104.08798 studies near-miss identities for ternary integral quadratic forms under congruence conditions, matching ES F03/F21/F31 and the exceptional-set theme F25.
why: Near-miss representation identities may explain why a quadratic-form proxy succeeds for most classes but leaves stubborn exceptions.
first_step: Extract one near-miss identity and see whether an ES quadratic-form reformulation admits an analogous identity with an explicit residual term.

title: Generalized Euclidean divisor search for ES certificates
connection: Arxiv:2410.05030 generalizes Lenstra's divisor search to additional Euclidean rings, matching ES F10/F32 and F16's algebraic word encodings.
why: Its algorithmic divisor approach may reveal an efficient search certificate for the particular divisor-in-a-class characterization of ES.
first_step: Check the paper's sequence construction in the ordinary integer case and determine whether the ES tied integer can be fed in without requiring the algorithm's S³>N range.

title: Ordering continuants by local transformations
connection: The operation increasing continuants in arXiv:1608.08322 matches ES F16/F17/F32: bounded continued-fraction words encode integers, and local word changes control their size.
why: A controlled transformation on the ES length-three word may normalize coordinates or push a witness into a useful congruence class.
first_step: Read the operation in the paper and test whether an analogous adjacent-letter move preserves n=tuv−u−v while changing the coordinate residue.

title: Periodic continuant formulas and ES residue periodicity
connection: The explicit periodic-continuant formulas in arXiv:2001.06213 match ES F16/F17/F03, since periodic continued-fraction words can encode structured congruence families.
why: This is a concrete identity toolkit for testing whether periodic ES word patterns generate infinite residue-class families.
first_step: Use the paper's periodic formula on a short periodic word and compare its resulting n-values modulo the ES covering modulus 840.

title: Shift two unit fractions while preserving exactness
connection: The Egyptian-fraction rewriting operator in arXiv:2003.13229 and ES F12/F14/F27: exact reciprocal decompositions admit local transformations while positivity/parity constrain the result.
why: A local rewrite may move a representation into the denominator congruence classes required by ES without changing the sum.
first_step: Read the operator identity and apply it to a two-term portion of a known three-term ES identity; check whether it preserves three terms and positivity.

title: Egyptian-fraction rewriting and S₃ normalization
connection: The rewrite identity of arXiv:2003.13229 matches ES F12/F14/F27: local transformations can interact with the S₃ symmetry of the three denominator variables and the positivity boundary.
why: A rewrite orbit could normalize a witness into a canonical ordering or residue pattern, reducing the search to fewer cases.
first_step: Generate the rewrite orbit of a single small ES triple under its stated operator and denominator permutations; check for a canonical congruence representative.

title: Markoff-type equations and logarithmic solution growth
connection: The generalized Markov–Hurwitz equations studied in arXiv:2605.05075 share ES F01/F13/F38 and F04w: positive integral surface solutions are organized by nonlinear equation structure and have a reported logarithmic asymptotic phenomenon.
why: The specific asymptotic theorem may inform how orbit size and witness counts behave in a Diophantine surface family.
first_step: Check the theorem's exact solution-counting variable and determine whether any ES parametrized subfamily has comparable tree growth.

title: Integral orbit tree versus finite ES residue covers
connection: The Markoff–Hurwitz positive-solution asymptotics in arXiv:2605.05075 match ES F13/F38/F34: an infinite orbit tree is a contrast to ES's need to cover every prime by families.
why: It suggests measuring whether a finite set of ES moves produces enough residue classes or only a thin orbit.
first_step: Compute the mod-840 action of candidate ES coordinate involutions and compare the orbit's residue coverage with the known Mordell covering.

title: Least prime in a progression and ES tied-divisor residues
connection: Arxiv:1309.3595 treats least primes in arithmetic progressions alongside least nonresidues, matching ES F10/F20/F29 and the residue-class existence question.
why: It gives verified conditional tools for small representatives in a residue class, potentially useful after ES is reduced to finding a suitable prime or divisor class.
first_step: Check whether any ES tied integer condition can be reformulated as a least-prime-in-progression condition without losing the same-parameter divisibility constraint.

title: A matrix-orbit test for ES certificate connectivity
connection: Markoff matrix/tree encodings in arXiv:0709.1499 match ES F18/F38/F39 and F32: the central question can be reframed as whether short transformations connect all required certificate states.
why: This suggests a finite-state or orbit-connectivity experiment on congruence reductions, directly aligned with the ES word-graph viewpoint.
first_step: Define vertices as ES word certificates modulo a small modulus and test whether candidate matrix generators connect every admissible residue state.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Problem 301: extremal distinct unit fractions
connection: Problem 301 ↔ ES F04, F12, F14, F27: reciprocal equations with distinct variables, symmetric witnesses, and positivity.
why: This extremal problem studies when a set avoids a unit-fraction equation; its disjoint-set argument could expose structural constraints on ES denominator choices.
first_step: Inspect the elementary argument summarized at https://www.erdosproblems.com/301 and test its disjoint blocks against denominator triples satisfying 4/p.

title: Problem 305: prime-target Egyptian fraction bounds
connection: Problem 305 ↔ ES F04, F12, F21, F29: prime-specific reciprocal representations and a pointwise existence/count problem.
why: The page records the upper bounds of Bleicher–Erdős, Yokota and Liu–Sawhney for general b. For prime b it records only the lower bound D(p) ≫ p log p, so it has no prime-specific construction. Check whether the upper-bound constructions behave differently at prime denominators.
first_step: Read Yokota [Yo88] and Liu–Sawhney [LiSa24] from the page; check whether their constructions treat prime b specially, and test the construction at targets 4/p.

title: Problem 308: Croot’s threshold for unit-fraction subset sums
connection: Problem 308 ↔ ES F01, F04, F12, F21: existence threshold, reciprocal subset sums and pointwise representation.
why: Croot’s result controls the least integer missed by subset sums of reciprocal sets; this could inform a greedy/supplementary-term strategy for ES.
first_step: Read Croot [Cr99] on the page and test whether its threshold argument can start from one ES denominator and complete with two terms.

title: Problem 314: Lim–Steinerberger reciprocal-sum exponent
connection: Problem 314 ↔ ES F04, F12, F21, F24: extremal reciprocal sum, representation scale and heuristic exponent.
why: Lim–Steinerberger show that consecutive harmonic sums Σ_{n≤k≤m}1/k can exceed 1 by as little as ≪ n^{-2}(log n)^{-5/4+δ} for infinitely many n. This calibrates how closely structured reciprocal sums can approach a target, which bears on ES's fixed three-term constraint.
first_step: Read Lim–Steinerberger [LiSt24] linked on the page and compare the exponent derivation with denominator size requirements for 4/p.

title: Problem 319: Croot reciprocal discrepancy construction
connection: Problem 319 ↔ ES F04, F05, F12, F21: controlled reciprocal sums, density and discrepancy.
why: Croot’s construction supplies a set with a specified reciprocal-sum behavior; discrepancy control could be tested against residues or denominator intervals in ES.
first_step: Read Croot [Cr01] from the page and compute the discrepancy of its constructed set in residue classes relevant to p modulo 8.

title: Problem 825: prime-factor threshold as feature flip
connection: Problem 825 ↔ ES features F01, F10, F12, with the flip being an imposed prime-factor restriction absent in ES.
why: The threshold theorem succeeds after restricting prime factors, highlighting whether ES can find a useful restricted subfamily of p-tied integers without losing coverage.
first_step: Read the theorem’s exact restriction in Larsen’s paper; enumerate which factorization conditions are compatible with 4Cp+1 and an ES divisor certificate.

title: Problem 300: Croot construction as a thin-set stress test
connection: Problem 300 ↔ ES F04, F05, F12, F24: sparse representation counts, density bounds and heuristic abundance.
why: A theorem disproving the expected scale for reciprocal subset representations is a reminder to test ES heuristics against deliberately sparse constructions.
first_step: Use the construction cited on the page to build a restricted denominator set and calculate whether its induced ES candidate count is atypically small.

title: Problem 309: coverage of many target values
connection: Problem 309 ↔ ES F04, F05, F12, F34: many represented values, almost-all coverage and families of representations.
why: A lower bound on the number of reciprocal-subset sums may identify a covering mechanism that can be restricted to prime targets.
first_step: Read Croot’s all-small-integers coverage argument and check whether the construction works uniformly on the sparse target sequence 4/p.

title: Problem 315: greedy expansion as a certificate algorithm
connection: Problem 315 ↔ ES F12, F17, F32: reciprocal expansion, bounded construction steps and certificate length.
why: The result’s comparison with the greedy expansion can be viewed algorithmically; testing its output on 4/p may expose bounded-continued-fraction patterns.
first_step: Implement only a hand-sized greedy expansion for 4/p and compare the first terms and residual with the argument in Kamio or Li–Tang.

title: Problem 300: almost-all reciprocal representation and ES exceptions
connection: Problem 300 ↔ ES F05, F12, F21, F25: abundance theorem versus explicit exceptional cases and pointwise demand.
why: Contrasting density results with known exceptional examples in neighboring unit-fraction problems may sharpen what an ES exceptional-prime theorem would need to exclude.
first_step: Read the explicit examples listed on the unit-fraction tag page and compare their mechanism with the known ES near-miss primes for restricted certificates.

title: Problem 312: multiset extraction and candidate denominator supply
connection: Problem 312 ↔ ES F01, F04, F12, F34: large supply forces a reciprocal sum, multiple candidate families cover targets.
why: A large multiset extraction theorem may be applied to a deliberately constructed supply of ES candidate denominators, if its multiplicity hypotheses can be met.
first_step: Read the exact threshold and test a candidate multiset formed from denominators in a chosen arithmetic progression; determine whether the resulting sum can equal a residual 4/p.

title: Problem 355: lacunary reciprocal sequence covers an interval
connection: Problem 355 ↔ ES F01, F12, F27, F32: reciprocal expansions, positivity and constructive coverage.
why: Van Doorn–Kovač prove a lacunary reciprocal sequence covers an interval of rationals, a concrete constructive coverage phenomenon worth testing on 4/p.
first_step: Read [DoKo25] linked on the page and inspect the interval-covering construction; ask whether 4/p lies in the covered interval with a three-term restriction.

title: Square-factor saturation for the trilinear form xy+yz+zx
connection: OEIS A025052 studies positive integers omitted by xy+yz+zx; the page records Borwein–Choi's theorem that every N with a square factor is represented except 4 and 18. This shares F01/F08w/F13/F16w: a universal representation problem, algebraic exceptional strata, and a cubic/trilinear polynomial encoding.
why: The explicit parametrization by square-factor decomposition could suggest a way to make ES certificates from a repeated factor, distinct from residue covering.
first_step: Translate the A025052 square-factor parametrization to ES: fix n=m r² and test whether the induced denominators can be made positive integers; enumerate small m,r and record exactly where integrality fails.

title: Uniquely represented trilinear integers as a model for witness multiplicity
connection: OEIS A093669/A093670, cross-referenced by A025052, classify numbers with a unique representation by ab+ac+bc. They share F04/F13/F14: count integral points on a symmetric cubic-form fibre, including unusually sparse one-witness fibres.
why: ES work often needs a pointwise lower bound on representation counts; the neighboring exact-one locus is a useful benchmark for how divisor factorizations control multiplicity.
first_step: For primes p, compare the number of ordered ES solutions up to permutation with the analogous factorization count on a small trilinear surface; look for a divisor-sum identity or a stable multiplicity statistic.

title: Egyptian fraction term-count threshold as a feature flip
connection: MO 212865 asks whether a/n (a > 4) is a sum of k < a unit fractions, e.g. 5/n with four terms; comments note this is open in general (citing Elsholtz, Trans. AMS 353 (2001)) while k ≥ a terms is easy by greedy. Matches F11/F12 and flips the term-count threshold relative to the numerator.
why: Understanding exactly why adding one term trivializes a family may identify which ES reductions must preserve the three-term constraint.
first_step: Read MO 212865 and the Elsholtz (2001) paper it cites; compare the easy k ≥ a regime with the k < a regime for a/n and isolate the algebraic step that fails when one term is removed.

title: Four-term ES decompositions as a triviality control
connection: The MathOverflow question on ES with four terms supplies a direct neighboring problem where term count changes, matching F12/F11/F32 and flipping the conjectural three-term bound to four terms.
why: A four-term baseline can validate enumeration and expose whether a proposed three-term construction loses only one controlled denominator or relies on a genuinely deep coincidence.
first_step: Implement a canonical greedy four-term decomposition for 4/p, then compare its denominator scale and residues with the shortest three-term witnesses for the same primes.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz proof on prime-sized cyclic seats
connection: A005097's comments cite Kohen–Sadofschi: a prescribed-distance seating problem on 2n+1 seats is solvable for every distance list iff 2n+1 is prime, proved using the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz. It shares F01/F03/F29/F31: universal finite-field conditions, prime residue structure, and an algebraic certificate.
why: This is a feature-flip: universality holds precisely on primes, rather than for every integer, and the proof is polynomial nonvanishing over a finite field.
first_step: Read Kohen's Nullstellensatz argument and test whether the polynomial coefficient-extraction method yields a nonzero count for ES witnesses modulo p, especially in the difficult p≡1 mod 4 class.

title: Residue restriction on exceptional additive representations
connection: A060003 notes that its terms greater than 3 all lie in 6n−1. This shares F03/F25/F29: congruence restrictions sharply constrain the exceptional set, while leaving a sparse residue class to investigate.
why: The exceptional set's congruence compression is an inexpensive analogue of ES square-class residue analysis, and can guide targeted rather than blind searches.
first_step: Compute ES witness counts by residue class modulo 840 and by prime splitting in Q(i), then check whether any analogous single congruence class carries almost all low-count primes.

title: Square-factor theorem as a route from a thin stratum to near-universality
connection: A025052's Borwein–Choi result covers all N with a square factor except 4,18, leaving squarefree inputs as the difficult stratum. It shares F01/F05/F08w/F25 and is a feature-flip: broad coverage is proved off the squarefree locus.
why: This is a useful structural decomposition template: establish a broad algebraic subfamily first and isolate the genuinely hard inputs explicitly.
first_step: Partition ES primes and general n by square factors in the tied divisor quantities (4Cp+1 or p+4d), and test whether the certificate family handles all but a squarefree residual condition.

title: Quadratic-form reinterpretation of a trilinear omission set
connection: A025052 links its omission set to integers lacking an indecomposable positive definite binary quadratic form of the corresponding discriminant (as reported in the entry). This shares F13/F25/F31: a representation problem on a cubic form is reframed through quadratic forms and a sparse obstruction list.
why: An independent quadratic-form characterization may expose arithmetic invariants not visible in the original ES fractions.
first_step: Trace the Zhu–Shao/Peters reference from A025052 and check whether any discriminant/class-number invariant can be attached to ES's divisor witnesses in Q(i).

title: Odd unit-fraction solution counts and polynomial lower bounds
connection: The same MO answer cites a result giving a lower bound on the number of odd-denominator solutions for larger odd term counts, while exact counts remain unknown. This matches F04w/F12/F21/F22: a lower-bound count for constrained reciprocal representations but a gap to exact pointwise behavior.
why: The proof's construction of many solutions under a congruence restriction may transfer to lower bounds for ES representations in selected residue classes.
first_step: Read Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang, cited in the answer (arXiv:1108.6118), and extract its solution-generating operation; test whether it produces multiplicative families of ES triples.

title: Strictly ordered cubic-form representations and symmetry reduction
connection: OEIS A093669 counts unique representations by ab+ac+bc under 0<a<b<c, removing permutation symmetry. It shares F04/F13/F14: a symmetric three-variable surface whose raw point count is converted to canonical unordered witnesses.
why: ES's S3 symmetry creates overcounting; the ordered-triple convention in this sequence offers an exact and transparent normalization.
first_step: For primes p, count only x≤y≤z ES triples and compare with the fully ordered count, separately tracking repeated-coordinate strata.

title: Factor-pair enumeration for a unique cubic-form witness
connection: A093669 provides a computation for unique ab+ac+bc representations by looping over a,b and testing whether n−ab is divisible by a+b, yielding c. This matches F10/F15/F32: each fibre is reduced to a divisor/congruence test and can be exhaustively certified.
why: It is a low-cost exact enumeration architecture analogous to fixed-variable ES hyperbola factorization, and can validate a new ES candidate-family search.
first_step: Implement the A093669 loop pattern for ES after fixing one denominator, using the exact split-hyperbola divisor condition; compare outputs against independent brute force for small p.

title: Collatz feature flip: almost-all control is not pointwise control
connection: Tao’s Collatz result shares ES’s universal target, computational verification, and a structured arithmetic map (F01,F23,F16w), but proves an almost-all weakened conclusion rather than all inputs (F05).
why: A feature-flip reminder: average-orbit control can coexist with unresolved exceptional inputs; it motivates studying ES exceptions structurally rather than inferring pointwise truth from density.
first_step: Check Tao’s theorem’s exact exceptional notion and test whether ES exceptional primes can be grouped by a corresponding large-deviation statistic.

title: Lonely runner: cyclic gap and symmetry reduction
connection: The lonely-runner problem shares F14,F23,F24,F01 through interchangeable runner labels, finite verified cases, and a universal conjecture. ES witness permutation symmetry is S₃ (F14), likewise reducing redundant cases.
why: A careful orbit/stabilizer reduction can make exhaustive searches over ES witnesses or residue configurations substantially smaller.
first_step: Inspect the survey’s symmetry reductions and implement canonical representatives for ES triples (x,y,z) and the corresponding residue constraints.

title: EFL feature flip: hypergraph structure versus arithmetic family
connection: EFL shares ES’s universal quantifier, finite local constraints, and proof-by-cover-plus-repair (F01,F03,F34), but its objects have a finite hypergraph decomposition while ES ranges over primes with multiplicative arithmetic (F33).
why: This feature flip identifies absorption as potentially portable only after finding an arithmetic analogue of the hypergraph reservoir.
first_step: Check whether ES certificate lines admit a bounded-overlap notion analogous to edge-disjoint color classes, then assess if an absorber can be defined.

title: Apollonian local-global feature flip: exceptional algebraic families
connection: Apollonian curvature results share ES’s local congruence restrictions, thin witnesses, and almost-all progress (F03,F05,F22), but explicit algebraic families can be missed, unlike a universal existential target. This is a feature-flip warning about exceptional subfamilies.
why: Testing for structured infinite exception families is more informative than only checking random integers.
first_step: Read the counterexample-family discussion in the 2024 paper and compare its quadratic/quartic obstructions with ES’s square-class obstruction.

title: Markov triples: mutation trees and orbit enumeration
connection: Markov triples share ES’s integral cubic equation, involutive transformations, thin witness families, and finite checks (F13,F30,F38,F23). Mutation organizes infinitely many solutions from a small seed.
why: A mutation-orbit perspective could reveal whether ES solutions partition into manageable parameter orbits rather than isolated divisor certificates.
first_step: Enumerate low-height ES triples modulo permutation and test for simple rational transformations preserving the defining cubic after fixing n.

title: Frobenius finite exceptions and parameter stratification
connection: Three-generated numerical semigroups share F11,F25,F32: parameter regimes can have exceptional cases and finite certificates. ES has numerator-dependent failures of related Egyptian-fraction statements and explicit finite counterexample lists.
why: Parameter stratification may help distinguish ES exceptional primes by the size or gcd pattern of a witness parameter.
first_step: The ref (Moreno-Frías–Rosales 2025) concerns numerical semigroups with a given Frobenius number and fixed gaps; check whether its parameter stratification (or that in Robles-Pérez–Rosales, dimension three) offers an exceptional-parameter template for ES square classes.

title: Matrix mortality: existence of a zero-product word
connection: Matrix mortality shares F16w,F18,F32,F23: a finite word in matrices witnesses a target property; bounded word search is computationally checkable. ES is likewise a word-reachability problem with a target entry.
why: Mortality techniques emphasize invariant sets and modular reductions that may prune ES word searches.
first_step: Review a matrix mortality reduction and check whether its modular invariant argument yields a useful obstruction or pruning rule for ES matrices.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Lüroth expansions and finite digit alphabets
connection: Lüroth and continued-fraction expansions share F17,F18,F32: digits encode rational values by short arithmetic words, with bounded-digit variants producing thin sets. ES also has bounded-length CF/SL₂ descriptions.
why: Alternative expansion algorithms may give a more natural parametrization of positive rational decompositions than continued fractions.
first_step: Search for a Lüroth representation of 4/p with constrained first digits and test whether three digit choices imply an ES decomposition.

title: Sandpile recurrence: finite states and critical group invariants
connection: Chip-firing/sandpile questions share F18w,F23,F32: reachability under local moves has finite-state invariants and short move-sequence certificates. ES matrix-word reachability offers a similar state-transition viewpoint.
why: Critical-group or modular invariants could cheaply eliminate impossible ES parameter words or classify search states.
first_step: Model ES matrix generators modulo m as a finite directed state graph and compare its conserved quantities with sandpile group invariants.

title: Zaremba: transfer-operator counting for restricted digits
connection: Restricted-CF denominator problems share F17,F18,F22,F24: thin matrix semigroups are counted via digit words and growth heuristics. ES’s bounded CF length and matrix-entry target invite analogous transfer operators.
why: A transfer operator may estimate how many ES-compatible words exist at a given prime, rather than merely count all integer triples.
first_step: Define a transfer operator for ES’s allowed three-step matrix digits and calculate its predicted count against small-prime data.

title: Collatz: density notions and logarithmic sampling
connection: Collatz and ES share F05,F21,F23,F24: strong almost-all/computational evidence leaves pointwise exceptional inputs unresolved. Tao’s logarithmic-density approach makes the quantifier gap explicit.
why: Comparing natural and logarithmic density may tell whether ES exceptional primes are genuinely sparse in the metric relevant to divisor-counting estimates.
first_step: Compute the logarithmic count of ES primes lacking each fixed certificate family over existing bounded data and compare with natural-density counts.

title: Kourovka group problems: SL₂(Z) word reachability
connection: Group word problems share F16w,F18,F32: whether a target element is represented by a word has a short explicit certificate and congruence quotients provide cheap tests. ES has a prescribed-entry SL₂ reachability form.
why: Quotient-group obstructions and normal forms can identify necessary conditions or canonical representatives for ES matrix words.
first_step: Take the ES generator matrices, compute their images in SL₂(Z/mZ) for small m, and compare reachable target-entry states by prime residue.

title: Addition-chain recurrences as ES multiplicative closure analogues
connection: Addition chains share F02w,F16w,F30,F32: recursive operations extend certificates from known inputs, and special infinite families follow. ES also has multiple-closure and thin recursive prime families.
why: A recurrence on ES certificates might extend a solution at p to a controlled family of related primes or numerators.
first_step: Search the addition-chain constructions for an explicit certificate-extension recurrence and test whether an ES identity can realize n↦2n+c.

title: Tiling problems: local rules and global periodic witnesses
connection: Tiling existence shares F01,F03,F23,F32: local compatibility constraints must yield a global object, finite patches provide certificates, and computational searches test instances. ES similarly combines local congruences with a global positive integral witness.
why: Compactness/patching arguments can distinguish local consistency from global realizability, mirroring ES’s local-global gap.
first_step: Choose a concrete Wang-tile undecidability example and compare its local-to-global obstruction with ES’s local solubility; do not assume the techniques transfer absent a finite-state reduction.

title: General fixed-numerator Egyptian fraction conjectures
connection: Schinzel-type equations m/n as bounded sums share F01, F02w, F11, F12, F25. The contrast between numerator 4 and neighboring numerators is structurally relevant.
why: A proof technique that exploits a special numerator could clarify exactly which arithmetic of 4 matters.
first_step: Compare the known m=4 and m>4 constructions and isolate the first point where constants cease to be uniform.

title: Conic bundles and integral fibres
connection: Conic-bundle families share F13, F15, F29 and make each base value a separate factorisation problem.
why: Uniform fibrewise estimates might turn many ES slices into a covering argument.
first_step: Express the ES surface as a conic bundle and inspect uniform integral-point bounds for its fibre discriminants.

title: Pell equations and thin prime families
connection: Pell-type problems share F02w, F30, F34, often proving infinite but thin parameterized families.
why: A family of ES-valid primes could serve as a rung in a covering system, even without positive density.
first_step: Search Pell parameterisations yielding ES identities and compute the induced prime residue classes symbolically.

title: Lyczak–Mitankin–Uppal cubic surfaces failing the integral Hasse principle
connection: LMU (2023) construct families of affine cubic surfaces with integral HP failures and count them; ES is an affine cubic family with no BM obstruction (BL).
why: Their counting of failures in families calibrates how often non-BM-explained failures appear.
first_step: Read LMU and check whether any of their families are of the form 'Cayley cubic minus triangle' (like U_n).

title: Rational points versus integral points on cubic surfaces
connection: The distinction shares F07, F13, F27: rational parametrisation need not preserve positive integral coordinates.
why: Studying integral models and denominators can pinpoint why a rationally soluble ES surface remains hard.
first_step: Take a rational parametrisation of the ES surface, track denominator divisibility, and compare with integral-point parametrisations in the literature.

title: Linear sieve and switching principles
connection: Thin sequence sieve problems share F05, F22, F40 and often gain from switching between primal and dual variables.
why: A switching step could exploit the tied parameter/divisor feature rather than treat candidates as an arbitrary sequence.
first_step: Recast the ES divisor condition in both numerator and divisor variables and check whether a switching identity improves level of distribution.

title: Chebotarev and splitting-sensitive Diophantine families
connection: Splitting problems share F06, F29, F36; Chebotarev controls average prime classes but not necessarily a witness for every prime.
why: Separating the distribution-of-primes issue from the per-prime construction can focus the ES reduction.
first_step: List which ES identity families require p split in Q(i), and check whether a compositum's Frobenius classes encode them.

title: Covering congruences in prime representation problems
connection: Finite congruence coverings share F03, F29, F34 and build a union of identity families over residue classes.
why: Covering-system optimization might reveal a broader set of usable identities, even if finite coverage is impossible.
first_step: Encode existing ES identity conditions as residue-class sets modulo a common modulus and search for minimal complementary covers.

title: Theta series and coefficient nonvanishing
connection: Theta-series problems share F19, F31, F32: arithmetic representations become coefficients of modular generating functions.
why: Coefficient formulas may isolate congruence obstructions or positivity contributions invisible in the original equation.
first_step: Inspect the ES theta-quotient identity and compare it with modular-form coefficient nonvanishing criteria at prime indices.

title: Additive combinatorics of reciprocal residues
connection: Reciprocal residue sets share F10, F22, F33, where modular inverses combine additively to hit a target residue.
why: Sumset expansion could show that allowed denominator residues cannot avoid all ES target configurations.
first_step: For a prime modulus, compute restricted reciprocal sumsets from the ES denominator conditions and test known sum-product expansion bounds.

title: Universal Diophantine statements with multiplicative closure
connection: Universal representation problems share F01, F02, F06; multiplicative closure reduces the domain to primes plus local cases.
why: The reduction template may identify a clean prime-only theorem and prevent wasted effort on composite inputs.
first_step: Formalize the ES multiple-closure map and compare it with closure reductions in other universal Diophantine representation problems.

title: Positivity in additive Diophantine equations
connection: Positive-variable problems share F27, F33, F01, while signed solutions can be plentiful and structurally misleading.
why: Positivity-aware methods may yield monotone bounds and compact search regions absent from the signed equation.
first_step: List all sign-sensitive inequalities in the ES parametrisations and test whether they define a convex feasible region for one denominator.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Genus theory and one-sided representation counts
connection: Genus-theory problems share F20, F29, F31 and can explain main terms while leaving a pointwise positive count unsettled.
why: Explicit genus-character decompositions may indicate whether the ES main term is forced or merely expected.
first_step: Decompose the ES count into genus characters and compare the local densities with the predicted main term for each prime class.

title: Exceptional primes for parametrised reciprocal identities
connection: Sparse algebraic failure sets share F08w, F25, F30, where a construction works except at explicit exceptional inputs.
why: A classification of failure sets may show that multiple parametrisations leave only a manageable intersection.
first_step: For each ES identity family, factor the obstruction polynomial and compare its prime roots with the failures of sister statements.

title: Andrews–Dyson–Hickerson precedent: a q-series whose coefficients are almost always 0 but unbounded
connection: ADH showed σ(q) has coefficients that are almost always zero yet take every integer infinitely often, via Hecke characters of Q(√6) and an indefinite form. The ES count is the opposite (expected ≍ log²n, never 0 conjecturally), but it is also an indefinite-form coefficient.
why: ADH is the template for exactly computing an indefinite-theta coefficient as a Hecke-character sum over ideals. That would make N₋(p) a sum over ideals of norm p in a quadratic field, i.e. a closed formula.
first_step: Try to express the χ-signed word count Σ_w χ(w) at prime p as a sum over ideals in some real quadratic field (ADH method); test numerically.

title: Strong symmetric genus spectrum (May–Zimmerman: every value occurs) as a ∀g∃G sibling via triangle groups
connection: May–Zimmerman: there is a group of every strong symmetric genus. Proofs use explicit group families acting with triangle signatures; Riemann–Hurwitz ties genus to 1/x + 1/y + 1/z (see triangle-orbifold item). Shares F01, F12.
why: A solved ∀∃ statement whose witness lives in the same unit-fraction equation (via Riemann–Hurwitz) — possibly a source of explicit families (x,y,z) with constrained 1/x+1/y+1/z.
first_step: Read May–Zimmerman's construction and check which signatures (x,y,z) and areas arise; see if area (p−4)/p is ever forced.

title: Salez's modular filters (verification to 10¹⁷) as an explicit infinite covering family
connection: Salez found new modular equations (identity families) and used them as sieving filters to verify ES to 10¹⁷ (F23, F03, F34).
why: The filters are a concrete enumerated set of 'lines'; their combined density deficit as a function of the number of filters is an explicit covering-rate curve to compare with the Poisson model.
first_step: Extract Salez's filter list and compute the density of primes left uncovered by the first k filters for k up to 10³; fit the decay rate.

title: Lagrange's four squares: closure (Euler identity) + prime case by pigeonhole and descent — template for F02
connection: Four squares reduces to primes by a composition identity; the prime case is done by finding a multiple mp represented (pigeonhole) and descending m to 1. ES reduces to primes by trivial closure; the prime case has no descent.
why: An ES descent ('from a solution of a structured 4/(mp)-type equation produce one with smaller m') would be a Lagrange-type proof.
first_step: Search for an operation turning ES-type data at mp (e.g. a solution where m divides two of the denominators) into data at m'p with m' < m.

title: Feature flip F14: weighted equation 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 2/z is trivial — symmetry/unit numerators are load-bearing
connection: Trivial: x = y = z = p gives 1/p + 1/p + 2/p = 4/p. Also for p ≡ 1 (mod 4), x = (p+3)/4 leaves 12/(p(p+3)) = 3/N with N = p(p+3)/4, and 3/N = 1/N + 2/N. Breaking the unit-numerator symmetry kills the problem.
why: Confirms the difficulty sits in the symmetric unit-numerator structure (F12, F14) — any proof must use that all numerators are 1.
first_step: List all weightings (a,b,c) with a+b+c small for which a/x + b/y + c/z = 4/p is trivially solvable; the first non-trivial weighting is a sub-problem ladder.

title: Feature flip F38: Markoff (quadratic in each variable ⇒ Vieta group) vs ES (multilinear ⇒ no Vieta) — what symmetry group does the ES cubic have?
connection: The ES surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is multilinear; its automorphisms include S₃ and Cremona-type maps (x ↦ 1/x turns it into a plane 1/x+1/y+1/z linear in reciprocals!). In reciprocal coordinates X = 1/x it is the plane X + Y + Z = 4/n.
why: The integral-points problem is 'points of the plane X+Y+Z = 4/n with all coordinates unit fractions' — the symmetry group of the problem is the affine group of that plane preserving the unit-fraction lattice condition; a new angle on F38/F39.
first_step: Determine the group of birational automorphisms of the ES surface over ℚ that preserve positivity and integrality for infinitely many n.

title: Heuristic exceptional-set size for ES and for (★) alone: Σ_n exp(−M(n)) vs. proved bounds
connection: Under the Poisson model with mean M(n) ≍ log²n the expected number of failures ≤ N is Σ exp(−c log²n) < ∞, while for single lines it diverges. Shares F24, F05, F40.
why: Quantifies the 'distance' between the proved exceptional bound (N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4})) and the heuristic truth (O(1)).
first_step: Compute Σ_{n≤N} exp(−M_BM(n)) numerically for N = 10⁸ with the measured zero-law constant; compare with observed (★) failure counts.

title: Feature flip F03: n ≡ 0, 2, 3 mod 4 and non-square classes mod 840 are covered by identities — what if the hard classes were non-squares?
connection: Mordell's identities cover every class except the six square classes mod 840 (F03, F08, F09). The squares are exactly the classes no polynomial family can reach — the reciprocity obstruction is the reason.
why: Problems with a finite congruence covering of ALL classes are solved by identities; ES's residual set is forced to be the squares by reciprocity — the same reason as in Apollonian packings (HKRS).
first_step: For moduli M = 840·ℓ (ℓ ≤ 50), confirm the set of uncovered classes stays 'squares mod M' and record the minimal identity degree needed per class.

title: Feature flip F11 downward: 3/n = 1/x + 1/y fails for p ≡ 1 mod 3 — the 'numerator = terms + 1' ladder starts with a genuine obstruction
connection: 3/p as two unit fractions requires a divisor condition that fails for primes p ≡ 1 mod 3 (local-type obstruction), while 4/p in three terms has no local obstruction. m/n in m−1 terms: m = 3 fails, m = 4 is ES.
why: Shows ES is the first rung where the obstruction disappears; the reason (one extra free parameter) is quantifiable.
first_step: Verify the 3/p criterion and check m = 4 with 2 terms (4/p = 1/x + 1/y ⟺ p ≡ 3 mod 4) to complete the small ladder table.

title: Feature flip F37: problems where a two-sided asymptotic for the pointwise count IS true (r₄(n) = 8σ*(n))
connection: Exact formulas (Jacobi) give two-sided control; ES provably has no two-sided polylog asymptotic (Linnik-type large values).
why: Confirms that ES requires a one-sided method; methods built on exact formulas (Jacobi-type) cannot be complete for ES.
first_step: List the exact formulae known for ES-like counts (theta-quotient normal form) and identify which term carries the Linnik large values.

title: Pratt-certificate analogy: recursive ES certificates via factors of p-tied integers
connection: Pratt certificates for primality recurse on factors of p − 1. ES witnesses are divisors of p-tied integers (F10). A recursive scheme: a witness for p from 'witness-like data' for prime factors of 4Cp+1.
why: Recursive certificate structures sometimes reveal inductive proofs (as for Pratt: every prime has a short certificate, by induction).
first_step: For hard primes, record which prime factors q of 4Cp+1 'produce' the class −1 (q ≡ −1 mod 4C or products) and whether q's own ES data predict it.

title: Graph-theoretic reformulation: bipartite 'divisor graph' between levels C and primes p; (★) ⟺ no isolated prime vertex
connection: Make a bipartite graph with an edge (C, p) when R_C(p) > 0 ((★) divisor form at level C). (★)(p) ⟺ p has degree ≥ 1 — false at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰, so an ES version must add edges from other lines (e.g. the b = 1 line). Degree distribution ≍ Poisson(log²p) heuristically.
why: Graph tools (expansion, Hall-type conditions, random-graph thresholds for isolated vertices) give a different language for the lower tail (F04, F24).
first_step: Compute the bipartite graph for p ≤ 10⁷, C ≤ 10³; check the isolated-vertex threshold vs. random bipartite graphs with the same degree sequence.

title: Small-prime-factor witnesses: q | 4Cp + 1 with q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) is itself a witness (d = q)
connection: If a prime q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) divides 4Cp + 1 then the cofactor is ≡ −1 too (product ≡ 1), so d = q is a (★) witness. For each prime q and each C with 4C | q + 1, q | 4Cp + 1 is a single congruence on p mod q.
why: So the set of p witnessed by (q, C) is one residue class mod q; (★)(p) for a hard prime p ⟸ p lies in some class {p ≡ −(4C)⁻¹ mod q : 4C | q+1} — an infinite covering by single residue classes (F34). These are (★) witnesses, so the covering misses the 14 (★)-failures ≤ 10¹⁰; for ES it must be combined with other lines. Note q ≥ 4C − 1, so q ≈ C scale.
first_step: For each hard prime p ≤ 10⁸, find the least prime q such that some C with 4C | q + 1 satisfies q | 4Cp + 1; study the distribution of that q.

title: Zhang / Polymath8 smooth-moduli level of distribution with modulus 4C smooth
connection: Zhang and Polymath8a get primes equidistributed in APs to smooth moduli beyond x^{1/2}; in ES Type I the tied modulus 4C (or 4cd) is free to be chosen smooth.
why: Choosing C among smooth numbers gives well-factorable moduli, which is exactly where beyond-1/2 equidistribution (dispersion + Kloosterman) is available.
first_step: Restrict the ES Type I/II search to C that are y-smooth (y = log^2 p) and measure on data whether R(p) restricted to smooth C keeps the log^2 p main term (p ≤ 10^7).

title: Fouvry–Radziwiłł level of distribution of unbalanced convolutions
connection: Fouvry–Radziwiłł show α*β with one short factor has level of distribution beyond 1/2 for all residue classes; ES divisor counts 1_{ab|N} are convolutions with one short divisor.
why: ES certificates typically use a small divisor a and a large cofactor — the unbalanced regime FR handle.
first_step: Express the Type II e-slice count as Σ_{a small} Σ_{b} 1_{ab = N} with class conditions and check whether FR's theorem (moduli to x^{1/2+δ}) applies when averaging over p in the exceptional-set argument.

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł at fixed p along the C-progression
connection: MR show bounded multiplicative functions have the same mean in almost all short intervals as in long ones; the integers 4Cp+1 (C varying) form an AP of modulus 4p at fixed p.
why: A short-AP version (Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen) could show divisor-class statistics of 4Cp+1 in short C-windows match long averages for one fixed p — pointwise in p, average over C.
first_step: Check whether Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen 'multiplicative functions in short arithmetic progressions' covers modulus q = 4p with interval length X = p^{θ}; compute what θ the ES Type I count needs.

title: Pilatte two-point log-Chowla improvement via graph spectra
connection: Pilatte (2023) gets (log X)^{−c} savings for two-point log Chowla using spectral bounds for random-like graphs on integers; same graph-on-divisibility template as Helfgott–Radziwiłł.
why: Quantitative spectral inputs are what a fixed-p C-average argument would need.
first_step: Read Pilatte's graph construction and check whether its vertex set can be replaced by an AP {4Cp+1}.

title: Friedlander–Iwaniec asymptotic sieve (x²+y⁴) for thin certificate families
connection: FI breaks parity for primes x²+y⁴ via bilinear forms on a thin quadratic sequence; ES Type I with d a square gives p² + (2cy)², sums of two squares.
why: Restricting to d = y² makes the Type I object a Gaussian norm, where FI-type bilinear technology is designed to work.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10^7, the fraction of primes with an ES Type I certificate having d a perfect square, and whether it stays bounded below.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Maynard primes with restricted digits → thin sets with Fourier control
connection: Maynard (Invent. 2019) counts primes with a missing decimal digit by strong Fourier bounds on the thin digit set; the set of ES-hard residue patterns (Mordell classes mod 840 and deeper digit-like conditions mod 4C) is a digit-like thin set.
why: Template for proving that a thin, Fourier-structured set of p's must intersect the ES-good set.
first_step: Compute the Fourier transform (mod M = 840·k) of the indicator of 'not covered by identities of modulus ≤ M' and compare its L1 norm with Maynard's digit-set bounds.

title: Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec / Tóth equidistribution of roots of quadratic congruences with modulus condition
connection: Roots ν/f of ν² ≡ −D (mod f) equidistribute (DFI 1995 primes, Tóth composite); ES Type I asks that p be such a root (p² ≡ −4c²d mod f) while f ≡ −p mod 4cd — a joint condition on root and modulus.
why: Joint equidistribution of (root mod f, f mod m) pairs is a natural theorem to aim for and would give averaged Type I counts in new ranges.
first_step: Compute empirically, for D = 4c²d fixed small and f ≤ 10^6, the joint distribution of (ν/f, f mod 4cd) and check for correlation.

title: Irving / Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang divisor function in APs to smooth or prime-power moduli
connection: Irving (2015) and Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang get τ(n) equidistributed in APs to smooth / prime-power moduli beyond 2/3; ES's tied modulus 4C can be chosen a power of 2 times smooth.
why: Choosing 4C = 2^k is a legitimate ES sub-family (TWO_POWER_LADDER) and prime-power moduli have extra equidistribution.
first_step: Compare TWO_POWER_LADDER.md counts with the divisor-in-AP-to-2^k asymptotic; check which range of k the LSZ theorem covers.

title: Ford–Maynard theory of prime-producing sieves
connection: Ford–Maynard analyse which sieve-theoretic information (Type I/II ranges) can and cannot produce primes, extending the parity problem; ES is a 'one witness among polylog' problem with a parity-like barrier.
why: A formal limit theory for sieve information could make the campaign's B-barriers precise or show a gap.
first_step: Check whether Ford–Maynard's framework (arXiv 2024) includes sequences where the target is 'has a divisor in a class' rather than 'is prime'.

title: Banks–Ford–Tao: probabilistic prime models fail → refine the ES zero law
connection: BFT (Invent. 2023) show Cramér-type random models of primes mispredict large gaps and propose corrected models; the campaign's (J)97 lottery zero law for ES failures is a random model of the same kind.
why: Siblings fail less than the zero law predicts (G4); a BFT-style correction (sieving by small primes first) could explain it.
first_step: Rebuild the ES lottery model with residue-class sieving by primes ≤ z (BFT 'Granville model') and refit to S_{n,−4} and ES_Q1 failure data.

title: Kozma–Samotij lower tails via relative entropy for R(p)
connection: Kozma–Samotij prove lower-tail large deviations for subgraph counts via relative entropy; R(p) is a count of 'arithmetic subgraphs' (divisor relations) in a random-like structure.
why: ES's core difficulty is the one-sided lower tail R(p) ≥ ε·M_BM(p); entropy methods are the modern lower-tail tool.
first_step: Map the ES certificate count to a polynomial in independent-ish Bernoulli variables (ℓ | 4Cp+1) and check the KS hypotheses (bounded influence) on data.

title: Granville–Soundararajan pretentiousness of the 'class of divisors' character
connection: Pretentious theory: a multiplicative function f is small on average unless it pretends to be n^{it}χ(n); the indicator of 'N has a divisor in class −1 mod m' expands via characters χ mod m into Σ_χ χ̄(−1) Σ_{d|N} χ(d).
why: The ES failure set is where all such character divisor sums conspire; pretentious distance gives a language for 'conspiracy'.
first_step: For each failing N (no divisor ≡ −1 mod m), compute the pretentious distance D(χ_m-twisted divisor sums) and see whether failures cluster at a pretentious character (e.g. the real character mod m).

title: Pierce–Turnage-Butterbaugh–Wood effective Chebotarev in families → small split primes
connection: PTW (Invent. 2020) prove effective Chebotarev for almost all fields in families, giving ℓ-torsion bounds; ES certificates need small primes split in Q(√−d)-type fields tied to p.
why: Families of fields indexed by d or C at fixed p are exactly where 'almost all fields' results bite.
first_step: Identify the field family {Q(√−d), ray class fields mod 4cd} relevant to Type I and check whether PTW's family hypotheses hold.

title: Drappeau–Pratt–Radziwiłł one-level density beyond (−2,2) via Kloosterman sums
connection: DPR extend one-level density support for Dirichlet L-functions using sums of Kloosterman sums (Deshouillers–Iwaniec spectral input); ES counts reduce to sums over characters mod 4C at fixed p.
why: Shows a pathway where spectral Kloosterman bounds give information about families of characters — the ES character expansion is such a family.
first_step: Check whether the ES Type I count summed over C ≤ X is a 'family of characters' average where DPR-style spectral input applies.

title: Kelley–Meka density increment on the multiplicative group (ℤ/e)^×
connection: Kelley–Meka get quasi-polynomial bounds for 3-AP-free sets via almost-periodicity + spectral positivity; the ES e-slice asks whether −1 lies in the quotient set Q = {ab⁻¹ : ab | N} ⊂ (ℤ/e)^×, an additive-combinatorial (multiplicative-group) statement.
why: KM's 'sifting' / dependent random choice finds structured pieces of a set with large Fourier mass; applied multiplicatively it might force Q to contain a coset of a large subgroup.
first_step: Compute |Q| and the multiplicative energy of the divisor set of N in (ℤ/e)^× at hard primes, and check whether Q is ever 'KM-structured' (large spectrum).

title: Balandraud's sharp subset-sum theorem in ℤ/p for the 'target −1' problem
connection: Balandraud: subset sums of k distinct nonzero residues mod a prime cover ≥ min(p, k(k+1)/2+1) elements; taking discrete logs, ES's subset-products of prime factors of N in (ℤ/e)^× is a subset-sum problem in ℤ/(e−1).
why: Gives the exact 'how many prime factors needed to hit a target' threshold in the cyclic setting; makes the ω(N) ~ log log N shortfall precise.
first_step: Tabulate, for N = (p+e)/4 at hard primes, ω(N) versus the Balandraud/Olson threshold for (ℤ/e)^× and record the gap.

title: −1 ∈ subgroup ⇔ even order: a parity reformulation of the e-slice event
connection: For prime e, −1 ∈ H ⊂ 𝔽_e^× iff |H| is even; the e-slice needs −1 in the quotient set Q (not the generated subgroup), but −1 ∈ ⟨Q⟩ is a necessary condition expressed via 2-adic valuations of multiplicative orders.
why: Converts part of the ES event into 2-adic order statistics of primes modulo e, a theme in Artin-type problems (OAI 029, Moree).
first_step: For hard primes, compute for each e-slice whether −1 ∈ ⟨factors⟩ and whether −1 ∈ Q; quantify how often the necessary condition holds but Q misses −1.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz for ES congruence certificates
connection: Alon's Nullstellensatz guarantees nonvanishing points in grids given a top-degree coefficient; mod-m versions of ES (local solubility with restricted coordinates) are polynomial non-vanishing questions over grids.
why: A grid-restricted solution mod many m simultaneously is a step toward ES with size-constrained denominators.
first_step: Write 'there exist x ∈ A, y ∈ B, z ∈ C with 4xyz ≡ n(xy+yz+zx) mod ℓ' and compute the relevant top coefficient to see when the Nullstellensatz applies.

title: Frankston–Kahn–Narayanan–Park fractional expectation thresholds / spread measures
connection: FKNP show spread measures on hypergraph edges imply threshold behaviour; ES certificates could be weighted by a spread measure over (C,d) pairs.
why: Constructing a spread measure on ES certificates is a concrete combinatorial goal that would imply a probabilistic 'certificate exists'.
first_step: Define the uniform measure on Type I certificate patterns and compute its spread parameter q on data.

title: Hypergraph containers for the set of possible ES failure sets
connection: Container lemmas (Balogh–Morris–Samotij, Saxton–Thomason) count independent sets in hypergraphs; the ES failure set is divisor-closed and must avoid every n with an identity — an independent set in an 'identity hypergraph'.
why: Containers bound how structured a failure set must be, a disproof-shape tool.
first_step: Count, for n ≤ 10^4 restricted to Mordell-hard residues, the number of divisor-closed sets avoiding identity coverage up to modulus M.

title: Talagrand / Kahn–Kalai expectation thresholds (OAI 175, claimed) for ES monotone events
connection: OAI family 175 claims integral and fractional expectation thresholds agree up to a constant; if ES(p) is modelled as a monotone event over random divisibility indicators, threshold statements tighten.
why: Removes the log factor from Park–Pham-type bounds in a model; calibration of the ES heuristic.
first_step: Read OAI 175 statement and recompute the ES random-model threshold without the log ℓ factor.

title: Green–Tao relative Szemerédi / dense model for ES-good primes
connection: Green–Tao transference finds structure in dense subsets of primes; the set of ES-hard primes (not covered by identities of modulus ≤ M) is a structured subset of primes.
why: Could prove infinitely many patterns (APs) among primes p whose ES solutions have a specific shape — an existence-of-structure statement.
first_step: Check whether 'primes with an ES Type I certificate with C ≤ K' has positive relative density in primes; if so Green–Tao yields APs of them.

title: Peluse–Prendiville polynomial Szemerédi with power saving
connection: Peluse–Prendiville give power-saving bounds for sets avoiding x, x+y, x+y² etc.; ES identities often involve quadratic expressions in the parameter (Mordell families).
why: Degree-lowering for polynomial configurations could detect quadratic ES families within dense sets of n.
first_step: List Mordell-family identities as polynomial configurations (n, n+P1(t), …) and check whether they are of PP type.

title: Moreira monochromatic {x, x+y, xy} and Hindman sums/products (OAI 164)
connection: Moreira (Annals 2017) found monochromatic {x, x+y, xy}; OAI 164 claims Hindman's finite sums and products conjecture; ES mixes additive (4Cp+1) and multiplicative (divisor) operations.
why: Ergodic sum-product Ramsey results show additive and multiplicative structure can be forced together.
first_step: Phrase ES Type I as a configuration {p, C, 4Cp+1, d, (4Cp+1)/d} with additive and multiplicative relations and check whether it is a 'sum-product configuration' in Moreira's sense.

title: Mattheus–Verstraëte algebraic pseudorandom graphs (R(4,t)) from Hermitian unitals
connection: MV built optimal R(4,t) lower bounds from algebraic graphs over 𝔽_{q²}; ES-like 'sterile' residue structures are algebraic objects avoiding configurations.
why: Suggests constructing explicit algebraic sterile structures as candidates for counterexample-shape tests.
first_step: Check whether the repo's sterile residue patterns (STERILE_EXPLICIT.md) define an algebraic graph with Hermitian-unital-like incidence.

title: Breuillard–Green–Tao approximate groups for the divisor quotient set
connection: BGT classify approximate groups as near nilpotent cosets; in abelian (ℤ/e)^× this is Freiman–Green–Ruzsa; the ES quotient set Q is a product set.
why: If Q is an approximate group, it is near a coset progression, and −1 ∈ Q becomes an explicit lattice question.
first_step: Test on data whether divisor quotient sets are approximate groups (|Q·Q| ≤ K|Q| for small K).

title: Magee–Oh–Winter uniform congruence counting for Schottky semigroups
connection: MOW give uniform spectral gap/congruence counting for thin Schottky semigroups; underlying tool for Zaremba-type local-global.
why: If ES₅ admits a Schottky-semigroup formulation with unbounded alphabet truncated at height T, uniform counting mod q gives local-global for almost all.
first_step: Check whether truncating ES₅ letters to digits ≤ A yields a Schottky semigroup and compute its Hausdorff dimension δ_A as A grows.

title: Bourgain–Fuchs / Bourgain–Kontorovich density-one Apollonian method for ES siblings
connection: Positive-density and density-one results for Apollonian curvatures use thin-orbit circle methods with a quadratic subfamily (shifted binary forms); ES certificates are also quadratic-form values (p² + 4c²d).
why: Transfer of the 'quadratic subfamily + large sieve' trick to ES certificate families.
first_step: Identify a sub-family of ES certificates that is a shifted binary quadratic form in two free parameters at fixed p, and apply the BK almost-all argument.

title: Discretised projection (Bourgain) / Furstenberg sets (Ren–Wang) for p-adic or real ES geometry
connection: Bourgain's discretised projection theorem and Ren–Wang's Furstenberg set resolution give sum-product in ℝ at scale δ; ES solution ratios (x:y:z) live on a real curve family.
why: Could bound concentration of solution directions, relevant to size-window (FORCED_WINDOW) statements.
first_step: Express the set of normalized ES solutions (x/n, y/n, z/n) as a δ-discretised set and test projection-dimension statistics numerically.

title: Wooley efficient congruencing / nested efficient congruencing for ES moments
connection: Efficient congruencing gives sharp mean values via p-adic concentration iteration; ES solution counts mod prime powers have a p-adic concentration structure (Hensel lifts of certificates).
why: Moment bounds Σ f(n)^k with sharp exponents constrain the distribution of R(p).
first_step: Compute numerically Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n)^2, f(n)^3 and fit exponents of log N; compare with decoupling-type predictions.

title: Reciprocal plane / Orlik–Terao algebra viewpoint
connection: In inverted coordinates (u,v,w) = (1/x,1/y,1/z), U_n is the plane u+v+w = 4/n; its closure in the x-coordinates is the reciprocal plane of an affine hyperplane (Proudfoot–Speyer), whose coordinate ring is an Orlik–Terao algebra.
why: Reciprocal linear spaces have explicit Gröbner bases, Hilbert series and degenerations (broken circuits); a combinatorial degeneration could organise integral points.
first_step: Compute the Orlik–Terao / Proudfoot–Speyer presentation for the arrangement {u,v,w,u+v+w−4/n} and see whether integral points correspond to lattice points in a broken-circuit fan.

title: Browning–Sofos–Teräväinen Bateman–Horn & polynomial Chowla with probability 1
connection: BST prove Bateman–Horn and polynomial Chowla for almost all polynomials in large families and deduce Hasse principle with probability 1 for families of varieties.
why: ES conditional results use Dickson/Bateman–Horn-type inputs (CONDITIONAL_ES.md); BST says such inputs hold for random polynomials.
first_step: List every polynomial whose Bateman–Horn behaviour would imply ES-type statements in CONDITIONAL_ES.md and check whether it lies in a BST family.

title: Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg: Hardy–Littlewood (finite complexity) ⇒ rational points on fibrations
connection: HSW use Green–Tao–Ziegler to prove HP for fibrations with split degenerate fibres over linear polynomials; ES fibrations have degenerate fibres over linear forms in x.
why: Unconditional finite-complexity linear prime patterns are available — the cheapest unconditional input to fibration methods.
first_step: Identify the degenerate fibres of U_n → A¹_x and test whether they are 'split over linear polynomials' in HSW's sense.

title: OAI 027 potential integral density on curve character varieties (claimed)
connection: OAI 027 claims integral points become Zariski dense (after finite extension) on SL_n character varieties of curves; if U_n is a character-variety component, potential density of integral points is known type.
why: Potential density is weaker than ES, but structural info about how integral points arise could be imported.
first_step: After the previous item's identification, read OAI 027's mechanism for producing integral points.

title: Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger uniform Mordell for curves in the ES certificate space
connection: DGH (Annals 2021) bound the number of rational points on genus ≥ 2 curves uniformly in terms of genus and rank; ES auxiliary curves (multiple simultaneous ES conditions) have such genus.
why: Uniform bounds limit how many n can share a structured multi-solution pattern — informative for repeated-certificate statistics.
first_step: Construct the curve 'n has two ES solutions sharing x and y-ratio t' and compute its genus as a function of the constraints.

title: Chabauty–Kim / quadratic Chabauty on ES-derived S-unit curves
connection: Chabauty–Kim computes integral points on P¹ − {0,1,∞} (S-unit equations) and higher-genus curves (Balakrishnan–Dogra–Müller–Tuitman–Vonk); ES-derived S-unit curves appear when two denominators are constrained to be S-units.
why: Explicit computation of the finitely many exceptions would turn the S-unit barrier into data.
first_step: For S = {2,3,5,7}, compute all solutions of 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z with x,y,z,n S-units by brute force / known S-unit solvers.

title: Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin: Hasse principle for random Fano hypersurfaces
connection: BLS prove HP for 100% of Fano hypersurfaces of fixed degree and dimension ordered by height; ES gives a one-parameter family (in n), not a random family.
why: Calibrates: one-parameter families are exactly where 'random family' methods do not apply.
first_step: Record the family dimension needed in BLS's argument and compare with the ES family {U_n} (dimension 1).

title: Graber–Harris–Starr sections exist over ℂ(t): why identities exist geometrically but not integrally
