connection: GHS: rationally connected fibrations over curves have sections; U → A¹_n has rational fibres, so sections exist over ℂ(n) and ℚ(n) (identities with rational denominators), but Mordell–Schinzel shows none integral covering square classes.
why: Makes the integrality defect precise: it's an 'integral section' problem, whose obstructions are at the special fibres (n = square).
first_step: Compute the degenerate fibres of the integral model over Spec ℤ[n] and interpret the Mordell–Schinzel barrier as nonexistence of integral sections through specific fibre components.

title: Ellenberg–Venkatesh–Westerland homological stability & Cohen–Lenstra over 𝔽_q(t)
connection: EVW prove Cohen–Lenstra-type statistics over function fields via homological stability of Hurwitz spaces; ES over 𝔽_q[T] has proved variants and class-group input in its Type I.
why: Class-group distribution in the function-field ES certificate families could be computed exactly via Hurwitz-space methods.
first_step: Identify which class groups (of 𝔽_q[T][√(−D(T))]) enter the function-field ES Type I and check whether EVW-type results give their 2-parts.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Chan–Koymans–Milovic–Pagano negative Pell lower bounds via 8-rank
connection: CKMP get the lower bound side of negative Pell densities via 8-ranks; template for proving lower bounds for '−1 attained' events.
why: ES needs a lower-bound (existence) statement — the side negative-Pell work had to prove separately.
first_step: Read the CKMP argument and identify the step converting 'distribution of ranks' into 'at least this proportion attain −1'.

title: Mordell–Weil / elliptic fibrations on the Cayley cubic resolution
connection: The minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic is a weak del Pezzo of degree 3; pencils of anticanonical sections give elliptic fibrations whose fibres carry group laws.
why: Group laws on fibres could produce new ES solutions from old (chord–tangent) with integrality tracked — a source of solution-generating operations.
first_step: Pick a pencil of plane sections through a node, compute the elliptic fibration, and test whether adding a torsion section maps integral ES points to integral ES points.

title: Igusa / Denef–Loeser uniform p-adic integration for local densities of U_n
connection: Uniform p-adic integration (Cluckers–Loeser motivic integration) computes local densities σ_ℓ(n) uniformly in ℓ and n; the ES main term M_BM is an Euler product of such densities.
why: Uniformity in n of local densities is needed for any pointwise main-term statement.
first_step: Compute σ_ℓ(n) symbolically for the Cayley-cubic model and check uniformity across n mod ℓ^k.

title: Condensed/analytic-stack adelic formalism for the integral BM set (honest low-value item)
connection: Clausen–Scholze condensed mathematics gives a uniform framework for topological algebra over all places; the integral Brauer–Manin set of U_n is an adelic topological object.
why: Only a formalism; possibly useful for a clean statement of 'non-BM integral HP failure' families, not for existence.
first_step: Check whether a condensed formulation changes anything in BL's computation; most likely not — record and close.

title: Geometric Langlands over function fields (Gaitsgory et al.; OAI 014) for function-field ES counts
connection: Over 𝔽_q(t), Hecke eigensheaves geometrise automorphic forms; function-field ES counts are point counts on varieties over 𝔽_q whose cohomology might be automorphic.
why: Function-field ES has proved variants; a sheaf-theoretic count could give exact formulas for solution numbers in degree d.
first_step: Compute the ℓ-adic cohomology (Betti numbers) of the variety of degree-d function-field ES solutions for small q,d by point counts over 𝔽_{q^k}.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Integral points on hyperplane-arrangement complements (very affine varieties) via tropical compactification
connection: The torus part of U_n (all coordinates nonzero) is P² minus 4 lines in reciprocal coordinates — a very affine variety; tropical compactifications (Tevelev) and Huh's likelihood geometry study such varieties.
why: Tropicalisation shows which valuation patterns (sizes of x,y,z relative to n) integral points can have — a size-pattern classification of ES solutions.
first_step: Compute the tropical variety of the reciprocal plane and compare its cones with the observed (log x, log y, log z)/log n patterns of ES solutions at p ≤ 10^6.

title: Einsiedler–Margulis–(Mohammadi–)Venkatesh effective equidistribution of closed semisimple orbits
connection: EMV/EMMV give effective equidistribution of closed orbits of semisimple groups (e.g. SO(Q) for ternary Q) with polynomial rates; ES has ternary-form and quaternion reformulations.
why: Closed-orbit equidistribution yields local-global for representations of large integers by forms — with effective rates, potentially of a whole genus.
first_step: Pick the repo's ternary/quaternion ES reformulation (QUATERNION_ES.md) and identify the closed orbit whose equidistribution would give the needed representations.

title: Blomer–Harcos hybrid subconvexity for effective ternary representations
connection: Blomer–Harcos give hybrid subconvexity for twisted L-functions, enabling effective representation results for ternary forms (with Siegel caveats); ES's ternary analogues would need such input.
why: Effective bounds combined with 10^18 verification are the only way a ternary route could close a range.
first_step: Quantify the size beyond which Blomer–Harcos yields representations, for the discriminants arising in any ES ternary reformulation.

title: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth cycle integrals for ES₅ geodesic data
connection: DIT express traces of modular functions over closed geodesics (indefinite forms) as coefficients of mock modular forms; ES₅/CF-length data is geodesic (Hirzebruch–Jung, Dedekind) data of rationals tied to p.
why: A mock-modular generating function for CF-statistics could encode ES₅ counts with exact modular transformation laws.
first_step: Compute the DIT-style generating function Σ_D Tr_D(f) for f = indicator-like modular function and check whether CF length-3 counts appear.

title: Holowinsky–Soundararajan: sieve + subconvexity combo for 'large on average, so not zero' at one form
connection: Holowinsky–Soundararajan proved mass equidistribution for holomorphic Hecke forms by combining two weak methods (sieve bounds for shifted sums, Soundararajan's weak subconvexity) that each fail alone; ES's pointwise lower tail resists every single method.
why: Template for 'two complementary partial methods cover all cases' — e.g. one method for p with many small factors in 4Cp+1, another for the rest.
first_step: Split hard primes by an 'anatomy' parameter (e.g. number of small prime factors of the first slices) and check whether different repo methods cover complementary regimes.

title: Supersingular isogeny graphs: certificates as short cycles / collisions in the ℓ-isogeny graph mod p
connection: Maximal orders in B_{p,∞} ↔ supersingular curves over F̄_p. Embeddings of CM orders ↔ endomorphisms. ES Type I ⇔ a CM-order collision, which might be a short closed walk in an isogeny graph (Pizer graphs, Ramanujan).
why: Ramanujan-graph expansion gives existence of short walks between any vertices, which is a pointwise existence mechanism (T-type thick object of size ~p/12).
first_step: For p < 500, compute which supersingular j-invariants have endomorphism rings containing the orders Λ_{d,m} and how ES levels map to isogeny degrees.

title: Siegel–Rogers mean value / random-lattice model for ES lattices L_ρ
connection: Siegel's mean value theorem and Rogers' higher moments give the distribution of lattice-point counts in random lattices; ES(p) ⟺ some lattice L_ρ(p) has a vector in a cone (LATTICE_MEETING).
why: A random-lattice model predicts P(no vector in cone) and its p-dependence — a cleaner heuristic than divisor lotteries.
first_step: Compute covolume and cone volume for L_ρ(p) and compare empirical 'empty cone' frequency with Rogers' Poisson prediction.

title: Katz equidistribution of Kloosterman angles for fixed-modulus ES counts
connection: Katz: Kloosterman angles at a fixed prime modulus equidistribute w.r.t. Sato–Tate as the argument varies; ES fixed-modulus counts (FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS) reduce to Kloosterman-type sums.
why: Gives exact variance/distribution of ES residue counts across p mod ℓ.
first_step: Compute the ES count mod a prime ℓ as a function of p mod ℓ and test Sato–Tate statistics of its fluctuating part.

title: Keating–Snaith / random-matrix models for families in the ES character expansion
connection: RMT predicts moments of L-function families; ES counts expand over Dirichlet characters mod 4C, i.e. involve families of L-values / character sums.
why: If the ES count's fluctuating part is governed by an L-function family, RMT predicts its distribution, including lower tails.
first_step: Identify the family of L-functions (if any) whose values weight the ES count (via Eisenstein coefficients) and check its symmetry type.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Heap–Radziwiłł–Soundararajan sharp fractional moments → lower tails
connection: HRS give sharp upper bounds for fractional moments of ζ; small-moment control is equivalent to lower-tail information for log-normal-like quantities.
why: If log R(p) were approximately Gaussian (log-normal counts), fractional moments of R would control P(R small).
first_step: Fit the distribution of log R(p) at p ≤ 10^8 (data exists) and test log-normality; compute fractional moments.

title: Radchenko–Viazovska Fourier interpolation applied to ES lattice theta data (speculative)
connection: Fourier interpolation reconstructs f from values at √n and f̂ at √n; ES lattice reformulations have theta series whose coefficients count certificates.
why: Interpolation formulas give exact identities linking counts at different scales — potentially forcing a nonzero coefficient.
first_step: Check whether ES certificate counts are coefficients of a theta series of a fixed-dimension lattice; if not, close.

title: Bruinier–Funke theta lifts / Borcherds products for ES generating functions
connection: Theta lifts produce modular generating functions of traces/cycle counts; Borcherds products give automorphic forms with prescribed divisors. ES counts across p could be coefficients of such a lift if they are traces over class groups.
why: A Borcherds-type product with zeros encoding ES failures would turn ES into a divisor statement for an automorphic form.
first_step: Test whether Σ_p f(p) q^p (or a class-group-trace version) is the holomorphic part of a weak harmonic Maass form by checking coefficient growth and congruences.

title: Hyperbolic circle problem in Γ₀(N) for e-slice counts
connection: Counting Γ₀(N)-orbit points in hyperbolic discs has spectral asymptotics with error controlled by exceptional eigenvalues; e-slice certificates ab | N with a ≡ −b (mod e) can be phrased via matrices with lower-left entry divisible by e.
why: Moves the e-slice count into a standard spectral counting problem.
first_step: Construct the matrix encoding of e-slice certificates and count numerically vs Γ₀(e) disc-count predictions.

title: Hirzebruch–Jung / Dedekind sums reciprocity as a forcing identity
connection: Dedekind-sum reciprocity s(a,c)+s(c,a) = (a/c + c/a + 1/(ac))/12 − 1/4 relates HJ continued fractions of a/c and c/a; ES certificates have HJ/CF data (DEDEKIND_ES).
why: Exact reciprocity laws are the only kind of 'charge identity' that work pointwise; the repo found the Dedekind–HJ discharging charge χ-blind.
first_step: Look for a twisted Dedekind sum (with a character mod 4C) whose reciprocity law is χ-sensitive and test on ES certificates.

title: Harvey–van der Hoeven O(n log n) multiplication / fast sieving for verification beyond 10^18
connection: Asymptotically optimal integer multiplication and modern segmented sieving speed up the ES verification pipeline (Salez 10^17, Mihnea–Dumitru 10^18).
why: Extending verification is calibration only, but cheap engineering improvements shift the 'explicit range' needed by any analytic tail.
first_step: Profile the repo's verify.py on a 10^9 block at 10^18 and identify whether multiplication, sieving, or modular inversion dominates.

title: Davies et al. ML-guided intuition: which features predict f(p)?
connection: Davies et al. (Nature 2021) used attribution on trained models to discover knot-invariant and Kazhdan–Lusztig relations; the repo has f_I, f_II for all p ≤ 10^8.
why: A saliency analysis might find an unexpected invariant (beyond p mod small moduli) controlling low-count primes — e.g. a CF or class-number feature.
first_step: Train gradient-boosted trees on features (p mod q for q ≤ 100, n₂(p), class numbers h(−p), h(−4p), CF of √p, Legendre symbols) to predict f(p)/log²p; inspect feature importance.

title: Ramanujan Machine-style search for polynomial-CF identities producing ES₅ words
connection: The Ramanujan Machine (Raayoni et al., Nature 2021) searches polynomial continued fractions for constant identities; ES₅ solutions are short CF words with entries polynomial in parameters (Mordell families).
why: Automated search over polynomial CF word families could find new parametric families covering more residue classes.
first_step: Enumerate length-3 ES₅ words whose entries are degree-≤2 polynomials in t with small coefficients and record which residue classes mod 840·k they cover.

title: Single-fold Diophantine representations (OAI 242, claimed) — uniqueness promise versions of ES
connection: OAI 242 claims every r.e. set has a single-fold Diophantine representation; ES counts solutions (f(n) ≍ polylog), the opposite of single-fold.
why: Records a logic/arithmetic contrast: ES's richness (many solutions) is what makes it plausibly true; single-fold encodings show uniqueness is achievable in general.
first_step: None beyond reading the OAI statement; close unless a uniqueness variant of ES ('exactly one solution of shape X') becomes interesting.

title: OAI 142 deterministic polynomial factorisation over 𝔽_p (claimed) for deterministic ES search mod p
connection: OAI 142 claims deterministic polynomial-time factoring of polynomials over prime fields; deterministic square roots mod p appear in Type I (p² ≡ −4c²d mod f).
why: Derandomising the local steps of ES search; minor but concrete.
first_step: Identify randomised steps in the repo's ES search code (square roots mod primes) and note whether deterministic alternatives matter.

title: Integer linear programming for minimal sterile residue systems
connection: Sterile residue classes (STERILE_*) are CRT systems where all certificates of bounded size fail; ILP can find minimal-modulus sterile systems or prove none exist below a bound.
why: Calibrates how deep sterility can go — the disproof-shape analogue of covering systems.
first_step: Encode 'class r mod M is sterile for all certificates with C ≤ K' as constraints and minimise M with an ILP solver for K ≤ 20.

title: Proof mining / Kohlenbach: extracting bounds from ineffective ES-adjacent proofs
connection: Proof mining extracts explicit bounds from ineffective proofs (Kohlenbach); ES-adjacent results (Siegel-dependent exceptional-set bounds) are ineffective.
why: May yield explicit forms without new analytic input.
first_step: Identify the ineffective step in the repo's 3/4-exponent note and check whether it's a Siegel zero use (needs real effectivity) or a compactness argument (minable).

title: Probabilistic primality + certification (ECPP) for adversarial hard primes
connection: Hard primes beyond 10^18 are BPSW-probable; ECPP certificates make them rigorous primes.
why: Small but necessary hygiene for any claimed record-hard prime.
first_step: Produce ECPP certificates (Primo/CM) for the repo's hardest primes (e.g. 2054098191162848070241).

title: Kolmogorov-complexity view: a least counterexample has a short description
connection: The least ES counterexample (if any) is defined by a short Π₁ formula, so has low description complexity; probabilistic models treat failing p as 'random'.
why: Low-complexity numbers are not random-like; a heuristic tension worth stating (cf. Chaitin) but unlikely to give mathematics.
first_step: Record as a heuristic remark; no computation.

title: Statistical change-point tests on hardness vs p (detecting new obstruction scales)
connection: Change-point and extreme-value statistics detect regime shifts; ES min-count/log²p over p ≤ 10^8 and adversarial data at 10^25 could reveal a scale where hardness behaves differently.
why: A detected trend in normalised minimum would inform P(ES false) calibrations.
first_step: Fit an extreme-value (Gumbel/GEV) model to block minima of f(p)/log²p over dyadic ranges and extrapolate the expected minimum at 10^30.

title: OAI 011 Poisson–Dirichlet law for prime factors of p−1 → law for factors of p+e
connection: OAI 011 claims the ordered normalised log prime factors of p−1 converge to PD(1); the e-slice integers (p+e)/4 are shifted primes for fixed e.
why: A PD(1) law for shifted primes p+e (fixed e) gives the distribution of the 'generator set' of the ES quotient set across p — the right random model for e-slice success.
first_step: Compute the empirical law of prime-factor log-ratios of (p+3)/4 for p ≤ 10^8 and compare with PD(1); then simulate e-slice success under PD(1).

title: OAI 021 quadratic Jacobsthal bound (claimed) for slices avoiding bad primes
connection: OAI 021 claims every interval of C·k²/(log log k)² integers contains one coprime to any m with ≤ k prime factors; ES e-slices form an interval of consecutive N_e.
why: Guarantees, within a short window of slices, an N_e coprime to any prescribed bad modulus — e.g. avoiding primes that obstruct (−1 ∉ Q). It forces avoidance, not hitting, but is a pointwise every-interval statement.
first_step: Identify a finite set of 'obstructing primes' for e-slice success at a hard prime and compute whether Jacobsthal-avoidance within the first slices helps.

title: OAI 026 positive lower density of large prime gaps (claimed) — calibration for sterile runs
connection: OAI 026 claims a positive proportion of prime gaps exceed C log p for any C; analogous 'long sterile runs' of slices at positive density would be a calibration point for ES heuristics.
why: Shows how 'rare-event at a fixed scale with positive density' results are proved — compare with ES's polylog windows.
first_step: Read the OAI 026 mechanism and test whether long failing slice-runs at fixed length have positive density among primes in data.

title: OAI 023 Patterson cubic Gauss sum first moment (claimed) — cubic analogue of ES characters
connection: OAI 023 claims Patterson's first-moment asymptotic unconditionally; ES's 'class of divisors' uses quadratic/Dirichlet characters, while 4/n ↔ cubic forms suggest cubic residue structure (cubic surface).
why: Low expectation; recorded because ES's cubic surface could have a cubic-character layer the campaign hasn't probed.
first_step: Test whether ES counts f(p) for p ≡ 1 (mod 3) correlate with the cubic residue character of 2 or 4 mod p.

title: OAI 028 Gaussian moat (claimed) — ES_Q1 Gaussian sibling geometry
connection: OAI 028 claims no infinite bounded-step walk through Gaussian primes; ES_Q1 over ℤ[i] has failures at Gaussian primes 2+5i, 4+5i, …
why: Coverage-transfer technique (sieve on Gaussian primes in sectors) might bound or locate Gaussian ES_Q1 failures by angle.
first_step: Plot ES_Q1 failure Gaussian primes by argument and norm; check for angular structure (the repo killed one angular-pinching claim).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: OAI 182 power savings for polynomial differences at primes (claimed)
connection: OAI 182 claims power-saving Sárközy-type bounds for differences P(p), p prime; ES certificate polynomials evaluated at primes are a polynomial-at-primes family.
why: Weak link; records that difference-set methods at prime arguments now have power savings.
first_step: Check whether any ES certificate condition is a 'difference set avoids P(primes)' statement; likely close.

title: OAI 002/030 BSD formula & modularity over imaginary quadratic fields (claimed) — ES has no elliptic curve
connection: These claimed results concern elliptic curves; ES's surface is rational (Cayley cubic) with no natural attached elliptic curve except via chosen fibrations.
why: Null result recorded; the only conceivable link is through elliptic fibrations of the Cayley cubic resolution (separate item).
first_step: Close.

title: Bergström–Diaconu–Petersen–Westerland moments of L-functions over function fields
connection: BDPW compute all moments of quadratic L-functions over 𝔽_q(t) for q large via homological stability; function-field ES counts expand over quadratic/Dirichlet characters.
why: Exact function-field moment formulas would test any ES lower-tail heuristic precisely.
first_step: Identify the character family in the function-field ES count and compare with BDPW's families.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sawin square-root cancellation for factorisation-type functions in short intervals over 𝔽_q[T]
connection: Sawin proved square-root cancellation for sums of arithmetic functions depending on factorisation type in very short intervals over 𝔽_q[T]; 'has a divisor in a class' depends on factorisation plus residues.
why: Short-interval control over 𝔽_q[T] is exactly the slice-window statement needed in a function-field ES lower tail.
first_step: Check whether 'N has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod M)' is a 'factorisation function' in Sawin's sense (it depends on residues of factors, so needs his twisted version).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Gaussian multiplicative chaos limit for divisor-class counting functions
connection: Critical GMC describes limits of random multiplicative functions' partial sums and of |ζ| on short intervals (Saksman–Webb); the ES count is a divisor-sum over a random-like factorisation.
why: GMC is the established mechanism behind non-Gaussian lower tails of such sums.
first_step: Compute the random-model R(p) distribution and check for GMC-type log-correlated structure (variance ~ log log).

title: Barban–Davenport–Halberstam variance for ES counts in APs of p
connection: BDH gives the variance of prime counts over all residue classes; an analogous variance for ES counts f(p) across p mod q would quantify residue-class structure of hardness.
why: The repo's 'failure profile carries nothing beyond p mod M' claim is a variance statement in disguise.
first_step: Compute Σ_{a mod q} (Σ_{p≡a, p≤x} f(p) − expected)² for q ≤ 1000 and compare with a BDH-type prediction.

title: Selberg–Delange for class-restricted divisor generating functions
connection: Selberg–Delange gives asymptotics for Σ a(n) when Σ a(n)n^{−s} ≈ ζ(s)^z G(s); the indicator 'N has no divisor ≡ −1 (mod m)' has Dirichlet series with a fractional zeta power (prime factors in a subgroup).
why: Exact asymptotics for counts of N with no class-divisor give the baseline failure probability per slice.
first_step: Compute the Selberg–Delange exponent z for 'all prime factors in a subgroup H ∌ −1 of (ℤ/m)^×' and the resulting density x(log x)^{z−1}.

title: Ford–Konyagin–Luca / multiplicative structure of shifted primes p+e for e-slice generators
connection: Results on prime factors of shifted primes (Baker–Harman largest prime factor of p−1, Fouvry; Erdős–Pomerance) control whether N_e = (p+e)/4 has many small factors (good for generating −1).
why: Shifted-prime anatomy across all p is known in averaged forms; a fixed-p statement over e is needed.
first_step: Compute the fraction of hard primes p for which the first 10 slices N_e are all y-rough (no factors ≤ y) and compare with independence.

title: Inverse Littlewood–Offord (Tao–Vu, Nguyen–Vu) for signed subset products hitting −1
connection: For squarefree N = ∏ℓ_i, the e-slice quotient ab⁻¹ (ab | N) is ∏ ℓ_i^{ε_i} with ε_i ∈ {−1,0,1} — a signed 'Littlewood–Offord walk' in (ℤ/e)^×. Inverse LO theorems say a walk concentrates on one value only if the steps are structured (lie in a small GAP/subgroup).
why: Gives the right language for ES's e-slice: the hitting probability of −1 vs the generic 1/|group|, and what structure is needed for systematic failure.
first_step: For hard primes compute, per slice, the distribution of ∏ℓ_i^{ε_i} over all 3^ω sign patterns and compare P(−1) with 1/φ(e); identify slices where steps lie in an index-2 subgroup.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Gowers' quasirandom groups: ABC = SL₂(𝔽_q) for dense A,B,C — local covering for ES₅ words
connection: Gowers (and Nikolov–Pyber) show that if |A||B||C| > |G|³/m (m = minimal nontrivial representation dimension) then ABC = G; ES₅ certificates are length-3 products of letters from fixed sets.
why: Gives a clean local (mod q) surjectivity criterion for length-3 words — the local layer of ES₅ — and quantifies how dense the letter sets must be mod q.
first_step: Compute the reductions mod q of the ES₅ letter sets A, B, C (with entries bounded by p-dependent ranges) and check the Gowers inequality for q ≤ 50.

title: Helfgott growth in SL₂(𝔽_p) for the set of ES₅ letters
connection: Helfgott: generating sets A of SL₂(𝔽_p) satisfy |AAA| ≥ |A|^{1+δ} unless A is nearly the group; the ES₅ letter set at p is a specific subset.
why: Growth explains how quickly length-k words cover the group; ES fixes k = 3 so the growth exponent needed is computable.
first_step: Measure |A|, |A²|, |A³| mod small primes for the ES₅ letter set restricted to letters of height ≤ p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Szemerédi–Vu long APs in subset sums → structure of rich divisor sets
connection: Szemerédi–Vu: subset sums of a set of size ≫ √n contain long APs; highly composite slices have rich subset-product sets.
why: For slices with large ω(N) the quotient set contains long 'geometric progressions' mod e, which may be forced to contain −1.
first_step: Identify slices with ω(N) ≥ 8 at hard primes and test whether their quotient sets contain long GPs in (ℤ/e)^×.

title: Munshi's delta-method variants (DFI δ with conductor lowering) for ES character sums
connection: Munshi's conductor-lowering trick proves subconvexity by inserting extra averaging; ES counts at fixed p could use an artificial extra average (over a dummy modulus) to gain cancellation.
why: Conductor lowering creates averages where none exist — precisely ES's 'no free average' problem.
first_step: Insert a dummy average over auxiliary primes q ~ Q into the fixed-p ES count expansion and see whether Poisson summation yields a gain.

title: Erdős discrepancy (Tao) — sign-sequence view of ES parity layers
connection: Tao proved every ±1 sequence has unbounded discrepancy along HAPs, via entropy decrement + Fourier on multiplicative functions; ES parity data (R(p)/2 mod 2) is a ±1 sequence on primes.
why: If ES parity were completely multiplicative-like, discrepancy theorems would constrain it; mainly a calibration lens.
first_step: Compute discrepancy of the sequence (−1)^{R(p)/2} along APs of primes for p ≤ 10^8.

title: Sarnak Möbius disjointness: is the ES-hardness sequence 'deterministic'?
connection: Sarnak's conjecture: μ is orthogonal to zero-entropy sequences; the indicator of 'ES-hard p' (low normalised count) is a sequence of unknown complexity.
why: Testing correlation of ES-hardness with μ(p−1)-type data or with low-complexity sequences gauges whether hardness has hidden deterministic structure.
first_step: Compute correlations of the hardness indicator with μ((p−1)/4), λ((p+3)/4) and with Sturmian sequences of p.

title: Lorentzian polynomials (Brändén–Huh) / log-concavity of certificate-count sequences
connection: Lorentzian polynomials prove log-concavity of combinatorial sequences (matroid independent sets, etc.); ES certificate counts by size class or by number of prime factors used form sequences whose log-concavity could constrain zeros.
why: Log-concavity + positive endpoints ⇒ no internal zeros: a positivity mechanism that is pointwise.
first_step: For hard primes, compute the sequence a_k = #certificates using C with ω(C) = k (or certificate size buckets) and test log-concavity; if robust, look for a Lorentzian generating polynomial.

title: Markov/Markoff via cluster algebra of the once-punctured torus — ES analogue?
connection: Markoff triples are cluster variables of the once-punctured torus cluster algebra; the Cayley cubic ↔ four-punctured sphere character variety; ES's U_n shares the Cayley cubic.
why: If U_n's integral points are cluster-like for the four-punctured sphere (Fomin–Shapiro–Thurston surface cluster algebras), mutation provides the missing group action.
first_step: Compute the cluster algebra of the four-punctured sphere and its exchange relations; test whether ES solution triples satisfy any mutation relation.

title: Hypothesis-testing view: sequential probability ratio of certificate search
connection: Wald's SPRT gives optimal stopping for detecting an effect; certificate search at p is a sequential search with known per-slice success probabilities.
why: Gives the expected search cost and a principled 'hardness score' for primes, standardising adversarial data.
first_step: Define per-slice success probabilities from the random model and compute the likelihood ratio of 'p is hard' after K failed slices for data primes.

title: Heath-Brown square sieve on the ES failure set (non-squareness exploitation)
connection: Heath-Brown's square sieve counts squares in a sequence via characters; T1 says Type I/II fail at squares — the square sieve could quantify 'how square-like' a non-square must be to fail.
why: Makes T1 quantitative: failure at non-squares requires mimicking squares at many primes ℓ ((p/ℓ) = 1).
first_step: Correlate f(p) with the number of small ℓ with (p/ℓ) = 1 (QR-richness) on data.

title: Ihara zeta / non-backtracking spectra of ES certificate graphs
connection: Ihara zeta functions encode cycle structure and Ramanujan property of graphs; the bipartite graph (C-values) ↔ (primes dividing 4Cp+1) at fixed p is a natural graph.
why: Spectral gap of this bipartite graph controls how dependent certificates are (Janson Δ).
first_step: Build the bipartite graph at a hard prime for C ≤ 10^4 and compute its non-backtracking spectrum.

title: Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec bilinear forms with Kloosterman fractions (classic) for ES dispersion
connection: DFI bound Σ α_m β_n e(a m̄/n) nontrivially in all ranges; ES dispersion involves e(h·\overline{4C}/f)-type fractions.
why: The basic input for Type II dispersion in divisor-of-quadratic problems.
first_step: Locate where the repo's exceptional-set work uses Weil bounds instead of DFI and assess the gain.

title: Hasse norm principle / Tate cohomology for ray-class formulations of Type I
connection: Type I as 'an ideal of norm f in a ray class mod 4cd in ℚ(√−d)' invokes norm groups; Hasse's norm theorem (cyclic) gives local–global for norms.
why: Turns part of the Type I condition into class field theory, possibly identifying a reciprocity layer (T1) as a ray-class character.
first_step: Compute the ray class group mod 4cd of ℚ(√−d) and identify the subgroup the Type I condition requires, for small c,d.

title: Inverse Littlewood–Offord for I3 at fixed t: walks in (ℤ/t)^×
connection: For I3 at fixed t, success needs a divisor of tn+1 ≡ −1 (mod t) — a signed subset-product hitting −1 in (ℤ/t)^× (t small!).
why: Small t means a tiny group: random-walk/local-limit arguments are much stronger than for ES's large e; I3 might be provable where ES isn't, isolating why.
first_step: For n ≤ 10^9 and t ≤ 20, measure the fraction of (n,t) with the event and the dependence across t at fixed n.

title: Brauer–Manin for the pencil S_{n,k} at k = −4 (sibling failures {2,9,21,165,945,1197})
connection: The repo proved a BM obstruction on S_{n,k} for positive squares k; at k = −4 failures exist but no invariant is known; Colliot-Thélène–Xu style integral BM with negative k is untried.
why: Explaining sibling failures by a BM class would refine the zero-law calibration and test whether ES-type failures are always 'lottery'.
first_step: Compute Br S_{n,−4} and evaluate the candidate quaternion classes at the failing n.

title: Kloosterman/KMS bounds applied to the I3 count averaged over t
connection: I3's divisor event involves tn+1 with class −1 mod t; averaging over t ≤ T at fixed n gives Kloosterman-type sums with modulus t (small).
why: Fixed-n averages over t is the I3 analogue of fixed-p averages over C — test bed for bilinear Kloosterman input.
first_step: Write Σ_t Σ_{d | tn+1} 1_{d ≡ −1 (t)} via Fourier in d mod t and identify the Kloosterman sums.

title: Maynard–Tao weights over the slice index e at fixed p
connection: At fixed p the slices N_e = (p+e)/4 are consecutive integers; MT weights over admissible tuples of slices could force several slices to be 'structured' (e.g. have a small prime factor in a chosen class) simultaneously.
why: Fixed-p, average over e: legitimate without averaging over p — and MT weights are designed for consecutive-integer tuples.
first_step: Choose an admissible k-tuple of slice offsets and compute (numerically) the MT weighted proportion of windows where ≥ 2 slices succeed.

title: Green–Sawhney-type Type II information for p² + 4c²d with d prime
connection: Restricting to prime d makes p² + 4c²d a sparse polynomial family close to Green–Sawhney's p² + nq² setting.
why: Sub-family selection to reach a known bilinear estimate; the count loses only a log factor.
first_step: Measure how often Type I certificates with d prime exist at p ≤ 10^7.

title: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard GCD graphs for I3 overlaps across t
connection: I3 events for different t at fixed n share prime factors through gcd(tn+1, t′n+1) | (t−t′)… structure; GCD graphs quantify such overlaps.
why: Second-moment control at fixed n over t is the key missing step; GCD-graph compression is designed for that.
first_step: Compute gcd(tn+1, t′n+1) statistics for t,t′ ≤ 100 at the hardest I3 n values.

title: Chen–Stein Poisson approximation for I3 counts at fixed n
connection: I3 counts at fixed n over t, u, v are sums of weakly dependent divisor events; Poisson approximation predicts P(count = 0).
why: I3 is verified to 10^9 with a known largest exception 2 433 600 — calibrates Poisson-model predictions of the largest exception.
first_step: Fit the Poisson model on n ≤ 10^8 and predict the largest exception; compare with 2 433 600.

title: Bhargava-style 'average over a family then sieve to the subfamily' for ES over n in APs
connection: Bhargava's method: count over a big family with geometry of numbers, then sieve to squarefree/maximal subfamilies via uniformity estimates; ES averaged over n in APs mod M is a sieve to sub-families.
why: Uniformity estimates ('tail' bounds) are exactly what pass from averages to subfamilies like Mordell-hard classes.
first_step: Compute averaged ES counts over n ≡ r (mod 840) for each Mordell-hard r and check uniformity in r of the main-term constant.

title: Davies-style ML on sibling failures: which local features predict S_{n,−4} and ES_Q1 failures?
connection: Sibling failures (S_{n,−4}: n ≡ 0 mod 3 odd failures; ES_Q1: Im n ≡ 1 mod 4 cell) were partly explained by low-count cells; attribution on a classifier could find further features.
why: If failures are fully explained by local count-lowering features, the lottery reading is strengthened.
first_step: Train a classifier on n ≤ 10^5 with local features (n mod q, Legendre symbols) to predict S_{n,−4} counts; inspect feature importance.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Kahn–Kalai / Park–Pham on the I3 random model (small groups, many events)
connection: I3's events per n are many (t ranges) with small moduli; threshold theory could predict exactly when 'expected ≥ 1' implies 'present w.h.p.'.
why: I3 is proved-false-free beyond 2 433 600 in data; matching threshold predictions is a sanity test of the method before ES.
first_step: Compute expectation thresholds for I3 events at n ~ 10^6–10^9 in the random model.

title: Quantitative Hilbert irreducibility (Cohen; Castillo–Dietmann) for ES certificate covers
connection: Quantitative HIT bounds the number of specialisations where a Galois group drops; ES certificate covers over the p-line have Galois groups whose specialisations at p determine certificate existence.
why: If the cover's Galois group stays large at all but few p, Chebotarev-type positivity follows for most p — and exceptional p are 'thin sets'.
first_step: Compute the Galois group of a single Type I certificate cover (fixed c,d) over ℚ(p) and its thin-set exceptions.

title: Kelley–Meka sifting for pooled multi-slice certificates
connection: Pooling several slices with a common modulus e (e.g. N_e and N_{e′} with e | stuff) creates larger generating sets; KM-type density increments find large structured pieces in the pooled divisor sets.
why: Pooling is the natural escape from B2's 'one integer' constraint; additive-combinatorial structure theorems are the tool to exploit pooled sets.
first_step: Identify ES certificate shapes that legitimately combine prime factors of two different p-tied integers in one group, if any (check SIGNED_REFACTOR.md / COMPOSITION_ES.md).

title: Mixing of the greedy/odd-greedy Egyptian map as a Markov chain on residues
connection: The map n ↦ remainder after subtracting the greedy unit fraction acts on residues; as a Markov chain its mixing describes the distribution of remainders (cf. Tao's Syracuse analysis).
why: Mixing estimates give 'almost all' success of fixed-depth greedy-with-choice algorithms and pinpoint residue traps.
first_step: Compute the transition matrix of the remainder residue mod M for the 2-step greedy-with-choice ES search and its spectral gap.

title: Relaxing the fan: which pairing classes occur among graphs with p spanning trees and k vertices
connection: Generalise item 1: the graph-theoretic analogue of 'ES with more terms' is 'some graph with ≤ k vertices and τ(G) = p has a non-square sandpile pairing'. ES₅ is the k = 4 fan case. (Not via cycles/trees: a tree has trivial critical group, and C_p has pairing class −1/p, which is a square for p ≡ 1 (4). For large k a non-square class should come from longer chains, i.e. from λ(p) ≤ k − 1, which is known for k ≫ log p.)
why: Gives a ladder of relaxations parametrised by vertex count, with a known extremal theory for τ(G) values (Sedláček's α(n)); the threshold k(p) at which the non-square pairing first appears is a new invariant to compare with λ(p).
first_step: Compute k*(p) = least vertex count with a non-square pairing and τ = p, for p < 10⁴; compare with λ(p) and with Stong/Azarija–Škrekovski bounds for α(p).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Modular spanning-tree realisation (Alon–Bucić–Gishboliner) as a model for the sign condition
connection: Alon–Bucić–Gishboliner show every residue u mod N is τ(G) mod N for some planar G on O(log N) vertices. ES₅ is a 'τ(G) = p exactly and pairing class prescribed' statement on 4 vertices.
why: Their short combinatorial proofs control τ(G) modulo N with few vertices; a version controlling the pairing class (a mod-p quadratic datum) would be a graph-theoretic analogue of an ES-type sign theorem.
first_step: Read arXiv:2503.23648; check whether their gadgets allow simultaneous control of τ(G) and the square class of the sandpile pairing.

title: Effective resistance A/p of a 3-node ladder network
connection: In the fan network with unit conductances, the effective resistance between a and the sink is (M⁻¹)₁₁ = A/p. So ES₅(p) ⇔ a three-node ladder network with integer conductances to ground and total 'tree count' p has R_eff(a,s) = A/p with A a non-residue mod p.
why: Electrical-network theory has exact theorems on which rationals are resistances of networks with k unit resistors (series–parallel ↔ continued fractions). The ES sign becomes a residuosity property of a physical quantity.
first_step: Enumerate rational resistances of networks with ≤ 12 unit resistors (OEIS A048211 family); check whether non-residue numerators A/p appear at small resistor counts for every p ≡ 1 (4) < 2000.

title: Heegaard Floer d-invariants of L(p,A) as an obstruction/selector for 3-chain plumbings
connection: d-invariants of lens spaces satisfy an explicit recursion (Ozsváth–Szabó), d(L(p,q),i) via d(L(q, p mod q), j). Plumbing length 3 constrains the negative-definite fillings, and the ES sign is the homotopy class.
why: d-invariants are a native tool for deciding which lens spaces bound which definite 4-manifolds (Lisca's rational-ball classification itself used Donaldson's theorem and lattice embeddings; d-invariants give complementary obstructions). They might give a closed-form test of 'some 3-chain filling exists in the non-square class'.
first_step: Implement the Ozsváth–Szabó recursion. For p < 2000, compare Σ_i d(L(p,A),i) statistics over the classes A with r(p/A) = 3 between (A/p) = ±1.

title: Lattice embedding of the 3-chain into the diagonal lattice ℤ^k (Donaldson-style)
connection: If a definite filling can be glued to another definite filling (of the reversed manifold) to give a closed definite 4-manifold, Donaldson's theorem forces the combined intersection lattice to be diagonal, so the plumbing lattice embeds in −ℤ^k (Lisca's method). For the chain (v,t,u), embeddings into ℤ^3 or ℤ^4 are explicit combinatorics, and the ES sign is a property of the complement lattice's discriminant.
why: This is the native toolbox of 4-dimensional topology for lens spaces, and it turns ES₅ into a finite combinatorial embedding question at each p.
first_step: Enumerate embeddings of chain lattices with det p into ℤ⁴ for p < 500; check whether the orthogonal complement's discriminant square class equals the ES sign.

title: Kollár–Shepherd-Barron P-resolutions and Wahl singularities 1/m²(1, ma−1) as the T1 locus
connection: T-singularities 1/(dm²)(1, dma−1) have ℚ-Gorenstein smoothings with Milnor number d − 1; the Wahl case d = 1, i.e. 1/m²(1, ma−1), has rational-homology-disk (QHD) smoothings. These sit at square orders m², exactly where T1 kills certificates. KSB P-resolutions of 1/p(1,A) are counted by zero continued fractions.
why: The T1 obstruction may be the shadow of 'square-order cyclic quotients admit QHD smoothings'. Smoothing theory would then give a geometric reason for the square/prime dichotomy.
first_step: Compute, for A ∈ L₃(m²), whether 1/m²(1,A) is a Wahl singularity or admits a QHD smoothing, and compare with the T1 certificate emptiness.

title: Tridiagonal ternary lattice of determinant p in the non-square genus
connection: The Gram matrix M(t,u,v) defines a positive definite ternary lattice of determinant p with basis e₁,e₂,e₃, e₁·e₃ = 0, e₁·e₂ = e₂·e₃ = −1. Its discriminant form is A/p on ℤ/p. ES₅(p) ⇔ the genus of ternary lattices of det p with non-square discriminant form contains a lattice admitting such a chain basis with norms ≥ 2.
why: This is the native language of ternary quadratic forms: genus/class tables (Brandt–Intrau), Siegel mass, and representation of binary sublattices. It brings Duke–Schulze-Pillot style tools.
first_step: For p < 2000, list the reduced ternary forms of det p in each genus (Eisenstein reduction). Count the classes admitting a chain basis, and check whether the non-square genus always has one iff ES₅(p).

title: Sylver coinage / numerical-semigroup games on the forest's Frobenius classes
connection: The forest edge relation uv | p+u+v identifies p as a 'Frobenius-shadow' point of ⟨u,v⟩. Conway's Sylver coinage is a game whose positions are numerical semigroups; P-positions are related to Frobenius data.
why: Game positions give a different combinatorial calculus on pairs (u,v); an ES-relevant invariant might appear as a Sprague–Grundy value. Low prior but not meaningless.
first_step: Compute Sprague–Grundy-type data for two-generator Sylver positions ⟨u,v⟩ with uv | p+u+v; look for any correlation with (uv/p).

title: Goeritz matrix of an alternating 2-bridge diagram equals the chain matrix
connection: For the plumbing description, the Goeritz form of a suitable 2-bridge link diagram should be (up to sign and stabilisation) the tridiagonal chain matrix (check the diagram convention: plumbing digits are not the same as twist-region counts of the standard diagram). Gordon–Litherland gives σ = sign(G) − μ.
why: This pins ES₅ to an explicit knot diagram: a 3-twist-region 2-bridge knot of determinant p. Knot tables could be scanned for the sign.
first_step: Check against KnotInfo: for 2-bridge knots with det p ≡ 1 (4), p < 200, and 3 twist regions in even CF form, record the linking-form class.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Plumbing calculus moves (blow-up/blow-down of ±1 curves) as certificate transport
connection: Kirby calculus moves change a plumbing chain without changing the boundary lens space. The boundary words (letters = 1) of LENGTH_THREE are formal words that become interior after blow-downs.
why: This gives a topological interpretation of the repo's boundary/interior word distinction and of 'transport' moves between certificates (boundary-preserving blow-ups do not change |det|, so transport between different n needs a non-boundary-preserving move such as a surgery/cobordism step; identify which).
first_step: Map LENGTH_THREE formal words (letter 1) to blow-down sequences; check whether ES transport laws (TRANSPORT_LAW.md) are Kirby moves.

title: Kirchhoff/Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte: squared rectangles from planar networks with p spanning trees
connection: A planar network with τ = p spanning trees gives a rectangle tiled by squares with sides of total scale p (BSST). The fan graph of item 1 is planar, so ES₅ gives a squared rectangle of a specific shape whose aspect ratio encodes the resistance A/p.
why: Squared-rectangle theory has a 'reduced side' (= τ) and aspect ratios = resistances. ES₅ becomes: some 4-vertex-network squared rectangle with reduced side p has aspect class non-residue.
first_step: Compute BSST rectangles for the fan networks at small p; check whether the aspect-ratio numerator class is visible geometrically (e.g. via tile parity).

title: Hoffman/spectral bound on the forest F_p with Legendre colouring (bichromatic edge existence)
connection: ES₅ for p ≡ 1 (8) ⇔ the word forest F_p has a bichromatic edge under v ↦ (v/p). Spectral graph theory bounds the size of monochromatic (independent-type) sets via eigenvalues.
why: It is the textbook first tool for 'every 2-colouring with given class sizes has a bichromatic edge'. The Legendre colouring has known sizes inside intervals (Burgess), but F_p is sparse.
first_step: Compute the spectrum of F_p for p < 10⁴; compare λ_max/λ_min with the size of the QR set inside vertices to see if Hoffman-type bounds are anywhere near.

title: Ising model on F_p: ES₅ failure = zero-energy configuration of a frustrated ferromagnet
connection: Put spins σ_v = (v/p) on F_p. ES₅ failure (no bichromatic edge) means the Legendre configuration is a ground state of the ferromagnetic Ising Hamiltonian on F_p. Statistical mechanics has Peierls/contour arguments for when ground states must have domain walls.
why: A Peierls-type argument combines an 'external field' (Legendre symbol bias on short intervals) with graph connectivity. It is a native tool not obviously tried.
first_step: Compute, per component of F_p, the fraction of +spins; check how large monochromatic components get (ES₅ only needs one bichromatic edge somewhere, so monochromatic components are compatible with ES₅).

title: Farey-graph geodesic of length 3 in the non-residue class
connection: HJ length r(p/A) is (up to normalisation) a combinatorial distance-type statistic in the Farey graph from ∞ to p/A via a specific path type. ES₅ asks whether the Farey ball of 'HJ radius 3' around ∞ contains a vertex p/A with A a QNR.
why: The Farey graph is hyperbolic geometry's combinatorial skeleton, and its metric theory (Beardon–Hockman–Short) is well developed.
first_step: Compare r(p/A) with Farey distance d(∞, p/A) for p < 10⁴; check whether the ES₅ condition is a Farey-distance condition for a known metric.

title: Closed geodesic of γ_w on the modular surface: trace N−m and word length 3
connection: γ_w is hyperbolic when |A+A*| > 2. Its closed geodesic has a cutting sequence of length governed by the word. Prime geodesic theorems with Jacobi-symbol twists (Sarnak's class-number sums) count such objects.
why: Prime geodesic theorems in conjugacy classes and with characters are fully developed; ES₅ is a twisted count of geodesics with very short cutting sequences.
first_step: Write trace(γ_w) = tu + tv − 2 = A + A* and list the conjugacy classes; check whether ES₅ is equivalent to a short-cutting-sequence geodesic of trace in a given set with a character condition.

title: Harpaz's log K3 surfaces: dP5 minus a pentagon and the frieze variety with coefficient N
connection: Harpaz classified log K3 surfaces with trivial geometric Picard group compactifiable to del Pezzos: dP5 with a boundary pentagon of (−1)-curves, which is the A₂ cluster variety. He proved non-Zariski-density of integral points when the Galois action is trivial. The ES₅ frieze (Ptolemy relations with frozen sides (1,1,1,1,N)) is a one-parameter deformation of this variety.
why: It is the closest proved arithmetic theorem about integral points on the exact variety class carrying ES₅ words, and it shows how Brauer–Manin fails to be the only obstruction there.
first_step: Check whether the N-fibre of the pentagon-with-coefficients variety is again dP5 minus a pentagon (a twisted A₂ cluster variety), and read Harpaz §§4–5 for the non-BM obstruction mechanism.

title: Conway–Coxeter triangulation count with a mod-4 marked quiddity entry
connection: Classical friezes ↔ triangulations (Conway–Coxeter). The slot lemma says the ES sign is −1 iff 4 divides one of the five pentagon entries (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1). So ES₅ asks for a frieze with coefficients having an entry ≡ 0 (mod 4).
why: 'Some quiddity entry ≡ 0 mod 4' is a reduction-mod-4 condition, and friezes over ℤ/4 (or SL₂(ℤ/4) Farey complexes) are finite objects with full classifications.
first_step: Enumerate the mod-4 reductions of all positive words for p < 10⁵ and record which mod-4 frieze types occur per p; compare with Morier-Genoud's counts of friezes over finite rings.

title: Tropical frieze / tropicalisation of the pentagon-with-coefficient
connection: Replacing (×,+) by (+,max) gives a tropical frieze: 2-adic valuations of the pentagon entries satisfy the tropical Ptolemy relations only as inequalities (v₂(a+b) ≥ min, with equality unless there is cancellation, e.g. 1 + 1 = 2), so they give tropical constraints, not a tropical frieze. The slot lemma condition is a 2-adic valuation event (v₂(entry) ≥ 2).
why: Tropical friezes are piecewise-linear and fully classifiable, so they might give a necessary-and-sufficient 2-adic shape of sign-(−1) words.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic valuation vectors (v₂ of the 5 entries) of all words for p < 10⁵ and the allowed tropical patterns; check whether every p has a pattern with some v₂ ≥ 2.

title: Positive points of cluster varieties ↔ tropical points (Fock–Goncharov duality) for the ES frieze
connection: Fock–Goncharov: positive-integer tropical points of a cluster X-variety parametrise a canonical basis of the dual A-variety. ES words are positive integer points of an A-type frieze variety with coefficient.
why: If ES words were tropical points of a dual variety, existence would become 'a certain polyhedral cone contains an integer point', which is linear.
first_step: Identify the dual (X-variety) of the A₂-with-coefficient frieze variety; compute its tropical points relevant to N; check whether the A-integer points (words) are in bijection with them.

title: Integral points on log CY surfaces: counting conjecture of order (log B)^k and the U_n fibre
connection: For log K3/log CY surfaces the expected integral point count up to height B is a power of log B (Harpaz; Wilsch-type works on integral points of bounded height). U_n has finitely many positive points, but its signed integral points can be counted.
why: The ES expected count ≍ log²n matches 'log-power' heuristics for log CY. Translating the n-dependence into height may connect ES's count to a Manin-type conjecture for integral points.
first_step: Count signed integral points on U_n of height ≤ B for fixed n and growing B (numerically); compare with a (log B)^b law and identify b with the boundary's dual-complex dimension.

title: The pencil S_{n,k}: 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) = k as a K3-type family with a singular fibre at k = 0
connection: Z52 proved a BM obstruction for k = m² (with congruence conditions) that dies at k = 0. In degeneration theory, the k = 0 fibre is the central fibre of a family of affine cubic surfaces. Brauer classes can extend over the family or ramify at k = 0.
why: Specialisation of Brauer classes in families (purity/residue maps) is a native tool. The residue along the exceptional conic was computed; nearby fibres give limiting information.
first_step: Compute Br of the generic fibre of the pencil over Q(k), and the residues at k = 0 and k = ∞; record whether any class survives as an unramified class on the k = 0 fibre's resolution.

title: Integral Hasse principle for U_n relative to a group action at infinity (ℝ⁺ component)
connection: BL treat the positive real component U_n(ℝ)⁺. Positivity of solutions is an archimedean condition; BM evaluation can see real connected components (as in BL's U_n(ℝ)⁺ version), but not finer positivity structure inside a component. Strong approximation with an archimedean constraint is studied for homogeneous spaces.
why: The repo's T1 is a reciprocity obstruction coupling the archimedean and finite places. The native tool is a 'Brauer–Manin with archimedean condition' (BL's U(ℝ)⁺ version).
first_step: Re-read BL §§5–7 for the exact role of U_n(ℝ)⁺; record which Brauer classes have non-constant evaluation on U_n(ℝ)⁺.

title: Elliptic fibration of the ES cubic by planes x + y + z = s
connection: Intersecting the projective closure with the pencil of planes x + y + z = sw gives plane cubic curves, an elliptic fibration (after base-point blow-ups). ES points are integral points on these elliptic curves with positive coordinates.
why: The elliptic-curve toolbox applies fibrewise: Mordell–Weil ranks, Néron–Tate heights and integral points. Ranks along the family could produce infinitely many signed points.
first_step: Compute the Weierstrass model of the s-fibre for fixed n (sympy), and the Mordell–Weil rank of the generic fibre over Q(s).

title: Toric degeneration of U_n to the torus complement xyz ≠ 0 and the Newton polytope
connection: As n varies, 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) degenerates (n → 0, n → ∞) to toric strata. Newton polytope methods (Bernstein–Kushnirenko, Khovanskii) count solutions in tori over finite fields; positive integer solutions relate to the polytope's interior lattice points.
why: Newton-polytope/tropical methods give exact solution counts over F_q (Ax–Katz divisibility of point counts) and might give mod-2 parity of solution counts.
first_step: Compute #U_n(F_q) exactly via the toric model and check Ax–Katz-type q-divisibility; record whether any parity information survives to positive integer points.

title: Hasse principle for the 'Type II at fixed level' variety: d | 4Cn+1, d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) as a norm-form/torus variety
connection: At fixed C, a solution is a factorisation 4Cn+1 = d·d′ with d ≡ −1 (mod 4C). This is an integral point on a torus-type variety (norm form for the trivial extension, with level structure). Ray-class-field reciprocity says the class of d is constrained.
why: Torus-variety integral points with level structure are governed by class field theory (ray class groups). ES at fixed C is exactly a ray-class question, B2.
first_step: Record the ray class group mod 4C whose Frobenius class decides it, and the explicit list of p's covered for C ≤ 20 (sanity link to Mordell covering).

title: Bhargava cubes: the Type II cube point (c,d,j) as a 2×2×2 integer cube
connection: FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS packages Type II data as a cube point; Bhargava's cube law composes three binary quadratic forms. If certificates are cubes with a fixed corner, composition gives relations among certificates of different n.
why: Bhargava's parametrisations come with orbit-counting (geometry of numbers on prehomogeneous spaces), which gives averages but sometimes also exact class-group relations.
first_step: Write a certificate as an explicit 2×2×2 cube and compute its three binary forms; check which one has discriminant related to p and what composition does to certificates.

title: Multiplicative subgroup generated by prime factors: Frobenius / Chebotarev form of 'divisor in coset'
connection: A divisor d of N in the class −1 mod 4C exists iff a subset product of the prime factors of N hits −1 in (ℤ/4C)^×. This is a zero-sum / subset-product problem in a finite abelian group (Davenport constant).
why: The Davenport constant D(G) says any sequence of length ≥ D(G) has a zero-sum subsequence. Subset-product hitting −1 needs ω(N) about D((ℤ/4C)^×) primes in general position.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ and C ≤ 30, compute ω(4Cp+1) and whether the prime classes' subset products cover −1; compare with Davenport-constant thresholds.

title: Burgess-type bounds for character sums over 'divisor sets' (multiplicative structure)
connection: ES₅ needs χ_p to be non-constant on S₃(p) = {A : r(p/A) = 3}, a set of size ≈ log²p built from divisors. Character sums over multiplicatively structured sets (products of two sets) admit Burgess/bilinear bounds.
why: S₃(p) = {(p+u)/v : v | p+u, …}: if it contains a product set A·B mod p with |A|,|B| ≫ p^ε, bilinear character-sum bounds would force a non-residue.
first_step: Check computationally whether S₃(p) (or the larger S_L(p)) contains large product sets A·B mod p.

title: The lattice Λ_A = {(x,y) : y ≡ Ax (mod p)}: ES₅ ⇔ a non-residue A whose lattice has a short vector in a hyperbolic region
connection: vA ≡ u (mod p) with v | p+u means (v, u) ∈ Λ_A with uv small. By Minkowski every Λ_A has a vector with |x||y| ≤ p. ES₅ needs (v, u) with vA − u = p exactly (not just mod p) and positive.
why: It is geometry of numbers in its native form: minima of the family of lattices Λ_A over A ∈ QNR. Successive minima of Λ_A relate to CF data, with a Hecke-type averaging over A.
first_step: For p < 10⁵ compute λ₁(Λ_A) for all A and the minimum over non-residue A of the product-norm minimum; relate to λ(p).

title: Backward-CF (Rényi-type) map T(x) = ⌈1/x⌉ − 1/x: infinite invariant measure and orbit length 3
connection: The HJ expansion is generated by a backward-CF (Rényi-type) map with an infinite invariant measure (parabolic fixed point). The coordinate convention matters: in the variable x = A/p the map T(x) = ⌈1/x⌉ − 1/x reproduces the HJ step, whereas the map x ↦ 1/(1−x) − ⌊⋯⌋ started at A/p does not (5/17 takes 4 steps, but its HJ length is 3). Short orbits to 0 in 3 steps are the ES₅ words.
why: Infinite-ergodic-theory tools (Aaronson, Thaler) describe return statistics near the parabolic point, and ES words are 'fast escapes', the complementary regime.
first_step: Compute the measure of points with exactly 3-step Rényi orbits to the cusp at resolution 1/p; compare with |L₃(p)|/p.

title: Farey-fraction spin chain (Kleban–Özlük) partition function and the ES words
connection: Kleban–Özlük's Farey spin chain has a partition function built from products of matrices [[1,0],[1,1]] and [[1,1],[0,1]], and its states are Farey fractions. ES words correspond to specific length-3 HJ blocks, so a restricted partition function counts them.
why: Statistical mechanics of number-theoretic chains has exact phase-transition results; a 'Legendre-field' coupling would make the ES sign a magnetization.
first_step: Define Z_p(β, h) = Σ_{A} e^{−β·r(p/A)} (A/p)^{h}; compute for p < 10⁴ and look at the h-derivative at β → ∞ (the min-length sign).

title: Hecke operators on the space of words: does T_ℓ map ES₅ words of p to words of ℓp or ℓ²p?
connection: Hecke operators act on SL₂(ℤ)-cosets/matrices with fixed determinant structure. Words are SL₂ matrices with upper-right entry p. Hecke correspondences relate matrices with entry p to entry ℓp.
why: It is the modular-forms-native way to get relations between different n. A Hecke-equivariant structure on certificates would allow induction.
first_step: Apply the coset representatives of T_2 to γ_w and check which images are words (positive, upper-right p or 4p) and how the sign transforms.

title: Gross–Keating / arithmetic intersection of CM cycles as certificate counts
connection: Gross–Keating compute intersection numbers of Hecke correspondences on modular curves in terms of quadratic forms. QUATERNION_ES shows Type I ⇔ an x = 2 collision of CM orders in B_{p,∞}, i.e. an intersection of CM points.
why: Intersection numbers are positive and given by explicit local formulas, which is a geometric positivity mechanism. The question is whether some intersection number equals (or bounds below) a certificate count.
first_step: Express the 'collision of CM orders' count as an intersection T_m · T_n of Hecke correspondences (Gross–Keating) for small p; compare with ES counts.

title: Duke–Schulze-Pillot: ternary forms represent all large n in their spinor genus — applied to the chain lattice
connection: DSP proved every sufficiently large integer (primitively, locally represented, outside spinor exceptions) is represented by a positive definite ternary form. ES₅ is not 'a fixed form represents p' but 'some form of det p has a special basis'; the dual question 'which binary forms does a ternary represent' (Ellenberg–Venkatesh) is closer.
why: It records the nearest pointwise representation theorem with ternary forms and why it does not apply directly (the form varies with p).
first_step: Find a reformulation where a fixed ternary form must represent a p-tied number with a sign (e.g. via QUATERNION_ES Λ_{d,m}) and check DSP's ineffectivity/effectivity.

title: Hurwitz class numbers and the level count M_t^lev(n) = (τ(N) − σ_{χ_{−t}}(N))/φ(t)
connection: The BM level count is a difference of divisor functions twisted by χ_{−t}. Sums over t of such twisted divisor sums resemble Hurwitz class-number relations (Kronecker–Hurwitz Σ_t H(4n − t²)).
why: Class-number relations are exact and positive. If Σ_t over BM levels matches a Hurwitz-type sum, the BM layer gets an exact formula.
first_step: Compute Σ_{t ≤ T} M_t^lev(n) and compare with Σ H(4tn − s²)-type expressions numerically for n < 10⁴.

title: Shimura curve / quaternion Shimura lift of the ES theta series
connection: The theta multiplier sign (bsB_theta_multiplier) is weight-1/2 data. The Shimura correspondence maps half-integral to integral weight. ES's sign function on certificate matrices might lift to a function on a Shimura curve's CM points.
why: It would place the sign inside an automorphic representation where nonvanishing theory exists. Zero-propagation was refuted (O175), so only the lifting is new.
first_step: Look at O175 notes (bsB_theta_multiplier) and identify which level and character a 'certificate theta series' would have; compute the first 50 coefficients.

title: Composition on V_n as ideal multiplication in ℤ[2√f]: certificates as a 'box' in a narrow class group
connection: COMPOSITION_ES: V_n values at μ are the fibre over a fixed order-2 narrow class δ of the box of primitive ideals of norm dividing μ. ES ⇔ the box meets δ with an extra condition (B = 1).
why: Class-group 'boxes' (ideals of bounded norm generating/hitting a class) are a native class-field-theory question, with results via Bach's bound under GRH and unconditional Lamzouri-type results.
first_step: Calibrate: for μ in a window, size of box vs narrow class number; check whether GRH-Bach bounds would put the box onto δ (they handle generation, not hitting one class with norm constraints).

title: Subconvexity for L(1/2, f × χ_{−4p}) and shrinking-target CM equidistribution
connection: Equidistribution of CM points in shrinking targets reduces (via Waldspurger) to subconvexity for twisted L-functions. ES certificates live in a target of measure ~p^{−1/2+o(1)}.
why: It gives the precise exponent gap: Weyl-strength subconvexity yields shrinking targets of size p^{−1/12}-ish, far from p^{−1/2}. It is a clean calibration.
first_step: Compute the target measure exactly, then the required subconvexity exponent; record the gap.

title: Quaternion order Λ_{d,m}: reduced-norm representation of p by a ternary sublattice
connection: QUATERNION_ES Lemma 1.2: Λ_{d,m} = ℤ⟨u,v⟩ with u² = −d, v² = −m, uv + vu = 1 is an order. Type I data are elements of prescribed norm/trace. ES becomes 'p is represented by a specific ternary norm form attached to (d,m)'.
why: Representation by ternary forms attached to orders has a theory: Gross lattices, Eichler orders, spinor genera. A family over (d,m) gives many forms, any of which suffices.
first_step: For each (d,m) ≤ 20 compute the Gross lattice (trace-zero part) and its genus; check whether p's representability by that genus is automatic (local conditions only) and whether spinor exceptions arise.

title: Hilbert modular / Hirzebruch–Zagier cycles for the pair (A, A*) with AA* = tp+1
connection: Hirzebruch–Zagier cycles T_N on Hilbert modular surfaces have intersection numbers given by class numbers. Pairs (A,A*) with AA* = tp + 1 are points of a 'norm' condition that might be intersection points of T_N with a modular curve.
why: Hirzebruch–Zagier gives exact intersection numbers as coefficients of modular forms; if certificates are intersection points, their count is a known modular coefficient.
first_step: Check whether pairs (A, A*) with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t) and AA* = tp+1 are naturally CM points / intersection points on X(1) × X(1) (i.e. on a Hecke correspondence T_{tp+1}).

title: Existential theory of (ℕ, +, |) (Lipshitz/Bel'tyukov) and fixed-C Type II statements
connection: At a fixed level C, 'p has a certificate' is ∃d,k: d | 4Cp+1 ∧ d = 4Ck − 1, an existential formula in (ℕ,+,|) with parameter p. Lipshitz proved the existential theory of (ℤ,+,|) decidable; the ∀p∃ fragment is a different matter.
why: It locates the logical complexity of finite-menu ES statements. A decidable ∀∃ fragment would make 'ES via levels C ≤ C₀' algorithmically decidable, although B1 says such statements are false.
first_step: Check the literature on the decidability of ∀∃ sentences of (ℕ,+,|) (Bel'tyukov, Lipshitz); record whether multiplication becomes definable there.

title: Gauss-sum / Fourier coefficient of 1_{S₃(p)} at the quadratic character
connection: ES₅(p) ⇔ Σ_{A ∈ S₃(p)} (A/p) < |S₃(p)|. In coding/Fourier terms, the quadratic Fourier coefficient of 1_{S₃} must not be maximal. Uncertainty principles (Tao's prime-field uncertainty, Biró–Meshulam) bound how concentrated a set and its Fourier transform can be.
why: Tao's uncertainty principle for F_p says |supp f| + |supp f̂| ≥ p + 1. Indicator sets that are subsets of QR have structured Fourier transforms, which gives a potential contradiction with S₃'s known Fourier structure.
first_step: Compute the Fourier transform of 1_{S₃(p)} for p < 5000; check whether 'S₃ ⊆ QR' would force a Fourier property contradicted by S₃'s divisor structure.

title: Statistical-mechanics partition function over all ES solutions and Lee–Yang zeros
connection: Define Z_n(β) = Σ_{solutions} (xyz)^{−β}. ES(n) ⇔ Z_n ≢ 0. Lee–Yang-type theorems locate zeros of partition functions with ferromagnetic structure. A family Z(n, β) analytic in n-related variables might have provably non-vanishing coefficients.
why: Speculative, but it is the stat-mech native form of 'nonempty'; the Dirichlet series Σ_n Z_n(β) n^{−s} is a height zeta function of the threefold 𝒰.
first_step: Compute the height zeta function Σ_n Σ_{sol} n^{−s}(xyz)^{−β} numerically; check for Euler-product structure.

title: Branching-process / tree-search model of the certificate search (Galton–Watson survival)
connection: Searching levels C = 1,2,… and divisor splits gives a search tree; the probability of finding no certificate is an extinction probability of a branching process with offspring ~ divisor counts.
why: Branching processes give exact extinction-probability equations, which give a sharper heuristic than Poisson when certificates cluster.
first_step: Model the per-level offspring distribution from data; solve the extinction equation and compare with observed zero frequencies for ES₅.

title: Maker–Breaker / Erdős–Selfridge criterion for covering-system strategies
connection: View 'adversary chooses p's residues prime by prime, prover covers with certificates' as a Maker–Breaker game on a hypergraph of congruence certificates. The Erdős–Selfridge criterion Σ 2^{−|e|} < 1/2 gives Breaker (adversary) a win.
why: It turns B1 (no finite covering) into a game-theory calculation and might quantify how large the certificate hypergraph must be for a covering, compared with the actual size.
first_step: Compute the Erdős–Selfridge potential of the certificate hypergraph up to level C₀ (edges = residue-class conditions on p); see where it crosses 1/2.

title: Machine-learned certificate selectors: features that predict the first working level
connection: Train a classifier on p ↦ least working level (or least u in I3_𝒞), with features such as Legendre symbols of small primes, p mod small moduli and factorisations of p+small. Interpretable models (sparse logistic, decision trees) may expose a structure.
why: This is the data-science native lens. Many repo results (I3_𝒞 u ≤ 39) suggest the selector is simple; a sparse rule could be a conjecture or a lemma candidate.
first_step: Using repo data for p ≤ 10⁹, fit a depth-6 decision tree predicting the least certifying u in I3_𝒞 from (q/p) for q ≤ 50; report accuracy and the tree.

title: Smith theory / ℤ/2-equivariant topology: fixed points of an involution on a ℤ/2-acyclic certificate complex
connection: Smith theory: an involution on a mod-2 acyclic finite complex has a non-empty mod-2 acyclic fixed set. A simplicial complex on solutions (or near-solutions) that is provably ℤ/2-acyclic, with an involution whose fixed points are certificates, would give existence.
why: It is the topological generalisation of 'odd number of fixed points', more flexible than plain parity because acyclicity can be proved by shellability or discrete Morse theory.
first_step: Define a complex on words of all p′ ≤ p (or on near-certificates) with faces from shared letters; compute mod-2 homology for small p.

title: Borwein–Choi's xy+yz+zx theorem as the closest proved sibling of I3/U(n)
connection: Borwein–Choi: there are at most 19 integers not of the form xy+yz+zx (x,y,z ≥ 1). Eighteen are known, and the 19th is excluded under GRH. The form is classified via class groups of Q(√−n), using (x+z)(y+z) = n + z². I3 is n = tuv−u−v ⇔ (tu−1)(tv−1) = tn+1.
why: It is structurally parallel (a factorisation of n + (shift) with constraints) and is proved up to one possible exception via idoneal-type class-number arguments. The I3/U analogue would be 'finitely many failures, all but one effective'.
first_step: Read Borwein–Choi (Exp. Math. 9 (2000)) and translate: for which discriminants does 'tn+1 has no factorisation (tu−1)(tv−1)' force a class-group condition (exponent ≤ 2) on Q(√−?)?

title: Restricted-denominator ES: which congruence restrictions on x, y, z keep ES true?
connection: Breusch/Stewart: every rational with odd denominator is a sum of distinct odd unit fractions (many terms). For three terms, all-odd is impossible (parity: 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) forces an even denominator). Classify restrictions (x,y,z in prescribed classes mod m) that are consistent with ES for all small p, and test which ones look 'every p'.
why: Restricted versions that hold numerically are stronger statements that may carry more structure for a proof (or reveal new obstructions).
first_step: Read arXiv:1108.6118 and arXiv:1606.02117; tabulate which three-term restricted variants of 4/n are known false and true.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Large-q limit (Katz–Sarnak) of the ES_q certificate count distribution
connection: As q → ∞ with deg P fixed, counts of certificates become equidistributed statistics governed by monodromy groups (Katz's equidistribution). The probability of zero certificates in the limit is computable.
why: It gives an exact 'random model' limit of the ES count distribution, a rigorous analogue of the Poisson heuristic, and possibly a proof of ES_q for q large relative to the degree.
first_step: Identify the monodromy group of the certificate-counting sheaf (divisor-in-class conditions) and compute the limiting P(count = 0) for small degrees.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: I3 at 2^k ± 1 by exponent coverings: Sierpiński-number technique
connection: I3 holds on 2^k ± 1 etc. by exponent coverings (I3_DEEP). This is exactly the Sierpiński/Riesel-number covering technique for k·2^n + 1 compositeness.
why: Covering congruences in the exponent are a native tool that is complete for its families. Extending to 'n = a·b^k + c' families tests how far exponent coverings go.
first_step: Try families n = 3^k ± 2, 5·3^k + 1 with exponent coverings for I3; record which ones close.

title: Unit-fraction graph on ℚ: 3-step walks from 0 to 4/n
connection: Define the graph on ℚ_{>0} with r ~ r + 1/k. ES(n) ⇔ dist(0, 4/n) ≤ 3. Farey neighbours a/b, c/d satisfy c/d − a/b = 1/(bd), so unit steps between Farey neighbours are edges.
why: It gives a metric-geometry view of Egyptian fractions. Bounds on the graph's diameter on {m/n : m ≤ 4} are exactly ES-type statements, and 'every m/n at distance ≤ c·log log n' results are known.
first_step: Compute the distance-2 neighbourhood of 4/p (pairs 1/y + 1/z) and its overlap with {4/p − 1/x}; record which Farey structure produces most certificates.

title: Pentagon identity of the dilogarithm on the coefficient-N pentagon
connection: The Rogers dilogarithm satisfies the 5-term relation along A₂ mutations: Σ L(X_i/(1+X_i)) = π²/2 on the positive real locus. With frozen coefficient N the relation acquires N-dependent terms. Words give rational points.
why: Dilogarithm identities encode K₂/Bloch-group data of the points. For rational points, Bloch-group elements are torsion, which gives exact identities; the sign might appear as a torsion class.
first_step: Compute Σ L over the five X-coordinates of each word for p < 100 numerically; look for a pattern in N and in the sign.

title: Commute time / escape probability on the fan: A/p as a random-walk quantity
connection: For the fan graph, R_eff(a,s) = A/p, so the commute time between a and the sink is 2|E|·A/p and the escape probability from a is 1/(v·R_eff) = p/(vA). The ES sign is a residuosity property of a commute time numerator.
why: Random-walk interpretations allow coupling/monotonicity arguments (Rayleigh monotonicity: adding edges decreases resistance), which could organise words by a partial order.
first_step: Use Rayleigh monotonicity to order words of p by resistance; check whether the sign changes monotonically along chains (data p < 10⁵).

title: Divisor class group of the toric ring k[σ^∨ ∩ M] ≅ ℤ/p and the canonical class: the sign as an Atiyah–Bott/Gorenstein index datum
connection: The cyclic quotient 1/p(1,A) has class group ℤ/p generated by a boundary divisor D₁. The canonical class K corresponds to −(1 + A)·[D₁]-type data, so the 'position of K in ℤ/p' is a quadratic-residue question about 1 + A or A.
why: Native singularity invariants (Gorenstein index, canonical class position) are computable and might rephrase the sign as 'K is a square multiple of a generator'.
first_step: Compute [K] ∈ Cl = ℤ/p for 1/p(1,A) and express its square class via A; compare with (A/p).

title: s-form: ES(p) ⇔ ∃ s ∈ ℕ³ with lcm_i 4s_i/gcd(4s_i, S) = p (value of an arithmetic function)
connection: GEOMETRY_ES: positive points ↔ primitive s with 4s_i | nS, and ES(p) ⟺ ∃ s with m(s) = lcm_i 4s_i/gcd(4s_i,S) = p. ES says the arithmetic function m on primitive triples hits every prime.
why: Surjectivity of an explicit arithmetic function on ℕ³ is the native form for additive/multiplicative combinatorics (value sets of lcm/gcd expressions, like the problem of values of lcm(a,b)/gcd(a,b)-type maps).
first_step: Compute the distribution of m(s) over s ≤ B and the smallest-height s with m(s) = p for p < 10⁶; look at the gcd(4s_i, S) pattern of minimal solutions.

title: Positivstellensatz / SOS degree of infeasibility certificates for bounded ES failures
connection: For bounded parameters, 'no certificate at p up to height B' is a finite infeasibility statement with a Positivstellensatz/SOS (or Nullstellensatz) refutation. The degree needed as a function of p and B is a proof-complexity measure.
why: If refutation degree must grow, low-degree 'algebraic' proofs of existence are impossible in a quantifiable sense (analogue of B1). If it stays bounded for some encoding, that encoding has hidden structure.
first_step: For p failing ES₅ at small B (e.g. p = 5, 13, 17, 2521 for I3_𝒞), compute minimal Nullstellensatz degree over F₂ of the bounded infeasibility system.

title: Banaszczyk transference / covering radius for BALANCED_LATTICE relation lattices
connection: BALANCED_LATTICE uses μ_∞(Λ) (covering radius) of relation lattices of small primes mod q. Banaszczyk's transference theorems tie covering radius to dual minima, and the dual minima correspond to characters that are nearly trivial on S.
why: It is the lattice-theory native tool and is already partly used; recorded for completeness. Sharper transference (Regev–Stephens-Davidowitz) could improve constants.
first_step: Check whether the R–SD reverse Minkowski / transference improvements change BALANCED_LATTICE's numerical thresholds.

title: Hecke (Rosen) continued fractions: ES-type statements for Hecke triangle groups G_q
connection: Replace SL₂(ℤ) by the Hecke group G_q and HJ fractions by Rosen λ_q-fractions. 'Every element of a cusp set has a length-3 expansion with a character condition' becomes a family of ES-analogues indexed by q.
why: Some Hecke groups are arithmetic (q = 3, 4, 6) and others non-arithmetic. Comparing ES analogues across them separates arithmetic from combinatorial ingredients.
first_step: Define the λ₄-analogue (G₄ is commensurable with Γ₀(2)) of words and check whether a T1-type obstruction occurs.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Integrable billiards / Sturmian cutting sequences of slope A/p in a square
connection: A billiard trajectory in the unit square with slope A/p has a cutting sequence (Sturmian/Christoffel word). HJ length is a renormalisation depth (number of Rauzy–Veech-type induction steps of a specific kind).
why: Rauzy–Veech induction is the dynamics-native renormalisation, and it has a version for square-tiled surfaces where arithmetic data (p) enters as the number of squares.
first_step: Identify HJ steps with a renormalisation algorithm on the square torus; check whether a square-tiled surface with p squares realises words as cylinder decompositions.

title: Artin-type: elements of L₃(p) with maximal 2-part of order; links to Artin's conjecture methods
