connection: ES₅ ⇔ some A ∈ L₃(p) has v₂(ord_p A) = v₂(p − 1). Artin-type problems (Heath-Brown, Gupta–Murty) prove that one of a few fixed integers is a primitive root mod infinitely many p. Here the candidate set depends on p.
why: It translates ES₅ into the language of multiplicative orders, where Chebotarev in Kummer extensions Q(ζ_{2^k}, A^{1/2^k}) is the native tool, but A depends on p (B2).
first_step: Check whether a fixed-A family (e.g. A = 2·3 − 1 = 5 from the word (2,3,v)) with v₂(ord_p 5) = v₂(p−1) covers a Chebotarev set of primes, and compute its density.

title: Weil representation of SL₂(ℤ/4p) and the sign as a matrix coefficient
connection: The theta multiplier is the Weil representation's character on Γ₀(4). The ES sign on γ_w is a matrix coefficient of the Weil representation of SL₂(ℤ/4p) (finite group). Representation theory of finite groups gives orthogonality relations for such coefficients.
why: Summing a matrix coefficient over a subset of the group equals an inner product. If the word set were a union of double cosets, orthogonality would give exact counts.
first_step: Reduce {γ_w} mod 4p and test whether it is (close to) a union of double cosets of a small subgroup (e.g. the Borel); compute the sign sum via characters.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Brown–Rödl partition regularity of 1/x + 1/y = 1/z and inhomogeneous colourings
connection: Brown–Rödl: in every finite colouring of ℕ the equation 1/x + 1/y = 1/z has a monochromatic solution. Croot: 1 = Σ 1/x_i monochromatic. ES is inhomogeneous (4/n), but 'colour n by ES status' and look for monochromatic structures.
why: Ramsey-theory native: a hypothetical ES-failure set F cannot contain configurations forced by partition regularity of related equations, which gives structural constraints on F.
first_step: Find equations E with E(n₁,…) ∧ ES(n₁) ∧ … ⇒ ES(n_k) (transport laws) and combine them with partition regularity to constrain F's structure.

title: Braid group B₃ lift of γ_w and link invariants of its closure
connection: SL₂(ℤ) is a quotient of B₃ (B₃ → SL₂(ℤ), kernel generated by (σ₁σ₂)⁶). Lifting γ_w to a braid and closing gives a link L_w. Link invariants (signature, Jones at roots of unity) are then functions of the word.
why: It gives another topological carrier of words, different from the 2-bridge/plumbing one, with Burau/Jones machinery.
first_step: Lift γ_w via M(b) ↦ σ₁^b σ₂^{−1}-type words; compute the signature of closures for p < 200 and compare with the sign.

title: Shioda's Mordell–Weil lattices: integral points of the ES elliptic fibration as small-height sections
connection: On a rational elliptic surface, integral sections (polynomial points) are exactly sections of small height in the Mordell–Weil lattice (Shioda). The plane-section fibration of the ES cubic gives an elliptic surface, and positive integer points restricted to fibres are its integral points.
why: MW lattices are explicitly computable (E₈-type root lattices for rational elliptic surfaces). Polynomial ES families (Mordell identities) would correspond to minimal-norm sections.
first_step: Compute the MW lattice of the x+y+z = s fibration of the ES cubic over Q(n)(s); list minimal sections and compare with Mordell identities.

title: Exceptional triples and the B₃ braid action: Markov-type invariant vs S_{n,D}
connection: Exceptional collections of 3 objects have Gram matrices [[1,a,b],[0,1,c],[0,0,1]], and the braid group acts by mutations preserving a² + b² + c² − abc (Bondal–Polishchuk). S_{n,D}: nA² + B² + D = ABC is a weighted variant, like a non-symmetric (n-twisted) category.
why: A categorical source of mutations for S_{n,D} would give the missing infinite group action (cf. BGS/Chen), and categories come with positivity (dimension vectors).
first_step: Check whether weighted Gram matrices [[1,a,b],[0,n,c],[0,0,1]]-type (objects with End of rank n) give the invariant nA² + B² + D − ABC under a braid action.

title: Hurwitz quaternions and metacommutation: ES certificates as factorisation patterns
connection: Lipschitz/Hurwitz quaternion factorisations of a norm-N element are unique up to metacommutation (Conway–Smith; Cohn–Kumar studied the metacommutation permutation). Certificates involve factorisations of p-tied norms in quaternion orders (QUATERNION_ES).
why: Metacommutation is a canonical permutation on factorisations with computable sign/cycle structure. The ES sign might be a metacommutation invariant.
first_step: For small p, compute the factorisations relevant to QUATERNION_ES Type I data in the Hurwitz order and the metacommutation permutation's sign.

title: Torus-equivariant localisation: counting words as fixed points of a T-action on a toric variety
connection: Lattice points in a polytope count T-fixed points / sections of line bundles (Brion, Lawrence–Varchenko). Words at fixed t are lattice points on a hyperbola, not a polytope, but at fixed (t,u) the v-condition is linear: the union over (t,u) is a union of 1-dim lattice point sets in progressions.
why: Equivariant localisation gives exact counts with signs (via Brion's formula) and might give a closed form for weighted word counts.
first_step: Write Σ_{words} x^t y^u z^v as a sum of rational generating functions (Brion-type) for each (t,u) cone; examine the analytic structure of the full sum.

title: Real quadratic order of γ_w: words as reduced cycles and the sign as a genus/narrow-class invariant
connection: γ_w ∈ SL₂(ℤ) hyperbolic determines a real quadratic order of discriminant (tr γ_w)² − 4 and an ideal class (Latimer–MacDuffee). The ES sign might be a genus character of that class evaluated at p.
why: Latimer–MacDuffee is an exact bijection between conjugacy classes of matrices and ideal classes. The sign then becomes a class-group statement in a family of real quadratic fields.
first_step: Compute the ideal class for γ_w (p < 300) and evaluate genus characters; check whether one equals (A/p).

title: Integral points on the 'word variety' as an affine homogeneous space under a unipotent group
connection: {γ ∈ SL₂ : b = p} is preserved by left and right multiplication by lower unipotents [[1,0],[k,1]] (left multiplication shifts d by kp, right multiplication shifts a by kp). Words are the integral points with level-structure congruences in a bounded region.
why: Homogeneous-space integral points with congruence conditions are governed by strong approximation (here for a unipotent group, which is trivial) and by the box. This explains why only the archimedean box matters.
first_step: Record: strong approximation for the unipotent group is automatic, so all ES₅ content is in the archimedean box (positivity, sizes). Use as a calibration item for future 'group-action' proposals.

title: Maynard–Tao: infinitely many primes p with many simultaneously prime 4Cp+1? (forced level failures; open whether it applies)
connection: If 4Cp + 1 is prime, its only divisors are 1 and itself (≡ 1 mod 4C), so level C fails. Maynard–Tao gives, for admissible tuples of linear forms, infinitely many n with ≥ m of them prime. If n can also be restricted to primes (check: Maynard's 'dense clusters' framework allows subsets such as the primes), this would give infinitely many primes p with ≥ m failed levels among C ≤ K.
why: It would be a PROVED statement about ES-hardness: arbitrarily many small levels fail infinitely often. It calibrates any proof that uses a bounded set of small levels, as a quantitative B1.
first_step: Check whether Maynard's 'Dense clusters of primes in subsets' (Compos. Math. 2016) applies with n ranging over primes and forms 4Cn + 1; state the resulting m(K).

title: V_n as values of the indefinite binary form nA² − 2μAB + B² on its Conway topograph
connection: V_n: nA² + B² + D = 2μAB means the form Q(A,B) = nA² − 2μAB + B² takes the value −D with D | μ. On Conway's topograph of Q (disc 4(μ² − n) = 4f), the values along the river are periodic, and ES points are river-adjacent values −D with D | μ at (A even, B = 1).
why: Topograph navigation gives all small values of an indefinite form exactly. ES becomes: for some μ, the river of Q_μ shows a value −D with D | μ at a B = 1 position.
first_step: For n = p < 500 and μ ≤ 3√p, draw/compute river values of Q_μ and mark ES points; look for a pattern in where they occur along the period.

title: Unexplained empty fibre S_{3861,4}(ℕ) = ∅: non-BM obstruction (Harpaz-type) or a second Brauer class?
connection: Z52 records unexplained zeros of the pencil fibres S_{n,k}(ℕ), e.g. S_{3861,4} with n ≡ 5 (mod 8). Harpaz shows that on some log K3 surfaces BM is not the only obstruction to integral points.
why: An explained zero would either give a new Brauer class (a new obstruction mechanism near ES) or the first example of a non-BM obstruction in the ES pencil. Both sharpen the map near k = 0.
first_step: Compute Br(S_{3861,4})/Br(ℚ) (algebraic part via the toric/conic structure) and evaluate all classes on local points; if all evaluations allow points, check the archimedean/positivity piece separately.

title: Semigroup orbit counting (Bourgain–Kontorovich, Kontorovich–Oh) for the ES word semigroup with entry p
connection: QUESTION_R casts words as elements of a semigroup Ψ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ)_{≥0}. Thin-orbit counting with congruence conditions gives asymptotic counts of orbit elements with entry ≤ N in progressions (level of distribution).
why: This gives averaged ES₅ results with power savings, and RS's local–global theorem shows that for fat semigroups the sporadic set is finite. The ES semigroup's exponent δ decides which regime applies.
first_step: Compute the critical exponent δ of the semigroup generated by the word letters (likely 1, i.e. not thin). If δ = 1, record that RS-type local–global for 'fat' semigroups is the relevant theorem class.

title: Minkowski question-mark function: ?(A/p) as a dyadic rational with prescribed run structure
connection: ?(x) maps the CF of x to a binary expansion with run lengths equal to the partial quotients. ES₅ asks for a QNR A whose ?(A/p) (or an HJ analogue) has a 3-block structure.
why: It gives a singular-measure (Minkowski measure) viewpoint: the set of A/p with short expansions is where ?-measure concentrates on few dyadic blocks. It is close to the Stern item but uses measure-theoretic tools.
first_step: Compute ?(A/p) for A ∈ L₃(p) and look for structure (e.g. ? values lie in a few dyadic intervals); compare QR vs QNR.

title: Borel–Cantelli heuristic: Σ_p P(no certificate at p) < ∞ under various independence models
connection: With P(fail at p) ≈ exp(−c log²p) the sum converges, so heuristically only finitely many failures exist and they would be small (all excluded below 10¹⁸). This is the probabilistic native statement of 'ES is true'.
why: Calibration: makes precise which correlation model must hold for the heuristic, and how much heavier the lower tail would have to be to allow infinitely many failures (log P(0) ≥ −log p).
first_step: From repo LDP data, fit log P(0|M) and compute the threshold tail behaviour that would make Σ_p diverge; compare with Markoff (Ghosh–Sarnak) where infinitely many failures occur.

title: ES₅ for p ≡ 5 (8) vs p ≡ 1 (8): different native fields for the two classes
connection: The five-slice equivalence λ(p) ≤ 3 is stated for p ≡ 1 (8). For p ≡ 5 (8), (2/p) = −1 gives cheap certificates. In lattice/sandpile terms, p mod 8 is the Gauss-sum class (Brown invariant) of the discriminant form, so different topological constraints apply.
why: Splitting by p mod 8 is natural in every field (Arf invariant of knots with det p, Brown invariant of linking forms). The hard class p ≡ 1 (8) is where the Arf invariant of a det-p knot is 0.
first_step: Record the per-class status (which classes are trivial, by which certificate) and check whether p ≡ 1 (8) hard primes correspond to knots with Arf = 0 and signature ≡ 0 (mod 8).

title: The multiplicative monoid (tn₁+1)(tn₂+1) = t(tn₁n₂ + n₁ + n₂) + 1: ES₅ transport n₁ ⋆_t n₂
connection: The set {N : N ≡ 1 (mod t)} is a multiplicative monoid, and n ↦ tn + 1 transports the operation n₁ ⋆ n₂ = tn₁n₂ + n₁ + n₂. Words of level t at n₁ and n₂ give factorisations whose products are factorisations of N(n₁ ⋆ n₂) with factors ≡ 1 (mod t), not −1. Mixing parities yields −1 classes.
why: It is an explicit transport law candidate: ES₅ data at n₁, n₂ might produce data at n₁ ⋆_t n₂. Iterated, the failure set must be closed under the inverse operation.
first_step: Compute: from words (A₁, A₁*) at n₁ and (A₂, A₂*) at n₂, does A₁A₂* (≡ +1 mod t) or A₁·(something) give a valid word at n₁ ⋆ n₂? Check by brute force for small n.

title: Honda's count of tight contact structures on L(p,A): (v−1)(t−1)(u−1) for p/A = [[v,t,u]]
connection: Honda: the number of tight contact structures on L(p,q) up to isotopy is ∏(b_i − 1) over the HJ digits of p/q. So ES₅ words are lens spaces of order p with exactly three-factor tight counts in the non-square homotopy class, and I3 (letters ≥ 3) means every factor is ≥ 2.
why: Contact topology adds a natural weight (the tight-structure count) to each word. Weighted counts Σ_A ∏(b_i − 1)(A/p) might be more regular than plain counts (e.g. given by a Heegaard Floer formula).
first_step: Compute the weighted sum W±(p) = Σ_{A ∈ L₃(p), (A/p)=±1} (v−1)(t−1)(u−1) for p < 10⁵ and look for a closed form.

title: K₄-multigraph rung: any 4-vertex multigraph with τ = p and non-square pairing
connection: Relax the fan shape to an arbitrary multigraph on 4 vertices (six edge multiplicities). Its τ is the Kirchhoff polynomial of K₄ in the multiplicities, and the pairing is read from the reduced Laplacian. This 6-parameter problem contains ES₅ (fan) as a 3-parameter slice.
why: It is the natural intermediate rung between ES₅ and 'any graph'. Its failure set might be empty for all p > small, which would locate exactly what the fan shape costs.
first_step: Enumerate 4-vertex multigraphs with τ = p, p < 2·10⁴, record non-square pairing existence; list failures.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Matrix relaxation: 4/n = 1ᵀM⁻¹1 for integer positive definite M in a class (diagonal = ES)
connection: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 1ᵀ diag(x,y,z)⁻¹ 1. Replacing diagonal matrices by tridiagonal chain matrices gives 1ᵀM⁻¹1 = (tu + tv + uv + 2u + 2v)/(tuv − u − v). The problem 'every 4/n is 1ᵀM⁻¹1 for M in a class 𝒞' interpolates between ES and lattice problems.
why: For rich classes 𝒞 (all positive definite integer M) it is trivially solvable; for diagonal it is ES. The threshold class is a measure of how special the diagonal (Egyptian) structure is. 1ᵀM⁻¹1 is an effective conductance.
first_step: Test 𝒞 = {diagonal + one off-diagonal −1}: is every 4/p = 1ᵀM⁻¹1 for such M? Compute for p < 10⁴.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Quadratic large sieve over p for the families S₃(p): exceptional-set bounds
connection: The large sieve for real characters (Heath-Brown) bounds Σ_p |Σ_{n} a_n (n/p)|². ES₅ failure at p needs (A/p) = 1 on S₃(p), but S₃ varies with p. EXCEPTIONAL_LARGESIEVE pursues this.
why: It is the native tool for exceptional sets; recorded to complete the map.
first_step: See EXCEPTIONAL_LARGESIEVE*.md for the current exponent; no new action here.

title: Standard-conjecture matrix: GRH, Elliott–Halberstam, Schinzel H, Chowla, Cramér vs ES/ES₅/I3
connection: FRONTIER says no standard conjecture is known to imply I3, ES₅ or ES. A matrix with rows = conjectures and columns = ES variants, recording what each gives (density, exceptional-set rate, pointwise), is the native 'conditional results' table.
why: It locates exactly which non-standard hypothesis is needed (e.g. 'divisors of one integer equidistribute in classes'), a useful formal target.
first_step: Check CONDITIONAL_ES.md; fill in missing cells (e.g. Chowla for (·/p) along words, EH for levels).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Pell-like recurrence: words at p from words at smaller primes via SL₂ conjugation by a fixed matrix
connection: Conjugating γ_w by a fixed S ∈ SL₂(ℤ) preserves trace but moves the entry p to a new value b′ = linear in (a,b,c,d). Integer orbits of the conjugation action on {γ with b prime} are Pell-like recurrences relating words of different primes.
why: It gives transport laws with group structure (like Vieta jumping). If a recurrence preserves the sign and sizes, failures would propagate along orbits.
first_step: For S = [[1,1],[0,1]] and [[1,0],[1,1]], compute how words transform (when the image is a word) and how the sign changes.

title: Egyptian fractions over the p-adics with archimedean positivity: a 'local-global' table per place
connection: For each place v, ES is solvable over ℤ_v (and positively over ℝ). The obstruction is global. An adelic-orbit/Tamagawa view gives the BM main term as ∏_v vol(U_n(ℤ_v)). The 2-adic factor carries the slot-lemma condition.
why: It records the native adelic computation that the repo already uses (BM_CORRECTED_COUNT); here the point is a per-place table of the slot-lemma 2-adic measure.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic measure of the set of words with some pentagon entry ≡ 0 (mod 4), as a function of p mod 8.

title: Quantum modular forms / Ẑ-invariants of the ES Seifert spaces
connection: WRT invariants and GPPV Ẑ-invariants of Seifert spaces with three exceptional fibres are false-theta functions, i.e. quantum modular forms (Lawrence–Zagier for the Poincaré sphere; Gukov–Pei–Putrov–Vafa). ES Seifert spaces M(0; 1/x,1/y,1/z) with e = −4/n form a family indexed by solutions.
why: Sum over solutions of a quantum invariant gives a generating object attached to n. Speculative, but it puts the solution set into an automorphic-adjacent structure different from Thm K.
first_step: Compute Ẑ (GPPV formula for Seifert spaces) for the ES Seifert spaces of small n and inspect the dependence on n.

title: Cohn matrices / Markov-tree calculus for products M(v)M(t)M(u)
connection: Markov numbers are entries of Cohn matrices, i.e. products of two generators along the Markov tree, and Christoffel words index them. ES words are length-3 products in the HJ generators. Cohn's calculus (trace identities, Fricke relations tr(AB) + tr(AB⁻¹) = tr A tr B) gives algebraic relations among such products.
why: Fricke trace identities make the Markoff equation appear from SL₂ traces. A trace-identity derivation of S_{n,D} from words would unify MARKOFF_ES and the HJ forms.
first_step: Compute tr(M(v)M(t)M(u)) and Fricke-related traces of pairs of word matrices; search for the relation nA² + B² + D = ABC among them.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Small levels as norm forms: level-t failure for t ∈ {3,4,6,8,12} ⇔ tp+1 is (roughly) a norm from Q(√−t)-type orders
connection: A divisor of tp + 1 that is ≡ −1 (mod t) exists iff some prime factor lies outside the subgroup generated by the classes splitting appropriately. For t = 4 this means 'some prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4)', so level-4 failure ⇔ 4p+1 has only prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) ⇔ 4p+1 is a sum of two coprime squares. Similar statements hold for t = 3 (norms from ℤ[ω]).
why: This makes the first levels' failure a Landau–Ramanujan-type 'values of a linear form that are norms' property. Writing 4p+1 = (2a+1)² + (2b)² gives p = a² + a + b², a quadratic polynomial in two variables. Iwaniec (1972) proved that suitable quadratic polynomials in two variables represent infinitely many primes; if his theorem applies here with the primitivity condition gcd(2a+1, 2b) = 1, it gives a PROVED infinite family of primes failing level 4 (check).
first_step: Compute the density of p for which all levels t ∈ {3,4,6,8,12} fail (simultaneous norm conditions), and the sieve-dimension of that set; compare with data.

title: Resistor-network rung: n/4 as the resistance of any 3-resistor integer network
connection: Three integer resistors in parallel give ES. The other 3-resistor topologies (series + parallel mixes: x + (y‖z), (x + y)‖z) give other Diophantine conditions. 'Every n/4 is realised by some 3-resistor network' is a rung that contains ES.
why: Calibration: it shows whether ES's difficulty is specific to the all-parallel topology. A cheap computation decides it for small n.
first_step: For n < 10⁶, check realisability of n/4 by each 3-resistor topology; list the n realisable only via the parallel one and those not realisable at all.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Values of rational symmetric functions on ℕ³: e₂/e₃ = 4/n
connection: ES(n) ⇔ the rational symmetric function e₂/e₃ = Σ 1/x_i takes the value 4/n on ℕ³. Value sets of symmetric rational functions on integer points connect to Vieta-type substitutions and to the 'totally split cubic' item.
why: It is a symmetric-function lens. Power-sum/elementary transitions might give alternative parametrisations, e.g. through e₁ (sum) or p₂.
first_step: Write ES in (e₁, e₂, e₃) with 4e₃ = n·e₂ and study integrality of the roots via the discriminant; compute which (e₁, e₂) give totally split cubics for small n.

title: Lattice of ES solutions under scaling: the 'primitive' solution poset and Möbius inversion over n
connection: Solutions for n give solutions for kn by scaling, and GEOMETRY_ES: each primitive s gives exactly the multiples of m(s). So f(n) = Σ_{d | n} g(d), with g(d) = #{primitive s : m(s) = d}. ES at primes ⇔ g(p) > 0.
why: Möbius inversion makes 'primitive solutions at exactly p' the core object, and its Dirichlet series is the height zeta function restricted to primitive points.
first_step: Compute g(d) for d < 10⁵ and its Dirichlet series behaviour; check the size of g at primes vs composites.

title: Conjugacy classes in SL₂(ℤ/4) and the slot lemma: '4 divides a pentagon entry' as a class condition on γ_w mod 4
connection: The slot lemma is a mod-4 condition on (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1), i.e. on γ_w mod 4 together with the frieze. SL₂(ℤ/4) has order 48; the sign may be a class function on SL₂(ℤ/4) restricted to word images.
why: A class-function description would let representation theory of the finite group SL₂(ℤ/4) (and its Weil representation) organise all sign computations.
first_step: Tabulate γ_w mod 4 and mod 8 for all words of p < 10⁴; check whether the sign is a function of the conjugacy class (or of the double coset) mod 4 or 8.

title: Thue ratio set (signed): {u/v mod p : 0 < |u|, |v| ≤ √p} = F_p^*; ES₅ adds the divisibility uv | p + u + v
connection: By Thue's lemma every residue is u/v mod p with |u|, |v| ≤ √p, so the signed ratio set of small numbers covers all QNRs (with positive u, v only it can fail: p = 5 misses 4). Words use positive u, v. Words give A ≡ u/v (mod p) with the extra exact condition uv | p + u + v. ES₅ ⇔ some QNR has a Thue representation u/v satisfying the divisibility.
why: It isolates the divisibility condition as the entire content (the ratio set is already everything). Results on ratios u/v with arithmetic constraints, such as u, v smooth or prime (Shparlinski-type), are the native next step.
first_step: For p < 10⁶, count Thue pairs (u,v) of QNRs and the fraction satisfying uv | p + u + v; compare with the heuristic 1/(uv) per pair.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sum-of-two-squares parametrisation p = a² + b² as an ES parameter space (Gaussian Type II)
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4) write p = a² + b². ES certificates might be organised by Gaussian integers: e.g. 4Cp + 1 = 4C(a² + b²) + 1 factors in ℤ[i]-related ways, and the divisor class −1 (mod 4C) might be read off a Gaussian factorisation.
why: It is a natural extra structure that exactly the hard primes possess (p ≡ 1 mod 4). If certificates correlate with (a, b), the Gaussian angle gives a new handle (Hecke equidistribution).
first_step: For p < 10⁶, compute (a mod 8, b mod 8, a mod 3, …) and the least certificate level; search for a deterministic rule using (a,b).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Additive energy / multiplicative energy of the word set and character-sum bounds via energy
connection: Bounds for Σ_{A∈S} χ(A) over a set S follow from its multiplicative energy E(S) (Shkredov, Chang). S₃(p) is small (log²p), so energy bounds are trivial, but over the union ∪_{L ≤ L₀} S_L(p) the energy might be small enough.
why: It is the native additive-combinatorics route to non-trivial character sums over thin sets, and it pins down the minimal L where energy methods start working.
first_step: Compute the multiplicative energy of S_L(p) for L ≤ 6 and p ~ 10⁵; find the least L where E(S_L) ≪ |S_L|³/p^δ.

title: Gauss–Bonnet / area argument: hyperbolic area of the 'certificate horoball region' vs number of words
connection: In the closed-horocycle or Farey picture, words correspond to cusp regions whose hyperbolic area can be computed by Gauss–Bonnet. Total area ≈ count × typical area gives a geometric derivation of the log²p main term.
why: A geometric derivation might reveal a monotonicity or tiling argument (regions tiling a fixed area) that forces at least one word in each 'colour' region.
first_step: Compute the hyperbolic area of the union of HJ-length-3 regions at level p and check whether it is asymptotically a constant (tiling-type) or grows.

title: The 4-adic structure of words as automata on digits (fixed-letter slices only)
connection: The slot lemma condition depends only on (t,u,v) mod 4 (and p mod 8). Combined with the word equation, the set of valid digit strings (base 2) of (t,u,v) is, for FIXED p, a finite set (so trivially regular). A uniform-in-p carry automaton is impossible because multiplication is not finite-state (Büchi arithmetic cannot define it). What is automatic are fixed-letter slices, e.g. (t,u) fixed and v varying (linear in v; compare tuv − u − v = p).
why: Automata over digits (as in Büchi arithmetic / automatic structures) give a decidable theory of such word sets for fixed p, and 2-adic 'carry' arguments are a native tool (as in Lucas/Kummer theorems).
first_step: Build the base-2 carry automaton for tuv − u − v = p with t,u,v as inputs; compute the language of sign-(−1) words for small p and look for structure across p.

title: Hilbert's irreducibility in the p-aspect: the word surface's fibres W_p as specialisations of a generic surface
connection: As p varies, W_p is a family over the p-line. Integral points on fibres correspond to integral points on the total space (t,u,v) with p = tuv − u − v, i.e. the total space is A³. ES₅ is surjectivity of a polynomial map ℤ³_{≥2} → primes with a sign condition.
why: 'Which values does a polynomial in several variables take at integer points with a sign restriction' is a native question about polynomial value sets (e.g. results on xyz + linear forms covering all large integers).
first_step: Look up results on value sets of polynomials of the shape xyz + ax + by + cz on integer boxes (e.g. 'every n is xyz + x + y' type theorems) and compare with Lorenzini's (W).

title: Smoothing as a decisive ingredient: smooth weights on (u,B,C) for a weighted R_w(p)
connection: Helfgott's minor arcs only closed after choosing smoothing functions optimally. ES: replace R(p) by R_w(p) = Σ w(u,B,C)1[4uBC−u−B=p] with smooth nonnegative w; R_w(p) > 0 ⇒ ES(p).
why: Error terms in Poisson/Voronoi-based treatments of R(p) depend heavily on sharp cut-offs of the hyperbolic region; smoothing is free for a positivity statement.
first_step: Numerically compare Var_p(R_w(p)/M_w(p)) over primes near 10⁷ for sharp vs. Gaussian/Beurling–Selberg weights; pick the weight minimising the left tail.

title: Goldbach exceptions are tied to one exceptional character — are ES/(★) failures tied to a character?
connection: In MV the only way to have many Goldbach exceptions is a Siegel zero. Analogue: (★)-failures (14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰) and b=1 failures (193, 2521, 66529) might share an extreme value of a single character statistic (e.g. least non-residue ℓ(p), or L(1, (·/p))).
why: If failures of sub-routes are 'explained' by one character, a Deuring–Heilbronn-type dichotomy becomes plausible.
first_step: For the 17 known sub-route failures and random controls compute ℓ(p), Σ_{m≤100}(m/p)/m, L(1,(·/p)) and the class number of Q(√p); compare ranks.

title: Almost-prime levels: choose C with 4Cp+1 = q₁q₂ (two primes) and study the class of q₁ mod 4C
connection: Chen-type results produce almost-primes in linear sequences. If 4Cp+1 = q₁q₂, the certificate condition at level C is q₁ ≡ −1 (mod 4C), a single-prime class condition.
why: Reduces a divisor-class problem to an equidistribution question for prime factors of almost-primes in a progression, a better-studied object.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁸ and C ≤ 10⁵ measure: fraction of C with 4Cp+1 = P₂, and the rate at which a factor hits −1 mod 4C versus the model 2/φ(4C).

title: Diophantine approximation spectrum of 4/p by three unit fractions
connection: Schnirelmann-type arguments start from approximate representations. Define δ(p) = min_{x,y,z} |4/p − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z| over x,y,z ≤ p^A (A large enough that all solutions are included); ES(p) ⟺ δ(p) = 0. Study the gap structure of the set of values near 4/p.
why: If near-solutions are abundant at scale p^{−k} and the set of 3-term sums has a 'no isolated gap' property near 4/p, existence might follow by a continuity/pigeonhole step.
first_step: Compute the k smallest nonzero |4/p − Σ| for p ≤ 10⁵ and look for universal patterns in the residual numerators.

title: Universal-form reduction: a map from representations by a universal quadratic form to ES certificates
connection: Linnik/Watson reduced 7 cubes to ternary forms; Hilbert used identities + Lagrange. Seek a quadratic form Q_p (or a fixed universal Q) and an explicit rational map Φ such that every representation Q(v) = g(p) yields an ES solution for p; universality/three-squares then proves ES.
why: Not a polynomial identity in p (so Mordell–Schinzel does not apply directly); the map may depend on the representation. Must be compatible with T1 (Type I/II fail at odd squares).
first_step: Search small Φ: take ES (★) triples (u,B,C) for many p and test whether u, B, C, or 4uC−1 are systematically sums of two/three squares with coordinates linked to p.

title: Ternary-form reduction with Duke–Schulze-Pillot as the closing theorem
connection: Linnik's 7 cubes: identity reduces the problem to n − (cubes) being represented by a ternary quadratic form in an AP, closed by ternary-form theory. ES: find an ES-certificate family equivalent to 'some N(p) is primitively represented by a positive ternary form in a fixed genus'.
why: DSP gives every sufficiently large n in the spinor genus (ineffectively) — an 'all large p' ES theorem even if ineffective would be new.
first_step: Search the (★)/b=1/ES₅ certificate shapes for a sum-of-three-squares interpretation (e.g. 4Cp+1 = d d' with d = x²+y²+z²-type constraint); test on data.

title: Divisor function in APs to a single modulus 4p as the base asymptotic
connection: Σ_{C≤X} τ(4Cp+1) is a divisor sum in the progression 1 mod 4p; asymptotics are known for X ≥ (4p)^{2/3+ε} (Selberg/Hooley/Heath-Brown/Fouvry–Iwaniec-type). The ES count refines τ to the class d ≡ −1 (mod 4C).
why: Starts from a pointwise-in-p theorem that is already true, and asks for a twist by the 'self-referential' modulus 4C — a precise, new-looking question.
first_step: Write D(4Cp+1; −1 mod 4C) via additive characters mod 4C and apply Voronoi summation in C to the twisted divisor sum; identify which terms are new.

title: Chord–tangent operations on the ES cubic surface family
connection: Euler's identity is a composition law on norm forms. The ES surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is a cubic surface; secant/tangent constructions (Manin) generate rational points from rational points.
why: Rational points are plentiful; the question is whether some composition preserves integrality or near-integrality across fibres n.
first_step: Implement the secant operation on U_n(ℚ) and measure denominators of the third point when the two inputs are integral points of nearby fibres (n, n') with n' | n·k.

title: Dedekind's Gaussian-integer proof analogue: an order where ES(p) ⟺ p is a norm
connection: Fermat two squares follows from ℤ[i] being Euclidean. Find a (possibly noncommutative) ring/order R and norm-like map such that ES certificates ↔ elements of 'norm' p with congruence side conditions; then a class-number-one/Euclidean property gives existence.
why: Quaternion orders and theta quotients already appear in the repo; the missing piece is a ring whose class number is 1 and whose norm condition matches the ES congruences.
first_step: Read the quaternion-order memos (git grep -il quaternion); compute class/type numbers of the orders arising there.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Class number one in the genus: search for an ES-encoding lattice with a one-class genus
connection: Gauss's three squares: local solvability + one class in the genus of x²+y²+z² ⇒ global. ES is locally solvable everywhere (Bright–Loughran); if ES(p) ⟺ a lattice L represents an invariant of p, and gen(L) has one class (or one spinor genus), ES follows.
why: The most classical local→global mechanism; repo has quaternion/lattice reformulations whose class numbers may never have been computed.
first_step: For each lattice reformulation in the repo, compute the class number of its genus (Sage/Magma genus enumeration) for small parameters.

title: Power-size main term requirement: lift ES to a variety with power-many points fibred over certificates
connection: Tartakowsky/Kloosterman work because the Eisenstein term ≍ n^{k/2−1} beats cusp-form bounds; ES's main term is log²p. Seek V_p → {ES certificates of p} with fibres of size p^δ (nontrivial geometry), so V_p's point count has a power-size main term that vanishes iff ES(p) fails.
why: Changes the competition 'polylog main term vs. error' into 'power main term vs. error' — the only regime where every-n theorems for forms were ever proved.
first_step: Construct candidates V_p (e.g. adjoin variables parametrising the Type II h-family or the factorizations of 4Cp+1 into 3 factors) and compute their point counts and singular series.

title: Linnik with a varying auxiliary split prime: ℓ = least prime with prescribed (p/ℓ)
connection: Linnik's ergodic method needed (−n/ℓ) = 1 for a fixed ℓ; varying ℓ with n is how one covers every n if the method is uniform in ℓ. ES: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9 shows the BM layer is pointwise free using the least ℓ with (n/ℓ) = −1; find an ℓ-adic dynamical argument for certificates using that ℓ.
why: Bounded ℓ ≤ 4ℓ(n) is already known to suffice for BM positivity; a dynamical/Hecke argument at that ℓ could control the next layer.
first_step: Look for an ℓ-Hecke correspondence on ES certificates (e.g. on the quaternion/SL₂ form: matrices of determinant ℓ acting on [[a,p],[c,d]]) and test whether it maps certificates of p to certificates of p.

title: Escalation of certificate menus: the ES 'truant' tree
connection: Bhargava's escalation: adjoin the smallest truant each time; finitely many escalators. ES: start with a certificate menu (Mordell identities, (★), b=1, ES₅, windows), find the least prime not covered, adjoin the cheapest family covering it, iterate; study the growth of the escalation tree.
why: Gives an empirical picture of how many families are needed up to X (B1 says bounded menus fail under Hypothesis H — the escalation rate measures how fast menus must grow).
first_step: Implement escalation over the repo's family menu up to 10⁸ and plot menu size vs. X.

title: Waldspurger-type formula: is some ES deviation a central L-value?
connection: Ono–Soundararajan proved Ramanujan's form under GRH because coefficient² ∝ L(1/2, f⊗χ_n) (Waldspurger), which GRH bounds. ES: look for an ES generating function with a cuspidal component whose p-th coefficient² is a twisted central value.
why: If such a formula existed, GRH (or subconvexity) would bound the deviation pointwise; METAPLECTIC says level series are Eisenstein + theta quotients, so a cusp form would have to come from a different construction (e.g. products/derivatives).
first_step: Decompose products of two level series (or the all-level series) into Eisenstein + cuspidal parts at small level numerically (Sage modular symbols) and look for nonzero cuspidal components.

title: A certificate scheme whose only hard condition is primality of linear forms (Green–Tao–Ziegler unconditional)
connection: Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg made Hypothesis-H-conditional fibration arguments unconditional when only linear polynomials must be prime, via Green–Tao–Ziegler. ES: search for a certificate parametrisation where, for fixed p, it suffices that a finite system of linear forms in free auxiliary variables be simultaneously prime.
why: GTZ would then give infinitely many such auxiliary tuples for each p — an unconditional every-p mechanism. Thm C (bounded witnesses fail under H) does not obviously forbid unbounded prime-based witnesses.
first_step: Enumerate ES certificate shapes where a denominator or factor is a free prime (e.g. Type I f prime, window prime q) and check whether remaining conditions can be made linear in auxiliary variables.

title: Exceptional character helps: Deuring–Heilbronn for ES families
connection: In Linnik's theorem a Siegel zero repels other zeros and makes primes more regular in other progressions. For ES, if (·/p) is 'exceptional' (QR at all small primes), the BM main term at small levels vanishes — but maybe other certificate families (b=1 line, windows with q where (q/p) = −1 is forced large) become abundant.
why: A dichotomy 'either the characters are regular (use H⁻_BM-type counting) or one is exceptional (use the repelled families)' is how Linnik/Heilbronn escaped worst cases.
first_step: Among primes with large least non-residue ℓ(p) (p ≡ 1 mod 840·k), compare counts of (★), b=1, ES₅ and window certificates to controls.

title: Erdős–Bertrand size contradiction: ES failure forces 4Cp+1 into thin multiplicative sets for every C
connection: Erdős proved Bertrand by showing C(2n,n) would be too small if no prime lay in (n,2n]. ES failure at p means: for every C, 4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C) (e.g. C=1: 4p+1 has only prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4; C=2: 8p+1's prime factors lie in {1,3} or {1,5} mod 8). Compare Π_C(4Cp+1) — whose prime-factor multiset is fixed by CRT — with these restrictions.
why: Converts ES into a sieve problem with explicitly known 'prime factor census' (each prime q divides 4Cp+1 exactly for C in one class mod q).
first_step: Formalise the constraint set S_C = {N : no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C} for C ≤ 32 and compute, for the hard primes, how many C ≤ X have 4Cp+1 ∉ S_C (each such C is a certificate).

title: Harman-style comparison sieve: R(p) versus the average of R(n) over a short interval around p
connection: Harman's sieve gets primes in every short interval by comparing a decomposition with a model where asymptotics are known, discarding only small nonnegative terms. ES: compare R(p) with ⟨R(n)⟩ over n ∈ [p−H, p+H] in the same residue class mod 840, using Type I/II information on the multiplicative structure of 4Cn+1.
why: Averages of R over short intervals are accessible (E(I) ≪ H exp(−c(log H)^{3/4})); the comparison step is the pointwise-transfer mechanism.
first_step: Numerically measure |R(p) − ⟨R⟩_H|/⟨R⟩_H for H = p^θ, θ = 0.1..0.5, and see which H makes the comparison tight.

title: Burgess shift trick on the level variable
connection: Burgess amplifies a short character sum by shifting n → n + ab and using multiplicativity. ES events at level C involve the residue of 4Cp+1 modulo divisors; shifting C → C + kd preserves 'd | 4Cp+1'. Use shifts to relate the certificate count on a short C-range to a complete sum handled by Weil.
why: A Burgess-type argument for divisor events in a short level range would give certificates with small C (C ≤ p^{1/4+ε}), a pointwise statement.
first_step: Write #{C ≤ X : ∃ d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)} with d in a fixed range as a character sum over C mod d and try the (n + ab) shift with Hölder.

title: Heath-Brown's 'one of three' for ES windows
connection: Heath-Brown: among three multiplicatively independent integers satisfying non-square conditions (e.g. three distinct primes), one is a primitive root for infinitely many p. ES windows: failure at window e requires the divisor classes of N_e = (p+e)/4 to avoid −1 in their ratio set (often: lie in an index-2 subgroup without −1). Show three suitably independent windows cannot all fail.
why: Pigeonhole over several candidate families is an every-type argument that needs no single family to work.
first_step: For (★)-failing primes, record for small windows e the subgroup generated by the prime factors of N_e mod e; look for algebraic relations among three windows that make simultaneous avoidance impossible.

title: Profinite zero–one law for ES certificate sets
connection: Gallagher's zero–one law makes metric Diophantine sets have measure 0 or 1. In the profinite completion of ℤ, the set of p̂ admitting a certificate at a finite level is open; its complement is closed of Haar measure 0 (almost-all theorem). Characterise the complement (contains square-mimicking points, B1).
why: The integers are a countable dense subset; ES says no integer lies in the closed null set. Knowing its exact shape (squares only? more?) is the profinite form of the problem.
first_step: Compute, for M = 840·k with k ≤ 30, the residues mod M not covered by certificates with all parameters dividing powers of M; compare with the squares mod M.

title: Is ES parity-sensitive? A Selberg-parity test for certificate counts
connection: FI/Heath-Brown matter because sieves cannot distinguish parity of Ω. Test whether the ES certificate indicator correlates with λ(4Cp+1) or λ of the divisor: if certificate detection is 'parity-blind', sieve-theoretic approaches are not blocked by parity.
why: Clarifies whether parity-breaking technology is needed at all.
first_step: Compute Σ_C λ(d)·1[d certificate at level C] over all certificates for many p; compare with the total count.

title: Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec well-factorable weights for the 'self-referential modulus'
connection: BFI pushed level of distribution beyond 1/2 for well-factorable weights. ES events have modulus 4C that is itself a factor of the divisor equation (d ≡ −1 mod 4C with d | 4Cp+1); exploit factorability of the weights in C.
why: The self-referential modulus is ES's distinctive structure; BFI-type dispersion is designed for moduli with flexible factorizations.
first_step: Rewrite R(p) with C = C₁C₂ factorable weights and check whether the resulting sums fit the BFI dispersion template (sum over moduli of a fixed residue).

title: ES along almost all polynomial families n = f(m)
connection: Skorobogatov–Sofos prove Schinzel on average over polynomial families. Ask: for 100% of quadratic families f (ordered by height), does Type II hold for all large m (or all m)? The square family m² is the T1 exception; maybe 'square-like' families are the only exceptions.
why: A different 'almost all' axis (over families, every member) that interacts directly with T1 and with the repo's exponential families.
first_step: For random quadratics f(m) = am² + bm + c with small height, compute the Type II failure set among m ≤ 10⁵ and see if failures concentrate on families that are squares up to linear change.

title: Ineffective lower bound for M_BM via Siegel instead of Burgess
connection: Thm 2.2 gets M_BM ≥ (3/16π²) log²p via Burgess. Siegel's L(1,χ) ≫ q^{−ε} might give the full M_BM ∼ M₀ for the dominant small-modulus part, ineffectively.
why: Would sharpen the unconditional main term (constant) at the cost of effectivity; useful for any ineffective all-large-p route.
first_step: Isolate the contribution of moduli 4uB ≤ (log p)^A in T(p), express it via L(1,·) values of characters of conductor ≤ (log p)^A twisted by (·/p), and apply Siegel–Walfisz-type input.

title: Almost-all exponents → all: Faltings-type finiteness for ES failure configurations
connection: Heath-Brown/Granville deduced FLT for almost all exponents from Faltings' finiteness. ES: find a family of curves X_p (genus ≥ 2, or of general type) whose extra rational/integral points are forced by ES failure at p; uniform finiteness would bound the failures.
why: Moves ES to finiteness of the exceptional set — a big intermediate step (finite exceptions + verification would finish).
first_step: Look for curves in the ES surface family U_p (e.g. intersections with x = λy) whose integral points correspond to certificates; compute genera.

title: Annihilator theory in (ℤ/4C)*: Stickelberger-type relations among divisor classes
connection: Mihăilescu's proof uses annihilators of cyclotomic class groups. The classes of prime factors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)* across many C are linked (the same p); look for annihilator-type relations that prevent all of them from avoiding −1.
why: Odd: ES failure is a statement about a family of subgroups indexed by C; group-ring relations between the families might be forced by the common p.
first_step: Compute for fixed p the vectors (class of q mod 4C) for primes q | 4Cp+1, C ≤ 200, and search for linear relations in the group ring that hold for all p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: 'At most one exception' phase: repulsion between ES-failing primes
connection: Heilbronn–Linfoot/Tatuzawa proved there is at most one exceptional discriminant before the full class-number-one solution. ES intermediate: show two (★)-failing or ES-failing primes p, p′ in a range [X, X²] cannot coexist (repulsion), e.g. because their characters would both be exceptional.
why: Finiteness/at-most-one statements are the classical stepping stone between almost-all and every.
first_step: Check the 14 (★)-failures ≤ 10¹⁰ for pairwise relations (p′/p) = 1, shared quadratic-residue profiles, and spacing; compare with random primes having the same individual profiles.

title: Continued-fraction periodicity vs. ES₅ length: Lagrange's proof structure
connection: Pell's solution comes from the periodic CF of √D. ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3 (a continued-fraction length condition for rationals with denominator p). Look for a quadratic irrational (depending on p) whose CF period contains an ES₅ witness, so periodicity forces existence.
why: Odd but concrete: links ES₅'s CF-length formulation to the one every-n theorem driven by CF structure.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, compute the CF periods of √p, √(4p+1), (1+√p)/2 and check whether an ES₅ witness can be read off from convergents.

title: Non-vanishing criterion (Gross–Zagier style) for the existence of a certificate
connection: Gross–Zagier: a Heegner point is non-torsion iff L′(E,1) ≠ 0 — existence from an analytic non-vanishing. ES: seek a curve/abelian variety A_p with a canonical point whose non-triviality is equivalent to (or implies) an ES certificate, so that a non-vanishing statement proves ES.
why: Converts existence into non-vanishing of a special value, where analytic tools work for every member of a family.
first_step: Look for elliptic fibrations of the ES surface U_p (e.g. fix x/y = λ) and compute whether the integral points relate to multiples of a canonical point.

title: Classify limit measures of normalised certificate data along hypothetical failing sequences
connection: QE (density one) comes from a variance bound; QUE (every) from classifying all possible limits (measure rigidity + entropy). ES: attach to each p a normalised measure (levels/shapes of certificates or profinite residue data); show that the only possible limit along any sequence p_k → ∞ is the 'Haar' one, incompatible with R(p_k) = 0.
why: Shifts from 'bound the variance' (almost all) to 'classify limits' (every) — the exact conceptual step of QUE.
first_step: Define μ_p on the profinite completion (or on (ℤ/M)* for growing M) from the residues of p; check what the square-mimicking points of B1 look like as limit measures.

title: Parametrise ES methods by L(1,(·/p)): one should improve as it grows, another as it shrinks
connection: Holowinsky's bound is in terms of Σ_ℓ (|λ(ℓ)| − 1)/ℓ, Soundararajan's in the opposite tendency. M_BM = M₀ − T(p) is hurt when the weighted sum of (−m/p) is large. Find a second certificate family whose expected count increases with T(p).
why: If the two main terms move in opposite directions with the same character statistic, their sum is bounded below uniformly — Holowinsky–Soundararajan in miniature.
first_step: Compute the expected counts of the b=1 line, windows and ES₅ as functions of the Legendre profile (m/p)_{m ≤ 100}; regress against T(p).

title: Mollified variance to identify which characters explain R's fluctuations
connection: Mollifiers (Selberg/Levinson/Conrey) dampen large values by a short Dirichlet polynomial. Fit R(n)/M(n) − 1 by a short combination of Legendre symbols (n/ℓ), ℓ ≤ L; the residual variance after mollification measures what remains beyond the genus/BM layer.
why: Tells whether ES fluctuations are dominated by a few small characters (then a Heilbronn-type split is promising) or are spread out (then they are 'X(p)' noise).
first_step: Least-squares fit on n ≤ 10⁷ in Mordell-hard classes; report explained variance as a function of L.

title: Minimal-counterexample descent: failure at p ⇒ failure at a smaller related prime
connection: Khare–Wintenberger: induction on conductor reduces to base cases. ES: find a map Φ such that if ES (or (★)) fails at p then it fails at some smaller Φ(p) (e.g. a prime factor of 4p+1 or of (p+e)/4); with verification to 10¹⁸ this proves ES.
why: Induction on the size of the counterexample is the cleanest every-n mechanism; data on (★)-failures can test candidate maps directly.
first_step: For the 14 (★)-failing primes, check whether any simple arithmetic function of p (prime factors of 4p+1, 8p+1, (p+3)/4, p−4k², …) systematically produces another (★)-failing prime.

title: Product of three sets in SL₂(ℤ): ES words as A·T·A with entry p
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd/Helfgott growth makes products of a few sets fill SL₂(F_q). ES words p = tuv − u − v are length-3 'minus continuants': the (1,1) entry of M(u)M(t)M(v) with M(a) = [[a,−1],[1,0]]. ES ⟺ some product in A·T·A (with t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p)) has the right entry.
why: Places ES in the product-set/growth framework where 'every element' theorems exist (at least modulo q).
first_step: Check numerically how the (1,1)-entries of M(u)M(t)M(v), u,v,t ≤ X, distribute modulo small q and whether all residues are hit with the expected frequency (local), then compare with the archimedean count.

title: Sum-product incompatibility: subgroup-avoidance across windows vs linear structure of N_e = (p+e)/4
connection: Bourgain–Katz–Tao: no set is nearly closed under both + and × in F_p. ES failure at many windows e forces the prime factors of N_e = (p+e)/4 into structured multiplicative sets mod e (e.g. squares when e is prime ≡ 3 mod 4), while N_e varies linearly in e.
why: If the multiplicative constraints at different e were incompatible with the additive progression N_e, ES would follow; sum-product is the canonical incompatibility principle.
first_step: For e prime ≡ 3 (mod 4), record whether all prime factors of N_e are QRs mod e for the hard primes; check how often this 'square-avoidance' happens across e ≤ 10⁴ compared to random.

title: Graph structure on certificates of a fixed p
connection: BGS/Chen study the connectivity of a graph on solutions. Define moves between ES certificates of the same p (change C keeping u, swap roles of u/B, Type I↔II transforms) and study components; 'one certificate ⇒ many' plus a counting congruence on component sizes might exclude zero.
why: Even if ES is not about connectivity, component structure can produce congruences (as in Chen).
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ build the move graph on all ES solutions and record component sizes; look for divisibility patterns.

title: Modular-Zaremba + size control: words with (1,2)-entry ≡ 0 (mod p) and size < 2p
connection: Moshchevitin–Shkredov solve a modular Zaremba problem by growth in SL₂(F_p). ES words: length-3 minus-continuant products; require the relevant entry ≡ 0 (mod p) and bounded by 2p, forcing equality with p. Equidistribution mod p of entries of words of archimedean size ≤ p is the needed input.
why: Separates ES into a modular part (growth, potentially 'every p') and a size part (counting words in a box).
first_step: Numerically test equidistribution mod p of the entries of length-3 words with entries ≤ p (count ≈ p log p) for p ~ 10⁶; measure deviations at 0 mod p.

title: Counting integral points on the quadric ad − pc = 1 (Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak / Eskin–McMullen)
connection: Oppenheim/Margulis and DRS/EM count integral points on affine homogeneous varieties via dynamics. The SL₂ form of ES: integer points of the affine quadric ad − pc = 1 (degenerate as a ternary quadratic polynomial: quadratic part ad of rank 2, linear in c — a family of hyperbolas ad = 1 + pc) with a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c), c ∈ 4ℕ, a, d ≥ 1. Decompose by c into congruence-subgroup cosets and count each via mixing.
why: Homogeneous-dynamics counts are pointwise in the variety (here: in p), unlike sieve averages.
first_step: For fixed c, the conditions define a coset of a congruence subgroup; compute the expected count Σ_c vol(coset ∩ region) and compare with R(p).

title: Shrinking-target property for every closed horocycle
connection: Logarithm laws (Kleinbock–Margulis) give deep excursions for almost every orbit; ES would need them for the specific closed horocycle of length p and depth ~ p^{θ}. Tseng (Math. Z. 2022) proves shrinking-cusp-target equidistribution for long closed horocycles (effective version included).
why: If a deep-excursion theorem for every closed horocycle exists at depth p^{θ}, the CF-length formulation might follow for a range of shapes.
first_step: Read Tseng, 'Shrinking target equidistribution of horocycles in cusps', Math. Z. 302 (2022), arXiv:2106.00836, and Kelmer, Israel J. Math. 229 (2019), arXiv:1708.08953 (both verified to exist); extract the deepest cusp target reachable for a closed horocycle of length p.

title: Large-p regime split by arithmetic configuration
connection: Tao handled different limiting zero configurations by different arguments. Split large p by configuration: (i) ℓ(p) small, (ii) ℓ(p) large but some small window works, (iii) (·/p) mimics a fixed character on all primes ≤ (log p)^A, … and design one certificate family per regime.
why: Each regime has extra structure to exploit; only finitely many regimes are needed if the split is by bounded data plus one 'pretentious' case.
first_step: Define the regime map on primes ≤ 10⁹ and check which certificate family is most robust in each regime.

title: Multiscale induction on level sizes
connection: Wang–Zahl proved 3D Kakeya by multiscale induction (sticky structure). ES certificates live at scales (C, u, B) with uBC ≈ p/4; formulate a statement S(X): 'every p has a certificate with C ≤ X or a structural reason to have one at scale X²' and attempt an induction on scales.
why: Scale induction is how several every-type geometric statements were proved recently; ES has a natural scale hierarchy.
first_step: From data, record for each p the smallest C with a certificate and the 'near miss' structure at smaller C; look for a recursive pattern across dyadic scales.

title: EGZ-style reduction: from 'composite' certificates to prime-level statements
connection: EGZ for n = ab follows from EGZ for a and b by iterated extraction. ES certificates at a level 4C = 4C₁C₂: is a certificate at level C obtainable from structure at levels C₁ and C₂ (e.g. a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C₁ and one ≡ −1 mod 4C₂ combined via CRT)?
why: If levels compose, it suffices to handle prime (power) levels, where character theory is simplest.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ test: when 4C₁p+1 and 4C₂p+1 have certificates, does 4C₁C₂p + 1 have one more often than chance?

title: Quasirandom 'one more factor' trick — size check for ES in SL₂(F_p)
connection: Nikolov–Pyber: if |A||B||C| > |G|³/m then ABC = G. For ES words A·T·A in SL₂(F_p), |A| ≈ |T| ≈ p while |G|³/m ≈ p⁸: the trick fails by a huge margin; quantify the deficit and check whether replacing SL₂(F_p) by a smaller quotient (Borel, affine group) helps.
why: Records why the canonical almost→every group trick does not apply directly, and where a smaller ambient group might restore it.
first_step: Compute |A|, |T|, |G| and m for G = SL₂(F_p), the Borel subgroup and the affine group F_p ⋊ F_p*; find the smallest ambient group in which ES becomes a product-covering statement.

title: Keevash template: algebraic identity families + random perturbation for square classes
connection: Keevash's randomized algebraic construction starts from an algebraic template and perturbs it. ES: Mordell identities cover all non-square classes mod 840 (algebraic template); perturb identity parameters randomly to handle the square classes, with an absorber for failures.
why: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities covering squares, but random perturbations of identities are not identities.
first_step: Take Mordell's identities, introduce free integer parameters (k-fold families), and measure how often random parameter choices give certificates for primes in square classes.

title: Extremal vs non-extremal split for ES
connection: EFL/Ringel proofs split into 'extremal' configurations (handled by hand) and 'random-like' ones (absorption). ES: random-like p (character values balanced) vs extremal p (QR at many small primes; square-like mod large M); handle extremal p by forced-congruence arguments (least non-residue) and random-like p by second-moment counting.
why: Gives a concrete division of labour where each part may be tractable; the extremal side is close to the Burgess/least-non-residue world.
first_step: Define an extremality score E(p) (e.g. number of primes ℓ ≤ 100 with (p/ℓ) = 1) and examine how certificate counts depend on it.

title: Minimal counterexample via the e-slice: ES(p) from data of N = (p+e)/4 < p
connection: Four-colour and many combinatorial proofs consider a minimal counterexample. ES(p) ⟸ a property P(N, e) of the smaller integer N = (p+e)/4. Find a property Q(n), inherited along n ↦ (n + e)/4 for some e, such that Q(n) for all n < p implies Q(p) and Q(p) ⇒ ES(p).
why: A successful Q would make ES a consequence of verification (10¹⁸) + induction.
first_step: Data mining: for each p ≤ 10⁷, list e for which N_e carries a certificate and look for a hereditary property of N_e.

title: Entropic Ruzsa distance between divisor-class distributions at different levels
connection: GGMT proved PFR via entropic Ruzsa distance and an entropy-decrement iteration. For fixed p, the distributions of divisor classes of 4Cp+1 across levels C could be compared via entropic distances; structured failure would force small distances to subgroup-uniform distributions.
why: An odd but well-defined way to quantify 'subgroup trapping' of divisor classes across levels.
first_step: Compute entropic distances of the divisor-class distributions to uniform-on-subgroup distributions for hard p.

title: Look-ahead greedy: provably terminating 3-term splitting rules
connection: Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy terminates because the numerator decreases; the odd greedy algorithm is open. For 4/p, analyse non-greedy first-step rules (choose x among ⌈p/4⌉ + k for k ≤ K by a look-ahead criterion) and characterise primes where every rule with K ≤ K₀ fails.
why: A finite-look-ahead rule is a bounded procedure (B1 says it must fail for some p under H), but the failure set's structure is informative and computable.
first_step: For each p ≤ 10⁸ compute the least k such that x = ⌈p/4⌉ + k leaves a two-term-solvable remainder; record the distribution and the extreme p.

title: Left-tail extrapolation: does Σ_p P(R(p) = 0) converge?
connection: Goldbach's other conjecture failed at 5777/5993 where the expected representation count was small. For ES, extrapolate the measured zero law (P(R* = 0 | M)) to estimate Σ_p P(no certificate) over p > 10¹⁸; if it is ≪ 10⁻⁶, the 'heuristic' evidence for ES is overwhelming, and the computation identifies which sub-route is safest to target.
why: Sanity-checks which formulations are heuristically true for all p (needed before trying to prove them).
first_step: Fit log P(R* = 0 | M) on the repo's data and integrate against the distribution of M(p) for p > 10¹⁸; do the same for (★), b=1, union.

title: Topological existence: Tucker/Ky Fan on a complex built from divisor lattices
connection: Lovász proved Kneser via Borsuk–Ulam; Tucker's lemma is its combinatorial form. Build a simplicial complex from divisor configurations of 4Cp+1 across levels with a free ℤ/2-action (d ↔ N/d swap or u ↔ B swap) such that an equivariant labelling without a 'complementary edge' is impossible, and complementary edges are certificates.
why: Topological methods give existence with no counting at all, immune to the polylog-main-term problem.
first_step: Toy version: for one level C, model divisors as vertices of a cross-polytope (±q_i) and check whether certificate-freeness defines an antipodal-free labelling; compute its index.

title: Representations with linear side conditions: ES certificates as constrained quaternion norms
connection: Machiavelo–Tsopanidis proved Sun's 1-3-5 conjecture (four squares with a linear condition) for every n. If ES certificates can be phrased as 'p (or 4Cp+1) is a norm from an order with a linear side condition on coordinates', their arithmetic arguments may transfer.
why: Linear side conditions on norm representations are exactly the shape of ES congruence constraints.
first_step: Read Machiavelo–Tsopanidis' method; try to phrase (★) as N(α) = 4Cp+1 with α in an order and a linear congruence on α's coordinates.

title: Tower of moduli with auxiliary primes (Shafarevich-style embedding problems)
connection: Shafarevich realised solvable groups by solving embedding problems step by step, choosing auxiliary primes to control local behaviour. ES: build a certificate as a sequence of lifts through moduli 4 → 8 → 24 → 840 → … with auxiliary prime factors of 4Cp+1 chosen at each step, keeping a global integer solution possible at each stage.
why: Gives a stepwise view of where integrality is lost; the final step (a genuine integer) is the crux.
first_step: Trace actual (★) certificates for hard primes: at which modulus in the tower does the certificate's structure become determined?

title: AKS-style 'too large and too small' group argument for a counterexample
connection: AKS: if n is not a prime power, a group of polynomials would be both ≥ a binomial lower bound and ≤ n^{√t}. ES: if p has no certificate, the set of divisor classes of 4Cp+1 across levels generates a structure (e.g. a subgroup of Π_C (ℤ/4C)* avoiding all −1's) that might be shown both large (many independent prime factors across C) and small (avoidance).
why: The most striking conditional→unconditional derandomisation used exactly this double counting.
first_step: Define G_K(p) = subgroup of Π_{C≤K} (ℤ/4C)* generated by the vectors (q mod 4C)_C over primes q > 4K dividing some 4Cp+1 (so q is a unit at every level); compute its index and whether it avoids the −1 pattern for hard p.

title: Partial-colouring pigeonhole: collisions of near-certificates yield certificates
connection: Spencer/Beck: exponentially many colourings fall into few buckets, two collide, their difference is a good partial colouring. ES: generate many near-certificates for p (objects mapping to a small 'defect' space), pigeonhole two into the same bucket, and combine them (difference/quotient) into an exact certificate — the Pell/Dirichlet mechanism with an entropy count.
why: The entropy count tells exactly how many near-certificates are needed versus the bucket count; if near-certificates are power-many while buckets are polylog-many, collisions are guaranteed.
first_step: Identify a combination law (SL₂ quotients, divisor ratios) and a defect space; count near-certificates vs buckets for test p.

title: Residue-class case split with per-class constructions (Ringel–Youngs) — and its limit
connection: Ringel–Youngs proved the Heawood bound by 12 residue cases, each with its own construction family. ES: Mordell's identities do this for non-square classes mod 840; the square classes need infinitely many sub-cases. Measure how the number of needed per-class families grows with the modulus (cf. B1).
why: Quantifies the 'case explosion' and hence how far case-analysis approaches can go.
first_step: For M = 840·k, count the minimal number of polynomial certificate families needed to cover all non-square classes mod M; plot vs M.

title: p-adic interpolation along exponential families (Skolem–Mahler–Lech)
connection: SML proves zero sets of linear recurrences are periodic + finite via p-adic analytic interpolation. ES along n_s = a·b^s + c: certificate conditions involve divisors of 4C·n_s + 1 = 4Ca·b^s + (4Cc + 1), an exponential sequence; p-adic interpolation of 'divisibility by a fixed d' gives periodic structure in s, possibly proving ES for open families like 15·2^s + 1 by periodic covering + finitely many checks.
why: The repo already proved several exponential families via windows; SML-type periodicity could organise the remaining ones.
first_step: For 15·2^s + 1 compute, for each small (C, d) with d ≡ −1 (mod 4C), the set of s with d | 4C·n_s + 1 (periodic in s); check whether a finite union of these covers all s.

title: Rademacher-type exact series for the ES level/word series
connection: Rademacher turned the Hardy–Ramanujan asymptotic into an exact convergent series for every n, with an explicitly bounded tail; Bringmann–Manschot extended exact expansions to some meromorphic Jacobi forms. METAPLECTIC Thm K writes the level series as Kronecker theta quotients θ(X²)/θ(X)² (meromorphic Jacobi-form-like); an exact Rademacher-type expansion of their coefficients would give R_t(p) as main term + explicit tail.
why: An exact formula with first term ≍ main term and an explicit tail is a pointwise-in-n statement by construction.
first_step: Check the modular/Jacobi properties of θ(X²)/θ(X)² as a function of (τ, z) and whether Bringmann–Manschot's framework (or Appell–Lerch sum expansions) applies; compute the first few terms numerically.

title: Monotone-quantity flow on certificate space
connection: Perelman finished Poincaré with a flow and monotone entropy that forces termination at a canonical object. ES: define a deterministic 'flow' on candidate triples (x, y, z) for 4/p (e.g. a descent on the defect 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) using local moves) with a monovariant that can only stop at a certificate, and prove no other stopping states exist (or classify them).
why: Odd but concrete: a local-move dynamical system on integer triples is easy to experiment with; classification of its sinks is a finite-ish problem per p.
first_step: Design local moves (change one coordinate by ±1, or by divisor-jumps) decreasing |defect| and compute sinks for p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Mordell's class-number formula for yz + zx + xy = p as an exact power-size count
connection: Duke/Iwaniec exploit class-number-sized representation counts. Mordell (1923) gives, for prime n, the number of positive solutions of yz + zx + xy = n as 3G(n) − 3 (G class-number type). ES solutions satisfy σ₂(x,y,z) = 4σ₃/p; scaling Type II solutions (y = pY, z = pZ) gives p·YZ = x(4YZ − Y − Z), a σ₂-type relation. Look for a bijection or injection from a subset of Mordell's solutions (power-many) to ES certificates.
why: Would tie ES to an exact class-number count (power-size, every p), the Duke template.
first_step: For small primes, list Mordell's solutions of yz + zx + xy = p (or = 4p, kp) and test which ones transform into ES solutions via simple rational maps.

title: Zeta-type packaging of Type I/II counts at p^k (T1 kills even k)
connection: Hasse–Davenport/Weil: point counts over all extensions assemble into a rational zeta function, so a few counts determine all. T1 gives f_{I,II}(p^{2k}) = 0 for odd p. Study f_{I,II}(p^{2k+1}) and the series Σ_k f(p^k) t^k: any rationality or recursion linking f(p³), f(p⁵), … to f(p) would make f(p) > 0 follow from large odd powers.
why: Odd powers of p may have solutions that do not come from p; a recursion would be a Hecke-type relation in the 'p-power direction'.
first_step: Compute f_I, f_II at p, p³, p⁵ for small primes p ≤ 200 and look for linear recurrences in k.

title: Rotation structure: fixing two word parameters makes ES a progression
connection: BGS's middle game uses 'rotations' (fix one Markoff coordinate → conic with a cyclic action). ES words p = tuv − u − v: fixing (t, u) gives v(tu − 1) = p + u, an arithmetic condition mod tu − 1; fixing (u, v) gives t·uv = p + u + v. Use these one-parameter 'rotations' to move between certificate-bearing and non-bearing configurations.
why: The local-to-global passage in BGS relies on such fibrations; ES has them in elementary form.
first_step: For hard p, compute for each (t,u) with tu ≤ T the residue of p + u mod tu − 1 and visualise the hit structure; look for orbit-like propagation.

title: 8/n exceptions as a built-in falsification test
connection: Kolmogorov/Kahane–Katznelson show almost-everywhere statements can fail on prescribed null sets. ES has a real-world analogue: 8/n fails at 131 and 241 while being 'almost all'. Any ES argument that is uniform in the numerator m without a threshold would prove 8/131 — use this as a mandatory test for every candidate mechanism.
why: Cheap and decisive filter for proof attempts (already in FRONTIER (J)41); worth applying to each upgrade template in this list.
first_step: For each template here (complementary methods, pigeonhole + group law, Hecke relations, …) check whether its ES version would also apply verbatim to 8/131.

title: Certificate-search complexity as a heuristic proxy
connection: Three cubes is 'computation only' because representations are astronomically large. ES certificates are tiny and fast to find; measure the asymptotic cost of the cheapest search (e.g. via Lenstra divisors-in-classes or e-slice scans) as p grows to quantify how 'easy' every p is.
why: If the search cost provably stays polylog for all p in a model, a proof by 'algorithm + analysis' (AKS-style) becomes a natural target.
first_step: Benchmark the cheapest certificate finder on the adversarial primes at 10¹⁸–10²⁵ and fit cost vs log p.

title: All-but-finitely-many with genuine small exceptions (Terjanian) — ES-type numerator analogues
connection: Ax–Kochen's statement is true for p > p₀(d) and false for some small p (Terjanian). The ES numerator family behaves similarly: 4/n has no known exception, but 8/n fails at 131, 241. A structural explanation of where p₀(m) lies for m/n would show what makes m = 4 special.
why: Understanding why 4 behaves like 'p₀ = 1' while 8 has small exceptions is a sharp test of any mechanism.
first_step: Tabulate the exceptions of m/n for m ≤ 30 (PW data) and search for a statistic predicting their largest exception (cf. Schinzel's exp(m^{1/3+o(1)})).

title: Escape of mass for ES: certificates drifting to extreme shapes
connection: Soundararajan's step was 'no escape of mass': limiting measures are probability measures. ES analogue: as p → ∞, could the certificates' normalized shape distribution (log C / log p, log u / log p) concentrate at the boundary (C ≈ 1 or C ≈ p), so that 'typical' regions are empty? Show mass stays in the bulk.
why: If certificates escape to extreme shapes for hard p, proofs focusing on bulk shapes miss them; if not, bulk counting suffices.
first_step: For hard primes vs controls, compute the empirical distribution of (log C/log p, log u/log p) of all certificates.

title: Entropy count of near-certificates vs defect buckets
connection: Spencer's partial colouring needs (#objects) > (#buckets)·(something). For ES, near-certificates of p with defect δ in a set of size Q number ~ p^{a}; buckets (defect, residues) number ~ Q^{b}. If a > b·log Q / log p, collisions are forced; compute a and b for concrete combination laws.
why: A pure counting check that tells whether any pigeonhole + combination mechanism can possibly work for ES.
first_step: For the SL₂-form near-certificates (det = 1 + δ with |δ| ≤ Δ), count objects with entries ≤ p and the number of congruence buckets needed for the quotient to be integral.

title: Parity of Ω(4Cp+1) and certificate existence
connection: Chen's theorem lives at the parity barrier (P₂ but not primes). Certificates at level C need a divisor in a class; if 4Cp+1 is prime, the only divisors are 1 and itself (class 1), so prime values of 4Cp+1 are useless. Measure the dependence of certificate probability on Ω(4Cp+1).
why: Tells whether ES needs 'many prime factors' (sieve-friendly almost-primes in reverse) and quantifies the loss from prime values.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁹ and C ≤ 10⁵ tabulate P(certificate at C | Ω(4Cp+1) = k) for k = 1..8.

title: Quaternion (Hurwitz) proof of four squares: Euclidean order as the 'every p' engine
connection: Lagrange's theorem has a proof via the Hurwitz order being (left) Euclidean: p = ππ̄ factors, giving p as a norm. ES quaternion reformulations (repo) would need an order with a Euclidean-like property relative to a congruence structure tied to 4C.
why: If the relevant order (or its Eichler sub-order of level 4C) has class number one for small C, ES at those levels follows from factorisation.
first_step: Compute class numbers of Eichler orders of level 4C in the Hurwitz quaternion algebra (Sage) for C ≤ 20 and compare with which levels never fail.

title: Corrected local-global: formulate ES sub-routes with their reciprocity exceptions removed
connection: After the Apollonian disproof, the corrected conjecture excludes the reciprocity families. For ES sub-routes, formulate 'corrected' versions (e.g. Type I/II for all non-squares; (★) for all p outside an explicit reciprocity-defined set) and test which corrected statements have finite exception sets.
why: Ensures the targets are the right ones before attempting proofs.
first_step: Use the repo's census data to fit, for each sub-route, its failure set to explicit reciprocity conditions; report residual sporadic failures.

title: Zero-sum over levels: among many levels, some combination of near-certificates is exact
connection: EGZ guarantees a zero-sum subsequence of prescribed length. ES near-certificates at different levels C carry 'defect classes' in groups (ℤ/4C)*; if defects lived in a common group, a zero-sum subsequence of defects could combine into an exact certificate (requires a combination law across levels).
why: Odd: needs a multiplicative combination law; but zero-sum theory exactly converts 'many near-misses' into 'one hit'.
first_step: Find a common quotient group for defects at levels C ≡ 0 (mod M) (e.g. (ℤ/M)*) and test whether products of near-certificates at different levels produce certificates at the lcm level.

title: Modularity of an ES generating object and a 'level-lowering' contradiction
connection: Ribet's level lowering forced a hypothetical form to level 2 where none exists. ES generating functions (Thm K level series) are modular of level t; a failure of ES at p might force some auxiliary modular form (e.g. a twisted combination vanishing at p) to have a special property that lowers its level or weight to a space that is empty.
why: Speculative, but 'empty space of modular forms' contradictions are the archetypal every-n mechanism.
first_step: Search for linear combinations of level-t series whose p-th coefficient is R(p) times a nonzero constant, and determine the space they live in; ask whether vanishing at all ES-failing p would force membership in a smaller space.

title: Frobenius count in SL₂(ℤ/q) for the SL₂ form of ES
connection: Ore-type proofs count solutions of word equations via Σ_χ χ(g)/χ(1). The SL₂ form asks for γ = [[a, p],[c, d]] with a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c); reduced mod q this is a count of elements in a double-coset-type subset of SL₂(ℤ/q); its character expansion has nontrivial terms bounded by 1/χ(1) ~ 1/q.
why: Shows how much cancellation is available 'for free' in a nonabelian encoding (local information only, but with strong decay).
first_step: Compute for primes q the number of solutions mod q via characters of SL₂(F_q) and compare with the abelian (genus) expansion's error.

title: Extreme-value statistics of the least certificate parameter
connection: Linnik-type theorems bound the least prime in a class. Measure the least certificate parameter (least C for (★), least e for windows) as p grows and fit an extreme-value law; a provable bound of the observed shape would be the 'Linnik constant' of ES.
why: Calibrates which quantitative statements are plausible (e.g. C(p) ≤ (log p)^A for all p?) before trying to prove any.
first_step: From the repo's census (and adversarial primes at 10¹⁸–10²⁵) tabulate max over p ≤ X of least C and least e versus log X.

title: Vinogradov's smooth-number trick for divisor classes
connection: Vinogradov bounded n(p): if every ℓ ≤ y is a QR, all y-smooth numbers are QRs, contradicting character-sum bounds since smooth numbers are plentiful. ES: if level C fails, no divisor of 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 (mod 4C); if additionally we know the classes of small primes, smooth parts of 4Cp+1 are constrained. Count C for which 4Cp+1 has a y-smooth divisor in a forced class.
why: Transfers a proven every-p argument shape (n(p) bounds) to divisor classes, using smooth numbers in APs (Granville, Harper).
first_step: Model: fix the classes mod 4C of primes ≤ y; count C ≤ X such that 4Cp+1 has a y-smooth divisor d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) using smooth-number distribution; compare with data.

title: Limiting distribution of R(p)/M_BM(p) (a Sato–Tate/Cohen–Lenstra-type law)
connection: Sato–Tate identified the exact limiting law of normalised a_p. For ES, determine the limiting distribution of R(p)/M_BM(p) (and of f(p)/log³p) as p → ∞ through Mordell-hard primes; its behaviour near 0 is what decides ES heuristically.
why: A precise conjectural law with a computable left tail sharpens the heuristic case for ES and indicates which normalisation is 'right'.
first_step: Histogram R(p)/M_BM(p) for primes in windows at 10⁶, 10⁸, 10¹⁰; test convergence and fit the left tail.

title: Class-number parity (genus theory, Rédei) as the source of oddness for a Zagier-type argument
connection: Heath-Brown's/Zagier's proofs use a set whose size parity is forced. Natural sets attached to p have sizes tied to class numbers h(−4p), h(−8p), whose parities/2-parts are governed by genus theory and Rédei symbols. Find an ES-related finite set whose cardinality equals (up to known even terms) such a class number with known parity.
why: Supplies the 'odd cardinality' input a parity proof needs from established theory.
first_step: Compute |S_p| for candidate sets (e.g. reduced forms of disc −16p with an extra congruence) and compare parity with h(−4p), h(−8p) and Rédei-symbol predictions.

title: Large prime factors in the AP {4Cp + 1 : C ≤ K} (Sylvester–Schur/Shorey–Tijdeman)
connection: Sylvester–Schur: products of consecutive integers have a large prime factor; Shorey–Tijdeman extend to AP terms. For ES, a single prime q | 4Cp+1 with q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) is a certificate. Large prime factors are guaranteed in the product over C ≤ K; the class condition q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) is the extra requirement.
why: Gives a guaranteed supply of large prime divisors; the problem reduces to a class-distribution question for these forced large primes.
