first_step: For p ~ 10⁹, list the largest prime factor of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10⁴ and test the rate at which it is ≡ −1 (mod 4C) against 2/φ(4C)-type models.

title: Instance transformation that preserves certificate existence but amplifies counts
connection: Reingold transformed every graph into an expander while preserving connectivity. ES: find a transformation p ↦ (structured object with power-many 'attempts') such that ES(p) ⟺ the object has a 'connected/nonzero' property that is robustly detectable (e.g. a spectral quantity), amplifying the polylog main term.
why: If the count can be amplified while preserving the zero/nonzero status, the polylog-main-term barrier (B2) changes character.
first_step: Look at the equivalence ES(p) ⟺ ∃e (e-slice form, Type I and Type II N's) and the implication (★)-level certificate ⇒ ES(p); build a graph on (e, divisors of N_e) whose connectivity property is equivalent to ES(p), and compute its spectral gap for small p.

title: Class-equation divisibility: Φ_n(q)-type obstruction to 'no certificate'
connection: Witt's proof of Wedderburn: the class equation has all terms but one divisible by Φ_n(q), forcing a contradiction. For ES, write an exact counting identity for a quantity attached to p (e.g. Σ_C τ(4Cp+1) over a full period, or a divisor-class census over (ℤ/4C)*) as a sum over 'orbits' where all non-certificate terms are divisible by some cyclotomic-type number.
why: A divisibility contradiction needs no asymptotic analysis.
first_step: Look for counting identities over complete residue systems (C mod q) where certificate-free contributions have a forced common factor.

title: Eventual periodicity of 'ES-easy' residue structures (Wilson-style)
connection: Wilson showed the set of orders admitting designs is eventually periodic, so finitely many residue classes need checking. For ES sub-routes, test whether 'the set of levels C at which the BM main term is positive for all p in a class r mod M' is eventually periodic in C, giving a finite description of guaranteed-positive levels.
why: Eventually periodic structures can be checked by finite computation and then fed into an every-p argument.
first_step: For M = 840, compute for each hard class r the set of C ≤ 10⁴ with M_C^lev > 0 for all p ≡ r (mod M·4C) and test periodicity in C.

title: Uncovered density of the (★) system restricted to moduli with bounded prime factors
connection: Hough's argument tracks how the uncovered set shrinks as primes are added to the moduli. Restrict ES congruences p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) to moduli 4uB built from primes ≤ y; compute the uncovered density δ(y) among integers in the hard classes and its decay in y.
why: A precise decay law for δ(y) (power of log y? exp?) quantifies how many prime 'layers' certificates need — a structural fingerprint of ES.
first_step: Compute δ(y) for y ≤ 50 by inclusion over moduli dividing a bounded smooth number, restricted to n ≤ 10⁸ in hard classes.

title: Primitive part of 4Cp+1 relative to smaller levels as a 'new divisor' source
connection: Zsigmondy isolates primes dividing a^n − 1 but no earlier term. For fixed p, call a prime factor q of 4Cp+1 'new' if q ∤ 4C′p+1 for C′ < C (equivalently c_q = C). New primes have c_q = C < q, and a new prime q is a single-prime certificate iff 4C | q + 1. Study the number of new primes at each level.
why: New-prime counts give an explicit, level-ordered supply of candidates with a clean certificate test.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁸ and C ≤ 10⁵ compute the new primes at each level and the frequency of 4C | q + 1.

title: Euler-system-style bounds on the 'obstruction group' of certificate-free levels
connection: Kolyvagin bounded Selmer groups with an Euler system of Heegner points. Define for p the 'obstruction group' O_p = set of levels/windows that fail with their local data; a norm-compatible system of near-certificates across levels (if it existed) would bound O_p and force it to be smaller than the set of all levels.
why: Highly speculative, but Euler systems are the one tool that converts a supply of compatible objects into a bound on an obstruction.
first_step: First check whether near-certificates at levels C | C′ satisfy any norm/trace compatibility (e.g. divisor classes mod 4C′ reducing to classes mod 4C).

title: Union-closed structure of the family of ES-solvable sets of numerators
connection: Gilmer's method applies to union-closed families. For each n, the set A_n = {m : m/n is a 3-term Egyptian fraction} — is the family {A_n} (or its complements) closed under unions/intersections in a way that forces a frequent element (a numerator m that works for most n)? For m = 4 the conjecture is 'all n'.
why: Odd, but the numerator–denominator incidence structure (with 8/n failing at 131, 241) is a natural set system to analyse with these tools.
first_step: Compute A_n ∩ [1, 30] for n ≤ 10⁵ and test closure properties and element frequencies.

title: Harmonic-sum thresholds for the denominator set of ES solutions
connection: Liu–Sawhney: a set A ⊂ [1, N] with Σ_{n∈A} 1/n ≥ (log N)^{4/5+o(1)} contains S with Σ_{S} 1/n = 1. ES solutions for p use denominators in {multiples of p} ∪ {numbers ≈ p/4 … p²}; compute the 'harmonic mass' of the possible denominator sets and compare with such thresholds (for 3 terms, thresholds are presumably different, but the bookkeeping shows the gap).
why: Quantifies how far ES is from the regime where density-based unit-fraction theorems apply.
first_step: Compute Σ 1/n over the set of denominators appearing in any ES solution for p (data) and over natural supersets.

title: Multiplicative-function structure of the level indicator at fixed p
connection: MR's method uses multiplicativity in n. At fixed p, the function C ↦ D_C(p) is not multiplicative in C, but N ↦ 1[N has a divisor ≡ −1 mod t] is 'multiplicative-ish' in N for fixed t. Study the Dirichlet-series/Halász structure of n ↦ D_t^−(tn + 1) for fixed t (its mean value over n is controlled by Halász-type theorems).
why: Halász/MR techniques give 'every interval of length h' results for multiplicative functions; level-t certificate indicators along n might be accessible.
first_step: Express 1[D_t^−(tn+1) > 0] via the multiplicative set S_t and compute its mean in short intervals of n numerically; compare with Landau–Ramanujan-type predictions.

title: Auxiliary-prime choice with prescribed local behaviour for windows
connection: Shafarevich's embedding-problem induction succeeds by choosing auxiliary primes with prescribed local behaviour at each step. For ES windows, choose the window prime q with prescribed splitting behaviour in fields built from p (e.g. q splits in ℚ(√p, i) or has given Frobenius in a Kummer extension) so that Rat_q(K) is forced to contain −1.
why: Chebotarev guarantees auxiliary primes with any prescribed Frobenius; if the window certificate were a Frobenius condition, existence would follow.
first_step: Test whether success of window q for p is predicted by the Frobenius of q in ℚ(ζ_8, √p) or in Kummer fields ℚ(ζ_4, p^{1/4}).

title: Hardest residue cases needed new constructions: identify ES's 'case 3 mod 12'
connection: In Ringel–Youngs some residue classes (e.g. cases 1, 9 mod 12) took years and ad hoc ideas. Among the six Mordell-hard classes mod 840 (1, 121, 169, 289, 361, 529), measure which is hardest (lowest counts, most sub-route failures) and focus constructions there.
why: Concentrating effort on the hardest class mirrors the historical endgame.
first_step: From census data, compute per-class mean/minimum of R(p)/log²p and sub-route failure counts.

title: Two square degeneracies: algebraic factorisation (p + m²) vs reciprocity (ES Type I/II)
connection: p + m² degenerates at squares because n − m² = (a − m)(a + m) allows at most one representation (m = a − 1); T1 makes Type I/II fail at odd squares through a reciprocity cancellation. Compare: exceptional-set technology for p + m² is power-saving (H. Li 2003: E(X) ≪ X^0.982; verified), more advanced than ES's; can ES's T1 be rewritten as an algebraic factorisation in some model (e.g. 4Cm² + 1 or (p + e)/4 at squares)?
why: If T1 becomes algebraic in some coordinates, Hardy–Littlewood-type machinery for 'non-square n' transfers more directly.
first_step: At n = m², examine 4Cm² + 1 and (m² + e)/4 for algebraic factorisations that explain the absence of certificates (e.g. Sophie Germain-type identities).

title: Brjuno-type sum as a certificate-difficulty index
connection: The Brjuno sum Σ log q_{n+1}/q_n measures cumulative small-divisor difficulty. Define an analogous additive difficulty index for p (e.g. Σ over small levels C of −log of the probability that level C fails given p's residues) and test whether ES certificate counts are governed by it.
why: A single scalar controlling difficulty would focus both proofs and adversarial searches.
first_step: Compute the index for primes ≤ 10⁹ and correlate with R(p), least certificate C and sub-route failures.

title: Jacobi-symbol parity forces a prime factor in a nonresidue class — how far toward the exact class?
connection: Elkies: (−D/H_D(j)) parity forces a prime factor inert in ℚ(√−D). ES windows: (N_e/e) = (p/e) for N_e = (p+e)/4, so if (p/e) = −1 then N_e has a prime factor q with (q/e) = −1 (FORCED_WINDOW's condition). ES needs more: a divisor ratio exactly ≡ −1. Identify what extra 'forcing' (higher-order characters, sign/size of N_e) could pin the class.
why: Clarifies the gap between the proven quadratic forcing and the needed exact-class statement; Elkies needed only a quadratic class.
first_step: For window primes e ≡ 3 (mod 4) with (p/e) = −1, measure the distribution of the forced nonresidue factors' classes and how often a complementary divisor completes −1.

title: Universality classification for the family a·tuv − b·u − c·v + d
connection: Bhargava classified universal quadratic forms by finite criteria. For the cubic family F(t,u,v) = a·tuv − b·u − c·v + d with lower bounds on t, u, v, classify which members represent every large integer (I3 is the member a = b = c = 1, d = 0, bounds ≥ 3) and find the nearest universal member to ES's constrained form.
why: Mapping the universality frontier in a family containing ES shows which constraint (4 | t, sign of d, bounds) is decisive.
first_step: Compute exception sets up to 10⁸ for small (a, b, c, d) and bounds; record which appear finite.

title: Exact CRT independence in the level variable at fixed p
connection: LLL/Janson need limited dependence. At fixed p, the events {q | 4Cp + 1} for distinct primes q are exactly independent and uniform over complete periods of C (CRT); the only C-dependence that breaks independence is the class condition modulo 4C itself. Separate the two: write certificate events as (CRT-random divisibility pattern) × (C-dependent class test).
why: Identifies a genuine source of exact independence at fixed p, which probabilistic arguments could exploit without averaging over p.
first_step: Formalise for C in a range [K, 2K] with periods Q = Π_{q ≤ y} q: the divisibility pattern is equidistributed over C mod Q; compute the conditional certificate probability given the pattern and the size of C.

title: Descent to universal torsors: more variables for the circle method
connection: Heath-Brown and others proved Manin-type results via universal torsors, which have more variables and simpler equations. ES's Type I/II parametrisations (Elsholtz–Tao) look like torsor coordinates; identify the universal torsor of the ES surface (BL computed its Brauer/Picard data) and count integral points on its twists with fixed p.
why: More variables after descent is the standard route to circle-method feasibility; the torsor equations may be quadratic in many variables.
first_step: From BL's description of Pic of the compactification of U_n, write torsor equations and compare with the ET parametrisation n = 4abcd − … ; count variables per equation.

title: Two-candidate version: (★) and b=1 as Heath-Brown's 'one of three' with two
connection: Heath-Brown's argument needs three candidates because two can both fail. ES data show (★) and b=1 never fail together ≤ 10⁸; test whether a third family (e.g. ES₅, small windows) is needed to make a proof-style argument robust, by finding primes where any two of three fail.
why: Determines the minimal number of families an 'at least one works' argument must juggle.
first_step: Compute joint failure sets of (★), b=1, ES₅ and the first-k windows up to 10⁹; report pairs/triples that fail together.

title: Moments in the level aspect at fixed p: Σ_C |D_C(p) − E_C|² via spectral methods
connection: Subconvexity proofs bound moments of families by spectral decomposition. At fixed p, the family of levels C gives the moment Σ_{C ≤ X} |D_C(p) − E_C|²; express it via sums of Kloosterman sums (Kuznetsov) and bound it pointwise in p.
why: A good level-aspect second moment at fixed p would show the deviations are small for most levels — then a positive proportion of levels with expected positive counts carry certificates.
first_step: Compute the moment numerically for p ~ 10⁸ and compare with Σ E_C (if Var ≈ mean, the moment is Poisson-like).

title: Multiplicative energy of divisor classes vs additive shifts N_e = (p + e)/4
connection: Sum-product: sets with small multiplicative energy have large sumsets. The divisor-class multisets of N_e across consecutive windows e (an additive progression in N) — compute their multiplicative energies; ES failure across many windows would force large multiplicative structure (subgroup trapping) along an additive progression.
why: Quantitative version of the sum-product incompatibility item, measurable on data.
first_step: For hard primes, compute E^×(classes of divisors of N_e mod e) for e ≤ 10³ and compare with random integers.

title: The trial-form sequence c_d/d at fixed p clusters at k/(4p): reparametrise by k
connection: Weyl-type equidistribution of sequences {f(d)} mod 1. In the trial form, R(p)/2 = #{d : 4c_d | d + 1, d² ≤ 4c_d p + 1} with c_d = −(4p)⁻¹ mod d. Reviewer repair: at fixed p these residues do NOT equidistribute — from 4p·c_d + 1 = k_d·d one gets c_d/d = k_d/(4p) − 1/(4pd) with k_d ∈ [1, 4p], so c_d/d clusters at the points k/(4p). The useful structure is the reparametrisation by k_d (equidistribution theorems for modular inverses average over both moduli and residues, not a fixed p).
why: The k-reparametrisation turns the trial form into a two-parameter divisibility problem (k_d·d = 4p·c_d + 1 with 4c_d | d + 1), a normal form in which the certificate event is explicit.
first_step: Tabulate, for fixed p, the pairs (k_d, d) and the certificate hits; check how the hit rate depends on k.

title: Fixed-length subproducts: ES with a prescribed number of prime factors in the divisor
connection: Kemnitz/Reiher control zero-sums of prescribed length. Refine ES: is there always a certificate whose divisor d has exactly k prime factors for some small k (e.g. k ≤ 2)? If 'k ≤ 2' holds empirically, ES reduces to a statement about prime pairs (q₁ q₂ ≡ −1 mod 4C) — a zero-sum of length 2.
why: A bounded-length version is much more structured (pairs of primes in classes) and amenable to sieve/character methods.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁸, record for each p the minimal Ω(d) over certificates; find primes requiring Ω(d) ≥ 3.

title: Distinct-denominator and ordering refinements as stronger every-n statements
connection: Breusch/Stewart required distinct denominators of a given parity. ES refinements: x < y < z distinct (automatic except special cases), x ≤ p/2, z ≤ p²/2, gcd conditions. Determine the strongest refinement that still holds for all p ≤ 10⁹; it defines the 'tightest' every-p target.
why: The tightest true statement carries the most structure for a proof and the most information for disproof searches.
first_step: Tabulate, for p ≤ 10⁹, the minimal max-denominator over solutions normalised by p², and other extremal statistics.

title: Distribution of R(p) modulo small primes ℓ (Ono-style equidistribution vs bias)
connection: Ono/Ahlgren studied p(n) modulo m: every residue class occurs. For ES, study R(p)/2 mod ℓ: equidistribution would be 'no structure', while a bias toward nonzero residues on some class would be a usable congruence. In particular check whether R(p)/2 ≡ 0 (mod ℓ) occurs with frequency ≈ 1/ℓ.
why: Cheap probe for hidden modular structure in the counts.
first_step: Compute the distribution of R(p)/2 mod 2, 3, 5, 7 over primes in each Mordell-hard class up to 10⁷.

title: Surgery on near-certificates: local modifications that remove a single obstruction
connection: Perelman's surgery removes singularities and continues the flow. For a near-certificate at level C (a divisor d of 4Cp + 1 in a class ≠ −1), define 'surgeries' changing one prime factor (moving to another level C′ sharing that factor via CRT) and study whether repeated surgery reaches a certificate.
why: Gives a local-move graph on near-certificates across levels, linked by shared prime factors.
first_step: Build the graph (nodes: (C, d); edges: share a prime factor q, C ≡ C′ (mod q)) for small p and search paths to certificates.

title: Landau–Siegel 'at most one exceptional modulus' analogue for ES levels
connection: Landau: at most one real character mod q ≤ Q has L(1,χ) tiny. ES analogue: among the characters χ_{−4uB} driving M_BM, show at most one (or boundedly many) can be 'exceptional' at p (strongly biased), so M_BM stays large except via one identifiable character whose effect can be handled separately.
why: The 'at most one exception' structure is what makes Siegel-type arguments work; ES's main term is a sum over many real characters.
first_step: Model T(p) as a sum over real characters and quantify how much a single character can reduce M_BM; compare with the observed minima of M_BM/L².

title: Thin-semigroup local-global with the ES constraint t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p): local obstructions?
connection: Bourgain–Kontorovich require knowing the local (congruence) obstructions of the semigroup before counting. Compute the reductions mod q of the ES-word set with the constraint on t (4ℤ for one branch, 8ℤ − p for the other, which depends on p!) and determine exactly which residues of p are locally admissible; check that only squares-related obstructions appear (T1-type).
why: The p-dependent constraint (8ℤ − p) is unusual for thin-orbit theory; its local analysis is a concrete, finite task.
first_step: For q ≤ 200 compute the set of p mod q (and mod 8q) hit by words with each constraint branch.

title: Erdős–Vaaler-type restricted versions: ES with levels restricted to squarefree or prime C
connection: Before Duffin–Schaeffer was proved in general, restricted cases (ψ supported on special sets) were proved first. Restrict ES (★) to prime levels C (or squarefree C): the overlap structure simplifies (gcd(C, C′) = 1). Study the prime-level-only (★) failure set and its overlap model.
why: Restricted versions with clean overlap structure are the natural first targets of a Duffin–Schaeffer-type method.
first_step: Compute (★) restricted to prime C for p ≤ 10⁹ and list failures; fit an independence model.

title: Siegel–Weil for indefinite ternary forms with congruence: ES's SL₂ quadric
connection: For indefinite forms in ≥ 3 variables representing a number, Siegel–Weil and strong approximation (spin groups) give local-global with spinor exceptions. The SL₂ form ad − pc = 1 is an affine quadric with degenerate quadratic part (rank 2, linear in c), so spin-group strong approximation does not apply as is; the ES congruence a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c) is not a lattice coset condition (modulus = coordinate), so classical theory does not apply directly. Find a reformulation where the congruence becomes a fixed-modulus coset condition.
why: If achieved, strong approximation for spin groups (no spinor obstruction ⇒ every locally represented integer is represented) would be the closing theorem.
first_step: Try substitutions a = ck − 1, d = cl − 1 and fix c's residue class; examine whether the resulting variety in (k, l, c) is homogeneous for a group with strong approximation.

title: Baseline: a single level already gives density one
connection: Level C = 1 works for p iff 4p + 1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) (it then automatically has two, so both cofactors are ≥ 3); the primes p for which 4p + 1 has only prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) have density zero (an upper-bound sieve gives ≪ X/(log X)^{3/2}; the matching order is the heuristic — check a source for the asymptotic). So 'almost all p' is cheap; all information sits in how fast the exceptional set of K levels decays.
why: A sanity baseline for every almost-all statement in this list: improvements must be measured in exceptional-set decay, not in 'density one'.
first_step: Compute the counting function of primes failing all levels C ≤ K for K = 1..10 up to 10⁹ and fit X/(log X)^{α_K}; compare α_K with Σ_{C≤K} δ_C from Landau–Ramanujan-type densities.

title: Pretentious distance D((·/p), 1; y) as the controlling statistic for ES difficulty
connection: Tao's EDP and Granville–Soundararajan's pretentious theory organise multiplicative functions by their distance to characters. The BM main term (via T(p)) and the least non-residue are governed by how much the Legendre symbol (·/p) 'pretends' to be 1 on small primes. Test whether all ES sub-route difficulty is a function of D((·/p), 1; y) for suitable y.
why: If one pretentious distance controls difficulty, the problem reduces to the 'pretentious case' (p a QR mod many small primes), where structure is strongest.
first_step: Compute D² = Σ_{ℓ ≤ y} (1 − (ℓ/p))/ℓ for primes ≤ 10⁹ and correlate with R(p)/M₀(p), least certificate C, and sub-route failures.

title: Supersingular points and maximal orders: ≈ p/12 objects attached to every p
connection: Every prime p has ≈ p/12 supersingular j-invariants, in bijection (Deuring) with left ideal classes of a fixed maximal order of the quaternion algebra ramified at p and ∞ (maximal-order types correspond to j up to Frobenius conjugation). These always exist, like Elkies's CM values; map them (or their small-norm elements, Eichler orientations) to ES certificate data.
why: Supplies power-many canonical objects for every p; if any natural map lands in certificates with positive probability, existence follows from their number.
first_step: Read the repo's supersingular/Eichler memos; for small p compute the maximal orders' reduced norms forms and test whether ES certificates appear as small vectors.

title: Reduction theory for ES solutions and congruence exclusion of all reduced representatives
connection: In Ghosh–Sarnak failures every orbit has a reduced representative in a bounded region, and congruence conditions can exclude all of them. ES: every solution has x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4] (x minimal); the 'reduced representatives' are the pairs (x, m = 4x − p). Ask whether congruence conditions modulo a fixed M can exclude all reduced representatives for infinitely many p (that would be a non-BM obstruction).
why: A concrete search space for genuinely new obstructions; if impossible for structural reasons, that fact is itself a (small) theorem.
first_step: For M = 840·k, compute which residues of p mod M admit a reduced representative whose two-term remainder is locally solvable mod M; check that no non-square class is fully excluded.

title: Positive proportion before density one (Bourgain–Fuchs) for bounded-shape certificates
connection: Bourgain–Fuchs proved a positive proportion of integers are Apollonian curvatures before density one. For ES, bounded-shape certificate families (u, B ≤ U fixed) cover a positive proportion of primes by Dirichlet; quantify the proportion covered by shapes with u, B ≤ U as U grows, versus the full ES density one.
why: Measures how much of ES is 'explained' by bounded shapes (Mordell-type) vs growing ones — the shape-growth rate needed for density one.
first_step: Compute coverage of primes ≤ 10⁹ by (★) with u, B ≤ U for U = 1..100.

title: Twists by characters mod 4C as 'twisted point counts' with an exactly known total
connection: Weil-type lower bounds use that twisted counts sum to an exact total. At level C, Σ_{χ mod 4C} χ(−1)·#{d | N : χ(d)…} expansions give D_C^−(N) = (1/φ(4C)) Σ_χ χ̄(−1) σ_χ(N) exactly; the trivial character gives τ(N)/φ(4C), others are twisted divisor sums. A lower bound needs |Σ_{χ ≠ 1} …| < τ(N): bound the twisted divisor sums σ_χ(N) pointwise (multiplicative, |σ_χ(q^a)| ≤ a + 1).
why: Pointwise bounds on σ_χ(N) are trivial-to-moderate; the issue is how many characters and how cancellation among them behaves for structured N = 4Cp + 1.
first_step: For hard p and small C, compute |Σ_{χ ≠ 1} χ̄(−1)σ_χ(N)| vs τ(N) and record how close it gets.

title: Switching between the two cofactors of 4Cp + 1 and the two ES types
connection: Chen's switching replaces a hard count by a dual count where the roles of variables swap. In (★), 4Cp + 1 = (4uC − 1)(4BC − 1) is symmetric; the b=1 line uses p + 4d with a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4d). Find an explicit bijection/switch between near-certificates of one line and of the other, so that an upper bound for near-misses of one yields a lower bound for hits of the other.
why: Switching is the concrete mechanism behind complementary-route arguments.
first_step: Search for maps (u, B, C) ↦ (d, w) between (★) data and b=1 data for the same p, and test on hard primes.

title: Finite base + closure: what finite verification would an ES closure theorem need?
connection: Graham's 77-theorem needed a finite check (78–333) plus closure maps. If any closure/transfer system for ES certificates were found (see closure items), compute the minimal 'base' of verified instances it needs; ES is verified to 10¹⁸, so any closure system with base ≤ 10¹⁸ would finish.
why: Turns closure-map searches into a concrete success criterion.
first_step: For each candidate closure map found by search, compute the set of primes it reaches from primes ≤ 10⁶ and check whether its complement thins out.

title: Reducibility check automation: verify 'configuration ⇒ certificate' lemmas by computer
connection: The four-colour proof verified each configuration's reducibility by computer. For ES, configuration lemmas of the form 'if p ≡ r (mod M) and 4Cp + 1 has factorisation pattern π then a certificate exists' can be verified symbolically for each (r, π); automate generation and checking of such lemmas.
why: Builds a library of machine-checked partial results that any case-analysis proof would need.
first_step: Implement a checker that, given (M, r, C, pattern), decides via CRT whether a certificate is forced; run over small M and patterns.

title: Limit objects of normalised divisor-class data as p → ∞ (Sendov's limiting measures)
connection: Tao's Sendov proof studies limiting zero distributions. For ES, attach to p the empirical measure of (log d / log N, class of d mod 4C) over levels C ≤ K and divisors d of 4Cp + 1; study its limit as p → ∞ (should be a product of uniform measures) and the rate; a counterexample sequence would converge to a measure avoiding a fixed 'certificate region'.
why: Gives a concrete limit object for compactness arguments.
first_step: Compute these empirical measures for p ~ 10⁶, 10⁸, 10¹⁰ and measure distance to the product-uniform model.
